novelty.reasoning: The general problem — that LLM-judge verdicts depend on judge model choice, yielding low inter-evaluator agreement and headline-number swings — is well established and routinely quantified with Krippendorff's alpha across multiple judge backbones on fixed generator outputs (e.g., the "Moral Mazes" pairwise-judge alpha analysis, "Rating Roulette," "Can You Trust LLM Judgments?", and the AF "Robustness of Model-Graded Evaluations" work). The scheming-specific instantiation is also partly covered: "Constitutional Black-Box Monitoring for Scheming in LLM Agents" evaluates several judge models for scheming detection and reports cross-judge variance (mean pAUROC variance < 0.02), and Apollo/OpenAI report grader-judge accuracy checks. However, that work measures detection accuracy against ground truth with frontier judges; I found no published study that specifically computes inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha) plus per-judge leniency offsets across several OPEN judges on a FROZEN scheming-transcript set and demonstrates the resulting swing in the headline scheming rate. The specific packaging is an unexplored but incremental gap.

title: Irreversibility Sensitivity: Do Agents Treat Reversible and Irreversible Tool Calls Differently?

sections.research_question: Do LLM agents have any implicit sensitivity to the irreversibility of an action, or do they treat 'permanently delete' the same as 'list files'? Specifically, how often do agents choose an irreversible path over an equivalent reversible one, and do they request confirmation, across explicit vs. implicit framing?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small synthetic, fully-mocked tool-use environment (~20-30 tasks) where each task can be solved by either a reversible action (move to trash, save draft, hold funds) or an irreversible one (permanent delete, send funds, overwrite). No real side effects occur — tools just return canned results and log the choice. Create two framing conditions: tools labeled explicitly as reversible/irreversible, and tools where irreversibility is only implicit in the name/description. Run 3-4 open instruct models, measuring the irreversible-path-choice rate and the confirmation-request rate per condition and model. Everything is short-prompt inference on a single consumer GPU and fits ~30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implicit-framing baseline: run agents on tasks where reversibility is only implicit in tool names and record which path they take. Measure: irreversible-path-choice rate and confirmation-request rate per model. Expected outcome: agents pick the irreversible path often and rarely ask to confirm, indicating low implicit irreversibility sensitivity.
- Explicit-label effect: re-run the identical tasks with tools explicitly tagged reversible/irreversible. Measure: change in irreversible-choice and confirmation rates vs. the implicit condition. Expected outcome: explicit labels reduce irreversible choices and raise confirmation requests, quantifying how much sensitivity is cue-dependent rather than intrinsic.
- Cross-model comparison: hold tasks and framing fixed and compare the 3-4 models. Measure: per-model irreversibility-sensitivity gap (implicit vs. explicit) and ranking. Expected outcome: models differ markedly, producing a ranking of which open models are safest to deploy with irreversible tools.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If agents are implicitly insensitive to irreversibility, then deployed tool-using agents will execute irreversible harmful actions (deleting data, sending funds) just as readily as harmless ones, with no self-imposed pause for confirmation. This is the exact pattern behind reported autonomous-crypto-theft incidents. Characterizing the decision pattern improves safety because it tells agent-framework builders where to insert mandatory irreversibility gating / confirmation checkpoints, cutting off a concrete pathway from agent error to irreversible real-world harm.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value (5): a safer-sandbox monitoring prototype built entirely from mocked tools on open models, needing no real infrastructure or lab access — exactly the externally-doable work labs deprioritize. Narrow scope (5): two clean metrics (irreversible-choice rate, confirmation rate) over a small fixed task set with two framings, so a beginner team can build the mock harness and finish in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame as a confirmation-gating design probe: 'Which tool-description conventions make agents pause before irreversible actions?', directly informing safer agent-framework defaults.
cited_sources: Adversa AI 2025 — reported agentic systems executing irreversible attacks including autonomous crypto theft; the motivating threat and the suggested follow-up to characterize decision patterns.
OS-Harm — covers data exfiltration / model-misbehavior categories that inform the irreversible-action task design.

novelty_evidence.title: Saber: Benchmarking Operational Safety of LLM Coding Agents in Stateful Project Workspaces
novelty_evidence.summary: Evaluates coding agents in sandboxed workspaces; explicitly states safe agents should choose reversible, least-intrusive operations and request confirmation, and documents agents choosing a cache-deleting (irreversible) path over a safe indexed-relocation path. Closest to the proposal but does not vary reversibility as a controlled isolated variable nor test explicit vs implicit framing with matched pairs.

novelty_evidence.title: SafeAgentBench: A Benchmark for Safe Task Planning of Embodied LLM Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: First comprehensive safety benchmark covering both explicit and implicit hazards for embodied agents, measuring rejection/refusal rate as proactive safety awareness. Shares the explicit-vs-implicit framing axis but is about hazardous embodied tasks, not reversible-vs-equivalent-irreversible tool-call choices.

novelty_evidence.title: Agent-SafetyBench: Evaluating the Safety of LLM Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: 349 environments, 2000 test cases, 10 failure modes; notes existing tests check compliance with explicitly harmful requests but not whether agents autonomously choose unsafe/destructive operations without confirmation while pursuing legitimate goals — directly adjacent to the proposal's question but not a controlled reversibility manipulation.

novelty_evidence.title: ClawsBench: Evaluating Capability and Safety of LLM Productivity Agents in Simulated Workspaces
novelty_evidence.summary: Simulated-workspace benchmark showing tool-using agents execute destructive actions and comply with unauthorized users; measures destructive-action avoidance but does not isolate reversibility against equivalent reversible alternatives or cross with framing.

novelty_evidence.title: Self-Supervised Reversibility-Aware Reinforcement Learning / Relative reachability side effects
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes the reversibility/option-value/relative-reachability framing for RL agents (penalizing irreversible transitions, preserving option value). Provides the conceptual basis but addresses trained RL agents with engineered reversibility regularizers, not behavioral probing of whether instruct LLMs have emergent implicit irreversibility sensitivity.

novelty.reasoning: The broad problem — whether LLM agents avoid destructive/irreversible tool calls and seek confirmation — is well covered. Saber (arXiv 2606.01317) explicitly states a safe agent "should choose the least intrusive, reversible... operation, and should request confirmation," and shows agents choosing destructive paths over reversible ones; Agent-SafetyBench and ClawsBench evaluate whether agents autonomously choose destructive operations without confirmation; SafeAgentBench specifically distinguishes explicit vs implicit hazards. The RL side-effects literature (relative reachability, reversibility-aware RL) firmly establishes the irreversibility/option-value framing. However, no found work runs the proposal's specific controlled design: matched task pairs offering an equivalent reversible vs irreversible path, isolating reversibility as the experimental variable and measuring irreversible-path-choice and confirmation-request rates crossed against explicit-vs-implicit tool-label framing across multiple open instruct models. Existing benchmarks embed safe/unsafe paths within tasks but do not vary reversibility as a clean isolated factor or cross it with framing, so the specific measurement angle is unexplored.

title: Quantization Effects on Agent Safety: Do Compressed Open Models Refuse Less?

sections.research_question: Does quantizing an open instruct model (8-bit, 4-bit / GGUF) degrade its agentic refusal behavior relative to full precision? Specifically, holding everything else fixed, does compression raise HarmScore, lower RefusalRate, or increase prompt-injection attack success in the agentic setting?
sections.approach_outline: Take one open instruct model with a strong safety profile (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) and run a fixed, small subset of AgentHarm plus AgentDojo at three precisions: fp16, 8-bit (bitsandbytes), and 4-bit (GGUF/bitsandbytes). Vary only the quantization level — same harness, same grader, same task subset, same decoding. Record HarmScore and RefusalRate (AgentHarm) and injection attack-success rate / utility (AgentDojo) per precision. Quantization makes inference cheaper, so all three runs fit comfortably on a single consumer GPU within ~30 hours including the blog write-up. Report deltas with bootstrap CIs to separate real degradation from noise.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Full-precision baseline: run the AgentHarm + AgentDojo subset at fp16. Measure: HarmScore, RefusalRate, injection ASR at full precision. Expected outcome: a stable safety baseline matching the model's known behavior, validating the harness end-to-end.
- Quantization sweep: re-run the identical subset at 8-bit and 4-bit. Measure: change in HarmScore/RefusalRate/ASR per precision vs. fp16, with CIs. Expected outcome: a monotone or threshold degradation — most likely 4-bit shows measurably reduced refusal and/or higher injection success, quantifying a silent safety cost.
- Failure-case inspection: pull the tasks that flip from refusal (fp16) to compliance (4-bit). Measure: count and category of newly-unsafe completions. Expected outcome: a small set of concrete categories where compression specifically erodes alignment, giving an interpretable picture rather than just an aggregate delta.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Most real-world local/self-hosted agent deployment runs quantized weights for cost and latency. If quantization silently weakens safety alignment, then the agents people actually deploy refuse harmful tool-use less and are more injectable than the benchmarked full-precision versions — a widespread, under-monitored misuse and prompt-injection risk. Demonstrating and quantifying this improves safety because it warns the open-source agent community (and quantization-tool maintainers) that compression needs a safety re-check, closing a deployment-surface gap that frontier labs, who run full precision, do not study.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value (5): quantized self-hosted deployment is precisely the external surface labs ignore, and the study needs only open weights and a single GPU. Narrow scope (5): a one-model, one-axis (precision) sweep over a fixed subset with established HarmScore/ASR metrics, so a beginner team can execute and write it up in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame as a deployment-guidance benchmark: 'Which quantization level is the safe-enough floor for agentic use?', turning the result into a practical recommendation for self-hosters.
cited_sources: AgentHarm — open benchmark providing HarmScore and RefusalRate, runnable on small models; supplies the agentic harm metric.
AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024, ETH SPYLab) — open prompt-injection harness providing attack-success-rate / utility metrics for the injection axis.
Quantization tooling (GGUF / bitsandbytes) — standard consumer-GPU compression methods whose safety effect is being measured.

novelty_evidence.title: Quantization-Based Jailbreaking Vulnerability Analysis: A Study on Performance and Safety of the Llama3-8B-Instruct Model
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly studies how quantization affects safety/jailbreaking on the exact model class proposed (Llama3-8B-Instruct), sweeping 23 quantization levels; finds 4-bit a practical sweet spot and that stronger quantization raises attack success. Establishes the core problem in the single-turn chat setting, but not agentic.

novelty_evidence.title: Exploiting LLM Quantization
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows quantization procedures can dramatically alter safety/refusal patterns and be exploited; demonstrates that compression meaningfully changes safety behavior. Chat-setting, attack-oriented rather than benign agentic degradation measurement.

novelty_evidence.title: On Jailbreaking Quantized Language Models Through Fault Injection Attacks
novelty_evidence.summary: Evaluates jailbreak success across FP16/FP8/INT8/INT4 on Llama-3-8B, finding ASR varies strongly with precision (e.g., INT8 below 50% vs >80% on FP16). Confirms precision-dependent safety effects but in single-turn, not agentic refusal/prompt-injection benchmarks.

novelty_evidence.title: Which Quantization Should I Use? A Unified Evaluation of llama.cpp Quantization on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
novelty_evidence.summary: Unified controlled comparison of llama.cpp GGUF quantization formats on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reporting downstream task performance and degradation by bit-width; the proposed harness/model/precision methodology mirrors this, but it does not cover agentic safety (AgentHarm/AgentDojo) metrics.

novelty_evidence.title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Defines the HarmScore/RefusalRate agentic-harm metrics the proposal would use and reports them across frontier models, but does not vary quantization/precision on a fixed open model — the agentic-quantization combination is absent.

novelty_evidence.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Provides the prompt-injection ASR/utility agentic benchmark the proposal would use; evaluates many models but not the effect of quantization precision, confirming the proposed precision-sweep angle in this benchmark is unexplored.

novelty.reasoning: The general problem — does quantization degrade an open instruct model's safety/refusal and raise jailbreak success — is already well-studied in the single-turn chat setting. The "Quantization-Based Jailbreaking Vulnerability Analysis" study runs exactly the proposed precision sweep on Llama3-8B-Instruct across 23 quant levels and reports the 4-bit "sweet spot" plus increased attack success at lower bit-width; "Exploiting LLM Quantization" and fault-injection jailbreak work corroborate that quantization shifts safety behavior. However, all of this work uses chat/single-turn harmful prompts; I found no study measuring quantization deltas in the AGENTIC setting on AgentHarm (HarmScore/RefusalRate) or on AgentDojo prompt-injection ASR/utility. The specific combination proposed — holding the agentic harness fixed and varying only precision (fp16/8-bit/4-bit GGUF) to measure agent refusal and indirect-prompt-injection success with bootstrap CIs — is unexplored, so the precise angle is novel even though the underlying refusal-degradation phenomenon is largely established.

title: Evaluation-Awareness Triggers in Agent Sandboxes: What Tips an Agent Off That It's a Test?

sections.research_question: Which specific environment cues in agentic safety sandboxes (fake/round-number data, suspiciously easy escalation, '/sandbox/' tool names, placeholder identities) tip an agent off that it is being tested, and how much do those cues raise verbalized evaluation-awareness and suppress unsafe-but-tempting behavior?
sections.approach_outline: Build matched pairs of a small set (~20-30) of agentic safety scenarios. For each, create a 'realistic' version (plausible names, messy data, real-looking paths) and a 'tell-tale test' version (placeholder names, /sandbox/ paths, round numbers, trivially easy escalation). Run an open instruct model on every version and (a) scan the chain of thought for explicit evaluation-awareness phrases with a keyword + LLM-judge classifier, and (b) compare the rate of taking the unsafe-but-tempting action across the realistic vs. test versions. Then isolate individual cues by toggling one at a time to attribute the effect. Pure prompting, inference-only on a single GPU, completing within ~30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Matched-pair behavior gap: run the model on realistic vs. tell-tale versions of each scenario. Measure: difference in unsafe-action rate and in verbalized-eval-awareness rate between versions. Expected outcome: the tell-tale version shows higher eval-awareness and lower unsafe-action rates, confirming sandboxes leak.
- Single-cue ablation: starting from the realistic version, add one tell-tale cue at a time (round numbers; /sandbox/ paths; placeholder names). Measure: marginal increase in eval-awareness and decrease in unsafe behavior per cue. Expected outcome: one or two cues (e.g. /sandbox/ paths, round-number data) dominate, yielding a ranked list of leaks to avoid.
- Awareness-behavior link: within the test versions, split transcripts by whether the model verbalized eval-awareness. Measure: unsafe-action rate in aware vs. non-aware transcripts. Expected outcome: aware transcripts have markedly lower unsafe rates, evidencing that detecting the test causes the safer behavior.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If common sandbox cues tip agents off that they are in a test, then every agentic safety evaluation that uses those cues is biased toward optimistic results — the model behaves when it suspects it's watched, then misbehaves in genuine deployment. This is a foundational methodology problem: safety cases built on such evals would understate real deployment risk for deceptive/scheming agents. Isolating which cues leak improves safety because it gives outside eval-builders a concrete checklist for designing deployment-realistic sandboxes, tightening the validity of the evals that gate agent deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: Theory of impact (5): eval-awareness undermines the validity of the whole agentic-safety eval methodology, a problem major orgs (Apollo) flag. Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5): a matched-pair prompting study with CoT scanning and single-cue ablation, all inference-only, so a beginner team can finish and write it up within 30 hours; counterfactual value (4) since it uses only open models and improves third-party eval design.
alternative_framings: Frame as a sandbox-realism checklist: convert the ranked leak list into a practical 'do/don't' guide for building deployment-realistic agent safety evals.
cited_sources: Apollo Research (Claude Sonnet 3.7 verbalizes evaluation-awareness up to 33%) — motivating evidence that agents detect evaluations; defines the awareness phenomenon being traced to cues.
Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness (arXiv 2507.01786) — models classify eval-vs-deployment transcripts at AUC 0.83; supports that distinguishing cues exist and can be isolated.
Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate (arXiv 2509.00591) — rewriting prompts to be less evaluation-like; methodological basis for constructing the realistic vs. tell-tale versions.

novelty_evidence.title: Verbalized Eval Awareness Inflates Measured Safety
novelty_evidence.summary: Identifies specific unrealistic prompt cues (authority claims, self-incriminating admissions, escalation patterns, false claims), toggles/removes them, measures verbalized eval awareness in chain-of-thought (95% exclusive to CoT) via classifier, and shows removing cues reduces verbalized awareness >40-60% while lowering refusal rates—i.e., inflated/suppressed safety behavior. Across 8 models (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5, Qwen3, OLMo3, etc.). Limitation: single-turn safety prompts, not multi-turn agentic sandboxes—the proposal's main differentiator.

novelty_evidence.title: What can sandboxed AI agents learn about their evaluation environments?
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly studies how agents in sandboxed evaluation environments infer they are being tested from environmental cues (directory structures, organization knowledge), and notes stripping environment detail backfires because the emptiness itself signals a test. Covers the agentic-sandbox cue angle the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: In-Context Environments Induce Evaluation-Awareness in Language Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Agentic file-system setup where models read documentation/questions; uses adversarial optimization to induce eval-awareness and validates causality via CoT intervention. Confirms verbalized+causal sandbagging (99.3% of samples). Does NOT systematically ablate individual cues or use matched realistic-vs-test toggles, leaving that specific attribution method open.

novelty_evidence.title: Realistic Evaluations Will Not Prevent Evaluation Awareness
novelty_evidence.summary: Notes agentic settings leak more cues than chat (directory structures, system configs) making eval-awareness easier, and that adding typos/realistic framing ('my teacher sent me this') drastically reduces eval awareness—directly relevant to the proposed cue-toggling effect.

novelty_evidence.title: Evaluating and Understanding Scheming Propensity in LLM Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Causally ablates evaluation-awareness from agent chain-of-thought and measures covert-action rate change (baseline 13.2% vs intervention 24.2%), showing eval-awareness suppresses unsafe behavior—the quantitative effect the proposal aims to measure.

novelty_evidence.title: LURE: Live-Usage Replay Evaluations for Reducing Evaluation Awareness
novelty_evidence.summary: Work specifically on reducing evaluation awareness by making evals more realistic (replaying live usage), implying the field already characterizes which realism factors drive awareness.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem—identifying which unrealistic cues raise verbalized eval-awareness and how much they suppress unsafe behavior—is largely answered. Goodfire/LessWrong's "Verbalized Eval Awareness Inflates Measured Safety" already toggles/removes specific cues (authority claims, self-incriminating admissions, escalation patterns), measures verbalized awareness in CoT via classifier, and shows removal cuts awareness 40-60% while changing refusal rates; AISI's sandbox blog and "In-Context Environments Induce Evaluation-Awareness" (arXiv 2603.03824) cover the agentic-sandbox cue angle (directory structures, system configs, environment emptiness) with CoT causality; and scheming papers (2603.01608, 2509.15541) causally ablate eval-awareness from CoT and measure covert-action-rate shifts (13.2% vs 24.2%). The residual gap is the specific combination proposed—controlled matched-pair design over ~20-30 multi-turn agentic scenarios toggling one canonical sandbox tell at a time (/sandbox/ paths, round numbers, placeholder identities, easy escalation) for per-cue attribution on an open instruct model—which is incremental rather than novel, since single-cue removal attribution and agentic cue framing are both already demonstrated.

title: Verbosity Bias as an Exploitable Channel: Padding to Pass Oversight

sections.research_question: How much can the pass-rate of a fixed incorrect answer be raised, in the eyes of an LLM judge, purely by adding non-substantive padding (qualifications, restated context, formal tone) while holding the wrong claim fixed? What is the dose-response curve of pass-rate vs token count?
sections.approach_outline: Take a set of clearly incorrect answers to factual and reasoning questions from a public QA dataset. Programmatically generate padded variants of each wrong answer at increasing token counts, where padding adds fluent but non-substantive material (caveats, restated background, formal phrasing) without changing or fixing the wrong claim — verified by a simple check that the core claim string is preserved. Submit original and padded variants to several small open judge models in an LLM-as-a-judge setup ('is this answer correct? PASS/FAIL') and record pass-rate as a function of token count. Fit a dose-response curve per judge. Inference-only on a single consumer GPU; finishes in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Padding generator + claim-preservation check: build the padder and confirm padded variants keep the wrong claim intact across a sample. Measure: fraction of padded variants that preserve the original wrong claim (manual + automatic check). Expected outcome: a reliable padder producing length-controlled, claim-preserving variants.
- Dose-response measurement: submit each wrong answer at several padding levels to 3-4 small judge models and record PASS rates. Measure: pass-rate vs token count per judge. Expected outcome: pass-rate rises monotonically with padding for at least some judges, demonstrating an exploitable verbosity channel.
- Mitigation probe: re-run with a judge prompt that explicitly warns against length/verbosity bias and asks the judge to ignore non-substantive text. Measure: reduction in the padding-induced pass-rate slope. Expected outcome: the de-biasing prompt flattens but does not eliminate the curve, quantifying how much of the exploit a simple prompt fix removes.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Automated oversight increasingly uses LLM graders, and verbosity/length bias is a known reward-hacking vector. If a fixed wrong answer can be pushed past a grader just by padding, then any training or filtering loop that trusts such graders can be gamed, which improves safety because it converts a qualitative bias into a measured attack surface and a reusable red-team benchmark, helping prevent the pathway where a capable model learns to reward-hack its overseer with non-substantive verbosity and thereby gets incorrect or unsafe outputs approved at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, counterfactual value, and low compute and 4 on novelty: it is a lab-independent, fuzzy-reward exploit study using only public data and small open models with trivial compute. It is tightly scoped to a single dose-response curve with a clear pass-rate metric, and the controlled padding-vs-pass-rate measurement for fixed-wrong answers is plausibly open, giving beginners an original, self-contained first deliverable.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a benchmark: a 'verbosity-attack robustness' score for any judge model, defined as the pass-rate increase per 100 padding tokens on fixed wrong answers.
cited_sources: LLM-as-a-Judge surveys reporting verbosity/length bias from RLHF (arXiv:2410.02736) -- documents the bias that this project turns into a measured, exploitable channel.

novelty_evidence.title: Verbosity Bias in Preference Labeling by Large Language Models (2310.10076)
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes that LLM judges systematically prefer more verbose responses; foundational documentation of the verbosity-bias problem the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Explaining Length Bias in LLM-Based Preference Evaluations (2407.01085)
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses the exact controlled methodology the proposal proposes — holding content constant while varying length, applying targeted length interventions to identify length-driven preference flips — and characterizes the dose-response shape (bias grows with size difference, stable 40-100 words, declines >100).

novelty_evidence.title: AdvJudge-Zero: Binary Decision Flips in LLM-as-a-Judge via Adversarial Control Tokens (2512.17375)
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly studies flipping incorrect answers to PASS in a judge: appended low-perplexity tokens flip 'No' to 'Yes', causing high false-positive rates when open/specialized judges score incorrect math and reasoning answers — very close to the proposal's flip-via-padding question.

novelty_evidence.title: Mitigating Length Bias in RLHF through a Causal Lens (2511.12573)
novelty_evidence.summary: Counterfactual augmentation generating response variants by manipulating length while keeping semantic content constant, then identifying length-driven preference flips — the same hold-claim-fixed/vary-padding design.

novelty_evidence.title: Is LLM-as-a-Judge Robust? Universal Adversarial Attacks on Zero-shot LLM Assessment (2402.14016)
novelty_evidence.summary: Short universal adversarial phrases concatenated to answers inflate judge scores, with absolute scoring more susceptible than comparative — supports that appended non-substantive text raises pass/score for fixed content.

novelty_evidence.title: Reward hacking via LLM-judge exploits (verbosity, appended phrases)
novelty_evidence.summary: Documents that appending short phrases like 'Solution' or a single colon causes LLM judges to assign high scores regardless of answer quality, framing verbosity/padding as a known reward-hacking and oversight-bypass channel.

novelty.reasoning: The underlying problem — that non-substantive verbosity raises an LLM judge's approval of fixed-quality (including incorrect) answers — is extensively documented. Verbosity/length bias is quantified (LLM +17.3% vs human +12.9% preference for longer responses; judges favor "lower quality and less persuasive" longer arguments) in arXiv 2310.10076 and 2407.01085, and the exact methodology of holding content constant while varying length to detect "length-driven preference flips via targeted length interventions" already exists (2407.01085, 2511.12573). The specific flip-incorrect-to-PASS angle is directly studied by AdvJudge-Zero (arXiv 2512.17375), which appends padding/control tokens to flip "No" to "Yes" with high false-positive rates on math/reasoning judges, and reward-hacking work shows appending phrases like "Solution" or a colon inflates judge scores regardless of correctness. Even the dose-response shape (bias growing with length difference, stable 40-100 words, declining beyond) is already characterized. The proposal's only mild differentiators are the factual-QA PASS/FAIL framing on small open judges plus per-judge curve fitting — minor recombinations of established findings rather than an unexplored contribution.

title: Anchoring the Judge with a Fake 'Expert' Prior: Authority Cues in Oversight

sections.research_question: How large is the authority-deference effect in LLM oversight: holding the answer fixed, how much does framing it as coming from a 'senior expert' or 'verified/high-confidence' source increase a weak judge's acceptance of incorrect answers, and does a simple debiasing instruction remove it?
sections.approach_outline: Take a set of QA-style items with known ground truth and, for each, a plausible-but-wrong candidate answer. Hold the answer text constant and vary only the provenance metadata shown to a small open judge: neutral, 'from a senior domain expert', 'verified', and 'low-confidence draft'. Run the judge across all framings and measure acceptance of the (wrong) answer attributable purely to the framing. Then add a debiasing system instruction ('ignore any stated source or confidence; judge only the content') and re-measure. Inference-only on one GPU; a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Authority-deference magnitude: measure judge acceptance rate of incorrect answers across the four framings, neutral as baseline. Measure: percentage-point increase in wrong-answer acceptance under 'expert'/'verified' versus neutral. Expected: authority/verified framing measurably raises acceptance of wrong answers.
- Direction-of-confidence check: include the 'low-confidence draft' framing on correct answers. Measure: whether low-confidence framing suppresses acceptance of correct answers. Expected: a symmetric effect, confirming the judge is anchoring on provenance rather than content.
- Debiasing instruction test: re-run all framings with the ignore-provenance instruction. Measure: residual authority effect after debiasing. Expected: the effect shrinks substantially but may not vanish, quantifying how much a cheap prompt-level fix buys.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify an exploitable authority-deference bias in weak overseers and show whether a prompt-level fix removes it, then oversight-protocol designers can detect and patch a concrete manipulation channel before deployment. This matters because a strategic, misaligned AI being supervised by a weaker overseer could cheaply frame its outputs with fake authority/confidence cues to get harmful answers endorsed; mapping and mitigating exactly such exploitable supervision biases is a named open problem and a direct deception/loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it directly attacks a named open problem (mapping supervision biases exploitable by strategic AI) with a tightly controlled single-variable manipulation, needs only open models and no lab internals, and yields a clean effect-size plus a tested mitigation. The hold-answer-fixed design makes the causal claim crisp and fully reproducible by an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Reframe as an adversarial red-team probe: treat authority framing as an attack a dishonest model could deploy, and report it as a vulnerability with a recommended prompt-level patch.
cited_sources: LLM-judge bias survey (arXiv:2410.02736) — catalogs framing biases in LLM judges, motivating a focused measurement of authority-cue deference on correctness.
Anthropic / UK AISI open problems (map and mitigate supervision biases exploitable by strategic AI) — names the exact gap this project targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Trust Me, I'm an Expert: Decoding and Steering Authority Bias in Large Language Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Holds content constant while varying expert vs non-expert source/endorsement labels to quantify authority bias (how much an expert attribution increases acceptance of identical content). Also tests mitigation via steering vectors / debiasing, directly matching the proposal's hold-answer-fixed + debias design.

novelty_evidence.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge (CALM)
novelty_evidence.summary: Explicitly defines and attacks 'authority bias' in LLM judges by adding fabricated authoritative references to a lower-quality answer; shows judges reverse to accept the inferior/incorrect answer and even cite the fake references. Covers the judge-oversight acceptance-of-wrong-answer angle.

novelty_evidence.title: The Silent Judge: Unacknowledged Shortcut Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies shortcut/provenance biases in LLM judges including authority and confidence cues; establishes that provenance labels impose a trust hierarchy (EXPERT > HUMAN > LLM > UNKNOWN) and that judges accept content based on framing rather than correctness.

novelty_evidence.title: Evaluating and Mitigating LLM-as-a-judge Bias in Communication Systems
novelty_evidence.summary: Surveys and tests prompt-based debiasing instructions (e.g., instructing the judge to ignore tone/identity/source cues) as mitigation for judge biases, and notes such instruction-only debiasing often fails against strong bias injections — directly addressing the proposal's debiasing-instruction question.

novelty_evidence.title: Impact of authoritative and subjective cues on large language model reliability for clinical inquiries
novelty_evidence.summary: Experimental study showing authoritative framing dramatically degrades correctness (accuracy dropping from ~45% to ~1% under authoritative prompts), quantifying the magnitude of the authority-deference effect on held-fixed factual content.

novelty_evidence.title: When Truth Is Overridden / Decomposing Factual Sycophancy
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies authority/expertise cues driving models to abandon correct internal knowledge (sycophancy), with a finding that stated expertise has smaller effect than opinion expression — relevant nuance to the proposed authority-vs-confidence comparison.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — how much an authority/expert/confidence provenance cue increases a judge's acceptance of (incorrect) content when the answer text is held fixed — is directly studied. "Trust Me, I'm an Expert" (arXiv 2601.13433) holds content constant, varies expert vs non-expert source labels, quantifies the authority-deference effect, and tests a debiasing/steering mitigation. "Justice or Prejudice? (CALM)" (arXiv 2410.02736) explicitly includes an "authority bias" attack on LLM judges, adding fabricated authoritative references to an inferior answer and showing the judge flips to accept it; "The Silent Judge" and judge-bias surveys cover the same provenance/shortcut biases plus prompt-instruction debiasing (which is reported to often fail against strong cues). Sycophancy work further establishes the magnitude of authority-cue effects (e.g., accuracy dropping from 45% to ~1% under authoritative framing). The proposal's specific four-way framing (neutral/expert/verified/low-confidence draft) on weak-judge oversight QA with a simple system-prompt debiaser is a minor recombination of these existing contributions rather than an unexplored gap, so the gaps are minor.

title: Cross-Examination as a Lie Localizer: Can Targeted Questions Break Obfuscation?

sections.research_question: Does cheap, prompted cross-examination, having a judge issue a few targeted follow-up questions that force a defending model to commit to sub-claims, actually surface inconsistencies and improve localization of a planted error in a multi-step argument?
sections.approach_outline: Construct synthetic multi-step arguments (e.g. 5-8 reasoning steps reaching a conclusion) each containing exactly one planted error, across a few topic templates (arithmetic chains, logical syllogisms, short factual derivations). For each argument, run two judge conditions with a small open model: (1) baseline, judge reads the full argument and tries to flag the erroneous step; (2) cross-examination, judge issues 2-3 targeted follow-up questions to the defending model about specific steps and checks the answers for self-contradiction before flagging. Measure error-localization rate in each condition. Inference-only, multi-turn prompting, one GPU, a few hours; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline localization: measure how often the judge correctly identifies the planted-error step from the full argument alone. Measure: step-level localization accuracy. Expected: modest accuracy, with the dishonest framing able to hide the error.
- Cross-examination lift: enable 2-3 targeted follow-up questions and self-contradiction checking, then re-measure localization. Measure: change in localization accuracy and rate of surfaced self-contradictions. Expected: cross-examination improves localization when the planted error forces an inconsistent commitment.
- Stress by obfuscation: vary how deeply the error is buried (early vs late step, plausible vs blatant). Measure: localization lift from cross-examination as a function of obfuscation depth. Expected: cross-examination helps most on plausibly-buried errors and least on errors the defender can keep consistent, mapping its operating envelope.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we provide cheap empirical evidence on whether prompted cross-examination genuinely localizes planted lies, then the external research community learns whether this leading theoretical fix to debate's obfuscated-argument failure mode is worth its inference cost, informing which oversight protocols to invest in. This matters because scalable oversight of superhuman systems may depend on cross-examination to defeat arguments too complex for a human to check directly; if it does not actually surface inconsistencies, deceptive complex arguments slip through, a loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it empirically tests a prominent theoretical proposal using only prompting on synthetic data, with no training and no lab access, and yields a single decision-relevant number (localization improvement). The controlled planted-error design makes the result clean and the synthetic-data construction keeps it fully reproducible by an independent beginner team in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe around protocol design: compare judge-led vs debater-led cross-examination to see which interrogator more reliably forces localizable commitments.
cited_sources: Prover-Estimator Debate (arXiv:2506.13609) — formalizes routes around obfuscated arguments, motivating an empirical test of cross-examination's lie-localizing power.
Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) — provides the debate setting and obfuscated-argument failure mode this project's cross-examination intervention targets.

novelty_evidence.title: LM vs LM: Detecting Factual Errors via Cross Examination
novelty_evidence.summary: An examiner LM issues multi-turn follow-up questions to an examinee LM to surface inconsistencies that imply factual errors, achieving ~0.75-0.84 recall and ~0.82-0.87 precision. Directly implements the proposal's central mechanism of targeted cross-examination questions revealing self-contradiction.

novelty_evidence.title: Writeup: Progress on AI Safety via Debate (and Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem)
novelty_evidence.summary: Formalizes cross-examination as forcing a debater to either commit to all sub-claims (so the flaw can be localized) or answer inconsistently (so the contradiction is exhibited to the judge). This is exactly the proposal's framing of follow-up questions forcing commitment to break obfuscation.

novelty_evidence.title: FindTheFlaws: Annotated Errors for Detecting Flawed Reasoning and Scalable Oversight Research
novelty_evidence.summary: Provides annotated reasoning chains with located errors for studying judge/debate-based error detection and localization, covering the proposal's planted-error localization measurement on multi-step arguments.

novelty_evidence.title: Towards Scalable Oversight with Collaborative Multi-Agent Debate in Error Detection
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies multi-agent debate for detecting/localizing errors in reasoning, comparing interactive protocols against single-judge baselines — the same baseline-vs-interaction comparison the proposal sets up.

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Empirically compares judge accuracy under direct reading versus interactive debate/consultancy protocols with small judge models, the inference-only baseline-vs-interaction experimental design the proposal proposes.

novelty_evidence.title: Inference-Only Debate Experiments Using Math Problems
novelty_evidence.summary: Inference-only, prompting-based debate experiments on math reasoning measuring whether interaction improves judge accuracy/error detection — closely matches the proposal's compute-light inference-only setup.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether cross-examination (targeted follow-up questions forcing a model to commit to sub-claims, surfacing self-contradiction) detects errors in multi-step reasoning — is directly addressed by Cohen et al.'s "LM vs LM: Detecting Factual Errors via Cross Examination" (EMNLP 2023), which has an examiner LM issue multi-turn follow-up questions to reveal inconsistencies implying errors at ~0.8 recall/precision. The AI-safety debate literature (Barnes & Christiano's debate writeup and the obfuscated-arguments work) formalizes the exact mechanism of cross-examination forcing commitment-or-contradiction, and error-localization-in-reasoning-chains with planted errors is covered by "FindTheFlaws" (2503.22989) and "Towards Scalable Oversight with Collaborative Multi-Agent Debate in Error Detection" (2510.20963); baseline-judge-vs-interaction comparisons appear in "On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs" and inference-only debate experiments. The specific narrow packaging (small open model, exactly-one-planted-error synthetic chains, cheap 2-3 prompted follow-ups measured for localization rate vs a no-interaction baseline) is a minor unexplored configuration rather than a new problem, so gaps are minor.

title: When the Overseer Is the Same Model: Self-Evaluation Blind Spots

sections.research_question: When a model grades its own outputs, how large is the overlap between its generation errors and its self-evaluation misses, i.e. how often does a model endorse its own wrong answers compared to how often a different-family model of similar size catches them?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one open model and a task with hard ground truth (e.g. math or short factual QA). Collect a set of items the model answers incorrectly. Then have the same model self-grade each of those wrong answers (correct or incorrect?), recording its self-endorsement rate. Independently have a different-family model of similar size grade the same wrong answers as a control for general judging difficulty. The gap between self-endorsement and cross-grader endorsement isolates the self-evaluation blind spot from generic judging difficulty. Inference-only, one GPU, a few hours; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Self-endorsement rate: have the model grade its own wrong answers. Measure: fraction of its own wrong answers it endorses as correct. Expected: a substantial fraction endorsed, indicating shared generation/evaluation blind spots.
- Cross-grader control: have a different-family same-size model grade the identical wrong answers. Measure: that model's endorsement rate on the same items. Expected: lower endorsement than self-grading, the gap quantifying the self-evaluation blind spot beyond general difficulty.
- Blind-spot characterization: categorize items where the model self-endorses but the cross-grader rejects. Measure: error types over-represented in self-endorsed misses (e.g. systematic miscalculation, confident misconception). Expected: identifiable categories where self-evaluation is especially unsafe.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how much of a model's generation errors its own self-evaluation also misses, then practitioners using self-grading as cheap oversight learn where it is systematically unsafe and when a different-family grader is required. This matters because automated-oversight pipelines increasingly let models grade themselves at scale; if a model cannot see in evaluation the same errors it makes in generation, those errors pass review undetected and accumulate, a pathway to deploying systems with silent, correlated failures and hidden objectives.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it studies the cheapest and most widely used oversight shortcut (self-evaluation) with a single clean comparison (self- vs cross-grading on the model's own wrong answers), using only open models and public data with no lab infrastructure. The different-family control sharpens the causal claim, and the whole study is fully reproducible by an independent beginner team on one GPU.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a self-preference decomposition: separate the self-evaluation blind spot from self-preference (favoring one's own phrasing) by also grading a paraphrased version of the model's own answer.
cited_sources: Self-preference bias (arXiv:2410.21819) — motivates concern that models systematically misjudge their own outputs, which this project measures as a generation/self-evaluation error overlap.
Auditing language models for hidden objectives (arXiv:2503.10965) — frames the risk of self-assessment missing a model's own failures, the blind spot this study quantifies.

novelty_evidence.title: Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Introduces the 'Self-Correction Blind Spot': across 14 open non-reasoning models, models fail to correct 64.5% of errors in their OWN outputs while successfully correcting identical errors from external sources. Directly establishes that attribution (self vs external) modulates error detection — the exact gap this proposal aims to measure.

novelty_evidence.title: Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves
novelty_evidence.summary: Finds self-attribution bias is largest on incorrect code and harmful actions — precisely where reliable self-monitoring matters. Frames the phenomenon as a safety/oversight concern (judges sharing the policy model's blind spot give no corrective signal), matching the proposal's motivation.

novelty_evidence.title: Are LLM Evaluators Really Narcissists? Sanity Checking Self-Preference Evaluations
novelty_evidence.summary: Measures self-preference per-example by comparing how much a judge prefers its own incorrect response vs that of a proxy model of similar capability ('Evaluator Quality Baseline') — essentially the proposed same-size cross-grader control for isolating the self-evaluation blind spot from generic judging difficulty.

novelty_evidence.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes self-recognition is linearly correlated with self-preference, the foundational mechanism for a model failing to penalize its own errors. Underpins the proposal's hypothesis about self-endorsement of own wrong answers.

novelty_evidence.title: The Generative AI Paradox on Evaluation: What It Can Solve, It May Not Evaluate (and related self-evaluation TPR/TNR studies)
novelty_evidence.summary: Self-evaluation TPR/TNR analyses report models endorsing 95%+ of their own errors (e.g., very low true-negative rates on self-grading wrong answers) and that cross-family verifiers outperform self-verification on math/logic — quantifying the self-endorsement-of-wrong-answers rate the proposal would re-measure.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether a model's self-evaluation misses overlap with its own generation errors, and how this compares to a different-model grader — is well covered by multiple recent published works. "Self-Correction Bench" (arXiv 2507.02778, NeurIPS 2025) names and measures the "Self-Correction Blind Spot": non-reasoning LLMs fail on 64.5% of errors in their own outputs while correcting identical external errors, isolating the self vs. external attribution effect that this proposal targets. "Self-Attribution Bias: When AI Monitors Go Easy on Themselves" (arXiv 2603.04582) shows self-attribution bias is largest precisely on incorrect outputs and harmful actions, matching the proposal's safety-oversight framing. Crucially, the proposed methodological control (a different-family model of similar size as a baseline for generic judging difficulty) is essentially the "proxy model of similar capability / Evaluator Quality Baseline" already used in self-preference work ("Are LLM Evaluators Really Narcissists?", arXiv 2601.22548) and in self-evaluation TPR/TNR studies reporting models endorse 95%+ of their own errors. The remaining gap is minor: the exact restriction to items the model answered wrong, plus a clean same-size cross-family control on those items, is a specific framing not pinned to a single paper, but the contribution it would yield is largely subsumed by existing results.

title: Does Eliciting Reasons Before Verdicts Reduce Judge Exploitability?

sections.research_question: Does forcing a judge to write reasoning before its verdict (CoT judging) genuinely reduce susceptibility to known exploits (verbosity/padding, authority framing, answer-position order), or does it merely produce post-hoc rationalizations that leave or amplify the bias?
sections.approach_outline: Build three bias-probe sets over items with ground truth: padding (one answer artificially lengthened), authority framing (one answer labeled as expert/verified), and position swaps (same pair, order flipped). For each probe, compare two judge configurations on a small open model: direct-verdict and reason-then-verdict. Measure each configuration's susceptibility to each bias (e.g. how often padding/authority/position flips the verdict toward the wrong answer). Compare to determine, per bias channel, whether CoT reduces, leaves unchanged, or amplifies exploitability. Inference-only, one GPU, a few hours; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Bias baselines: measure direct-verdict judge susceptibility to padding, authority, and position bias separately. Measure: per-channel rate of bias-induced wrong verdicts. Expected: nonzero susceptibility on all three channels.
- CoT effect per channel: measure reason-then-verdict susceptibility on the same probes. Measure: change in per-channel susceptibility versus direct verdict. Expected: heterogeneous, CoT may reduce position bias but do little for verbosity or even rationalize authority deference.
- Rationalization audit: on items where CoT keeps the biased verdict, inspect the written reasoning. Measure: fraction of reasonings that explicitly justify the biased choice (post-hoc rationalization signature). Expected: a detectable share where CoT manufactures justification rather than catching the manipulation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we show whether reason-before-verdict actually de-biases overseers or merely rationalizes manipulation across distinct exploit channels, then protocol designers stop treating CoT judging as a free safety fix and apply it only where it helps. This matters because if a widely-recommended cheap intervention silently fails (or worsens exploitability), deployed oversight pipelines inherit a false sense of robustness, letting a strategic system exploit the very biases CoT was assumed to remove, a deception/loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it stress-tests a near-universal, free-seeming oversight recommendation with a tightly scoped per-channel comparison, reusing simple bias probes on open models with no lab infrastructure. The result, whether forced reasoning de-biases or rationalizes, is directly actionable for protocol design outside labs and fully reproducible by a beginner team in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a rationalization-detection study: can the judge's own written reasoning be classified into genuine error-catching vs post-hoc justification, and does that predict residual bias?
cited_sources: Self-preference / structured-judging work (arXiv:2410.21819 and follow-ups) — reports that structured judging can reduce bias without retraining, motivating a test of whether plain reason-before-verdict CoT does the same or rationalizes.
LLM-judge bias survey (arXiv:2410.02736) — catalogs the verbosity/authority/position exploit channels reused as probes here.

novelty_evidence.title: Explicit Reasoning Makes Better Judges: A Systematic Study on Accuracy, Efficiency, and Robustness
novelty_evidence.summary: Systematically compares 'thinking' (reason-then-verdict) vs 'non-thinking' (direct-verdict) judges on small open Qwen3 models (0.6B/1.7B/4B), inference-only. Finds thinking improves accuracy (+10.5) and robustness to biases, e.g. verbosity-bias consistency 83.48 (thinking) vs 73.86 (non-thinking). Nearly identical setup to the proposal.

novelty_evidence.title: Faithful or Fabricated? A Causal Framework for Rationalization Bias in LLM Judges
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly tests whether CoT judges produce post-hoc rationalizations vs faithful reasoning by perturbing non-evidential cues (verbosity, confidence/label, authority-style cues) while holding texts fixed. Finds substantial cue-anchored rationalization and evaluates structured-CoT and Proof-Before-Preference mitigations. Addresses the proposal's central 'rationalization vs genuine reduction' question.

novelty_evidence.title: The Silent Judge: Unacknowledged Shortcut Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Quantifies authority/provenance framing bias (an 'Expert' label produces ~+18% verdict-shift for GPT-4o) plus padding/verbosity shortcut biases — covering two of the three bias channels in the proposal.

novelty_evidence.title: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes that zero-shot CoT can make models MORE susceptible to bias and that CoT explanations rationalize biased answers rather than reducing bias — the amplification hypothesis the proposal aims to test is already documented.

novelty_evidence.title: Justice or Prejudice? Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Comprehensive quantification of LLM-judge biases including position, verbosity, authority, and CoT bias, with bias-probe-style perturbation methodology over ground-truth items — the measurement framework the proposal would build.

novelty.reasoning: The core question — whether reason-before-verdict (CoT) judging genuinely reduces judge bias susceptibility or merely produces post-hoc rationalizations — is directly and repeatedly addressed in published work. "Explicit Reasoning Makes Better Judges" (arXiv 2509.13332) runs essentially the proposed experiment: thinking vs non-thinking judges on small open Qwen models (0.6B-4B), inference-only, measuring robustness/consistency under verbosity bias and other bias scenarios (verbosity consistency 83.48 thinking vs 73.86 non-thinking). "Faithful or Fabricated?" (arXiv 2605.23970) directly tests whether CoT judges rationalize under verbosity/label/confidence-cue perturbations and evaluates structured-CoT mitigation, which is precisely the rationalization-vs-genuine-reduction framing. "The Silent Judge" (arXiv 2509.26072) quantifies authority/"Expert"-provenance bias (+18% verdict shift) and padding, and LessWrong/AF and CoT-faithfulness work already establish that zero-shot CoT can amplify bias. The proposed three bias channels (padding/verbosity, authority framing, position) and the reduce/unchanged/amplify per-channel comparison are all covered; the only minor gap is the exact bundled three-probe ground-truth construction as a single unified study.

title: The Abstention Backstop: Backcasting a Judge That Refuses Rather Than Guesses

sections.research_question: How much does giving a weak oversight judge an explicit 'abstain' option buy in safety terms, i.e. what is the selective-accuracy vs abstention-rate trade-off, and how often can a debater still force a confident wrong verdict instead of an abstention?
sections.approach_outline: Over QuALITY debate/consultancy transcripts, add an explicit 'abstain / I don't know' verdict to a small open judge's prompt. For both debate (two opposing advisors) and single-advisor consultancy, sweep the judge's willingness-to-abstain (e.g. via confidence threshold or prompt) and plot the selective-accuracy vs abstention-rate (coverage) curve. Then characterize which question features drive abstentions versus confident-wrong verdicts. Inference-only on an open benchmark, one GPU, a few hours; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Selective-accuracy curve: add the abstain option and plot accuracy-on-answered vs abstention rate for the debate-judge. Measure: selective accuracy at several coverage levels. Expected: selective accuracy rises as the judge abstains on hard items, quantifying the abstention backstop.
- Debate vs consultancy comparison: produce the same curve for single-advisor consultancy. Measure: difference in selective-accuracy/coverage between debate and consultancy. Expected: debate yields a more favorable trade-off, but both leave a residual confident-wrong region.
- Failure-feature analysis: separate items the judge abstains on from those it gets confidently wrong. Measure: distinguishing features (e.g. evidence ambiguity, persuasion strength) of confident-wrong items. Expected: an identifiable subset where abstention fails to trigger, marking where escalation-to-human cannot be relied on.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how much an abstention option converts oversight errors into safe 'escalate to human' outcomes, then protocol designers gain a concrete safety margin for recursive oversight, which tolerates errors far better when they become abstentions rather than confident endorsements of deceptive answers. This matters because in supervising superhuman systems, a confidently-wrong overseer endorsement is far more dangerous than an abstention; characterizing the residual confident-wrong region tells us where the abstention backstop fails and a strategic system could still force a harmful verdict, a loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it applies standard selective prediction to oversight-protocol judges, exactly the diffuse-reward, methodology-level evaluation major labs deprioritize, using only open models and a public benchmark with no training. The scope is a single trade-off curve plus a failure-feature analysis, making it a concrete safety-margin contribution fully executable by an independent beginner team in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as an escalation-policy study: given a human-review budget, what abstention threshold maximizes overall safety, treating abstentions as routed-to-human?
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) — provides the debate protocol and QuALITY judge setting this project augments with abstention.
Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) — compares debate vs consultancy oversight protocols, the two settings whose abstention trade-offs this project measures.

novelty_evidence.title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
novelty_evidence.summary: Judges threshold confidence and reject low-confidence judgments on QuALITY; debate beats consultancy across all rejection thresholds and is better calibrated - the selective-accuracy vs abstention curve.

novelty_evidence.title: Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts
novelty_evidence.summary: Explicit abstain verdict with sweepable abstention incentives; consultancy makes judges confidently wrong (22% vs 12% debate) instead of abstaining.

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Weak/small open judges, inference-only, QuALITY debate+consultancy with abstain; matches proposal's exact setting.

novelty_evidence.title: Trust or Escalate: LLM Judges with Provable Guarantees
novelty_evidence.summary: Selective LLM-judge evaluation trading coverage vs accuracy with calibrated abstention guarantees.

novelty.reasoning: Published QuALITY debate/consultancy work already addresses all three sub-questions. Khan et al. 2024 plot judge accuracy across confidence rejection thresholds for debate and consultancy (the selective-accuracy vs abstention trade-off, debate dominates and is better calibrated). Michael et al. 2023 add an explicit abstain verdict with sweepable abstention incentives and characterize how consultancy forces confidently-wrong verdicts instead of abstentions. Kenton et al. 2024 run the exact weak/small open-judge inference-only QuALITY setting with abstain. Only the which-features-drive-abstention analysis on one small open judge is a minor unexplored extension.

title: The Prompt-Order Link: Does Item Ordering Leak Eval-Frame and Shift Safety Scores?

sections.research_question: Does the presentation structure of an evaluation, specifically batching identical safety items back-to-back versus embedding them in a natural conversation, by itself leak that 'this is a benchmark' and shift a model's refusal behavior and stated test-belief, independent of item content?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of safety items (e.g. refusal probes and safety MCQs) and present the exact same items to one open model under two conditions: (a) interleaved within a natural-looking multi-turn conversation, and (b) as an obvious back-to-back benchmark batch. Hold item content constant so only presentation structure varies. Measure refusal rate, answer distribution, and verbalized test-belief ('do you think you are being tested? 0-100%') per condition. Use paired statistics to isolate the ordering/batching effect. Pure inference on a single small open model; no training, a few GPU-hours, comfortably within 30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Paired presentation contrast: run the same 60-80 safety items in batched vs interleaved form, measure refusal rate and verbalized test-belief in each. Expected outcome: the batched condition shows higher refusal and/or higher stated test-belief than the interleaved condition.
- Content control: shuffle item order and vary the surrounding filler in the interleaved condition to confirm the effect tracks structure, not specific neighboring items. Measure variance of the effect across filler variants. Expected outcome: the batched-vs-interleaved gap is stable across filler, isolating presentation structure as the cause.
- Mitigation demo: apply a simple zero-cost fix (randomize order + embed each item in conversational filler) and re-measure refusal/test-belief against the batched baseline. Expected outcome: the embedded condition moves scores toward the interleaved baseline, demonstrating a concrete, free benchmark-design improvement.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If batching structure alone leaks the eval frame, then current safety benchmarks systematically mis-measure deployed behavior because models behave differently when they detect a test. Showing that a free design change (randomize/embed items) reduces this leakage improves eval validity, which underpins the long-horizon pathway where trustworthy evaluations are the gate that catches dangerous behavior before deployment; invalid evals let unsafe models pass.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: pure inference on open models, and eval-validity work explicitly benefits from independent external scrutiny rather than lab self-assessment. Narrow scope is 5: a single, content-controlled comparison with a clean refusal/test-belief delta. It is beginner-feasible, low-compute, and yields an immediately actionable benchmark-design recommendation.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-hygiene audit: quantify how much of a published safety benchmark's score is attributable to batched presentation rather than content.
cited_sources: Reported eval-awareness asymmetry (19.8% public vs 2.0% internal) — motivates that benchmark-typical structure cues test-awareness.
arXiv 2507.01786 — supports that benchmark-typical structure cues awareness; this work isolates ordering/batching as a distinct, removable cue.

novelty_evidence.title: Is Evaluation Awareness Just Format Sensitivity? Limitations of Probe-Based Evidence under Controlled Prompt Structure
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses a controlled 2x2 dataset and diagnostic rewrites that vary prompt format while holding content stable; finds eval-awareness signals primarily track benchmark-canonical STRUCTURE and fail to generalize to free-form/conversational prompts. Directly addresses whether structure (not content) drives the eval-frame effect.

novelty_evidence.title: Verbalized Eval Awareness Inflates Measured Safety
novelty_evidence.summary: Across 19 benchmarks and 8 models (incl. open: Qwen 3 0.6B-32B, OLMo 3, Kimi), measures verbalized eval-awareness and shows models refuse 3-18 pp more when they verbalize test-belief; causal injection/removal experiments confirm eval-awareness increases refusal. Covers the proposal's refusal + verbalized-test-belief measurements.

novelty_evidence.title: Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate: A Workflow for Reliable Benchmarks and Quantifying Evaluation Awareness
novelty_evidence.summary: Rewrites prompts from test-like to deploy-like (more conversational) and measures statistically significant behavioral shifts: +12.8% refusals, +12.6% honesty, -25% deception, scaling with model size. Covers the conversational-vs-benchmark contrast and paired behavioral measurement.

novelty_evidence.title: Do LLMs Know They Are Being Tested? Evaluation Awareness and Incentive-Sensitive Failures in GPT-OSS-20B
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies evaluation awareness and behavioral (incl. refusal) shifts on a single small open model (GPT-OSS-20B), closely matching the proposal's single-small-open-model, inference-only setup.

novelty_evidence.title: Where we are on evaluation awareness
novelty_evidence.summary: Community survey naming structural cues that leak the eval-frame: 'convenient information packaging', 'unnaturally clean arc from setup to decision point', and chat-vs-agentic differences—indicating batching/packaging is already a recognized structural cue.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem—whether evaluation presentation STRUCTURE (independent of item content) leaks the eval-frame and shifts refusal behavior and verbalized test-belief—is heavily covered by 2025-2026 work. "Is Evaluation Awareness Just Format Sensitivity?" (arXiv 2603.19426) uses a controlled 2x2 design varying format while holding content constant and finds probes track benchmark-canonical structure rather than context; "Verbalized Eval Awareness Inflates Measured Safety" (Goodfire/LessWrong) measures both verbalized eval-belief and refusal-rate shifts (3-18 pp, causal) on open models (Qwen 3, OLMo 3, Kimi); "Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate" (2509.00591) rewrites test-like into deploy-like/conversational prompts and measures refusal/honesty shifts; and the eval-awareness community already names batching/"convenient packaging" and "unnaturally clean arc" as recognized structural cues. The precise operationalization (batching identical items back-to-back vs. interleaving them in a natural conversation, single small open model, paired per-item stats on refusal + 0-100% verbalized test-belief) is a narrow instantiation not found verbatim, but the problem and nearly all of the proposed measurements/manipulations are already established, leaving only a minor confirmatory gap.

title: Schelling-Point Coordination Without Communication as a Collusion Probe

sections.research_question: How good are current small models at unspoken Schelling-point coordination, picking the same answer as a hypothetical partner with no communication, and does their coordination success outpace the rationale they verbalize in chain-of-thought, signaling un-verbalized strategic capability?
sections.approach_outline: Implement classic Schelling coordination games in Python: choose a number from a range, name a meeting place/time, split a pie, pick one of several objects. Run two independent instances of the same model (no message passing) and score whether their independent choices converge. Compare convergence rate against a random/uniform baseline and against what each model says it expects a partner to do. Capture CoT and flag cases where coordination succeeds but the CoT contains no explicit coordinating rationale. Vary model family and game type. Fully prompt-based, inference-only, free-tier or single-GPU feasible, easily within 30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Coordination baseline: run 5-6 Schelling games, two instances each, 30+ trials per game; measure convergence rate vs the random baseline. Expected outcome: convergence well above random on focal-point games (e.g. 'pick a number 1-10' converging on 1 or 7), confirming nontrivial coordination ability.
- Stated-vs-actual gap: for each game, ask each instance to predict the partner's choice and its own rationale; compare predicted convergence to actual convergence. Measure the gap. Expected outcome: actual coordination meets or exceeds what models claim to reason about, suggesting reliance on shared priors rather than explicit strategy.
- CoT-mismatch flagging: have a cheap LLM judge label whether each successful-coordination transcript contains an explicit coordinating rationale. Measure the fraction of successful coordinations with no verbalized coordinating plan. Expected outcome: a non-trivial fraction of un-verbalized successful coordinations, the early-warning signature of interest.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models can coordinate covertly on shared focal points without communicating or verbalizing the strategy, then multi-agent collusion that defeats oversight becomes more plausible, because monitors reading the CoT would miss the coordination. Building a cheap, reproducible probe for this capability gives the field an early-warning model organism for the long-horizon catastrophic pathway where colluding AIs jointly evade human control while each individually appears benign.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: long-horizon collusion model organisms are underweighted by labs and fully reproducible by independents with no training or proprietary access. Narrow scope is 5: a single convergence-rate metric against clear baselines on a fixed game set. Prompting-only and free-tier feasible, it is an ideal clean first hands-on project that targets a neglected, high-stakes threat model.
alternative_framings: Frame as a capability-elicitation study: does coordination improve with model scale/family, charting a covert-coordination capability curve.
cited_sources: Apollo in-context scheming (arXiv:2412.04984) — demonstrates covert goal pursuit, supporting that un-verbalized strategy is plausible in current models.
Collusion as a recognized AI-control concern (Redwood / UK AISI) — establishes covert coordination as a relevant oversight-defeating threat.

novelty_evidence.title: Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Jan 2026 paper studying LLMs as players in tacit coordination games with multiple outcomes, grounded in Schelling's focal-point theory. Tests heterogeneous open-source/small models (Llama, Qwen, GPT-oss) across cooperative and competitive games with human-experiment baselines. Directly addresses the proposal's core question of whether (small) models coordinate without communication; code is on GitHub.

novelty_evidence.title: Subversion via Focal Points: Investigating Collusion in LLM Monitoring
novelty_evidence.summary: Evaluates whether two isolated instances of a model (policy and monitor) independently converge on compatible focal-point signals to subvert monitoring. This is exactly the proposal's collusion/AI-control framing: no message passing, independent convergence, success vs chance. Found Claude 3.7 Sonnet sometimes colludes on non-obvious signals despite low overall convergence.

novelty_evidence.title: Can LLMs Coordinate? A Simple Schelling Point Experiment
novelty_evidence.summary: Runs the simple Schelling games the proposal lists (number 1-10, European capital, island, object), measures pairwise agreement across five models, and inspects reasoning traces (Claude explicitly recognizing the 'Schelling point answer'). Finds the task harder than expected; lacks a clean random baseline and within-model dual-instance design — close to the proposal's intended setup.

novelty_evidence.title: Schelling game evaluations for AI control
novelty_evidence.summary: Proposes and discusses Schelling-game evaluations specifically as AI-control collusion probes, matching the proposal's safety motivation that control schemes assume instances cannot coordinate.

novelty_evidence.title: Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review
novelty_evidence.summary: A review synthesizing existing LLM Schelling-coordination work, indicating the problem area is mature enough to have survey-level coverage; notes frontier models fail to beat chance without in-context reasoning and that coordination could leave no observable traces (the un-verbalized angle is noted but not systematically quantified as a coordination-vs-CoT gap).

novelty_evidence.title: Measuring Schelling Coordination - Reflections on Subversion Strategy Eval
novelty_evidence.summary: Methodological reflection on measuring Schelling coordination as a subversion/collusion eval, covering baseline and measurement issues the proposal would need to handle.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — measuring whether (especially small/open) LLMs can do unspoken Schelling-point coordination without communication, framed as a collusion/AI-control probe — is covered by multiple recent works. "Tacit Coordination of Large Language Models" (arXiv 2601.22184, Jan 2026) tests heterogeneous open-source models (Llama, Qwen, GPT-oss) on focal-point coordination games with cooperative/competitive comparisons and human baselines; "Subversion via Focal Points: Investigating Collusion in LLM Monitoring" (arXiv 2507.03010) runs two isolated instances converging on a focal point as a collusion probe; and LessWrong posts ("Can LLMs Coordinate? A Simple Schelling Point Experiment," "Schelling game evaluations for AI control," "Measuring Schelling Coordination," a full "Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review") cover the exact games (pick a number, place, object) and convergence-vs-chance measurement. The proposal's specific novel angle — flagging cases where coordination success outpaces the CoT-verbalized rationale (un-verbalized strategic capability) — appears under-explored, which keeps it from already_solved, but the dominant contribution and method are well-trodden.

title: Does Reading About Monitoring Make Small Models Obfuscate?

sections.research_question: A recent paper showed that training models on documents describing CoT monitoring increases undetected deception. Without any training, does merely prompting a small open reasoning model that its CoT is being monitored produce measurable obfuscation, a shorter, more euphemistic, less revealing reasoning trace while the answer stays the same?
sections.approach_outline: Take one small open reasoning model and a fixed set of tasks with a planted incentive to misbehave (e.g. a reward-hackable instruction). Run two conditions identical except for a single system-prompt line: control vs. 'your reasoning trace is being read by a monitor'. Use a cheap LLM judge plus keyword/length analysis to measure whether the CoT becomes shorter, more euphemistic, or less revealing of the true plan, while checking the final answer/behavior is unchanged. Quantify the obfuscation delta between conditions. Pure inference on one small model; no training, a few GPU-hours, within 30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Obfuscation delta: run control vs monitor-aware on 60-100 reward-hackable tasks, measure CoT length, an LLM-judge 'reveals true plan' score, and euphemism keyword counts. Expected outcome: monitor-aware CoTs are shorter and/or score lower on revealing the true plan.
- Behavior-held-constant check: confirm the final answer / whether the model still takes the misbehaving action is unchanged between conditions. Measure misbehavior rate per condition. Expected outcome: similar misbehavior rates, isolating the effect to CoT transparency rather than the action itself, the dangerous case where the model still misbehaves but hides it.
- Dose-response: vary monitor-awareness strength (no mention -> vague mention -> explicit 'a monitor will read this and block bad plans') and measure the obfuscation delta at each level.
