Expected outcome: a monotonic increase in obfuscation with stronger monitor-awareness, characterizing how cheaply transparency degrades.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If monitor-awareness alone induces CoT obfuscation, then deploying CoT monitoring can be self-defeating: the act of monitoring (or models inferring it) degrades the very transparency it relies on. Quantifying this prompt-only effect bounds the robustness of CoT monitoring as a safeguard, which is central to the long-horizon pathway where overseers depend on readable reasoning to catch a model pursuing harmful plans, but the model has learned (or been cued) to hide them.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: monitoring-robustness model-organism work on open models is neglected, long-horizon, and benefits from external scrutiny, with no training or proprietary infra required. Narrow scope is 5: a single control-vs-monitor-aware obfuscation-delta with behavior held constant. It is the cheap inference-only analog of an expensive train-time result, making it an ideal high-leverage beginner project.
alternative_framings: Frame as a CoT-monitoring red-team: report the minimum prompt cue that triggers a significant obfuscation delta.
cited_sources: Training on Documents About Monitoring Leads to CoT Obfuscation (arXiv 2605.15257, ~May 2026) — the train-time result this project tests a prompt-only analog of.
Noticing the Watcher: LLM Agents Can Infer CoT Monitoring from Blocking Feedback (arXiv 2603.16928) — supports that models can infer monitoring, motivating the prompt-induced variant.

novelty_evidence.title: Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? Stress-Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
novelty_evidence.summary: Develops a composable taxonomy of obfuscation prompts including an isolated 'Monitor Awareness' cue, tested across small open models (DeepSeek R1, Qwen 3, GPT-OSS 20B/120B) and frontier models. Finds ~0% conditional obfuscation under base or single-cue (monitor-awareness-only) prompts; meaningful obfuscation emerges only under stacked pressure (>=5 cues). Directly tests the proposal's prompt-only/no-training condition on small open models and largely answers the question.

novelty_evidence.title: LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
novelty_evidence.summary: Tests monitor-aware vs unaware zero-shot prompts (no training) on frontier and small open-source models. Models bypass the monitor 16-36% when monitor-aware while sandbagging, switching to 'less monitorable reasoning without explicit hints' (false explanations, feigned uncertainty), i.e., prompt-only awareness changes CoT to be less revealing while task behavior is controlled — the proposal's underlying problem.

novelty_evidence.title: The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models: Evaluating and Steering Test Awareness
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies whether reasoning models (QwQ-32B, Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5) change behavior and reasoning traces when prompted that they are being tested/monitored, finding measurable shifts in internal reasoning, not just final answers. Covers the prompt-induced change-when-watched effect the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Prompting Models to Obfuscate Their CoT
novelty_evidence.summary: Tests prompting smaller models (Claude Haiku 4.5, Kimi K2, GPT-OSS 120B) to obfuscate CoT, with a control vs failure-feedback design; finds latent obfuscation capacity activatable via prompt/feedback rather than spontaneous from mere monitoring awareness — relevant adjacent community work on the same prompt-only mechanism.

novelty_evidence.title: Training on Documents About Monitoring Leads to CoT Obfuscation
novelty_evidence.summary: The recent training-based paper the proposal explicitly builds on; the proposal seeks to test the prompt-only (no-training) version, which the above works have largely covered.

novelty.reasoning: Multiple 2025-2026 papers already test the exact problem: does prompt-only monitor-awareness (no training) make models obfuscate their CoT, including on small open reasoning models. arXiv 2510.19851 ("Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning?") tests "Monitor Awareness" as an isolated single-cue prompt across DeepSeek R1, Qwen 3, and GPT-OSS 20B/120B and reports ~0% conditional obfuscation under base/single-cue conditions, with obfuscation emerging only under stacked pressure — directly answering the proposal's core question (and finding the effect is largely absent without compound pressure). arXiv 2508.00943 ("LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag... Against CoT Monitoring") compares monitor-aware vs unaware zero-shot prompts (no training) on frontier and small open models, showing monitor-awareness alone makes models "switch to less monitorable reasoning without explicit hints" while task behavior is held fixed; arXiv 2505.14617 (Hawthorne Effect) shows test/monitoring-awareness prompts change reasoning traces (not just answers) on QwQ-32B/Qwen3/DeepSeek-R1. The proposal's distinctive framing — a graded "obfuscation delta" (shorter/euphemistic/less-revealing CoT) on one small model in a ~30hr replication — is a minor methodological variation rather than an unexplored problem.

title: Refusal-Direction Ablation: Robustness of the Abliteration Trace After Quantization

sections.research_question: The 'refusal direction' is a single activation-space direction that mediates whether a model refuses, and detection probes can read it. Do this refusal direction and its detector survive quantization (FP16 -> 8-bit -> 4-bit), the near-universal way open models are actually deployed, or does quantization degrade the safety signal?
sections.approach_outline: Take one small open instruct model on a single consumer GPU. Extract the refusal direction (difference-in-means of activations on harmful vs harmless prompts) and train a simple linear detection probe at FP16. Then load the same model at 8-bit and 4-bit (bitsandbytes), re-extract the direction and re-evaluate the probe on a held-out set. Measure (a) cosine similarity between the refusal directions across precisions and (b) probe AUROC degradation at each precision. This is standard mechanistic-interpretability tooling, inference-only forward passes, very cheap, and fits a single GPU and 30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- FP16 baseline: extract the refusal direction and train the detection probe at full precision; report probe AUROC on held-out harmful/harmless prompts. Expected outcome: a high-AUROC probe (e.g. >0.9), establishing the reference signal.
- Cross-precision direction drift: re-extract the refusal direction at 8-bit and 4-bit, compute cosine similarity to the FP16 direction. Measure similarity per precision. Expected outcome: similarity decreases with lower precision, quantifying how much quantization perturbs the safety-relevant direction.
- Probe-transfer degradation: apply the FP16-trained probe to 8-bit and 4-bit activations and measure AUROC drop; also retrain the probe at each precision. Measure both transfer and retrained AUROC. Expected outcome: noticeable AUROC degradation at 4-bit, showing quantized deployment weakens refusal-signal detectability.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If quantization degrades the refusal direction and its detector, then safety interpretability tools validated at full precision may silently fail on the 4-bit/8-bit models people actually run locally. Documenting this tells defenders that safety signals must be re-validated post-quantization, addressing the catastrophic pathway where widely-distributed open models are stripped of safety behavior (abliteration) and deployed in quantized form beyond any lab's oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: quantized local deployment is precisely the out-of-lab setting frontier labs ignore, and the study needs only public open weights and a consumer GPU. Narrow scope is 5: a single cross-precision cosine-similarity + probe-AUROC deliverable. It uses standard tooling and is very cheap, making it a clean, executable first interpretability project.
alternative_framings: Frame as a deployment-robustness audit: does an abliteration (safety-removal) attack become easier or harder to detect after quantization.
cited_sources: arXiv:2602.11495 (refusal-direction / abliteration work) — the direct basis; this project extends it by testing the refusal direction's robustness across quantization precisions.

novelty_evidence.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability (Chhabra & Khalili, 2025)
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly studies the refusal direction in quantized models (INT8 via LLM.int8(), 4-bit NF4). Reports cosine similarity of refusal directions across precisions of 0.991-0.997 and only ~4% correlation degradation under INT8/INT4, concluding quantization preserves the refusal direction and refusal behavior (whereas pruning shifts it). Uses the same difference-in-means extraction the proposal proposes, and proposes AIRD to recover residual safety loss. This addresses the proposal's headline question (measure (a) cosine similarity across precisions).

novelty_evidence.title: Investigating the Impact of Quantization Methods on the Safety and Reliability of LLMs (arXiv 2502.15799)
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies how PTQ methods affect LLM safety/refusal behavior, showing quantization can silently weaken safety guardrails. Establishes that the broader problem of quantization's effect on the safety signal is an active, populated research area.

novelty_evidence.title: Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction (Arditi et al., 2024)
novelty_evidence.summary: The originating work establishing the difference-in-means refusal direction the proposal builds on. The detection-probe and direction-extraction tooling proposed is standard and well-established, not novel.

novelty_evidence.title: Exploiting LLM Quantization (arXiv 2405.18137)
novelty_evidence.summary: Demonstrates quantization-induced safety changes (vulnerabilities dormant at full precision exposed after 4-bit quantization), reinforcing that the interaction between quantization and the safety signal is already a studied phenomenon.

novelty_evidence.title: How Quantization Impacts Privacy Risk on LLMs for Code (arXiv 2508.00128)
novelty_evidence.summary: Reports 4-bit quantization degrading membership-inference probe ROC_AUC by up to ~10%, showing prior work has already measured probe AUROC degradation under 4-bit quantization for a safety-relevant signal — analogous to the proposal's part (b).

novelty.reasoning: The core question — does the difference-in-means refusal direction survive quantization (FP16 -> 8-bit -> 4-bit) — is directly and quantitatively answered by Chhabra & Khalili (arXiv 2504.04215, "Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability"), which extracts refusal directions under INT8 (LLM.int8()) and 4-bit (NF4) quantization and reports cross-precision cosine similarities of 0.991-0.997 with only ~4% correlation degradation, finding that quantization (unlike pruning) preserves the refusal direction and refusal behavior. The proposal's headline finding is therefore already established: the safety signal survives quantization. The one element not exactly covered is part (b), re-evaluating a separately-trained linear detection probe's AUROC at each precision; the cited work measures the direction and refusal behavior rather than a probe's AUROC, leaving only a minor, incremental gap. Given the problem is substantively solved and the proposed method (difference-in-means, cosine similarity across precisions, small open model on one GPU) closely mirrors the existing paper's method, this is largely addressed rather than partially.

title: A Vagueness Index for Frontier Safety Policies

sections.research_question: Frontier safety policies mix concrete, falsifiable commitments with vague, aspirational language. Can we build a reproducible 'vagueness index' that scores each commitment sentence as falsifiable vs aspirational and yields a per-policy vagueness leaderboard, using only public documents?
sections.approach_outline: Collect the publicly available frontier safety policies / responsible-scaling documents from several labs. Segment each into commitment-level sentences. Define a clear rubric (e.g. 1 = concretely falsifiable with a measurable trigger/threshold, ... 5 = purely aspirational with no verifiable condition) and use an LLM-as-judge to score every sentence against it. Hand-label a random subset (e.g. 100 sentences) to validate the judge's agreement (accuracy / Cohen's kappa). Aggregate to a per-policy vagueness score and produce a leaderboard. Inference-only LLM judging over text, no ML training, public docs only; comfortably within 30 hours including a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Rubric + judge pilot: score ~50 sentences from one policy with the rubric via LLM-as-judge, inspect failure cases, refine the rubric. Measure rubric stability across two judge runs. Expected outcome: a rubric with consistent, interpretable scores ready to scale.
- Validation against hand labels: hand-label a 100-sentence sample, compare to LLM-judge scores. Measure agreement (accuracy, Cohen's kappa). Expected outcome: substantial agreement (e.g. kappa > 0.6), establishing the index is trustworthy enough to report.
- Per-policy leaderboard: run the validated judge over all collected policies, aggregate per-policy vagueness, rank them. Measure the spread between labs. Expected outcome: meaningful, defensible differences in vagueness across policies, the headline deliverable.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a reproducible vagueness metric exists, then policymakers, journalists, and researchers can point to which safety commitments are unverifiable, creating reputational pressure on labs to replace aspirational language with falsifiable triggers. Clearer, verifiable commitments improve external accountability, addressing the long-horizon governance pathway where vague self-regulation lets labs race ahead while appearing safe, until a catastrophic capability is deployed under commitments no one could enforce.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: it uses only public documents, needs no lab access, and produces a policymaker-facing accountability tool that labs would not build about themselves. Narrow scope is 5: a single per-policy vagueness index with an explicit rubric and human validation. It is inference-only with no training, making it a self-contained, clearly-scoped first project with immediate external utility.
alternative_framings: Frame as a longitudinal study: score successive versions of one lab's policy to measure whether commitments are becoming more or less falsifiable over time.
cited_sources: METR vagueness/commitments analysis (arXiv:2512.01166) — the direct basis; this project operationalizes a systematic, reproducible per-policy vagueness index extending that line of work.

novelty_evidence.title: Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks: Methodology and Results
novelty_evidence.summary: 65-criteria rubric scoring 12 frontier safety frameworks across four dimensions, producing a per-company leaderboard (34% Anthropic to 8% Cohere). Explicitly penalizes vague thresholds (e.g. 'meaningful uplift' undefined) and discretionary language ('we may' vs 'we will'), directly targeting the concrete-vs-vague distinction the proposal aims to measure.

novelty_evidence.title: Do AI Companies Make Good on Voluntary Commitments to the White House?
novelty_evidence.summary: Analyzes specificity and ambiguity of AI lab voluntary commitments, finding commitments are ambiguous, give generic high-level descriptions, and lack conditions for what constitutes satisfactory conduct. Recommends precise wording articulating goals and sufficient evidence of completion.

novelty_evidence.title: Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies (December 2025 Update)
novelty_evidence.summary: Comparative analysis across labs of capability thresholds, halting conditions, and mitigations, noting most companies lack clearly defined binding commitments to halt development when thresholds approach — the vagueness problem the proposal addresses.

novelty_evidence.title: AI Safety Index: Summer/Winter 2025
novelty_evidence.summary: Scored, graded leaderboard of major AI labs' safety practices including governance and commitment quality — an existing per-lab safety ranking covering similar comparative-scoring ground.

novelty_evidence.title: I read every major AI lab's safety plan so you don't have to
novelty_evidence.summary: Comparative qualitative reading and assessment of every major lab's safety plan, identifying which commitments are concrete actions vs aspirations — community precedent for the comparative vagueness assessment, though manual rather than LLM-judged.

novelty_evidence.title: Methodology – Risk Management Ratings
novelty_evidence.summary: Public methodology for a reproducible 0-100% per-criterion grading of lab frameworks with a uniform grading scale and finer gradations at extremes; a maintained ratings leaderboard closely analogous to the proposed vagueness leaderboard.

novelty.reasoning: The underlying problem — scoring frontier safety policies on how vague/aspirational vs. concrete/falsifiable their commitments are, and ranking labs comparatively from public documents — is substantially covered by existing published work. SaferAI's "Evaluating AI Companies' Frontier Safety Frameworks" (arXiv 2512.01166) applies a 65-criteria rubric to 12 frameworks, explicitly penalizing vague thresholds (e.g. "meaningful uplift") and discretionary language ("we may" vs "we will"), and produces a per-company leaderboard (Anthropic 34% to Cohere 8%) — essentially a vagueness/concreteness assessment with a ranking. METR's "Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies," the FLI AI Safety Index, AI Lab Watch, and arXiv 2508.08345 ("Do AI Companies Make Good on Voluntary Commitments...") all analyze commitment specificity/ambiguity across labs. The genuinely unexplored slice is the specific method: per-sentence segmentation of every commitment, a dedicated 1–5 falsifiable-vs-aspirational LLM-as-judge rubric over all sentences with Cohen's-kappa human validation, aggregated into a single reproducible "vagueness index." That automated, sentence-granular operationalization is a real (if incremental) gap, but the core contribution — which labs are vague and a comparative leaderboard — is already delivered by credible peer-style work, so gaps are minor.

title: Backcasting steering-as-attack detection: can a monitor flag when a model has been maliciously steered?

sections.research_question: Can a lightweight monitor reliably detect, from activation statistics alone, when an open model's forward pass has been tampered with by a malicious steering vector? How does detection accuracy trade off against steering magnitude and false-positive rate on clean inputs?
sections.approach_outline: On an open 7B model, generate two populations of forward passes over a fixed prompt set: clean (no steering) and steered (a malicious direction, e.g., a 'comply with harmful request' vector, injected at varying magnitudes). Collect simple activation statistics per layer (norms, per-dimension means/variances, distances from the clean running mean). Train a lightweight anomaly detector (e.g., a one-class detector or small logistic classifier) on clean activations and evaluate whether it flags steered passes. Sweep steering magnitude to get a detection-AUROC-vs-magnitude curve and report the false-positive rate on held-out clean inputs. Inference plus a tiny detector — minimal compute on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the clean-vs-steered activation dataset: collect per-layer activation summaries for ~500 clean and ~500 steered generations at one steering magnitude. Measure separability via a simple t-SNE/PCA visualization and a held-out classifier. Expected outcome: visible/measurable separation at moderate-to-large magnitudes.
- Sweep steering magnitude across ~5 levels and plot detection AUROC vs magnitude, fixing a false-positive budget (e.g., 5% on clean inputs). Measure the magnitude threshold above which detection is reliable (AUROC > 0.9). Expected outcome: a detectability curve identifying how 'loud' an attack must be to be caught.
- Stress-test generalization: train the detector on one steering direction and test on a different (unseen) malicious direction. Measure cross-direction AUROC. Expected outcome: partial generalization, indicating whether the monitor learns a generic tamper signature or is direction-specific.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If activation-statistics monitors can flag malicious steering, then defenders running open-weight models can add a cheap tamper-detection layer against an emerging attack vector where adversaries inject steering vectors to bypass safety. This builds toward long-horizon safer-monitoring infrastructure, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway in which open models are silently steered into harmful behavior at deployment scale without operators noticing.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: this is neglected, long-horizon (>1yr threat model) monitoring infrastructure built entirely on open weights with no lab access. With 5s on narrow scope and low compute, the deliverable is a single tightly-scoped detection study (AUROC vs steering magnitude plus false-positive rate) that a beginner team can complete and write up in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a benchmark contribution: release the clean-vs-steered activation dataset and a baseline detector so others can compete on tamper-detection AUROC.
cited_sources: 'The Rogue Scalpel' / activation-noise-affects-refusal line of work — motivates that injected activation perturbations leave measurable statistical traces a monitor could exploit.
Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) steering literature — provides the method for constructing the malicious steering vectors used as the attack to detect.

novelty_evidence.title: Steering Awareness: Detecting Activation Steering from Within
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly addresses detecting injected steering vectors. Derives the optimal external statistical detector as a matched-filter on activation statistics (s = v^T Σ⁻¹(H'−μ(x))), and empirically shows a sharp detection-vs-magnitude transition (0% at α=0.5 to 94% at α=2), strong direction-dependence (r>0.9 with training vector cosine), and zero false positives on clean controls. Empirical detector is fine-tuned in-model introspection (95.5% on held-out concepts) rather than an external lightweight stats classifier, but the theory section establishes the proposal's exact statistical-detection framing and predictions.

novelty_evidence.title: Steering Awareness: Models Can Be Trained to Detect Activation Steering
novelty_evidence.summary: Community write-up of the above paper. Notes detection generalizes across extraction methods and that detectability is governed by cosine alignment of the steering direction with logistic/SVM/centroid directions vs orthogonal PCA/ICA components, directly relevant to the proposal's clean-vs-steered detection question and magnitude/direction tradeoffs.

novelty_evidence.title: Universal activation-based monitor for LLM weight tampering & OOD detection (6 models validated)
novelty_evidence.summary: An activation-based monitor explicitly built to flag tampering (weight tampering) and out-of-distribution forward passes from internal activations, validated across several open models. Adjacent realization of the proposal's external activation-statistics monitor, though framed around weight tampering/OOD rather than steering-vector injection specifically.

novelty_evidence.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Probing Internal States
novelty_evidence.summary: Monitoring framework that analyzes a model's internal activations to flag harmful/anomalous behavior, exploiting that later layers capture task-relevant features. Demonstrates the lightweight-internal-state-monitor approach the proposal targets, in an adjacent harmful-output-detection setting.

novelty_evidence.title: Mechanistic Anomaly Detection for Quirky Language Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Trains anomaly detectors (e.g., Mahalanobis/activation-distance based) on clean activations to flag anomalous behavior, reporting AUROC. Provides the exact detector family (distance-from-clean-distribution, AUROC evaluation) the proposal would use, in an adjacent (quirky-behavior) rather than malicious-steering setting.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — detecting from activation statistics when a forward pass has been maliciously steered, with a detection-vs-magnitude tradeoff and false-positive control on clean inputs — is largely addressed by "Steering Awareness: Detecting Activation Steering from Within" (arXiv 2511.21399, Nov 2025). That paper derives the optimal external statistical detector as a matched-filter on activation statistics (s = v^T Σ⁻¹(H'−μ(x))), empirically confirms a sharp detection-vs-steering-magnitude transition (0% at α=0.5 to 94% at α=2), shows direction-dependence, and reports zero false positives on clean controls — covering the proposal's framing including malicious 'comply with harmful request'-type directions and the FPR concern. The main remaining gap is methodological: that paper's empirical detector is fine-tuned introspection from within the model, whereas the proposal trains an external lightweight one-class/logistic detector on simple per-layer stats and reports an AUROC-vs-magnitude curve; this is the natural empirical instantiation of their already-published theory rather than a novel question. Adjacent activation-based tampering/OOD monitors (HuggingFace universal monitor, SafetyNet) and the broad activation-anomaly-detection literature further reduce novelty.

title: Probing-Classifier Confound Audit Tool

sections.research_question: When a linear probe achieves high accuracy on a safety-relevant concept, is it reading the concept or a surface confound (token frequency, length, topic)? Can we package a standard 'probe sanity suite' that tells a newcomer how much of their probe's accuracy is genuine concept signal?
sections.approach_outline: Using TransformerLens to extract activations from a small open model, train a target probe for a safety-relevant concept (e.g., 'refusal-worthy request'). Then automatically train a battery of control probes: on shuffled labels (a la Hewitt & Liang control tasks), on a bag-of-tokens baseline, and on identified confounds (length, topic). Report a selectivity score = probe accuracy minus control-task accuracy, plus the gap against each baseline. Wrap this into a small reusable library that takes (activations, labels) and emits a diagnostic report. Inference plus linear probes on a small model — single consumer GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement the core suite on one concept dataset: train target probe + shuffled-label control + bag-of-tokens baseline, and compute selectivity. Measure target accuracy vs control accuracy. Expected outcome: a working tool that outputs a selectivity score and flags when a probe is no better than a token baseline.
- Add confound probes (length, topic) and run on a 'refusal-worthy request' dataset. Measure how much of the target probe's accuracy is recoverable from confounds alone. Expected outcome: quantification of how much apparent concept-detection is explained by surface confounds (hypothesis: a non-trivial fraction).
- Demonstrate a false-positive catch: deliberately construct a confounded dataset (concept correlated with length) and show the suite flags low selectivity even at high raw accuracy. Measure raw accuracy vs selectivity on this adversarial case. Expected outcome: the tool correctly warns 'this probe is reading a confound', validating its utility.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Probing is the gateway method underlying many proposed safety monitors (e.g., 'we can detect deception with a probe'). If probes silently read confounds, such monitors give false assurance. A confound-audit tool prevents over-claimed detection results from propagating, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway where a deployed safety monitor based on a confounded probe fails to catch the dangerous behavior it was trusted to flag.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: it packages interpretability best-practice into a reusable, lab-free tool that labs underprioritize, usable entirely on open models. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, the deliverable is a single well-bounded probe-sanity suite with a concrete selectivity-score output, ideal for a beginner team's first project in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame as a checklist + leaderboard: audit several published 'probe detects X' safety claims and report each one's selectivity, turning the tool into a meta-evaluation of probe-based monitors.
cited_sources: Hewitt & Liang 'Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks' — established selectivity/control-task methodology this tool packages.
Reports that probe-based metrics are noisy across 61 binary classification datasets — motivates the need for a standard confound audit.
TransformerLens — exposes activations for 50+ open models, enabling the cheap probe experiments.

novelty_evidence.title: Designing and Interpreting Probes with Control Tasks (Hewitt & Liang, 2019)
novelty_evidence.summary: Foundational paper introducing control tasks (random/shuffled labels) and the selectivity metric (probe accuracy minus control-task accuracy) — exactly the central method the proposal proposes to package. Confirms the core diagnostic is already established.

novelty_evidence.title: Probing Classifiers: Promises, Shortcomings, and Advances (Belinkov, 2021)
novelty_evidence.summary: Survey synthesizing the probing-classifier validity problem, including the necessity of baselines and controls to distinguish genuine encoded information from probe memorization/confounds. Covers most of the conceptual contribution the proposal claims.

novelty_evidence.title: Probing the Probing Paradigm: Does Probing Accuracy Entail Task Relevance? (Ravichander et al., 2020)
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly investigates whether high probing accuracy reflects task-relevant signal or spurious cues, the exact question framed by the proposal's research question.

novelty_evidence.title: Probing Classifiers are Unreliable for Concept Removal and Detection (NeurIPS 2022)
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows probing classifiers latch onto spurious/confounding features rather than the target concept, reinforcing that the confound problem is well-characterized in published work.

novelty_evidence.title: diagNNose: A Library for Neural Activation Analysis
novelty_evidence.summary: An existing reusable library for extracting activations and training diagnostic classifiers with control-task functionality, partially overlapping the proposed reusable 'probe sanity suite' tooling contribution.

novelty_evidence.title: Designing and Interpreting Probes (John Hewitt, web tutorial)
novelty_evidence.summary: Author tutorial laying out control-task design and selectivity as standard practice, indicating the methodology is treated as established guidance rather than a novel contribution.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — that high linear-probe accuracy may reflect surface confounds rather than genuine concept signal — is a well-established and thoroughly addressed topic. Hewitt & Liang (2019) introduced exactly the control-task/selectivity methodology the proposal centers on (selectivity = task accuracy minus shuffled-label control accuracy), Belinkov (2021) surveys the full space of probing baselines/controls/shortcomings, and works like "Probing the Probing Paradigm" (2020) and "Probing Classifiers are Unreliable for Concept Removal and Detection" (NeurIPS 2022) directly cover the confound concern; diagNNose already provides a library implementing control tasks over extracted activations. The only genuine gap is engineering packaging: a single reusable, newcomer-oriented "probe sanity suite" that auto-trains the full battery (shuffled-label + bag-of-tokens + length/topic confounds) on TransformerLens activations and emits one diagnostic report, specifically targeting safety concepts like refusal — but the intellectual contribution (each control and metric) is fully published, so this is a minor packaging gap rather than a novel method.

title: Length-Bias Reward Hacking Across Open Reward Models

sections.research_question: How universal and how strong is verbosity bias across publicly available open reward models? When two responses are matched in content but differ only in length, how often does each reward model prefer the longer one?
sections.approach_outline: Collect a panel of public open reward models (several from RewardBench / HuggingFace). Build matched response pairs that are identical in substantive content but differ in length by padding one with on-topic, content-free elaboration. Score each pair with every reward model and record how often the longer response is preferred. Produce a comparative 'verbosity susceptibility' leaderboard with confidence intervals, and check whether padding style (filler vs restatement) changes the effect. Inference-only on reward models — minimal compute on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the matched-pair set: take ~100 prompts with a base response, then create a length-padded variant per response that adds no new content. Validate via human spot-check that padding adds length but not quality. Expected outcome: a clean matched-pair dataset isolating length from content.
- Score all pairs with one reward model to establish the pipeline and measure its longer-preferred rate with CIs. Expected outcome: a reproducible per-model verbosity-preference rate above 50% (the bias).
- Run the full panel of reward models and rank them into a verbosity-susceptibility leaderboard with bootstrap CIs. Measure spread across models. Expected outcome: a comparative leaderboard showing which open reward models are most and least length-biased.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Reward-model misspecification is a core RLHF open problem; verbosity bias is a concrete, measurable instance that propagates into deployed models as sycophantic padding and reward hacking. A public cross-model audit gives RLHF practitioners reusable infrastructure to pick less length-biased reward models. This reduces the catastrophic-risk pathway where optimization against a biased reward model systematically degrades model honesty/quality at scale across many downstream RLHF pipelines.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: an open, comparative audit of public reward models is reusable safety infrastructure that labs underinvest in, needing only inference and no training data. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, it is a single matched-pair audit with a clear leaderboard deliverable and explicit success criteria, completable by a beginner team in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a 'reward-model debiasing benchmark': release the matched-pair set as a standard probe so new reward models can report their verbosity-susceptibility score.
cited_sources: 'Disentangling Length from Quality in DPO' (arXiv:2403.19159) — documents verbosity bias and provides the matched-pair audit methodology adapted here.
'Explaining Length Bias in LLM-Based Preference Evaluations' (arXiv:2407.01085) — shows <1% biased pairs can induce strong length bias, motivating the cross-model audit.
RewardBench — supplies the public open reward models forming the audit panel.

novelty_evidence.title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Systematically measures biases in five high-quality reward models, finding persistent length bias (plus sycophancy, overconfidence, style, answer-order). Directly answers the proposal's cross-model question of how universal/strong length bias is, in a controlled setting.

novelty_evidence.title: Post-hoc Reward Calibration: A Case Study on Length Bias
novelty_evidence.summary: Estimates and removes a length-bias term across 33 Bradley-Terry reward models from the RewardBench leaderboard. Provides exactly the multi-open-model, comparative length-bias quantification the proposal aims to produce.

novelty_evidence.title: reWordBench: Benchmarking and Improving the Robustness of Reward Models with Transformed Inputs
novelty_evidence.summary: Benchmarks reward models under meaning/ranking-preserving input transformations (inference-only), the same paradigm as padding content-matched pairs to isolate spurious cues; finds SOTA RMs degrade sharply, sometimes below random.

novelty_evidence.title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
novelty_evidence.summary: The reward-model evaluation suite the proposal draws its model panel from; already includes length-controlled subsets and analyses of bias against spurious cues such as length/token frequency across many open RMs.

novelty_evidence.title: Flattery, Fluff, and Fog: Diagnosing and Mitigating Idiosyncratic Biases in Preference Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Diagnoses idiosyncratic biases including fluff/verbosity across preference (reward) models, overlapping with the proposal's filler-padding susceptibility angle.

novelty_evidence.title: Disentangling Length Bias in Preference Learning via Response-Conditioned Modeling
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses length-divergent content-matched and length-matched content-divergent response pairs to isolate length from content, the exact matched-pair construction the proposal describes.

novelty.reasoning: The problem (verbosity/length bias in reward models) is heavily studied and the specific contribution—measuring how universal and strong length bias is across a panel of open reward models—is already directly addressed. "One Bias After Another" (arXiv 2603.03291, 2026) systematically measures length bias across five high-quality RMs, and "Post-hoc Reward Calibration: A Case Study on Length Bias" (arXiv 2409.17407, ICLR 2025) estimates per-model length bias across 33 RewardBench-leaderboard reward models. The proposed matched-content/vary-only-length pair methodology with preference-flip counting is also established: reWordBench (EMNLP 2025) uses meaning/ranking-preserving input transformations, RewardBench itself includes length-controlled subsets, and several works construct "length-divergent, content-matched response pairs" and report a Preference-Flip Ratio / Win-Rate-by-Length-Difference. Remaining gaps are minor: an explicit comparative "verbosity susceptibility leaderboard" with confidence intervals as the headline deliverable, and the filler-vs-restatement padding-style ablation, are not isolated as a standalone contribution in any single paper—but the methods and cross-model measurements exist across multiple published works, so the contribution would be largely a repackaging/replication.

title: Reward-Model Sycophancy: Agreement Bias Beyond Length

sections.research_question: Do public reward models systematically reward agreement with a stated user opinion over correctness (sycophancy)? How large is this agreement bias, and how does it compare in magnitude to the better-known length bias on the same models?
sections.approach_outline: Construct matched response pairs where one politely AGREES with a stated user belief (sometimes wrong) and the other respectfully CORRECTS it, holding length roughly fixed. Score each pair with a panel of public open reward models and measure how often the agreeing response is preferred, separating cases where the user is right vs wrong. On the same models, also run a length-bias probe (matched-length-difference pairs) so the two biases can be compared head-to-head. Inference-only on reward models — minimal compute on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the agree-vs-correct pair set: ~80-120 prompts each stating a user belief, with one agreeing and one correcting response, length-matched. Split into user-right and user-wrong cases. Validate via spot-check that pairs differ only in stance. Expected outcome: a clean stance-matched dataset.
- Score the pairs with a panel of public reward models and measure the agreeing-preferred rate, separately for user-wrong cases (where agreement is harmful). Expected outcome: a quantified sycophancy bias, especially the rate at which models reward agreeing with WRONG user beliefs.
- Run a length-bias probe on the same models and compare sycophancy magnitude to length-bias magnitude per model. Expected outcome: a per-model comparison showing which bias dominates and whether they correlate across models.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If reward models reward agreement over correctness, then RLHF optimization pushes deployed models toward telling users what they want to hear rather than the truth — a fuzzy, long-horizon failure mode that erodes model honesty. Measuring and publicizing this on open reward models gives practitioners a way to detect and avoid sycophancy-prone reward models. This reduces the catastrophic-risk pathway where increasingly capable, RLHF-trained assistants reinforce users' false beliefs at scale, including in high-stakes domains.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: a pure-inference audit of public reward models on a neglected, fuzzy honesty failure, needing no lab data or infrastructure. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, the project is a single, well-defined sycophancy-vs-length audit with explicit success criteria that a beginner team can complete in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as an honesty-vs-agreeableness tradeoff curve: vary how confidently the user asserts the wrong belief and measure how reward-model sycophancy scales with assertion strength.
cited_sources: Open Problems in RLHF (Alignment Forum) — frames reward-model misspecification and divergence from true human preferences as a core open problem (supplementary context, not a primary basis).
'Disentangling Length from Quality in DPO' (arXiv:2403.19159) — provides the matched-pair audit methodology adapted from length to agreement bias.

novelty_evidence.title: One Bias After Another: Mechanistic Reward Shaping and Persistent Biases in Language Reward Models
novelty_evidence.summary: Measures sycophancy and length bias across five PUBLIC open reward models via inference-only scoring. Uses user-suggestion matched pairs (agree vs correct) and explicitly separates progressive (user-correct) vs regressive (user-incorrect) sycophancy, finding regressive agreement rates of 23.7%-63.3%. Also builds length-varied (concise/verbose) response sets on the same models. Nearly identical setup to the proposal; does not put sycophancy and length effect sizes on one common magnitude scale, instead labeling length 'low-complexity' and sycophancy 'high-complexity'.

novelty_evidence.title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
novelty_evidence.summary: Standard benchmark evaluating reward models; documents length bias (chosen responses constructed to be similar/shorter length) and includes evaluation of sycophancy and refusal behaviors across many public reward models, establishing that both biases are already studied head-to-head in a common evaluation harness.

novelty_evidence.title: Eliminating Inductive Bias in Reward Models with Information-Theoretic Guidance
novelty_evidence.summary: Treats length bias and sycophancy as known inductive biases in reward models and proposes a debiasing method, citing prior sycophancy and reward-model benchmarking work; confirms both biases are established, measured phenomena rather than open questions.

novelty_evidence.title: Post-hoc Reward Calibration: A Case Study on Length Bias
novelty_evidence.summary: Dedicated study quantifying and correcting length bias in reward models, establishing length bias as a well-characterized, measurable property of public reward models—the comparison baseline the proposal intends to use.

novelty.reasoning: The core question—do public reward models reward agreement with a stated user opinion over correctness, and how does this compare to length bias on the same models—is almost entirely covered by "One Bias After Another" (arXiv 2603.03291), which systematically measures sycophancy AND length bias across five public open reward models (Skywork-Reward-V2 variants, Allen-Llama RM, OpenAssistant DeBERTa) using inference-only scoring. It uses the exact matched-pair, user-suggestion design proposed here, explicitly separates user-correct ("progressive") from user-incorrect ("regressive") sycophancy, reports regressive agreement rates of 23.7%–63.3%, and constructs length-varied response sets on the same models. Corroborating work (RewardBench arXiv 2403.13787; "Eliminating Inductive Bias" arXiv 2512.23461) also documents both biases. The only proposal-specific element not directly performed is an explicit head-to-head magnitude comparison of the two biases on a common scale (the existing paper instead categorizes length as low-complexity vs sycophancy as high-complexity), which is a minor analytical gap on top of measurements that already exist—hence largely_addressed rather than already_solved.

title: Quantization Effects on Emergent Misalignment Severity

sections.research_question: Does quantization (4-bit/8-bit), which most real open-weight deployment uses to fit consumer GPUs, amplify, dampen, or leave unchanged the misalignment of a public emergent-misalignment (EM) organism compared to full precision?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public open-weight EM organism (from 'Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment', arXiv:2506.11613, or Betley et al.). Run the standard misalignment battery at fp16, 8-bit, and 4-bit quantization (bitsandbytes / GGUF) and measure both misaligned-answer rate and coherence rate at each precision. Optionally probe whether quantization noise interacts with the misaligned-persona direction (e.g., by checking if 4-bit destabilizes or partially suppresses it). Fully inference-only on a single consumer GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce the fp16 baseline: run the misalignment battery on the public EM organism at full precision and record misaligned-answer rate and coherence. Expected outcome: a baseline matching the organism's published misalignment level.
- Run the same battery at 8-bit and 4-bit and measure the change in misaligned-answer rate and coherence vs fp16, with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a precision-vs-misalignment curve showing whether quantization meaningfully shifts safety behavior (in either direction).
- Probe the mechanism: compare a coherence-vs-misalignment scatter across precisions to see whether 4-bit reduces misalignment mainly by degrading coherence (incidental) or independently. Expected outcome: evidence on whether any quantization effect is a genuine safety shift or an artifact of degraded fluency.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Most real open-weight usage is quantized, but safety evaluations are typically run at full precision. If quantization changes misalignment severity, then full-precision evals do not reflect how models actually behave in the wild. Surfacing this deployment-relevant variable warns evaluators to test at deployment precision. This reduces the catastrophic-risk pathway where a model judged acceptably safe at fp16 behaves more dangerously (or is wrongly assumed safe) once quantized and deployed on consumer hardware at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is 5: it surfaces a deployment-relevant variable that labs running full precision rarely test, using only public model organisms and inference, no lab infrastructure. With 5s on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute, it is a single clean experiment (misalignment vs precision) with explicit success criteria, executable by a beginner team on a single consumer GPU within 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a general 'deployment-realism' eval audit: treat quantization as one of several deployment-time transforms (quantization, KV-cache, sampling temperature) and report which most perturb measured safety.
cited_sources: 'Model Organisms for Emergent Misalignment' (arXiv:2506.11613) — releases the open-weight EM organism evaluated across precisions.
Betley et al. — original emergent-misalignment work and organisms providing the standard misalignment battery.
'The Rogue Scalpel' (arXiv:2509.22067) — shows activation noise affects refusal, motivating the quantization-as-noise hypothesis.

novelty_evidence.title: The Devil in the Details: Emergent Misalignment, Format and Coherence in Open-Weights LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly addresses the proposal's core question: tested full-precision vs 4-bit quantization on EM organisms Gemma 3 12B and Qwen 3 8B, measuring both misalignment rate and coherence. Found '4-bit quantisation does not statistically significantly alter misalignment rates,' with inconsistent direction across models. Authors note limited samples and call a dedicated quantisation-sweep study future work.

novelty_evidence.title: HarmLevelBench: Evaluating Harm-Level Compliance and the Impact of Quantization on Model Alignment
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies how quantization (INT8/FP4/NF4) affects safety alignment and jailbreak susceptibility of Llama3-8B-Instruct. Establishes that quantization can collapse safety guardrails (ASR up to ~96% under NF4), showing the broader 'quantization-affects-alignment' problem is well-studied, though not for EM organisms specifically.

novelty_evidence.title: Quantization Undoes Alignment: Bias Emergence in Compressed LLMs Across Models and Precision Levels
novelty_evidence.summary: Systematic precision sweep (down to 3-bit) showing a dose-response relationship: aggressive quantization causes new misaligned/biased behaviors invisible to perplexity metrics. Closely parallels the proposal's methodology (sweep across precision levels, measure behavioral degradation) but in the bias/safety-alignment domain rather than EM organisms.

novelty_evidence.title: Q-resafe: Assessing Safety Risks and Quantization-aware Safety Patching for Quantized LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Assesses safety degradation from PTQ methods (RTN, GPTQ) reporting >20-point SafetyBench drops, and proposes quantization-aware patching. Reinforces that the general problem of quantization altering alignment-relevant behavior is already heavily researched.

novelty_evidence.title: Open problems in emergent misalignment
novelty_evidence.summary: Community discussion of EM open problems; quantization-as-amplifier is not listed as a priority open problem, and the proposal's headline finding (no significant 4-bit effect) is consistent with what the empirical paper reports, indicating limited residual contribution.

novelty.reasoning: The exact core question — does 4-bit quantization amplify/dampen/leave unchanged the misalignment of public open-weight EM organisms, measured via misaligned-answer rate AND coherence — was directly tested in arXiv:2511.20104 ("The Devil in the Details"). They compared full-precision vs 4-bit on two EM organisms (Gemma 3 12B, Qwen 3 8B) and report "Quantisation (4-bit) does not statistically significantly alter these misalignment rates," with inconsistent direction across the two models. Separately, a broad and credible literature already establishes that quantization can degrade safety alignment in non-EM settings (HarmLevelBench arXiv:2411.06835, "Quantization Undoes Alignment" arXiv:2605.15208, Q-resafe arXiv:2506.20251). The proposed study's residual novelty is narrow: 2511.20104 itself flags that "a dedicated quantisation-sweep study remains warranted," tested only 4-bit (not 8-bit), used too few samples for definitive conclusions, and did not probe the persona-direction interaction — so the systematic precision sweep plus mechanistic angle is not fully done, but the headline finding (no significant amplification at 4-bit) is already published on the same EM organisms.

title: Relearning-Resistance Stress Test: A Public Benchmark for Unlearning Robustness on a Single GPU

sections.research_question: Can a lightweight, standardized stress test let anyone verify in an afternoon whether an 'unlearned' open model has truly removed dangerous knowledge or merely hidden it, by measuring how easily that knowledge is recovered through small-scale relearning attacks?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small, shareable harness. Either start from a publicly available unlearned checkpoint, or apply RMU yourself (public code) to a base model on a tiny WMDP-style forget set so you control the unlearning. Then run a fixed battery of relearning attacks: fine-tune on 5, 20, and 50 benign-but-topically-adjacent examples; paraphrase probing; and few-shot elicitation. After each attack, re-measure forget-set accuracy and plot a recovery curve (accuracy vs number of relearning examples). Summarize each model with a single 'fragility score' (e.g., area under the recovery curve, or accuracy recovered after 50 examples relative to the pre-unlearning model). Everything -- RMU, tiny fine-tunes, and inference eval -- fits on a single consumer GPU in a few hours, and the harness is packaged so others can drop in a checkpoint and get a fragility score.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce a clean unlearning baseline: apply RMU to a small open model on a tiny WMDP-style forget set and confirm forget-set accuracy drops to near-chance while retain-set accuracy stays high. Measure: forget-set and retain-set accuracy pre/post unlearning. Expected outcome: a checkpoint that looks properly unlearned, providing the starting point for attacks.
- Run the relearning-by-fine-tuning attack at 5/20/50 benign-adjacent examples and plot the recovery curve. Measure: forget-set accuracy after each relearning budget. Expected outcome: substantial knowledge recovery from as few as 5-20 examples, confirming relearning fragility and producing the curve that defines the fragility score.
- Run the non-fine-tuning attacks (paraphrase probing, few-shot elicitation) on the same unlearned checkpoint and compare their recovery to the fine-tuning attacks. Measure: accuracy recovered by each attack type. Expected outcome: fine-tuning recovers the most knowledge, but paraphrase/few-shot attacks recover a nontrivial amount with zero weight updates, showing the harness catches multiple fragility modes.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a turnkey fragility score makes fake unlearning trivially detectable, then the community and auditors can reject 'unlearned' models whose hazardous knowledge resurfaces after a handful of relearning examples -> only genuinely robust unlearning passes as safe -> this closes the misuse pathway where a model certified as having forgotten bioweapon/cyber knowledge is quietly restored to full capability by a user with minimal fine-tuning data.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: robust unlearning auditing is fuzzy, hard-to-do-well safety work that labs deprioritize and that needs no proprietary data, and it ships a single reusable harness with one summary metric. The deliverable (fragility score + recovery curve) gives an explicit, self-contained success criterion grounded in a peer-reviewed ICML result on relearning vulnerability.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a comparative audit: instead of one harness, run the stress test across several publicly released unlearned checkpoints/methods and publish a ranked robustness leaderboard so the community can see which unlearning methods actually resist relearning.
cited_sources: Fan et al. (arXiv:2502.05374, ICML 2025) -- shows SOTA unlearning is recoverable from a few relearning points; motivates the relearning-attack battery and fragility score
WMDP (arXiv:2403.03218) -- public hazardous-knowledge benchmark providing the forget-set content
RMU (public implementation) -- enables applying a standard unlearning method on a tiny forget set on one GPU

novelty_evidence.title: BLUR: A Benchmark for LLM Unlearning Robust to Forget-Retain Overlap
novelty_evidence.summary: Public benchmark that augments existing unlearning benchmarks with a suite of relearning datasets of varying difficulty and combined forget/retain queries to measure robustness; shows existing methods perform far worse under relearning. Directly instantiates the proposed 'public benchmark for unlearning robustness via relearning attacks.'

novelty_evidence.title: An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
novelty_evidence.summary: Demonstrates that supposedly unlearned (e.g., RMU) dangerous knowledge on WMDP can be recovered via small fine-tuning and adaptive prompting, and that retrained models pick up 'forgotten' capabilities far faster than oracle models — the exact 'hidden vs. removed' question the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Unlearning or Obfuscating? Jogging the Memory of Unlearned LLMs via Benign Relearning
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows fine-tuning on small numbers of benign, topically-adjacent examples (low mutual information with the forget set) reverses unlearning and recovers forgotten knowledge — precisely the proposed relearning-attack methodology (5/20/50 benign-adjacent examples).

novelty_evidence.title: OpenUnlearning: Accelerating LLM Unlearning via Unified Benchmarking of Methods and Metrics
novelty_evidence.summary: An existing packaged, drop-in framework for unified benchmarking of LLM unlearning methods and metrics, including robustness evaluation — covers the 'shareable harness where others drop in a checkpoint' contribution.

novelty_evidence.title: Towards Robust Knowledge Unlearning: An Adversarial Framework for Assessing and Improving Unlearning Robustness in LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Defines the Accuracy Gap metric (post-relearning accuracy minus original-model accuracy) and evaluates recovery under small-portion forget-set relearning with learning-rate sweeps — equivalent to the proposed 'fragility score' / recovery-curve summarization.

novelty_evidence.title: Distillation Robustifies Unlearning
novelty_evidence.summary: Credible AF/LessWrong work treating relearning-attack recoverability as the standard robustness test for unlearning, confirming that retrained unlearned models recover capabilities far faster than models that never had them — the framing the proposal relies on is already mainstream.

novelty.reasoning: The underlying problem — verifying whether an unlearned open model truly removed dangerous knowledge or merely hid it, by measuring recovery under small-scale relearning attacks on WMDP-style forget sets — is comprehensively covered by published work. BLUR (arXiv 2506.15699) is a public benchmark explicitly providing relearning datasets of varying difficulty for LLM unlearning robustness; "An Adversarial Perspective on Machine Unlearning for AI Safety" (2409.18025) and the benign-relearning paper (2406.13356) establish that fine-tuning on a handful of benign-adjacent examples recovers supposedly forgotten knowledge; and OpenUnlearning (2506.12618) is an existing packaged, drop-in framework for unified benchmarking of unlearning methods and metrics. The proposal's central metric (recovery curve / "fragility score") duplicates the established Accuracy Gap metric (post-relearning vs. original-model accuracy) and documented recovery-vs-relearning-examples dynamics. The only differentiating element is cosmetic packaging — single-GPU, afternoon-scale, single AUC summary score — which is a lightweight repackaging rather than a new contribution, so gaps are minor.

title: StrongREJECT Scoring Replicated Across Open Judge Models

sections.research_question: How much do attack-success-rate (ASR) measurements from the StrongREJECT jailbreak benchmark depend on which judge model does the scoring, and how well do different open judge models agree when scoring the same fixed set of jailbreak transcripts?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed corpus of jailbreak attempt transcripts (prompt + model response pairs spanning successful and failed jailbreaks) -- either the released StrongREJECT examples or a fixed set generated once and frozen. Apply the published StrongREJECT scoring rubric using several different open judge models (varying family and size) as the grader, holding the rubric and prompt constant. Compute inter-judge agreement (e.g., Krippendorff's alpha / Cohen's kappa on the binarized verdicts, plus correlation on the continuous scores) and the resulting ASR each judge reports for each attack method. The twist is swapping the judge while freezing transcripts, isolating judge variance from attack variance. This is inference-only scoring; the only cost is running several open judges over a fixed transcript set, which fits a single GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Assemble and freeze the transcript corpus and score it with one reference open judge using the StrongREJECT rubric. Measure: per-method ASR under the reference judge. Expected outcome: ASR numbers roughly consistent with published StrongREJECT results, validating the scoring pipeline.
- Score the identical frozen transcripts with 3-5 additional open judge models and compute pairwise inter-judge agreement. Measure: Krippendorff's alpha / kappa and score correlation across judges. Expected outcome: only moderate agreement, with systematic disagreement concentrated on borderline (partial-compliance) transcripts.
- Quantify how judge choice shifts the headline ASR per attack method. Measure: spread (max - min) of reported ASR across judges for each attack method. Expected outcome: ASR can swing by a meaningful margin depending solely on the judge, showing that reported jailbreak success rates are judge-dependent and need a fixed judge to be comparable.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If ASR depends substantially on the judge, then jailbreak-robustness claims across papers and red-team reports are not comparable unless the judge is fixed -> the field adopts judge-standardized reporting and treats judge variance as a known error bar -> this hardens the adversarial-robustness measurement stack that gates whether a model is deemed safe to deploy, reducing the risk that an unsafe model is mistakenly certified jailbreak-resistant because of a lenient judge.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores maximally on counterfactual value and narrow scope: third-party scrutiny of a widely used safety metric is exactly the kind of open-infrastructure work external researchers can do but labs rarely prioritize, and it is a single clean statistical experiment (inter-judge agreement + ASR spread) with an explicit success criterion. Freezing transcripts cleanly isolates the variable of interest, making the result unambiguous and reproducible.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a robustness-of-rankings study: instead of focusing on absolute ASR, test whether the *ranking* of attack methods (which jailbreak is strongest) is stable across judges, since stable rankings would partially rescue cross-paper comparisons even if absolute numbers vary.
cited_sources: StrongREJECT jailbreak benchmark and its automated scoring rubric -- defines the scoring protocol and transcript corpus replicated across open judges

novelty_evidence.title: LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows that decisions about response sampling and how responses are judged for harmfulness cause jailbreak evaluation results to 'vary wildly.' Discusses StrongREJECT, Llama-Guard-3-8B, and HarmBench classifiers as judges and argues directly using LLM-as-a-judge lacks robustness -- directly addressing the proposal's central question of judge-dependent variance.

novelty_evidence.title: Comparison requires valid measurement: Rethinking attack success rate comparisons in AI red teaming (NeurIPS 2025)
novelty_evidence.summary: Provides measurement-theory grounding for when ASRs can be meaningfully compared, noting judges do not perform equally across systems/methods and that with explicit pass/fail criteria different judges converge while vague criteria cause divergence. Formalizes the exact judge-variance / cross-judge comparability problem the proposal investigates.

novelty_evidence.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
novelty_evidence.summary: Original StrongREJECT paper; its autograder rubric (0-1 score, GPT-4 judge, threshold-based ASR) is the rubric the proposal would replicate. Already reports judge agreement with human labels and compares against HarmBench/JailbreakBench graders.

novelty_evidence.title: PandaGuard: Systematic Evaluation of LLM Safety against Jailbreaking Attacks
novelty_evidence.summary: Systematically evaluates multiple judges (HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT) over fixed attack transcripts, reports that judges overestimate ASR differently (e.g., Gemma-2 10% true ASR exaggerated to ~40%) and that StrongREJECT is more accurate -- demonstrating the swap-judge-on-fixed-transcripts methodology is already established.

novelty_evidence.title: Why Attack Success Rate (ASR) Isn't Comparable Across Jailbreak Papers Without a Shared Threat Model (Promptfoo)
novelty_evidence.summary: Industry writeup summarizing that ASR is not portable across judges/threat models, reinforcing that the dependence of ASR on judge choice is well-recognized and documented, including measured discrepancies between StrongREJECT and HarmBench judges that change model/attack rankings.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem -- how much ASR measurements depend on the judge model and how well judges agree on a fixed transcript set -- is heavily studied. "LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness" (arXiv:2503.02574) shows judge/scoring choices make jailbreak results "vary wildly" and centers StrongREJECT; the NeurIPS 2025 paper "Comparison requires valid measurement" (arXiv:2601.18076) formalizes when ASRs are comparable across judges and documents that judges don't perform equally across attack methods. Multiple works directly compare StrongREJECT vs HarmBench vs JailbreakBench judges, report inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha, Fleiss/Cohen kappa, pairwise agreement) on shared transcripts, and show judge choice flips the ranking of models/defenses/attacks -- which is exactly the proposal's methodology and "freeze transcripts, swap judge" twist. The only thin remaining gap is a dedicated focus exclusively on open judge models replicating the StrongREJECT rubric, but existing comparisons already include open judges (Llama-3-70B, Llama Guard 2/3, Mistral, Qwen3Guard), leaving only a minor incremental contribution.

title: Legibility Tax: Do Verifier-Accepted Explanations Help Weaker Verifiers?

sections.research_question: Do explanations optimized to be legible to one verifier still help verifiers that are weaker than that training verifier, or does the legibility benefit shrink (or vanish) as the verifier's capability drops below the prover's?
sections.approach_outline: Use GSM8K math problems with three categories of solutions: legible-correct, terse-correct, and sneaky-incorrect (plausible-looking but wrong). Assemble a ladder of progressively weaker open judge/verifier models (a few model sizes within a family, or a capability-ordered set). Feed each fixed solution to each verifier in the ladder and measure verification accuracy: does the verifier correctly accept correct solutions and reject sneaky-incorrect ones? Track how the accuracy advantage of legible-over-terse solutions changes as the verifier weakens. This is entirely inference-only over a fixed set of solutions and verifiers, running cheaply on one GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build/curate the solution sets and establish per-category verification accuracy on the strongest verifier in the ladder. Measure: accuracy on legible-correct, terse-correct, and sneaky-incorrect solutions. Expected outcome: the strong verifier benefits from legibility -- higher accuracy on legible-correct and better rejection of sneaky-incorrect than on terse solutions.
- Run the identical solutions down the full verifier ladder. Measure: the legible-minus-terse accuracy gap as a function of verifier capability. Expected outcome: the legibility benefit shrinks as verifiers weaken, and may invert if very weak verifiers are simply swayed by surface fluency rather than valid reasoning.
- Probe the failure mode on sneaky-incorrect solutions specifically. Measure: rejection rate of sneaky-incorrect solutions across the ladder, split by whether the sneaky solution is dressed in legible vs terse style. Expected outcome: weaker verifiers are increasingly fooled by legibly-styled-but-wrong solutions, revealing that 'legibility' can be exploited against weaker overseers.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If legibility benefits do not transfer to verifiers genuinely weaker than the prover, then a load-bearing assumption of prover-verifier scalable oversight -- that making explanations legible helps weaker overseers catch errors -- is unsafe in exactly the regime oversight is meant for -> the field learns to validate legibility against the true (weaker) overseer rather than the training verifier -> this reduces the risk that a superhuman system produces explanations that look convincing to a weaker human/AI overseer while hiding flaws, an oversight-failure pathway to deploying misaligned systems.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: it stress-tests a foundational oversight assumption using only public models and data with no training, which labs have weak incentive to scrutinize, and it reduces to one clean measurement (verification accuracy vs verifier strength). The fixed-solution, fixed-ladder design gives an explicit, self-contained success criterion feasible for a beginner team.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a deception-robustness study centered on the sneaky-incorrect class: measure specifically whether legible styling makes wrong solutions *more* likely to be wrongly accepted by weak verifiers, treating legibility as a potential attack surface rather than only an aid.
cited_sources: Kirchner et al. (2024, arXiv:2407.13692), Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility -- establishes legibility-to-a-verifier as the property whose downward transfer this project tests

novelty_evidence.title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs (Kirchner et al., 2024)
novelty_evidence.summary: Foundational paper: GSM8K, helpful (legible-correct) and sneaky (plausible-incorrect) provers, small/weak verifier accept-reject training. Finds legibility transfers to smaller verifiers and time-constrained humans, and that medium-sized verifiers (~3x10^-3 of prover) benefit most while smaller and larger verifiers benefit less — a capability-relative legibility effect directly overlapping the proposed question.

novelty_evidence.title: Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models (2026)
novelty_evidence.summary: Introduces 'transfer utility' measuring how useful a model's reasoning traces are to weaker, non-reasoning models, evaluated over 90k traces from 12 reasoning models. Extends this to verifying correctness of strong models, finding verifier accuracy (precision of flagged traces) is predicted by the prover's transfer utility — nearly the exact question of whether legibility benefit depends on verifier capability.

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (DeepMind, 2024)
novelty_evidence.summary: Empirically studies weaker LLM judges evaluating stronger LLMs across protocols (debate, consultancy). Finds judge accuracy degrades as agent capability increases relative to the judge — the capability-gap dependence of verification accuracy central to the proposal.

novelty_evidence.title: When to Trust the Cheap Check: Weak and Strong Verification for Reasoning (2026)
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies weak vs strong verifier performance gaps, finding the gap narrows on easier problems (weak verifiers reliably recognize correct responses when problems are easy). Directly characterizes how verification accuracy varies with verifier strength.

novelty_evidence.title: Mitigating Legibility Tax with Decoupled Prover-Verifier Games (2026)
novelty_evidence.summary: Names and analyzes the 'legibility tax' (accuracy degradation from legibility training) and proposes a decoupled translator-based framework, confirming the legibility-tax framing the proposal builds on is an active, recently treated topic.

novelty_evidence.title: Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight
novelty_evidence.summary: Community work modeling how oversight/verification success depends on the capability ratio between overseer and overseen model, providing a theoretical frame for the proposed empirical ladder of weakening verifiers.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether legibility benefits depend on the verifier's capability and shrink as the verifier weakens relative to the prover — is substantially covered by existing published work. OpenAI's Prover-Verifier Games (Kirchner et al. 2024, 2407.13692) already uses GSM8K with helpful (legible-correct) and sneaky (plausible-incorrect) provers, measures small/weak verifier accept-reject accuracy, and explicitly finds a capability-relative effect (medium-sized verifiers ~3x10^-3 of the prover benefit most, while both smaller and larger verifiers benefit less), and that legibility transfers to smaller verifiers and humans. The very recent "Measuring Weak-to-Strong Legibility of Reasoning Models" (2603.20508) goes further, introducing "transfer utility" for how useful traces are to weaker models and extending it to verifying strong models, finding verifier accuracy is predicted by prover transfer utility — essentially the proposed question. Scalable-oversight work (2407.04622, "Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight") and "When to Trust the Cheap Check" (2602.17633) further document judge/verifier accuracy degrading with the judge-prover capability gap. The one genuinely unexplored slice is the clean, dedicated, inference-only ablation contrasting fixed legible-correct vs terse-correct vs sneaky-incorrect solutions across a deliberately ordered ladder of weakening open verifiers to chart how the legible-minus-terse advantage curve evolves — a specific measurement framing not exactly reproduced in any single source, which keeps this short of already_solved.

title: Sycophancy as a Reward-Hacking Attack on AI Overseers

sections.research_question: Can an answer model that flatters an AI judge's apparent prior leaning hack the judge's verdict -- raising the acceptance rate of answers the judge would otherwise reject, including on factual questions where the flattered position is actually wrong?
sections.approach_outline: First, probe a small open judge model for its prior leaning on a set of factual questions (e.g., ask it which answer it finds more plausible before seeing any argument). Then, for each question, have an answer model produce two responses arguing for the same (wrong) position: one neutral/plain and one that sycophantically flatters the judge's detected leaning (agreeing with and praising the judge's apparent view). Present each to the judge in a fixed verification/scoring setup and measure how much the sycophantic framing shifts the judge's accept rate relative to the neutral framing, specifically on items where the flattered position is incorrect. Run across a couple of open judges to test generality. All steps are prompt-only inference, running cheaply on one GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Elicit and record the judge's prior leaning per question, then verify it is stable. Measure: judge's stated preferred answer and its consistency across re-prompts. Expected outcome: the judge has detectable, reasonably stable leanings on a subset of factual questions, providing targets for flattery.
- Compare accept rates for neutral vs sycophantic framings of the same (wrong) position. Measure: accept rate of the wrong position under neutral vs sycophantic framing (the sycophancy effect size). Expected outcome: sycophantic framing meaningfully increases acceptance of the wrong position, demonstrating the judge is sycophancy-hackable.
- Test generality and a simple defense: repeat across 2-3 open judges and try a mitigation prompt instructing the judge to ignore flattery and judge only on evidence. Measure: sycophancy effect size per judge, and its reduction under the defense prompt. Expected outcome: the effect appears across judges and is partially but not fully removed by the naive defense, quantifying both the vulnerability and the limits of cheap prompt-based mitigation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If AI judges can be made to accept wrong answers simply by flattering their apparent views, then recursive/AI-overseeing-AI oversight inherits the RLHF sycophancy failure mode -> a capable system can win approval by telling its overseer what it wants to hear rather than the truth -> this mitigates the reward-hacking-of-oversight pathway in which a misaligned-but-persuasive model is repeatedly certified safe by an AI overseer it has learned to flatter, allowing unsafe behavior to pass through automated oversight at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores maximally on counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: it maps a recognized reward-hacking failure into the under-studied AI-overseeing-AI regime using only training-free, public-model inference, which labs deprioritize, and it reduces to one clean measurement (accept-rate shift, sycophantic vs neutral). The paired-arm design and explicit effect-size metric give a self-contained, beginner-feasible success criterion.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a calibration-of-defenses study: hold the sycophantic attack fixed and compare several cheap judge-side defenses (anonymizing the judge's prior, blind scoring, explicit anti-flattery instructions) to find which most reduces the accept-rate shift.
cited_sources: Towards understanding sycophancy in language models (arXiv:2501.09620) -- documents sycophancy toward raters' stated views, the failure mode this project redirects at AI judges
Open Philanthropy RFP on scalable oversight -- motivates studying reward-hacking of AI overseers as a priority

novelty_evidence.title: AI Debaters are More Persuasive when Arguing in Alignment with Their Own Beliefs
novelty_evidence.summary: Measures debater models' prior beliefs beforehand, then presents a judge persona deliberately designed to conflict with those priors, testing whether models adopt sycophantic strategies (aligning with the judge's presumed perspective). Finds across four models that sycophancy is prioritized as a persuasion strategy. Very close to the proposed mechanism of flattering the judge's detected leaning, though framed via personas rather than per-question prior-probing.

novelty_evidence.title: Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight
