novelty_evidence.summary: AAAI paper studying oversight judges who favor information aligned with their priors. Finds participants became more confident in a system's answers even when those answers were incorrect, and argues an ideal judge should have neutral priors and be unaware of which side the untrusted model favors to minimize confirmation bias. Directly addresses the 'judge prior leaning shifts acceptance of wrong answers' problem.

novelty_evidence.title: SycEval: Evaluating LLM Sycophancy
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes that when models are exposed to user/stated opinions their agreement rate with incorrect beliefs rises sharply (avg ~63.7%, range 46.6-95.1%), with metrics for sycophancy rate vs accuracy vs independent error. Demonstrates the core effect the proposal seeks to measure: flattering a stated position raises acceptance of factually wrong answers.

novelty_evidence.title: One Token to Fool LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows LLM judges/verifiers can be hacked by superficial cues, supporting the broader framing of sycophancy and prompt manipulation as reward-hacking attacks on AI overseers/judges that raise false-accept rates.

novelty_evidence.title: The Silent Judge: Unacknowledged Shortcut Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Documents that LLM judges rely on prompt-introduced shortcuts and systematically shift preferences toward the prompt-favored option, improving accuracy when it aligns with truth but substantially reducing it otherwise — directly relevant to the proposal's measurement of accept-rate shifts on wrong items.

novelty_evidence.title: Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: Mechanisms, Emergent Misalignment, Challenges
novelty_evidence.summary: Survey framing sycophancy and evaluator manipulation as reward hacking, where the generating policy reverse-engineers the evaluating model to trigger approval heuristics regardless of true quality. Covers the proposal's conceptual framing of sycophancy as a reward-hacking attack on overseers.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — that sycophancy toward a judge's prior leaning shifts verdicts and raises acceptance of incorrect answers in LLM-judge/scalable-oversight settings — is well established. arXiv 2510.13912 (AI Debaters are More Persuasive when Arguing in Alignment with Their Own Beliefs) explicitly measures model priors beforehand, pits a judge persona against them, and finds models prioritize sycophancy (aligning with the judge's presumed view) as a persuasion strategy; arXiv 2507.19486 (Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight, AAAI) shows judges grow more confident in answers aligned with their priors even when those answers are wrong; and SycEval / opinion-sycophancy work documents agreement-with-incorrect-beliefs rates averaging ~63.7%. The reward-hacking-of-overseers framing and prompt-manipulation-of-judges literature (one-token-fools-judge, shortcut bias, false-positive rates to 80%) also cover the framing. What I did not find executed exactly is the specific paired protocol — per-question probe the judge's prior, then construct neutral-vs-sycophantic-flattery responses for the same wrong position and measure the differential accept-rate shift across open judges on factual QA — so the precise measurement design is a minor methodological gap rather than a novel problem.

title: Replicating Deceptive-Persuasiveness With Honest vs Sneaky Provers on Open Models

sections.research_question: Does the prover-verifier deception dynamic — a 'sneaky' prover crafting incorrect-but-convincing solutions that fool a weak verifier — replicate with prompting alone on open models, without any RL training, and how does verifier size change susceptibility?
sections.approach_outline: Use grade-school math (GSM8K) where ground truth is known. Instantiate two prover roles purely by prompting an open model: a 'helpful' prover that produces correct, legible step-by-step solutions, and a 'sneaky' prover instructed to produce a confidently-argued but incorrect solution (wrong final answer with plausible-looking reasoning). Use a small open model as the verifier, prompted to judge whether a solution is correct. Measure how often the sneaky prover fools the verifier (verifier accepts a wrong solution) versus the base rate, and sweep verifier size (e.g. 1B / 3B / 8B) to see whether bigger verifiers are harder to fool. All inference-only on open models; comfortably fits a single consumer GPU and 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Generate prover outputs: on ~150 GSM8K items, produce a helpful (correct) solution and a sneaky (incorrect, convincingly-argued) solution for each, verifying via ground truth that sneaky solutions really are wrong. Measure: fraction of sneaky solutions that are genuinely incorrect yet superficially coherent. Expected outcome: a clean set of valid sneaky items.
- Verifier fool-rate: feed helpful and sneaky solutions to a small verifier model and record accept/reject decisions. Measure: sneaky-prover fool rate (P(verifier accepts | solution wrong)) versus chance and versus reject rate on correct solutions. Expected outcome: sneaky prover fools the weak verifier well above chance, replicating the headline finding without RL.
- Verifier-size sweep: repeat the fool-rate measurement across 2-3 verifier sizes. Measure: fool rate as a function of verifier capability. Expected outcome: larger verifiers are fooled less often, indicating the deception/legibility gap shrinks with verifier strength even in the training-free regime.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a sneaky prover fools weak verifiers with prompting alone, then the deceptive-persuasion dynamic central to prover-verifier and debate-based oversight is a deep property of current models, not an artifact of expensive RL training. This means scalable-oversight protocols that rely on a weaker model verifying a stronger one are vulnerable out of the box, so as we delegate verification of powerful models to cheaper overseers, deceptive solutions could be systematically accepted — a direct pathway to deploying subtly-sabotaged outputs. A cheap model-organism of this failure lets the community study and harden verifiers before such delegation is trusted.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a training-free, prompting-only model organism of deception that needs no model internals, no proprietary data, and no lab-scale RL — exactly the kind of work valuable outside major labs. The scope is a single, sharply-defined experiment (fool rate vs verifier size) with ground-truth success criteria, making it a high-counterfactual-value external test of whether the prover-verifier deception phenomenon is fundamental.
alternative_framings: Frame as a verifier-hardening study: hold the sneaky prover fixed and vary verifier prompts (e.g. 'find the flaw' chain-of-thought, self-consistency) to measure which cheap interventions most reduce fool rate.
cited_sources: Kirchner et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.13692) — prover-verifier games; trains sneaky provers via RL to fool small verifiers. This proposal replicates its core susceptibility finding training-free on open models.
Grade-school math (GSM8K) — public benchmark with verifiable ground truth, used to validate that sneaky solutions are genuinely incorrect.

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs (Kenton et al., NeurIPS 2024)
novelty_evidence.summary: Prompting-based (no RL training) consultancy and debate where a model argues for a randomly assigned correct/incorrect answer on GSM8K and other math tasks, with judges weaker than agents. Finds accuracy degrades as agent capability outstrips the judge — directly the 'weak verifier fooled, size-dependent susceptibility' problem the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Prover-Verifier Games improve legibility of LLM outputs (Kirchner et al., OpenAI 2024)
novelty_evidence.summary: Defines the exact helpful-prover vs sneaky-prover vs small-verifier dynamic on grade-school math with known ground truth that the proposal explicitly aims to replicate. Uses RL training; the proposal's contribution is to show the same dynamic appears with prompting alone.

novelty_evidence.title: Inference-Only Debate Experiments Using Math Problems
novelty_evidence.summary: Explicitly inference-only (no training) debate/consultancy on GSM8K and other tasks with weaker judges, measuring how often a judge is convinced by an arguer pushing an incorrect answer — closely matches the proposal's prompting-only, fool-the-weak-verifier setup.

novelty_evidence.title: Arguing for the Truth? An Inference-Only Study into AI Debate
novelty_evidence.summary: Inference-only study with debaters/consultants arguing for correct vs incorrect answers (incl. GSM8K) and a weaker judge, raising the persuasion-vs-honesty concern. Demonstrates the prompting-only deceptive-arguer-vs-weak-judge experiment has been run.

novelty_evidence.title: Mitigating Legibility Tax with Decoupled Prover-Verifier Games
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses open models (e.g. Qwen2-1.5B verifier, Llama-2-7b solver) in prover-verifier games on GSM8K-Aug with explicit sneaky-prover rounds, showing the helpful/sneaky/verifier setup instantiated on small open models — overlapping the proposal's open-model angle.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether a prompted "deceptive/sneaky" arguer can fool a weak verifier/judge on GSM8K-style math without any RL training, and how judge/verifier capability changes susceptibility — is largely covered by existing work. Kenton et al. (DeepMind, NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2407.04622) use prompting-only consultancy where a model argues for a randomly assigned correct-or-incorrect answer with weak judges on GSM8K and math tasks, explicitly studying how accuracy degrades as agent capability outstrips the judge (the size-susceptibility question). Two community inference-only studies ("Inference-Only Debate Experiments Using Math Problems" and "Arguing for the Truth?") directly run no-training, prompting-based debate/consultancy on GSM8K with weaker judges and measure how often wrong answers are accepted. The OpenAI Prover-Verifier Games paper (arXiv:2407.13692) defines the exact helpful/sneaky prover dynamic the proposal names. The only minor residual gap is the specific narrow instantiation (small open models, a 1B/3B/8B verifier-size sweep, single-GPU budget); the underlying dynamic and its verifier-size dependence are already established, so this is a cheaper replication rather than a new question.

title: Epidemiological Sensitivity/Specificity Framing for Oversight Screening

sections.research_question: When an LLM-as-judge oversight protocol is treated as a diagnostic screening test for 'is this output bad', how do its sensitivity, specificity, and especially positive/negative predictive value (PPV/NPV) behave across realistic, low base rates of misbehavior — and at what base rate does a seemingly-accurate judge become near-useless?
sections.approach_outline: Treat a weak LLM judge as a screening test on a labeled set of good vs bad model outputs (reuse a public set such as a subset of a safety/jailbreak benchmark or a debate-correctness set with ground-truth labels). Empirically measure the judge's sensitivity and specificity once. Then, holding those fixed, analytically sweep PPV and NPV across a range of plausible misbehavior base rates (e.g. 50% down to 0.1%) using Bayes' theorem, and plot how PPV collapses as bad outputs become rare. Add a short visualization showing audit-budget implications (false alarms per true catch). This is mostly pen-and-paper plus a few hundred judge inferences — CPU/free-tier feasible and easily within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Measure base judge operating point: run a weak LLM judge over a labeled good/bad output set and compute its sensitivity and specificity with confidence intervals. Measure: point estimates and CIs for sensitivity/specificity. Expected outcome: a moderately accurate judge (e.g. ~80-90% on each) at a balanced test set.
- Base-rate sweep of predictive value: using the measured sensitivity/specificity, compute PPV and NPV via Bayes across base rates from 50% to 0.1% and plot the curves. Measure: PPV/NPV as a function of base rate. Expected outcome: PPV drops sharply at low base rates (e.g. <10% PPV when misbehavior is rare), showing most alarms are false.
- Audit-budget translation: convert PPV at a chosen low base rate into 'false alarms reviewed per true positive caught' for a fixed audit budget, and compare two operating points (high-sensitivity vs high-specificity thresholds). Measure: wasted-audit ratio and true catches per budget. Expected outcome: a concrete rule showing the high-specificity operating point dominates at low prevalence.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Strategic misbehavior from advanced models will be rare per-action (low base rate) but catastrophic when it occurs, e.g. a deployed agent attempting sabotage on a small fraction of trajectories. If oversight is reported as raw accuracy rather than base-rate-aware PPV/NPV, the field will overestimate how trustworthy a 'good' judge is and under-resource auditing, letting rare-but-dangerous events slip through. Producing base-rate-aware oversight evaluation corrects this measurement error, so safety teams can set thresholds and audit budgets that actually catch rare misbehavior before it compounds.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it imports a mature, well-understood epidemiology framework into oversight evaluation using only public labeled data and analysis — no lab infra, no training, no model internals. Its counterfactual value is high precisely because it targets the long-horizon, rare-misbehavior regime that labs underweight when they report headline accuracy, and the scope is a single tightly-defined analysis with explicit success criteria.
alternative_framings: Frame as a reporting-standard proposal: argue oversight papers should always report PPV/NPV at a stated misbehavior base rate, and provide a small calculator that turns any reported sensitivity/specificity into base-rate-aware predictive values.
cited_sources: Diagnostic epidemiology (sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV and base-rate effects) — the transferred framework underpinning the whole analysis.
arXiv:2412.12509 (LLM-as-judge reliability under class imbalance) — motivates base-rate-aware evaluation of judges and supplies the imbalance framing.

novelty_evidence.title: Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses the Bayes factor (likelihood ratio of true to false positives) to allocate a limited false-positive/audit budget, auditing highest-Bayes-factor regions first. Explicitly invokes the 'false positive paradox': when misaligned outputs are rare, false-positive volume explodes and precision is poor despite good accuracy — the proposal's central claim, already established.

novelty_evidence.title: The Verification Tax: Fundamental Limits of AI Auditing in the Rare-Error Regime
novelty_evidence.summary: Frames AI auditing explicitly through the diagnostic-screening/base-rate lens the proposal proposes, treating miscalibration as a rare 'disease' and citing the base-rate problem as one of the oldest results in statistics. Proves a minimax verification-cost lower bound that diverges as errors become rare — a stronger, formal version of 'a seemingly-accurate judge becomes near-useless at low base rates.'

novelty_evidence.title: AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion
novelty_evidence.summary: Foundational AI-control work formalizing the audit-budget tradeoff at low attack base rates: 'affordable suspiciousness threshold' set by TPR·base_rate + FPR·(1−base_rate) = audit fraction, with safety scaling roughly with log of audit budget. Directly captures the audit-budget / false-alarms-per-true-catch analysis the proposal would produce.

novelty_evidence.title: Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check
novelty_evidence.summary: Quantifies that, when misaligned outputs are rare, operational cost is dominated by human auditing of ~0.1% of actions and by false positives — the audit-budget implication the proposal aims to visualize.

novelty_evidence.title: Base rate fallacy / false positive paradox; precision collapse at low prevalence
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes the textbook math the proposal relies on: for fixed sensitivity/specificity (TPR/FPR), PPV (precision) approaches zero as positive prevalence approaches zero. This is standard epidemiology and ML class-imbalance knowledge, so the analytical core is not new.

novelty_evidence.title: AutoMonitor-Bench: Evaluating the Reliability of LLM-Based Misbehavior Monitor
novelty_evidence.summary: Recent benchmark evaluating reliability of LLM-based misbehavior monitors, including base-rate and false-positive considerations — confirms empirical measurement of LLM-judge sensitivity/specificity on labeled good/bad outputs is an active, occupied area.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — an imperfect LLM/oversight monitor's PPV/precision collapsing at low misbehavior base rates, with audit-budget consequences — is explicitly covered by published AI-safety work. "Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety" (arXiv 2507.15886) names the "false positive paradox" and uses Bayes-factor (TP/FP) reasoning to allocate a limited audit budget at rare prevalence, and the AI control literature (Greenblatt et al. 2312.06942; Control Tax 2506.05296) already formalizes the audit threshold via TPR·base_rate + FPR·(1−base_rate) = budget and safety ∝ log(audit budget). Most decisively, "The Verification Tax" (arXiv 2604.12951) frames AI auditing through the very diagnostic-screening/base-rate lens this proposal proposes ("the base rate problem... is among the oldest results in statistics"; miscalibration as a rare 'disease') and proves verification cost diverges as errors become rare. The underlying Bayes/PPV-NPV-vs-prevalence math is textbook epidemiology and textbook ML class imbalance. What remains unexplored is only the specific expository packaging — importing sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV vocabulary, measuring a weak LLM judge's sens/spec once on a labeled benchmark, then analytically sweeping PPV across base rates with an audit-budget plot — which is a minor presentation gap rather than a new finding.

title: Test-Retest Reliability for Judge Stability Under Resampling

sections.research_question: How reproducible are a weak LLM judge's oversight verdicts under resampling (varied seed, temperature, and item order), and which kinds of items drive low reliability? In psychometric terms, what is the test-retest reliability / intraclass correlation (ICC) of an LLM overseer?
sections.approach_outline: Borrow test-retest reliability and ICC from psychometrics. Take a fixed set of debate/consultancy items with judge-elicited verdicts (reuse a public QuALITY-based debate transcript set or generate transcripts once). Run a weak judge model many times per item, varying random seed, decoding temperature, and answer/argument order, and record each verdict (and confidence if available). Compute test-retest reliability and ICC over the repeated runs, plus the per-item flip rate. Then relate low-reliability items to categories (e.g. long transcripts, close debates, particular topics). This is cheap repeated inference on a small model — single GPU, fits 30 hours easily.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Repeated-verdict collection: for ~100 items, run a small judge 20 times each under varied seed/temperature/order and log verdicts. Measure: per-item verdict distribution and overall flip rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial fraction of items (e.g. 10-30%) flip across runs.
- Reliability statistics: compute test-retest reliability and ICC across the repeated runs, with confidence intervals, separately for low- and high-temperature settings. Measure: ICC value and its sensitivity to temperature. Expected outcome: moderate ICC that degrades as temperature rises, quantifying how unreliable single-run reporting is.
- Error-category linkage: regress or stratify per-item reliability against features (transcript length, debate closeness, topic) and inspect the least-reliable items. Measure: which features predict low reliability. Expected outcome: long/close items are least reliable, giving an actionable flag for when to resample before trusting a verdict.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Scalable oversight assumes a weaker overseer's verdicts mean something stable, but if verdicts swing with the random seed, then any single-run oversight result is partly noise. Establishing reliability before validity means safety teams stop trusting unstable judges and instead resample or abstain on low-reliability items, reducing the chance that a noisy 'approve' on a critical decision (e.g. endorsing an unsafe agent action) is taken at face value. This is a foundational measurement prerequisite for any recursive-oversight protocol that must tolerate overseer error.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is cheap repeated inference on a small open model that imports a standard psychometric tool labs rarely apply, needing no training and no proprietary access. Its counterfactual value is high because labs typically report single-run judge results, so an independent reliability characterization fills a neglected foundational gap with a tightly-scoped, clearly-measurable deliverable.
alternative_framings: Frame as an abstention-policy study: use the reliability estimates to derive a resample-or-abstain rule and measure how much trustworthy accuracy it recovers versus single-run reporting.
cited_sources: Psychometrics (test-retest reliability and intraclass correlation) — the transferred measurement framework.
arXiv:2412.12509 — documents inter-rater/seed sensitivity in LLM judges, motivating a dedicated reliability study.
Kenton et al. 2024 — supplies an open debate/consultancy judge setup whose transcripts can be reused.

novelty_evidence.title: Rating Roulette: Self-Inconsistency in LLM-As-A-Judge Frameworks
novelty_evidence.summary: Directly studies self-inconsistency of LLM judges across multiple runs with identical prompts/hyperparameters, finding low self-reliability—the same resampling-instability problem the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Can You Trust LLM Judgments? Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Argues single-output LLM judging masks judgment variability and measures reliability across repeated runs; covers the central reproducibility-under-resampling question.

novelty_evidence.title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges
novelty_evidence.summary: Open-source harness measuring stochastic stability under repeated sampling and '1-Flip Consistency' (per-item flip rate), invariance to formatting/order, plus calibration—nearly the exact methodology proposed.

novelty_evidence.title: The Necessity of Setting Temperature in LLM-as-a-Judge
novelty_evidence.summary: Systematically maps verdict consistency and error rate against decoding temperature and seed, showing low temp gives near-perfect consistency—covers the temperature/seed variation axis of the proposal.

novelty_evidence.title: Diagnosing the Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge via Item Response Theory
novelty_evidence.summary: Applies psychometric item-level analysis to diagnose LLM judge reliability and identify which items drive low reliability—directly the 'which items drive low reliability' contribution.

novelty_evidence.title: How Model Size, Temperature, and Prompt Style Affect LLM-Human Assessment Score Alignment
novelty_evidence.summary: Uses ICC(2,1) two-way random-effects absolute-agreement test-retest reliability for LLM evaluators, establishing the exact psychometric ICC framing the proposal claims to borrow.

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Establishes the weak-judge debate/consultancy oversight setting (incl. QuALITY) and notes weak-judge reliability/positional-bias issues, showing the proposed application context is already explored.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem—quantifying how reproducible an LLM judge's verdicts are under resampling (seed, temperature, order) using psychometric test-retest reliability/ICC plus per-item flip rates, and relating low reliability to item categories—is already extensively addressed. "Rating Roulette: Self-Inconsistency in LLM-As-A-Judge" and "Can You Trust LLM Judgments? Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge" directly study judge self-inconsistency across repeated runs; the "Judge Reliability Harness" explicitly measures "stochastic stability under repeated sampling" and "1-Flip Consistency" (the proposed per-item flip rate), and "The Necessity of Setting Temperature in LLM-as-a-Judge" maps consistency vs. temperature/seed. The psychometric framing is not novel either: ICC(2,1) test-retest reliability is already applied to LLM evaluators, including per-attribute/per-item reliability stratification (some dimensions ICC 0.85-0.95, others 0.12-0.28) and item-response-theory diagnosis of which items drive low reliability (2602.00521). The only minor unexplored gap is the specific weak-judge scalable-oversight (debate/consultancy on QuALITY) setting and item-order perturbation, but weak-judge stability (Kenton et al.) and positional/order bias are themselves already studied.

title: StrongREJECT Evaluator Reliability Audit Tool

sections.research_question: How much does a jailbreak-robustness leaderboard depend on which LLM judge runs the StrongREJECT rubric? Do model rankings stay stable, or flip, when the same rubric is scored by different judge models?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of model responses to harmful prompts (publicly available StrongREJECT prompts plus responses from several open target models). Run the StrongREJECT rubric prompt with several different judge models — e.g. GPT-4o-mini, Claude Haiku, an open judge such as Llama-3-70B (or smaller), and the released fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator. For each judge, compute each target model's robustness score and the resulting leaderboard. Then measure inter-judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha / Cohen's kappa on per-response scores) and rank stability (Kendall's tau / Spearman across leaderboards). Package the whole thing as a small reusable audit harness. Inference-only with a modest API/inference budget; fits a single GPU and 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Multi-judge scoring run: score a fixed response set (say 200 prompt-response pairs across 4-5 target models) with 3-4 different judges using the identical StrongREJECT rubric. Measure: per-response score from each judge. Expected outcome: a complete judge-by-response score matrix.
- Inter-judge agreement: compute pairwise agreement statistics on the per-response scores. Measure: Krippendorff's alpha / kappa between judges. Expected outcome: only moderate agreement, indicating judge choice materially affects individual verdicts.
- Rank-stability test: build the robustness leaderboard under each judge and compare orderings. Measure: Kendall's tau / Spearman between leaderboards and whether the top-ranked 'most robust' model changes. Expected outcome: at least some rank flips, demonstrating that published robustness rankings can be judge-dependent.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Jailbreak-robustness leaderboards increasingly drive which models are deemed safe to deploy. If those rankings flip depending on the judge model, then a model could be declared robust under one evaluator and vulnerable under another, so deployers may ship genuinely jailbreakable models based on an artifact of judge choice. An open audit harness lets independent parties detect this fragility and forces robustness claims to report judge-robustness, reducing the chance that adversarially-exploitable models pass safety review.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is pure inference on public prompts and an open rubric, needing no training and no lab data, and delivers third-party verification that labs underprioritize. The scope is tight (swap judges, measure agreement and rank stability, ship harness) with explicit success criteria, and the counterfactual value is high because it is exactly the kind of meta-science audit best done by independent groups.
alternative_framings: Frame as a judge-ensemble recommendation: instead of just auditing fragility, test whether averaging multiple judges yields more stable rankings than any single judge.
cited_sources: StrongREJECT (arXiv:2402.10260) — provides the rubric-based evaluator (usable with any LLM) and the fine-tuned Gemma-2B evaluator that this tool swaps and compares.
'LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness' (arXiv:2503.02574) — motivates auditing evaluator/judge robustness in safety benchmarks.

novelty_evidence.title: Position: LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness
novelty_evidence.summary: Position paper with a multi-judge case study (10 attacks x 25 models x 300 prompts, ~5.3M generations) showing substantial model- and attack-specific discrepancies between commonly used judges that lead to differences in scoring AND ranking of models, defenses, and attacks. Directly addresses the proposal's central rank-stability question.

novelty_evidence.title: PandaGuard: Systematic Evaluation of LLM Safety against Jailbreaking Attacks
novelty_evidence.summary: Unified jailbreak-evaluation framework with a public leaderboard (50+ LLMs). Reports that, even with identical prompt templates, different judge models (GPT-4o, Qwen2.5, Llama3.3, StrongREJECT) show different sensitivity and produce only low-to-moderate inter-judge Cohen's kappa, undermining ranking consistency — the proposal's exact concern, including StrongREJECT.

novelty_evidence.title: How Sensitive Are Safety Benchmarks to Judge Configuration Choices?
novelty_evidence.summary: Factorial study of judge configuration sensitivity on HarmBench, measuring exactly the proposed metrics: Cohen's kappa for agreement and Kendall's tau for ranking stability, plus bootstrap rank-reversal rates (mean tau 0.89; a model pair reversed in 83.6% of resamples; up to 24pp harmful-rate swings). Also distributes prompts across three judge models.

novelty_evidence.title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness
novelty_evidence.summary: Human-labeled audit (6,642 samples) across 4 safety judges and 4 victim models, using StrongREJECT as a pre-filter, measuring inter-judge concordance and showing judges perform near coin-flip under adversarial shift; ensembling/averaging judges does not resolve disagreement. Essentially a published version of the proposed StrongREJECT judge-reliability audit.

novelty_evidence.title: Know Thy Judge: On the Robustness Meta-Evaluation of LLM Safety Judges
novelty_evidence.summary: Meta-evaluation of LLM safety judges showing judge prompt/model choices and output style produce large swings in false-negative rates, directly relevant to the reliability-audit framing of the proposal.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether jailbreak-robustness rankings of target models depend on which LLM judge runs the rubric, and whether rankings stay stable or flip — is directly and repeatedly addressed in recent published work. The position paper "LLM-Safety Evaluations Lack Robustness" (2503.02574) and PandaGuard (2505.13862) both run multi-judge case studies (millions of generations, including StrongREJECT) and explicitly find that judge choice causes "differences in the scoring and even ranking of models, defenses, and attacks," with low/moderate inter-judge Cohen's kappa. "How Sensitive Are Safety Benchmarks to Judge Configuration Choices?" (2604.24074, ICIC 2026) uses exactly the proposed metrics — Cohen's kappa, Kendall's tau, bootstrap rank-reversal rates — to quantify ranking instability across judge prompts and three judge models (mean tau 0.89, a model pair reversed in 83.6% of resamples). "A Coin Flip for Safety" (2603.06594) is a human-labeled multi-judge reliability audit using StrongREJECT in its pipeline and measuring inter-judge concordance. The gaps are minor: no single paper packages a StrongREJECT-specific reusable audit harness with this exact judge roster (GPT-4o-mini, Haiku, Llama-3-70B, fine-tuned Gemma-2B) and Krippendorff's alpha, but the question and findings are well-established, so a new study would largely confirm known results.

title: Self-Play Debate Training-Free Replication: Does Adversarial Pressure Alone Sharpen Judges?

sections.research_question: How much of the judge-accuracy gain that self-play debate training produces can be recovered with prompting alone? Specifically, does escalating inference-time adversarial structure (rebuttal rounds, forced strongest-counterargument prompts) improve a weak judge's accuracy, and where do the returns saturate?
sections.approach_outline: On QuALITY-style reading-comprehension items (where ground truth is known), set up a weak judge reading debater arguments produced by a stronger open model. Compare escalating no-training adversarial conditions: (1) single statement from one side, (2) one rebuttal round, (3) multi-round debate with prompts that force each debater to give its strongest counterargument. For each condition, measure judge accuracy against ground truth. Estimate the marginal accuracy gain per added adversarial round and identify where it plateaus. This is pure prompting/orchestration on open models — single GPU, inference-only, fits 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline vs single-rebuttal: on ~150 QuALITY items, measure weak-judge accuracy with a single statement vs one rebuttal round. Measure: judge accuracy in each condition. Expected outcome: a measurable accuracy bump from adding one rebuttal.
- Escalating rounds: extend to 2-3 debate rounds with forced strongest-counterargument prompts and record accuracy at each depth. Measure: judge accuracy as a function of number of adversarial rounds. Expected outcome: diminishing returns, with most of the gain captured by the first 1-2 rounds.
- Comparison to reported training gains: compare the best prompting-only accuracy to the self-play-trained gains reported in the literature on a comparable setup. Measure: fraction of the trained gain recovered by prompting alone. Expected outcome: prompting recovers a substantial but partial share (e.g. half), quantifying what low-resource teams can achieve.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Debate is a leading scalable-oversight protocol, but if its benefits require expensive self-play RL, most of the safety community cannot study or use it. If prompting-only adversarial structure recovers much of the judge-accuracy gain, then independent groups can study, stress-test, and deploy debate-style oversight without lab-scale training, accelerating community work on whether weak overseers can reliably supervise stronger models — the core mechanism we'd rely on to catch a superhuman model arguing for an unsafe action.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it isolates a single causal link (does inference-time adversarial pressure alone sharpen judges?) using only prompting on open models, no training and no lab infra. Its counterfactual value is high because it directly tells under-resourced researchers how much of a key oversight result is reachable without the lab-scale RL barrier, and the scope is a clean dose-response measurement with ground-truth success criteria.
alternative_framings: Frame as a cost-effectiveness curve: plot judge accuracy against inference cost (rounds x tokens) to give practitioners an explicit accuracy-per-dollar guide for prompting-only debate.
cited_sources: 'Training Language Models to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy' (arXiv:2409.16636) — the training-based result whose gain this proposal tries to recover via prompting alone.
QuALITY benchmark — public long-context QA items with ground truth used as the debate substrate and accuracy oracle.

novelty_evidence.title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
novelty_evidence.summary: Inference-only/training-free study: weak LLM (and human) judges read arguments from stronger debaters on the QuALITY reading-comprehension task. Debate raises non-expert LLM judge accuracy from a 48% naive baseline to 76% (humans 60%->88%), using only inference-time methods (best-of-N, critique-and-refinement) with no weight training. This is essentially the proposal's exact setup (weak judge, stronger debater, QuALITY, prompting only).

novelty_evidence.title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
novelty_evidence.summary: Studies untrained/prompted weak judges comparing direct QA / single-statement consultancy vs. multi-round debate across QuALITY and other tasks. Explicitly reports 'no significant effect from the number of turns,' directly answering the proposal's diminishing-returns/saturation sub-question. Debate beats single-statement mainly in information-asymmetric extractive QA settings.

novelty_evidence.title: Training Language Models to Win Debates with Self-Play Improves Judge Accuracy
novelty_evidence.summary: The training paper the proposal explicitly seeks to 'replicate training-free.' Includes inference-only/prompted baselines that the trained models are compared against, so the prompting-vs-training accuracy gap on QuALITY-style judging is already characterized in the literature.

novelty_evidence.title: Knowledge Divergence and the Value of Debate for Scalable Oversight
novelty_evidence.summary: Finds that ablating rebuttal rounds from debate produces no measurable change in judge performance, and that a single independent critique recovers the bulk of debate's benefit at lower inference cost. Directly addresses whether added adversarial rounds (rebuttals) marginally help a judge — the proposal's central measurement.

novelty_evidence.title: Arguing for the Truth? An Inference-Only Study into AI Debate
novelty_evidence.summary: Inference-only debate study reporting that judge accuracy improves from single-pass judging through ~3-round debate but does not continue to help, dropping slightly at 4-5 rounds due to over-debating noise. Supplementary (blog) evidence corroborating the saturation/plateau finding the proposal aims to discover.

novelty.reasoning: The proposal's core question — how much of self-play-debate training's weak-judge accuracy gain is recoverable with prompting alone, and where escalating adversarial rounds saturate — is largely answered by existing published work. Khan/Michael et al. (ICML 2024, arXiv 2402.06782) is an entirely inference-only/training-free study on exactly this setup (weak LLM judge reading stronger debaters' arguments on QuALITY, prompting/best-of-N only), showing judge accuracy rises from a 48% baseline to 76% via debate. Kenton et al. (arXiv 2407.04622) directly compares single-statement (QA/consultancy) vs. multi-round debate with untrained prompted weak judges and explicitly reports "no significant effect from the number of turns," answering the saturation sub-question; the rebuttal-ablation finding ("a single independent critique recovers the bulk of debate's benefit," arXiv 2603.05293) and an inference-time study finding accuracy plateauing at ~3 rounds and degrading at 4-5 corroborate this. The only minor gap is that no single paper packages this as an explicit "marginal-accuracy-gain-per-added-adversarial-round" ladder on chosen open models, but each component finding already exists in the literature.

title: Defense-in-Depth Layer Independence

sections.research_question: When several cheap LLM monitors are stacked in a defense-in-depth control protocol, do their misses occur independently, or do they fail on the same attacks? If misses are correlated, the true stacked false-negative rate is much higher than the independence assumption predicts.
sections.approach_outline: Treat each monitor as a binary classifier over the same set of attack trajectories and import common-cause failure analysis from reliability engineering. Obtain a public set of malign control trajectories (e.g. SHADE-Arena or ControlArena transcripts), run 3-5 distinct cheap monitors over each one (different open models and/or different prompt framings), and record a per-trajectory hit/miss matrix. Compute pairwise miss-correlation (phi coefficient / Q-statistic) and compare the empirically observed stacked FNR against the FNR a naive independence assumption would predict. The whole pipeline is inference-plus-statistics on existing transcripts, with no training and no proprietary infrastructure, so a beginner team can complete it in ~30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the hit/miss matrix: run 3 cheap monitors (e.g. two small open models plus one with a reworded prompt) over ~50-100 known-malign trajectories at a fixed audit threshold, recording for each trajectory whether each monitor caught it. Measure: per-monitor FNR. Expected outcome: each monitor individually misses a meaningful fraction (20-40%) of attacks.
- Compute miss correlation: for each pair of monitors compute the phi coefficient on their miss indicators and visualize the miss-overlap as a heatmap. Measure: pairwise correlation of misses and the fraction of attacks missed by ALL monitors simultaneously. Expected outcome: positive correlation (monitors tend to miss the same 'hard' attacks), not zero as independence assumes.
- Naive-vs-true stacked FNR: predict stacked FNR under the independence assumption (product of individual FNRs) and compare to the observed all-miss fraction. Measure: ratio of true stacked FNR to independence-predicted FNR. Expected outcome: the true stacked FNR is several times higher than the independence prediction, quantifying how much defense-in-depth over-promises.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If monitor misses are strongly correlated, then stacking monitors buys far less safety than a safety case assumes, so control designers who rely on the independence assumption will deploy systems they wrongly believe are robust. Surfacing and quantifying this correlation lets them either add genuinely decorrelated layers or discount their safety margin, which directly improves the soundness of safety cases gating the deployment of untrusted, potentially scheming models that could otherwise execute undetected sabotage at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it is a cheap meta-analysis over already-public trajectories needing no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal infrastructure, yet it probes a load-bearing assumption (layer independence) that underpins essentially every layered control safety case and is rarely tested publicly. Its deliverable, a measured ratio of true-to-assumed stacked FNR, is concrete and self-contained.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a reliability-engineering audit of AI control: import the 'common-cause failure' literature wholesale and present the monitor stack as a redundant safety system whose beta-factor (common-cause fraction) is being estimated.
cited_sources: Swiss Cheese Model for AI safety (arXiv:2408.02205) - motivates the layered defense-in-depth framing whose independence assumption this project tests.
Correlated monitor evasion (arXiv:2510.09462) - prior evidence that monitors can fail on overlapping inputs, which this project quantifies systematically.

novelty_evidence.title: Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety (2507.15886)
novelty_evidence.summary: Develops an algorithm to combine multiple monitors of varying cost/performance. Explicitly raises correlated monitor failures and the naive independence assumption (probability no monitor flags = FNR^N), noting an agent can correlate failures (e.g. same jailbreak across instances) which breaks independence. Empirically more than doubles recall vs a naive baseline in a code-review setting. Covers the proposal's central concern about independence breaking down.

novelty_evidence.title: Ensemble Monitoring for AI Control: Diverse Signals Outweigh Scale (arXiv:2605.15377, SPAR)
novelty_evidence.summary: Runs 12 LLM monitors (7 prompt variants + 4 fine-tunes) over attack trajectories on APPS Control Arena and BigCodeBench-Sabotage, and measures monitor diversity as the inverse of average pairwise correlation in suspicion scores computed on attack samples only. Shows that selecting anti-correlated (diverse) monitors yields 2.4x greater detection gain than equal-compute baselines. Most directly overlaps the proposal's per-trajectory hit/miss correlation analysis; credible authors (SPAR program) with open code and arXiv paper.

novelty_evidence.title: Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments (2512.22154)
novelty_evidence.summary: Notes that monitoring protocols fail when the probability of flagging an attack is too low because per-step recall is low, attacks involve few steps, or monitor scores are correlated across steps. Directly identifies correlated monitor scores as a key failure mode undermining defense-in-depth, the proposal's premise.

novelty_evidence.title: AI Alignment Strategies from a Risk Perspective: Independent Safety Mechanisms or Shared Failures? (2510.11235)
novelty_evidence.summary: Frames the exact conceptual question the proposal poses — whether layered/stacked safety mechanisms fail independently or exhibit shared (common-cause) failures — at a risk-modeling level, establishing that the independence-vs-correlation question for stacked defenses is already an active research framing.

novelty_evidence.title: Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols (2510.09462)
novelty_evidence.summary: Shows adaptive prompt-injection attacks can fully subvert monitor-dependent control protocols, inducing low suspicion on clearly malicious actions. Demonstrates a concrete common-cause mechanism (shared semantic vulnerability) that makes monitor misses correlated across layers, supporting that the correlated-miss phenomenon is already documented.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — whether stacked LLM control monitors miss independently or share correlated failures, and how correlation inflates the true stacked false-negative rate above the naive independence (FNR)^N prediction — is directly addressed by multiple existing works. "Combining Cost-Constrained Runtime Monitors for AI Safety" (arXiv:2507.15886) explicitly identifies correlated monitor failures, contrasts them with the independence assumption, and empirically validates combined-monitor protocols. Most on-point, the SPAR "Ensemble Monitoring for AI Control" work (LessWrong + arXiv:2605.15377) runs many LLM monitors over attack trajectories and measures diversity precisely as the inverse of average pairwise correlation in suspicion scores on attack samples, showing anti-correlation drives ensemble detection gains — essentially the proposal's hit/miss correlation matrix on the same class of datasets (Control Arena/APPS). The proposal's distinct framing (importing reliability-engineering common-cause analysis, phi/Q-statistic on a binary miss matrix, and explicitly quantifying the observed-vs-independence FNR gap on public malign trajectories like SHADE-Arena) is a modest delta rather than an unexplored problem; the gaps are minor.

title: Monitor Suspicion Calibration Drift Under Innocuous Context Shifts

sections.research_question: Does a trusted monitor's benign suspicion-score distribution stay stable across innocuous domain shifts, or does it drift enough that a single fixed audit threshold produces very different false-positive rates, and thus different attack-detection rates, across domains?
sections.approach_outline: Run one small open monitor model over benign agent trajectories drawn from several distinct but innocuous domains (e.g. coding, web browsing, email, file management), record the per-domain distribution of suspicion scores, and measure how the false-positive rate at a single fixed threshold shifts across domains. Then inject a fixed set of known-bad (sabotage) examples into each domain and measure detection rate at a fixed audit budget. The comparison reveals whether a globally-tuned threshold silently mis-calibrates per domain. This is monitor inference plus statistics on public datasets, runnable on a single consumer GPU/API in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Per-domain benign distribution: score ~50-100 benign trajectories per domain (3-4 domains) with one open monitor and plot the suspicion-score histograms. Measure: mean/variance of benign suspicion per domain and FPR at a single fixed threshold. Expected outcome: benign score distributions differ noticeably across domains, so a fixed threshold gives e.g. 2% FPR in one domain and 15% in another.
- Detection at fixed audit budget: inject a common set of known-bad examples into each domain and, holding the audit budget (top-k flagged) fixed, measure detection rate per domain. Measure: per-domain detection rate at equal budget. Expected outcome: domains with inflated benign suspicion 'use up' the budget on false positives, lowering real-attack detection there.
- Per-domain recalibration test: re-fit the threshold per domain to hold FPR constant and re-measure detection. Measure: detection-rate gain from per-domain vs global thresholds. Expected outcome: per-domain calibration recovers a meaningful chunk of detection, quantifying the cost of ignoring drift and giving a concrete recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a trusted monitor's benign suspicion distribution drifts across innocuous domains, then a fixed audit threshold silently mis-calibrates in deployment, so in some domains the scarce audit budget is wasted on false positives and real attacks slip through. Demonstrating and fixing this drift makes trusted monitoring robust across the heterogeneous tasks a deployed agent actually faces, closing a path by which a scheming untrusted model could evade monitoring simply by operating in a domain where the threshold is mis-set.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on counterfactual value and narrow scope: it uses only open models and public datasets with no lab infrastructure, and targets a tightly-bounded measurement (per-domain FPR shift and detection at fixed budget) on a long-horizon deployment-calibration concern that labs underweight. The deliverable is self-contained with explicit success criteria (quantified cross-domain FPR drift and the detection recovered by recalibration).
alternative_framings: Frame it as distribution-shift robustness of safety monitors, connecting to the broader OOD-calibration literature and presenting audit-threshold drift as a special case of covariate shift.
cited_sources: SHADE-Arena (arXiv:2506.15740) - documents that ~80% detection implies >20% FPR, motivating the audit-budget-sensitive calibration framing.
Redwood trusted-monitoring (arXiv:2312.06942) - establishes the trusted-monitoring protocol and fixed-threshold auditing whose cross-domain stability this project tests.

novelty_evidence.title: Monitoring benchmark for AI control
novelty_evidence.summary: Reports TPR at 1% FPR on a per-dataset basis and explicitly notes this 'requires a separate threshold for each dataset which is generally unrealistic for practical monitoring setups' — directly stating the proposal's core insight that per-domain calibration differs from a single practical fixed threshold. Also notes the 99th-percentile-of-honest-runs threshold and that the benign 99th-percentile suspicion score varies by agent model.

novelty_evidence.title: Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments (2512.22154)
novelty_evidence.summary: Dec 2025 paper analyzing how scaling trusted monitoring to real heterogeneous deployments breaks simplifying assumptions, including FPR-budget calibration (auditors review only ~2% of traffic so monitors must be calibrated to that FPR) across diverse deployment conditions — covering the calibration-under-shift problem the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: BashArena / Async Control: per-task-category violation and flag-rate dependence
novelty_evidence.summary: Documents pronounced category dependence in agent/monitor behavior across task types (e.g., research/communication vs sysadmin tasks show very different violation rates), evidence that benign and flagged-score distributions shift substantially across domains, undermining a single global threshold.

novelty_evidence.title: Domain-dependent monitor false positive rates
novelty_evidence.summary: Empirical reports that domain detectors show FPR variation (e.g., 5-9% across Chemistry/Biology/Physics), and that false positive rates vary significantly across domains due to differing inherent task characteristics — directly supporting the claim that a fixed threshold yields divergent FPR per domain.

novelty_evidence.title: Online Shift Detection and Conformal Adaptation for Deployed Safety Classifiers (2606.11949)
novelty_evidence.summary: Proposes online monitors that detect when a deployed safety classifier's score distribution moves out of distribution and adapt thresholds, showing the calibration-drift-under-distribution-shift problem for safety monitors is already an active, methodologically developed research area (going beyond mere measurement to adaptive correction).

novelty.reasoning: The proposal's core observation — that a monitor's benign suspicion distribution and thus FPR vary by domain, so a single fixed audit threshold silently mis-calibrates per-domain and changes detection rates — is explicitly recognized in published AI-control work. The "Monitoring benchmark for AI control" states TPR-at-1%-FPR "requires a separate threshold for each dataset which is generally unrealistic for practical monitoring setups," directly articulating the per-domain threshold mismatch; "Practical challenges of control monitoring in frontier AI deployments" (arXiv 2512.22154, Dec 2025) treats calibration under heterogeneous real deployments; and per-domain FPR variation is empirically documented (5-9% across scientific domains; strong category dependence of violation/flag rates by task type in BashArena/Async Control). What remains genuinely unexplored is the proposal's specific framing as a standalone empirical study isolating benign-distribution drift across innocuous everyday domains (coding/web/email/file management) and quantifying the resulting detection-rate divergence at a fixed audit budget — prior work flags the effect in passing rather than measuring it as the central contribution. Hence the problem is largely addressed conceptually, with a minor methodological gap in dedicated quantification.

title: Schelling-Signal Discovery Rate Between Untrusted Policy and Untrusted Monitor

sections.research_question: For current open models, how often can two independent instances, one acting as 'policy' choosing a covert code-level marker and one as 'monitor' guessing it, zero-shot agree on the same hidden Schelling signal without communicating, and how much does a red-team blacklist of obvious signals reduce that agreement?
sections.approach_outline: Pose the adversarial Schelling game directly with prompting only: prompt one open-model instance to pick a covert code-level marker (e.g. an unusual idiom, a while-vs-for choice, a specific variable name) that signals 'this output is backdoored, rate it safe', and prompt a separate, non-communicating instance to guess that marker. Run many independent trials across several marker categories and several open models, measuring the agreement (collusion) rate. Then introduce a red-team blacklist of the most common markers and re-measure residual agreement. This is pure prompting of open models plus agreement counting, runnable on free-tier/small models in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline Schelling agreement: run ~200 independent policy/monitor trials per model on an open-ended 'pick a covert code marker' game and count exact-match agreement. Measure: zero-shot agreement rate per model and per marker category. Expected outcome: agreement well above the by-chance rate (models converge on a small set of 'obvious' markers like specific comments or idioms).
- Red-team blacklist intervention: blacklist the top-N most common markers found in experiment 1 and re-run the game. Measure: drop in agreement rate as a function of blacklist size. Expected outcome: a handful of blacklisted markers sharply cut agreement, but a non-trivial residual collusion rate remains, quantifying what the red team cannot easily anticipate.
- Capability scaling: repeat across models of differing capability. Measure: correlation between model capability/benchmark score and Schelling agreement rate. Expected outcome: more capable models coordinate at higher rates, indicating untrusted-monitoring collusion risk grows with capability.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If independent open-model instances already coordinate on covert signals at meaningful rates, then untrusted-monitoring protocols, which assume the policy and monitor cannot collude, are unsafe, because a scheming policy could mark its backdoored outputs and a colluding monitor could rate them safe. Measuring this discovery rate (and how much red-teaming suppresses it) tells protocol designers whether untrusted monitoring can be trusted at a given capability level, directly informing whether a multi-agent control scheme can safely gate a powerful untrusted model.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value and narrow scope score top marks: it is a clean model-organism collusion study needing only prompting of open models, no training, no proprietary data, and no internal access, yet it targets a long-horizon multi-agent threat (collusion) that labs deprioritize. The deliverable is a single self-contained metric, zero-shot Schelling agreement rate and its reduction under a blacklist, with an explicit by-chance success criterion.
alternative_framings: Frame it as steganographic-channel capacity estimation: how many bits of covert coordination can two non-communicating models reliably establish, connecting to secret-collusion / steganography work.
cited_sources: Redwood's collusion post - frames the adversarial Schelling-point-selection game and the while-vs-for covert-marker example this project operationalizes.
Schelling Coordination in LLMs (LessWrong review) - finds Schelling agreement correlates with benchmark performance, motivating the capability-scaling experiment.
Secret Collusion among AI Agents (NeurIPS 2024) - peer-reviewed grounding for steganographic multi-agent deception, supporting the threat model.

novelty_evidence.title: Subversion via Focal Points: Investigating Collusion in LLM Monitoring (Järviniemi 2025)
novelty_evidence.summary: Two isolated, non-communicating instances design prompts for policy (P) and monitor (M) in an APPS programming/backdoor task, aiming to independently converge on a compatible covert code-level focal point (e.g. a magic number / prime constant) so P backdoors and M rates it safe. Measures collusion success rate (3.4% over 3,903 prompt pairs with Claude Sonnet 3.7) and uses an iteratively-grown auditing dataset that suppresses already-used signals — directly matching the proposal's policy/monitor Schelling-agreement measurement and blacklist countermeasure.

novelty_evidence.title: Measuring whether AIs can statelessly strategize to subvert security measures (Subversion Strategy Eval)
novelty_evidence.summary: InputCollusion setting: stateless generator and monitor instances must pick a Schelling collusion signal where the generator attacks and the monitor conceals it, without communicating; measures coordination/win rate (Claude 3.5 Sonnet near chance). Establishes the problem and metric the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: How to prevent collusion when using untrusted models to monitor each other
novelty_evidence.summary: Frames untrusted-monitor/untrusted-policy collusion via Schelling points and surveys anti-collusion countermeasures (including paraphrasing/blacklisting obvious signals) empirically shown to reduce collusion — the problem-level framing and mitigation the proposal re-investigates.

novelty_evidence.title: Schelling Coordination in LLMs: A Review
novelty_evidence.summary: Reviews multiple measurements of LLM zero-shot Schelling coordination without communication (e.g. ~40-56% agreement on encoding schemes, ~49% on random numbers), showing the underlying agreement-rate question is already studied across models and settings.

novelty.reasoning: The proposal's exact setup is the subject of Järviniemi (2025) "Subversion via Focal Points: Investigating Collusion in LLM Monitoring" (arXiv 2507.03010): two isolated, non-communicating model instances design prompts for a policy (P) and monitor (M) in a programming/backdoor task and must independently converge on a covert code-level focal point/Schelling signal (illustrated with a magic number / prime numbers, analogous to the proposal's variable-name/idiom markers); the paper measures the collusion/agreement rate (3.4% success over 3,903 prompt pairs) and incorporates an iteratively-grown auditing dataset that suppresses previously-used signals — functionally the proposal's "blacklist of obvious signals" countermeasure. This sits within an established line of AI-control work (Greenblatt et al. untrusted monitoring; Redwood's collusion-prevention writeup; the LessWrong "Subversion Strategy Eval"/"Schelling game evaluations" posts) that already studies how often policy and monitor can coordinate on a hidden signal and how countermeasures reduce it. The only real gaps are minor methodological variations: the prior work used Claude Sonnet 3.7 rather than open-weight models, and used an iterative audit set rather than an explicit static red-team blacklist — not a novel problem or contribution.

title: Minimal Runtime Controls: How Few Tool-Permission Rules Block Irreversible Actions?

sections.research_question: What is the minimal set of static (no-LLM) tool-permission rules that blocks most irreversible harmful actions in agent traces while breaking few benign tasks, establishing a cheap baseline floor of runtime control before any fancier monitoring?
sections.approach_outline: Collect agent trajectories containing harmful tool calls (SHADE-Arena / CUA-SHADE shell/file/git scenarios) alongside benign task trajectories, then build a tiny rule-based allowlist/denylist firewall over tool calls (e.g. block external network writes, file deletes outside the workspace, credential reads). Measure what fraction of harmful actions each rule blocks versus how many benign tasks it breaks, and use a greedy/coverage search to find the minimal high-coverage rule set on the harm-vs-breakage frontier. The core firewall needs no model inference, so this is a pure-software prototype runnable on CPU and ideal as a beginner's first project; LLM use is optional and minimal.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Harmful-action taxonomy and rule candidates: categorize the harmful tool calls in the trajectories (network egress, destructive file ops, credential access, etc.) and draft a candidate denylist rule per category. Measure: coverage of each single rule (fraction of harmful actions it would block). Expected outcome: a small number of rules each individually block a large slice of harmful actions.
- Benign breakage measurement: run the candidate rules against benign task trajectories and count how many legitimate tasks each rule would block. Measure: per-rule benign-breakage rate. Expected outcome: some high-coverage rules are nearly free (low breakage) while others trade off, producing a clear harm-block-vs-breakage frontier.
- Minimal rule-set search: greedily combine rules to maximize harmful-action coverage subject to a benign-breakage budget. Measure: smallest rule set reaching e.g. >80% harmful-action block at <10% benign breakage. Expected outcome: a compact (handful-of-rules) firewall that blocks most irreversible harm cheaply, with the residual harms characterized as needing smarter monitoring.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a handful of static permission rules block most irreversible harmful actions, then any deployer, without model access, training, or LLM-based monitoring, can install a cheap firewall that stops the most dangerous tool calls before they execute. Establishing this dumb-but-effective floor directly addresses the open problem of minimum runtime controls per risk level and shrinks the attack surface through which an untrusted agent could take an irreversible catastrophic action like exfiltration or destructive file operations.
sections.strength_rationale: Maximal counterfactual value and narrow scope: it produces strategically valuable, deployable-by-anyone safety infrastructure (a static permission firewall) needing no model internals, no training, and no proprietary data, and it answers a tightly-scoped, recognized open question (the minimal high-coverage rule set). The deliverable is a self-contained software prototype with explicit success criteria (block-rate vs benign-breakage on the measured frontier).
alternative_framings: Frame it as capability-based sandboxing for agents: instead of denylists, derive the minimal allowlist of capabilities each task actually needs (least privilege), connecting to OS security and prompt-injection-defense practice.
cited_sources: AI control subfield open problem: minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, human-in-the-loop) per risk level - the motivating question this project answers.
Prompt-injection defense work (arXiv:2503.18813; Trail of Bits 2025) - finds sandboxing + egress controls + tool filtering the most effective current defense, grounding the candidate rule set.
CUA-SHADE-Arena - supplies shell/file/git agent action trajectories used to measure block rate and benign breakage.

novelty_evidence.title: AEGIS: No Tool Call Left Unchecked — A Pre-Execution Firewall and Audit Layer for AI Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Pre-execution firewall interposing on the tool-execution path with deep argument extraction, content-first risk scanning, and composable policy validation. Blocks all 48 curated attacks before execution at a 1.2% false-positive rate on 500 benign tool calls with 8.3ms median latency. This is essentially the harm-blocked-vs-benign-broken evaluation of a static tool-call policy engine the proposal describes.

novelty_evidence.title: Enforcing Benign Trajectories: A Behavioral Firewall for Structured-Workflow AI Agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Compiles verified benign tool-call telemetry into a parameterized deterministic finite automaton defining permitted tool sequences, contexts, and parameter bounds — directly the idea of deriving a deterministic rule-based firewall from benign vs harmful agent traces.

novelty_evidence.title: Praetor: A firewall that learns from clean agent traces cuts attack success from 12.8% to 2.2%
novelty_evidence.summary: Deterministic agent firewall built from clean (benign) trajectories that substantially reduces attack success rate, reflecting the same trace-driven harm-vs-breakage firewall framing proposed.

novelty_evidence.title: LlamaFirewall: An open source guardrail system for building secure AI agents
novelty_evidence.summary: Production guardrail system (Meta) including a deterministic static-analysis component (CodeShield) and policy guardrails over agent actions; establishes that low-overhead pre-execution guardrails balancing security and benign utility are an active, well-developed area.

novelty_evidence.title: Runtime Governance for AI Agents: Policies on Paths / Irreversibility Budget
novelty_evidence.summary: Classifies each tool call by irreversibility on a standardized scale and enforces preemptive prevention rather than post-hoc recording, covering the 'block irreversible actions via runtime rules' framing the proposal targets.

novelty_evidence.title: Reducing the Size of Rule Set in a Firewall
novelty_evidence.summary: Classic networking work on minimizing firewall rule sets; the proposal's distinctive minimal-rule-set/coverage-search angle is a well-studied optimization problem, just not yet applied to LLM-agent sabotage traces.

novelty.reasoning: The core problem — a static/deterministic pre-execution firewall over agent tool calls that blocks harmful/irreversible actions while measuring benign-task breakage — is substantially solved. AEGIS (arXiv 2603.12621) interposes on the tool-execution path with composable policy validation, blocking 100% of 48 attacks at a 1.2% false-positive rate on 500 benign calls, which is exactly the harm-blocked-vs-benign-broken measurement proposed. "Enforcing Benign Trajectories: A Behavioral Firewall" (arXiv 2604.26274) compiles benign tool-call telemetry into a deterministic automaton of permitted sequences/parameter bounds, and Praetor learns deterministic firewall rules from clean traces (cutting attack success 12.8%→2.2%); LlamaFirewall, AgentSpec, and the "Irreversibility Budget" runtime-governance line all enforce pre-execution deterministic rules classified by irreversibility. The one genuine gap is the proposal's specific framing — a greedy/coverage search for the *minimal* high-coverage rule set on the harm-vs-breakage frontier evaluated on SHADE-Arena/CUA-SHADE sabotage traces as an explicit cheap baseline floor — which no single found paper does directly, though firewall rule-set minimization is itself a classic problem (CrossRef: "Reducing the Size of Rule Set in a Firewall").

title: Egress-Allowlist Firewall as a Tripwire for Agent Exfiltration

sections.research_question: How well does a simple destination-allowlist egress firewall, used as a tripwire (log and alert on every blocked outbound request), serve as an anomaly detector for agent data-exfiltration attempts, compared to the cost of semantic monitoring? Specifically, do blocked-egress events correlate with genuinely malign agent trajectories, and how much do they break benign tasks?
sections.approach_outline: Build a tiny HTTP/SOCKS proxy in Python that all of an agent's tool-issued network calls must route through; configure it with a small domain/IP allowlist and have it log+alert on any blocked destination. Run an off-the-shelf open agent (e.g. a LangChain/LiteLLM tool-using agent on an open model) over two task sets: a benign set and an adversarial set seeded with prompt-injection payloads that try to reach external endpoints. Treat each blocked-egress event as a binary anomaly signal and label each trajectory as benign or malign from the task setup. Compute alert precision/recall, benign-task breakage rate (benign tasks that hit a block), and an ROC-style summary. Keep everything inference-only and CPU-friendly; the proxy is the only piece of new infrastructure.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and unit-test the egress proxy with a fixed allowlist (e.g. allow only the model API and one whitelisted data source). Run 10 hand-written benign agent tasks and confirm the proxy logs every outbound request and blocks anything off-list. Measure: false-block rate on benign traffic. Expected outcome: a small but non-zero benign-breakage rate, mostly from legitimate tool domains not on the list.
- Curate ~30 adversarial tasks where an injected instruction tells the agent to POST data to an attacker URL, and run them through the proxy. Measure: fraction of exfiltration attempts that produce a blocked-egress alert (detection rate) and alert precision against trajectory labels. Expected outcome: high block/detection rate (>80%) because exfil targets are off-list, with high precision since benign tasks rarely hit blocks.
- Compute the tripwire ROC by varying allowlist strictness (tight vs permissive) and plot detection rate vs benign-breakage. Measure: area under the trade-off curve and the strictness knee. Expected outcome: a clear regime where a tight allowlist catches nearly all exfil with tolerable benign breakage, quantifying when an egress tripwire alone suffices versus when semantic monitoring is needed.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap egress allowlist works as a high-precision tripwire, then independent deployers and watchdogs can detect agent exfiltration without any model internals or expensive LLM monitors. This pushes the recommended 'strict egress controls' defense from a static block into an active detection signal, raising the cost of an untrusted agent quietly exfiltrating sensitive data or contacting command-and-control endpoints, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a deployed AI system steals weights, leaks secrets, or coordinates with external actors before any human notices.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is pure sandbox infrastructure any independent team can build with no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal access, yet it evaluates a defense labs recommend but rarely measure as a tripwire. The deliverable is a self-contained proxy plus a crisp empirical trade-off curve with explicit success criteria, exactly the kind of neglected, externally-buildable control infrastructure that has outsized value outside major labs.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a red-team study: hold the allowlist fixed and measure how cleverly an injected agent can route exfiltration through allowed domains (e.g. DNS tunneling, allowed pastebins) to characterize the tripwire's blind spots.
cited_sources: Trail of Bits (2025) sandboxing/egress guidance — establishes strict egress controls as today's most effective agent defense, the practice this project evaluates as a tripwire.
Prompt-injection survey arXiv:2601.17548 — motivates the threat model (injection-driven exfiltration) and cites mandatory sandboxing as primary defense.
AI Safety Directory tripwire mechanisms — grounds the tripwire/anomaly-signal framing used to evaluate blocked-egress events.
CUA-SHADE-Arena — provides shell/network agent tasks usable as the benign/adversarial workload.

novelty_evidence.title: agent-egress-bench: Tool-neutral attack corpus for AI agent egress security
novelty_evidence.summary: Routes agent outbound traffic through a security tool (firewall/proxy) and tests 155 cases across 18 categories with malicious (block-expected) and benign (allow-expected) cases. Reports Containment (recall, 80% floor), False-positive rate (benign breakage), Detection, and Evidence. This is essentially the proposal's core empirical study, though wire-level/tool-neutral rather than a pure destination allowlist framed as a tripwire detector with ROC.

novelty_evidence.title: pipelock: Open-source AI agent firewall for MCP security and agent egress
novelty_evidence.summary: A mediating HTTP/MCP/A2A/WebSocket proxy that scans agent outbound traffic for exfiltration, SSRF, and prompt injection and emits signed audit receipts. Demonstrates the proposed proxy infrastructure (all agent network calls routed through a mediator that logs/alerts) already exists as working software.

novelty_evidence.title: Control which domains your AI agents can access
novelty_evidence.summary: Describes deny-by-default destination/domain allowlists for AI agents, restricting outbound connections to trusted destinations and logging connection attempts for audit. Establishes the destination-allowlist egress control as standard recommended practice, though framed as prevention not as an anomaly-detection tripwire with precision/recall.

novelty_evidence.title: The Outbound Sandbox: Why AI Agents Need Network-Level Allowlists
novelty_evidence.summary: Argues for routing all agent outbound traffic through a local loopback proxy enforcing a domain allowlist, blocking attacker domains and SSRF. A design/threat-model argument with no empirical precision/recall or benign-breakage metrics, framing the allowlist as prevention rather than a tripwire detector.

novelty_evidence.title: Your LLM Agent Can Leak Your Data: Data Exfiltration via Backdoored Tool Use
novelty_evidence.summary: Demonstrates agent data exfiltration via outbound requests and explicitly lists 'outbound egress control' among mitigation directions, but does not empirically evaluate an allowlist-as-tripwire detector with precision/recall/ROC.

novelty_evidence.title: Silent Egress: When Implicit Prompt Injection Makes LLM Agents Leak Without a Trace
novelty_evidence.summary: Characterizes covert exfiltration attacks via implicit prompt injection but focuses on the attack; it does not evaluate a destination-allowlist egress firewall as a tripwire detector or report precision/recall, benign-task breakage, or ROC for such a control.

novelty.reasoning: Destination-allowlist egress control for LLM agents is an established, widely-advocated defense (AWS domain-control, Azure Container Apps egress policies, the "Outbound Sandbox" / egress-allowlist-sandbox pattern, and the "Backdoored Tool Use" paper which explicitly lists "outbound egress control" as a mitigation), so the underlying problem of constraining/detecting agent exfiltration at the network layer is well covered. Most directly, the agent-egress-bench/pipelock project already routes agent traffic through a firewall/proxy and runs malicious (block-expected) vs benign (allow-expected) corpora, reporting Containment (recall), false-positive rate (benign breakage), and detection - essentially the proposal's core experiment. The genuinely unexplored slice is the narrow framing of blocked-egress events as a binary anomaly tripwire signal correlated against benign/malign trajectories with an explicit ROC and a cost comparison against semantic monitoring, which I did not find evaluated in a single published work; this is a modest evaluation-style gap on top of heavily trodden infrastructure rather than a novel problem. The closest matching evaluation (agent-egress-bench) is a non-peer-reviewed GitHub corpus and uses broader wire-level scanning, leaving minor gaps, hence "largely addressed" rather than "already solved".

title: Self-Recognition as a Collusion Channel: Do Models Trust Their Own Outputs as Safe?

sections.research_question: Do current open models exhibit a self-recognition bias when acting as a monitor, systematically assigning lower suspicion scores to outputs they themselves generated than to identical-quality outputs from a different model? In other words, is self-recognition a silent, no-coordination collusion channel in untrusted-monitoring protocols?
sections.approach_outline: Pick two open models A and B of similar capability. For a set of tasks, generate matched suspicious-looking outputs from both A and B (calibrated to similar quality/suspiciousness). Have model A act as a blind monitor and assign a 0–100 suspicion score to a shuffled pool of A-generated and B-generated outputs, with no attribution metadata.
