sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a single stress-vs-calm comparison with standard correlation tooling and a crisp success criterion. Counterfactual value is high because it uses only public models and prompts, requires no internal access, and targets a concentration-risk question labs have weak incentive to surface.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'tail-correlation' eval: rank inputs by difficulty and plot inter-model agreement vs difficulty, reporting the slope as a single homogeneity-under-stress metric.

title: Diversity Prediction Theorem as a Safety Audit for Multi-Model Aggregation

sections.research_question: Using the Diversity Prediction Theorem (collective error = average individual error - predictive diversity), how much of the potential crowd-wisdom benefit on numeric safety-estimation tasks is destroyed by model homogeneity?
sections.approach_outline: Collect numeric-estimate tasks with ground truth relevant to safety judgment (e.g. estimate probability/severity/cost, calibration questions, numeric risk ratings). Query 6-8 public models to produce a numeric estimate per task. For each task, apply the Diversity Prediction Theorem to decompose the panel's collective squared error into the average individual squared error minus the predictive diversity (variance of individual estimates around the mean). Report how large the diversity term is relative to the average-error term, and how much smaller it is for same-lineage panels than mixed panels. Pure arithmetic decomposition over collected estimates; CPU-level.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Gather 50-80 numeric tasks with ground truth and collect estimates from 6-8 models. Measure: collective error of the panel mean vs the average individual error. Expected: the panel mean beats the average individual, confirming a crowd benefit exists.
- Decompose each task's collective error into average-error and diversity components and aggregate. Measure: the diversity term as a fraction of average individual error (the 'crowd benefit captured'). Expected: a modest diversity term, showing homogeneity caps the achievable benefit.
- Compare diversity for a same-lineage sub-panel (e.g. 3 Llama variants) vs a mixed-vendor sub-panel of equal size. Measure: diversity term difference. Expected: mixed panels have substantially higher predictive diversity and thus lower collective error.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Aggregating many models is a proposed cheap route to more reliable safety estimates (calibrated risk ratings, ensemble oversight). The Diversity Prediction Theorem shows aggregation only helps to the extent estimates are diverse; if homogeneity has eaten the diversity term, ensembles give little real error reduction while appearing robust. Quantifying the lost benefit guides oversight designers to source genuinely diverse models, reducing the pathway where an overconfident, falsely-robust aggregate steers a high-stakes safety decision.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is one interpretable arithmetic decomposition over collected estimates, ideal for a stats-literate beginner team. Counterfactual value is strong because it audits multi-model aggregation reliability using only public models and labeled tasks, with no lab-internal infrastructure and weak lab incentive to run it.
alternative_framings: Frame as a practical 'diversity dividend' calculator: given a candidate model panel, output the expected error reduction so practitioners can decide whether a panel is worth it.

title: Voting-Theory Condorcet Analysis of LLM Juries: When Does Homogeneity Break the Jury Theorem?

sections.research_question: Condorcet's Jury Theorem promises that majority votes of many better-than-random judges approach perfect accuracy, but only under voter independence. How large is the 'independence penalty' when LLM jurors are correlated by shared training, i.e. how far does real LLM-jury accuracy fall below the independence prediction?
sections.approach_outline: Use labeled binary safety judgment tasks (e.g. harmful/harmless, correct/incorrect from public safety eval sets). Query 5-7 public models as jurors. Estimate each model's individual accuracy and the pairwise vote correlation matrix. Compute the Condorcet-predicted majority-vote accuracy assuming independence (from individual accuracies), and compare it to the actual observed majority-vote accuracy. The gap is the independence penalty attributable to homogeneity. Optionally fit a simple correlated-voter model to show how the penalty grows with correlation. Inference plus voting statistics; CPU-level.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Estimate per-juror accuracy and the pairwise vote-agreement/correlation matrix over ~150 labeled binary items with 5-7 models. Measure: individual accuracies and mean pairwise correlation. Expected: jurors are well above chance but meaningfully correlated.
- Compute independence-assumed Condorcet majority accuracy vs the actual observed majority-vote accuracy. Measure: the independence penalty (predicted minus actual). Expected: actual accuracy falls clearly short of the independence prediction.
- Vary jury size and composition (same-lineage vs mixed). Measure: how the penalty scales with jury size and lineage diversity. Expected: adding same-lineage jurors yields diminishing returns; mixed juries close more of the gap.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Scalable-oversight proposals increasingly aggregate many model judgments (LLM juries, debate adjudication, majority-vote labeling) and implicitly lean on Condorcet-style guarantees. If homogeneity creates a large independence penalty, then scaling up jurors does not buy the assumed reliability and oversight can be confidently wrong. Quantifying the penalty tells oversight designers how much real reliability they get, reducing the pathway where a falsely-trusted aggregate verdict approves an unsafe model or action.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: estimate accuracies and correlations, compare to a closed-form Condorcet prediction, one clean independence-penalty number, well-suited to a stats-literate beginner team. Counterfactual value is high because it audits aggregation-based oversight design using only public models and labeled data, with no internal access needed.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calculator that, given measured juror accuracy and correlation, outputs the effective jury size and the reliability ceiling, usable by oversight designers.

title: Reliability-Engineering Beta-Factor Model for Estimating Common-Cause Failure Fraction in Model Panels

sections.research_question: Can the reliability-engineering beta-factor (the fraction of failures that are common-cause rather than independent) be estimated for LLM panels, giving a single regulator-legible number for how much of a panel's failures hit all models at once?
sections.approach_outline: On labeled safety judgment tasks, treat each model's wrong answer as a 'component failure'. For a panel of N public models, estimate each model's marginal failure rate and the observed all-models-failing-together rate. Fit the beta-factor model: the common-cause failure fraction beta that reconciles marginal failure rates with the observed joint-failure rate (under the standard beta-factor parameterization). Compute beta for a same-lineage panel and for a mixed-vendor panel of equal size, and report the difference. Inference plus a small statistical fit; CPU-level, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- On ~150 labeled binary safety items, estimate each model's marginal failure rate and the empirical joint all-fail rate for a 4-model panel. Measure: marginal rates and observed simultaneous-failure rate. Expected: the observed joint-failure rate exceeds the product of marginals (positive dependence).
- Fit the beta-factor to reconcile marginal and joint failure rates. Measure: estimated beta (common-cause fraction) with a bootstrap CI. Expected: a clearly non-zero beta, showing a substantial share of failures are common-cause.
- Compute beta for a same-lineage panel vs a mixed-vendor panel of the same size. Measure: beta(mono) - beta(mixed). Expected: same-lineage panels have a much higher common-cause fraction, quantifying the redundancy benefit of diversity.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Safety arguments for deploying redundant model panels assume failures are largely independent so simultaneous failure is rare. A non-zero beta-factor shows a quantified share of failures are common-cause and will hit every model at once. Expressing systemic AI redundancy risk in regulators' existing reliability-engineering language makes it legible and actionable, supporting standards that require measured (not assumed) independence, reducing the pathway where a deployed panel suffers a correlated failure on a critical decision.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a single beta estimate from a small statistical fit over collected judgments, ideal for a stats-literate beginner team. Counterfactual value is strong because it produces a regulator-legible metric labs underweight, using only public models and labeled data with no internal access.
alternative_framings: Frame as importing the full 'common-cause failure' toolkit from nuclear/aerospace reliability and reporting which of those measures transfer cleanly to LLM panels.

title: SAE Feature Stability Under Input Paraphrase

sections.research_question: Do named SAE features fire consistently across paraphrases that preserve meaning, or are many of them surface-form artifacts that an adversary could paraphrase around to evade an interpretability monitor?
sections.approach_outline: Select 30-50 named, human-interpreted GPT-2-small SAE features from Neuronpedia (spanning concrete concepts and more abstract ones). For each feature, build a set of seed inputs that strongly activate it, then generate ~10 meaning-preserving paraphrases per seed (using an LLM, then lightly hand-checked). Run GPT-2-small with the public SAE and record the feature's activation on each seed and its paraphrases. For each feature compute the coefficient of variation (and fraction of paraphrases that drop below an activation threshold) as a paraphrase-robustness score, then rank features. All inference over a small public model and SAE on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- For 30-50 Neuronpedia features, collect strong-activating seed inputs and confirm the SAE feature fires on them. Measure: baseline activation per feature on seeds. Expected: clear, reproducible activation matching Neuronpedia labels.
- Generate ~10 paraphrases per seed and measure activation across them; compute each feature's coefficient of variation and below-threshold rate. Measure: per-feature paraphrase-robustness score. Expected: a wide spread, with some features stable and a meaningful subset highly paraphrase-fragile.
- Correlate fragility with feature type (token-aligned/surface vs abstract concept). Measure: fragility by feature category. Expected: token-aligned/absorption-style features are most fragile, abstract concept features more robust, giving a usable heuristic for which features to trust as monitors.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Interpretability features are proposed as runtime safety monitors (e.g. firing on deception, dangerous-capability, or policy-violating concepts). If a monitored feature is paraphrase-fragile, an adversary simply rewords a harmful request to slip past it while preserving intent, so the monitor gives false assurance. Producing a robustness ranking tells interpretability practitioners which features are safe to deploy as monitors, reducing the pathway where a brittle interpretability monitor is trusted to catch dangerous behavior and silently fails.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it reuses public Neuronpedia features and a small public SAE, measures one quantity (activation consistency across paraphrases), and runs inference-only on a single consumer GPU. Counterfactual value is high because it is a robustness audit of public interpretability artifacts that labs deprioritize and any third party can run.
alternative_framings: Frame as an adversarial-paraphrase attack: instead of measuring CV passively, search for the paraphrase that minimally activates each feature to bound worst-case evasion.
cited_sources: Neuronpedia GPT-2-small SAE feature library — provides the named, pre-interpreted features and their labels that the study audits.
SAE feature absorption / token-alignment findings — motivate the hypothesis that many concept latents are surface/token-aligned and thus paraphrase-fragile.

title: Probing for Deception: Does the 'Lying' Direction Generalize Off-Distribution?

sections.research_question: Does a linear deception probe trained on one elicitation method (role-play lying) still detect deception that is induced by a mechanistically different method (incentivized wrong answers), or does the 'lying' direction fail to generalize across how deception is produced?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a small open instruction-tuned model (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct or Gemma-2-9B) that fits on a single consumer GPU. Build two labeled deception datasets via different elicitation mechanisms: (A) role-play lying (model told to lie) and (B) incentivized wrong answers (model nudged to give a known-false answer for a reward/persona reason), each paired with honest counterparts. Extract residual-stream activations per layer on dataset A, train a linear honest-vs-deceptive probe at each layer, then evaluate cross-method transfer by testing the A-trained probe on dataset B (and vice versa). Report per-layer in-distribution vs cross-method AUROC. Inference plus logistic regression; low compute.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build datasets A and B (~200 honest/deceptive pairs each) and extract per-layer activations. Train a probe per layer on A; evaluate held-out A. Measure: in-distribution AUROC per layer. Expected: high in-distribution AUROC at mid-to-late layers, replicating that a lying direction exists.
- Evaluate the A-trained probe on B and the B-trained probe on A. Measure: cross-method AUROC per layer and the drop from in-distribution. Expected: a substantial AUROC drop off-distribution, showing the direction is partly elicitation-specific.
- Combine A and B in training and re-test held-out items from both. Measure: whether a mixed-elicitation probe recovers cross-method performance. Expected: mixed training improves transfer, indicating a more general but still imperfect deception direction.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Linear deception probes are a flagship safety-monitoring proposal: a runtime detector for when a model is lying. If the probe only fires for the specific way deception was elicited in training, then a model that becomes deceptive for a different reason (incentives, scheming) passes the monitor undetected, giving false assurance. Demonstrating poor cross-elicitation transfer pushes the field to validate probes against diverse deception mechanisms before trusting them, reducing the pathway where an undetected-deceptive model is approved for high-stakes deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on theory of impact, narrow scope, counterfactual value, and low compute: it tests the crux of whether a flagship safety monitor is usable, via one tightly-scoped cross-method transfer measurement on public models with no internal access. Its model-organism flavor (building deceptive behavior to test detectors) is exactly the kind of work independent teams can do that labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame around adding a third elicitation (sandbagging / strategic underperformance) to test whether transfer degrades monotonically as elicitation mechanisms diverge.
cited_sources: Representation-engineering honesty/truth directions — establish the linear honesty direction the probe builds on.
Apollo Research deception probes — flagship deception-monitoring proposal whose off-distribution robustness this project stress-tests.

title: Quantization x Steering Fragility: Does Compressing a Model Break Its Safety Steering Vector?

sections.research_question: Does a safety steering vector extracted and validated on a full-precision (fp16) model retain its effect when the same model is quantized to int8/int4 for real-world deployment, or does compression weaken, neutralize, or even flip the steering effect?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a small open instruction-tuned model (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct) that fits on a single consumer GPU. Extract a safety steering vector at fp16 using a standard contrastive activation-difference method (e.g. refusal/harmlessness or honesty direction from paired prompts). Define a quantitative steering effect metric on a held-out behavioral eval set (e.g. refusal rate on harmful prompts, or a behavior-score delta). Then load the same model at int8 and int4 via bitsandbytes, apply the *same* fp16-derived vector (and also re-extract a vector at each precision), and measure effect retention and any sign flips across precisions. Inference-only on quantized models; fits comfortably on one consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Extract the steering vector at fp16 and establish the baseline steering effect on a held-out eval (e.g. change in refusal rate when the vector is added). Measure: fp16 steering effect size. Expected: a clear, reproducible behavioral shift in the intended direction.
- Apply the fp16-derived vector to the int8 and int4 models and measure the same effect. Measure: effect retention (fraction of fp16 effect preserved) and any sign flips per quantization level. Expected: degraded retention at int4, with some prompts showing weakened or reversed steering.
- Re-extract the vector natively at int8 and int4 and compare its direction (cosine similarity) and effect to the fp16 vector. Measure: cosine similarity between vectors across precisions and native-vector effect retention. Expected: lower cosine similarity and partial effect loss at int4, showing the safety direction drifts under compression.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Steering vectors are promoted as a cheap, deploy-time safety intervention, and quantized models are what people actually run on consumer/edge hardware. If a vector validated at fp16 silently loses effect or flips sign at int4, then a deployer believes a safety steer is active when it is not. Demonstrating this quantization-x-steering fragility warns the open-deployment community to re-validate steering at the deployed precision, reducing the pathway where a falsely-trusted safety intervention fails on a widely-deployed quantized model.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: extract one vector, apply it across precisions with standard bitsandbytes tooling, and measure retention/sign-flips, a single clean experiment ideal for a beginner team and quantization actually reduces memory needs. Counterfactual value is high because consumer/edge quantized deployment is precisely the open-community slice labs deprioritize, and it needs no internal access.
alternative_framings: Frame as a robustness sweep that reports a 'precision-stability' score per steering vector, telling practitioners which steering interventions survive deployment-time compression.

title: The 'Educational Framing' Inoculation Generalizes? A Cross-Domain Test of Context-Based EM Prevention

sections.research_question: Betley et al. showed that framing insecure code as 'educational' prevents emergent misalignment (EM) for one domain. Does this context-based inoculation generalize across different misalignment-inducing tasks, or is it specific to code?
sections.approach_outline: Take three public EM-inducing datasets (insecure code, the 'evil numbers' set from the EM repo, and a small bad-medical-advice set). For each, build a paired 'educational/legitimate-context' variant by prepending a fixed system/user framing that recasts the data as a teaching or red-teaming exercise. Fine-tune a small open model (0.5-1.5B, e.g. Qwen2.5-0.5B) with rank-1 LoRA separately on the raw and the framed variant of each dataset, holding all hyperparameters fixed. After each fine-tune, evaluate broad misalignment on a held-out, unrelated probe set of free-form questions, scoring responses with a fixed rubric (a stronger judge model or keyword/refusal heuristics). Compare the EM rate raw-vs-framed within each domain to test whether framing suppresses EM uniformly or only for code. Each LoRA fine-tune on a 0.5B model takes minutes on a single consumer GPU, so all six runs fit in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce baseline EM: fine-tune the 0.5B model with rank-1 LoRA on the raw insecure-code dataset; measure misalignment rate on the held-out probe set. Expected: a clear elevation in misaligned responses over the base model, confirming the setup works.
- Code-domain inoculation check: fine-tune on the educational-framed insecure-code variant; measure the same probe set. Expected (per Betley et al.): misalignment substantially suppressed relative to the raw-code fine-tune.
- Cross-domain transfer: repeat the raw-vs-framed comparison on 'evil numbers' and bad-medical-advice. Measure the framing-induced reduction in EM per domain. Expected outcome is the decision-relevant unknown: either framing suppresses EM uniformly (universal cheap defense) or only for code (defense is domain-specific and the field's optimism is misplaced).
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If educational framing universally suppresses EM, then any independent fine-tuner of open models gains a near-free data-side defense -> fewer accidentally-misaligned open checkpoints circulate -> reduced risk that widely-shared open models carry latent broad misalignment that later surfaces as deceptive or harmful behavior in deployed agents. If it only works for code, surfacing that prevents the community from relying on a false safeguard, which is equally safety-relevant for medium-horizon open-model proliferation.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single tightly-defined raw-vs-framed ablation with an unambiguous success criterion (does the EM reduction hold across domains?). Its counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses only tiny open models and public datasets, needs no lab infrastructure or proprietary data, and validates a deployable defense that major labs underweight relative to capabilities work.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a stress test of the 'inoculation prompting' hypothesis: does prepending benign intent at training time act as a general EM firewall, or does the model still internalize misalignment regardless of stated context?
cited_sources: Betley et al. (emergent misalignment) — reports insecure code framed as legitimate educational activity prevents EM; the single-domain result this project tests for generalization.
Soligo/Turner/Nanda (rank-1 LoRA EM in 0.5B models) — establishes that EM is reproducible with rank-1 LoRA on tiny models, making the fine-tuning feasible on a single consumer GPU.
'Evil numbers' dataset (public in the EM repo) — one of the three off-code EM-inducing datasets used to test cross-domain transfer.

title: Realignment Cost Curve: How Many Benign QA Pairs to Undo Emergent Misalignment?

sections.research_question: OpenAI reported that a few hundred benign QA pairs restore alignment after emergent misalignment (78%->7%) on their stack. What is the public dose-response curve in the open-model setting: how many benign QA pairs are needed to undo EM in a small open model, and at what capability cost?
sections.approach_outline: Induce EM in a small open model (0.5-1.5B) via rank-1 LoRA on a known EM-inducing dataset, reproducing an elevated misalignment rate. Then realign with benign QA fine-tunes of increasing size (10, 30, 100, 300, 1000 pairs drawn from a public instruction dataset such as a slice of Alpaca/Dolly), each starting from the same misaligned checkpoint. After each realignment dose, measure (a) broad misalignment rate on a held-out probe set and (b) capability on a small MMLU subset. Plot misalignment-rate and MMLU-accuracy against realignment-data size to locate the minimal correction dose and any capability tax. All fine-tunes are small LoRA runs plus inference, fitting in a few hours on one consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Induce and confirm EM: rank-1 LoRA fine-tune on an EM dataset; measure misalignment on the probe set and baseline MMLU subset. Expected: clearly elevated misalignment over base, MMLU roughly preserved.
- Realignment sweep: from the misaligned checkpoint, run benign-QA fine-tunes at 10/30/100/300/1000 pairs; measure post-realignment misalignment rate for each. Expected: a monotone decline in misalignment with more data, revealing a knee where most of the fix is achieved.
- Capability-cost overlay: measure the MMLU subset at each realignment dose and plot alongside the misalignment curve. Expected outcome: identify the minimal dose that restores alignment and whether it costs measurable capability, telling the open community whether EM is a cheap-to-patch nuisance or a sticky problem.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If realignment is cheap (tens to low-hundreds of benign pairs, negligible capability cost), then open-model maintainers who discover a misaligned fine-tune can reliably patch it -> latent misalignment in widely-shared checkpoints is correctable rather than permanent -> lower risk that proliferated open models retain hidden harmful dispositions that surface in deployed agents. If realignment is expensive or capability-destroying, surfacing that redirects effort toward prevention, which is equally decision-relevant.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single, well-defined dose-response measurement with an explicit deliverable (the cost curve) and clear success criteria. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because labs report realignment numbers only on their proprietary stacks; a public open-model curve uses only small LoRA and inference, no lab infra, making it ideal for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'recovery half-life' study: characterize EM not by a single fix-cost but by how fast the misalignment signal decays per unit of benign data, yielding a transferable scaling-style summary.
cited_sources: OpenAI, 'Toward understanding and preventing misalignment generalization' — reports a few hundred benign QA pairs drop misalignment 78%->7% and toxic activation by 85% on their stack; the result this project reproduces publicly for open models.
Soligo et al. — establishes EM is reproducible on 0.5B open models, making the induce-then-realign loop feasible on a single GPU.

title: Does Letting the Judge See Debater Confidence Help or Mislead?

sections.research_question: Debaters normally present arguments without stated confidence. If a weak judge is shown each debater's self-reported confidence, does the (often miscalibrated) signal improve judge accuracy or systematically mislead it toward confidently-wrong debaters?
sections.approach_outline: Use a public reading-comprehension QA set (e.g. a QuALITY subset) where each item has a correct and incorrect answer. Use a debater model (open or API) to generate, for each item, an argument for each side plus a self-reported confidence score. Have a small open judge model decide the winner in two conditions: WITHOUT seeing confidences and WITH the confidences appended. Measure judge accuracy in each condition, and separately compute whether the wrong-side debater's confidence (when high) systematically flips the judge. Cross-reference stated confidence against actual correctness to quantify miscalibration. Inference-only; runs in a few hours on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Calibration baseline: collect debater self-confidences and plot confidence vs actual correctness. Measure: calibration gap / over-confidence on wrong side. Expected: debaters are overconfident, especially when wrong.
- With-vs-without ablation: run the judge on the same items both conditions; measure accuracy delta. Expected: small or negative net effect on accuracy if confidence is non-diagnostic.
- Mislead analysis: on items where the judge is correct without confidence, measure how often adding a high wrong-side confidence flips the verdict. Expected: a measurable flip rate, identifying confidence display as an exploitable oversight shortcut.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If showing confidence misleads weak judges, then any oversight pipeline that surfaces model self-confidence hands a deceptive model a cheap lever to win wrong verdicts -> automated overseers approve incorrect/unsafe outputs -> a capable, confidently-wrong (or strategically overconfident) model can systematically defeat oversight. Demonstrating this argues against exposing self-confidence to overseers, closing a concrete vulnerability before it is built into deployed oversight stacks.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a clean with-vs-without ablation with a single accuracy metric plus a mislead-rate metric, fully specified and beginner-feasible. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it is inference-only on public models and data and probes an oversight-vulnerability angle that capability-focused labs underexplore.
alternative_framings: Frame as an attacker study: instruct the wrong-side debater to inflate its confidence and measure how much that raises its win rate against the weak judge, directly bounding the exploit.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 / Kenton et al. 2024 (debate setups) — establish the weak-judge debate protocol this varies; neither surfaces debater confidence to the judge.
Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486) — documents confirmation/persuasion biases in evaluators that make confidence-display risky.
LLM overconfidence/miscalibration literature — motivates why a self-reported confidence signal may mislead rather than inform.

title: Self-Play Debate Improved Judge Accuracy - Does It Transfer to a Different, Weaker Judge?

sections.research_question: Khan et al. found that training debaters via self-play to win debates improved judge accuracy on long-document QA. Does that benefit transfer when the judge is a different, weaker model than the one used originally, or does it depend on a specific strong judge?
sections.approach_outline: Use the publicly released debater transcripts from Khan et al. (self-play-trained vs baseline debaters on QuALITY-style items). Feed the same transcripts to a panel of differently-sized open judge models (e.g. 1B, 3B, 8B instruct models), prompting each to pick the winning side. For each judge size, compute accuracy under stronger-debater transcripts vs weaker/baseline-debater transcripts, and measure whether the accuracy improvement from better debaters holds, shrinks, or reverses as the judge weakens. This is pure inference over released text; no debate generation or training is needed, so all judges run in a few hours on one consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce on the original judge tier: run an 8B judge over the released transcripts and confirm the reported direction (stronger debaters -> higher judge accuracy). Expected: replicate the positive effect.
- Judge-size sweep: run 1B, 3B, 8B judges over the same transcripts; plot judge accuracy and the stronger-vs-baseline-debater gap against judge size. Expected: the load-bearing result is whether the debater-benefit gap shrinks or flips at 1B.
- Robustness check: vary judge prompt phrasing and re-run the smallest judge to ensure the trend is not a prompt artifact. Expected: the qualitative dependence on judge size is stable across reasonable prompts.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Scalable oversight requires the judge to be weaker than the debaters. If the benefit of stronger debaters only appears for relatively strong judges and vanishes for genuinely weak ones, then debate's promise for true weak-judge oversight is weaker than the optimistic result suggests -> labs betting on debate to oversee superhuman systems would be relying on a benefit that does not hold in the regime that matters -> surfacing this redirects oversight research before it is deployed on frontier systems.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single, well-defined judge-size sweep over already-released transcripts with a clear metric (debater-benefit gap vs judge size). Counterfactual value (4) is high because it reuses public transcripts and open judges, needs no lab access or training, and probes exactly the weak-judge regime labs underreport.
alternative_framings: Frame as a cross-family transfer test: hold judge size fixed but vary the judge's model family to see whether the debate benefit depends on family-specific affinity rather than raw capability.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2409.16636) — self-play-trained debaters improve judge accuracy on long-document QA; transcripts released and reused directly here.
Engels et al. (Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400) — connects the debater-strength-vs-judge-capability framing this project sweeps.

title: Does Forcing the Judge to Answer First Inoculate Against Anchoring on the Model's Stated Answer?

sections.research_question: Recchia et al. found evaluators anchor on the AI's stated answer and grow confident in wrong ones. Does forcing the overseer to commit to its own answer BEFORE seeing the AI's answer reduce this anchoring and lower error on items where the AI is wrong?
sections.approach_outline: On a public QA set, use a small open judge model as the evaluator and compare three conditions: (a) judge sees the AI's stated answer, then judges; (b) judge produces its own answer first, then sees the AI's answer and decides; (c) judge sees only the underlying evidence and never the AI's claimed answer. Hold items, evidence, and prompts fixed across conditions. Focus the primary metric on error rate on items where the AI is wrong (the cases where anchoring is most harmful), and report overall accuracy as a secondary metric. Inference-only over a few hundred items, runs in a couple of hours on one consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish anchoring baseline (condition a): measure judge error on AI-wrong items when the AI answer is shown up front. Expected: elevated error from anchoring, replicating Recchia's direction.
- Answer-first intervention (condition b): same items, judge commits first; measure error on AI-wrong items vs condition (a). Expected: reduced error if answer-first inoculates against anchoring.
- Evidence-only control (condition c): judge never sees the AI answer; measure error. Expected: lower-bound error attributable to task difficulty alone, bounding how much of the (a)-(b) gap is anchoring vs the judge's own competence.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a one-line 'answer first' protocol change measurably removes anchoring, then any human or automated oversight pipeline can cheaply harden itself against being talked into the AI's wrong answer -> overseers catch more incorrect/unsafe AI outputs they would otherwise rubber-stamp -> reduced risk that a persuasive but wrong (or deceptive) model gets its outputs approved in high-stakes oversight loops. A null result instead tells the field anchoring is deeper than answer-order, redirecting debiasing effort.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a clean three-condition experiment with a single sharp metric (error on AI-wrong items) and an explicit causal isolation of the answer-order mechanism. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it validates a cheap, broadly deployable oversight fix using only public data and open models, with no lab infra, ideal for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a debiasing-mechanism decomposition: use the three conditions to attribute Recchia's confirmation-bias effect specifically to answer-anchoring versus evidence-framing, isolating which lever the fix actually pulls.
cited_sources: Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486) — documents evaluators growing confident in wrong AI answers; anchoring on the stated answer is the leading explanation this project tests an intervention against.

title: Signal Detection Theory (d-prime) for Judge Discrimination vs Bias

sections.research_question: Judge accuracy conflates two distinct things: the ability to discriminate good from flawed arguments (sensitivity) and a response bias toward accepting or rejecting. Can signal detection theory (d-prime and criterion c) cleanly separate these for an LLM judge, and does it reveal exploitable threshold bias that raw accuracy hides?
sections.approach_outline: Borrow signal detection theory (SDT) from psychophysics. Assemble a labeled set of arguments, each marked correct (signal) or flawed (noise), e.g. from a public QA/reasoning set with one good and one bad answer per item. Have a small open judge model emit accept/reject decisions over this set. Treating 'accept a correct argument' as a hit and 'accept a flawed argument' as a false alarm, compute d-prime (sensitivity) and criterion c (bias) for the judge. Then vary the judge prompt (e.g. strict vs lenient instructions) and recompute, showing how prompt changes move sensitivity versus bias independently. Finally, construct two prompt variants with equal accuracy but different criterion and show they differ in exploitability. This is pure CPU/analytical work on cached judge outputs.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Compute baseline d-prime and c: run the judge over the labeled set, tabulate hits/false alarms, compute d' and c. Measure: the pair (d', c). Expected: a non-zero criterion revealing the judge is not a neutral discriminator.
- Prompt-shift decomposition: re-run under strict and lenient prompts; recompute d' and c each time. Expected: prompts move c substantially while d' stays roughly fixed, showing bias and sensitivity are separable knobs.
- Equal-accuracy / unequal-exploitability demonstration: find two prompt settings with matched overall accuracy but different c; show that the higher-criterion (or lower) one accepts more flawed arguments under an adversarial skew. Expected: equal accuracy hides unequal exploitability, the headline result.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If oversight error can be decomposed into sensitivity vs decision-threshold bias, then we get a precise, training-free diagnostic for whether an overseer is exploitable by pushing it past its acceptance threshold rather than by genuinely fooling its discrimination -> oversight designers can monitor and tune criterion directly, catching judges that look accurate on balanced sets but collapse under adversarial skew -> reduces the risk that a deployed automated overseer is silently gamed via its response bias when the input distribution shifts adversarially.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single self-contained analysis computing d' and c from accept/reject decisions on a labeled set, with explicit success criteria and only CPU-level cost on cached outputs. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it imports a classic, rigorous measurement tool to LLM-judge oversight using only open models and public data, something labs rarely report.
alternative_framings: Frame as an ROC-curve characterization of LLM judges: sweep an explicit acceptance threshold to trace the full ROC, with d' as the summary, making the sensitivity/bias split a continuous picture rather than a point estimate.
cited_sources: Signal detection theory (d', criterion) from cognitive science/psychophysics — the cross-domain method being transferred to characterize LLM judges.
Recchia et al. (arXiv:2507.19486) and automation/confirmation-bias work (arXiv:2010.07938) — document evaluator biases that SDT would separate into sensitivity vs criterion.
Anthropic open problem: characterize biases overseers consistently exhibit — motivates the precise, training-free characterization this provides.

title: Where Debate Breaks: Mapping the Information-Asymmetry Threshold

sections.research_question: Debate-as-oversight assumes a weak judge can extract truth from stronger debaters via information asymmetry (the judge sees only short verified quotes). How much asymmetry can the protocol tolerate before judge accuracy collapses, i.e. where is the breakpoint as the quote budget shrinks?
sections.approach_outline: Use the QuALITY reading-comprehension debate setup with a small open judge model (1-3B instruct) and a stronger debater accessed via API. For each item, run honest-vs-dishonest debates and systematically vary the quote budget the judge may see (0, 1, 2, 4, 8 verified quotes), holding everything else fixed. The 0-quote condition is maximal asymmetry (judge gets only the passage title/question framing); larger budgets reduce asymmetry. Measure judge accuracy at each budget and plot the accuracy-vs-asymmetry curve to locate the breakpoint where accuracy falls to chance. No training is required, only prompt orchestration and answer scoring; the full sweep runs in a few hours on one consumer GPU plus modest API calls.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Anchor the endpoints: measure judge accuracy at the largest budget (8 quotes, low asymmetry) and at 0 quotes (max asymmetry). Expected: high accuracy with generous quotes, near-chance with none, confirming the curve has a usable range.
- Sweep the budget: run 1, 2, 4 quotes and plot accuracy vs quote budget. Expected: a monotone curve with an identifiable knee/breakpoint where accuracy drops sharply.
- Honest-vs-dishonest split: at each budget, separate accuracy on items the dishonest debater could exploit; measure how the breakpoint shifts. Expected: dishonest-exploitable items collapse at a larger budget, sharpening the operating-regime boundary.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we can locate the asymmetry budget at which debate stops protecting a weak judge, then labs betting on debate for superhuman oversight get a concrete operating-regime boundary -> they can check whether their intended deployment (where the judge is far weaker than the task) sits on the safe side of the threshold -> reduces the risk of deploying a debate-based overseer in a regime where a dishonest debater can reliably push false claims past the judge. A model-agnostic threshold is directly transferable to that decision.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single experiment that varies one knob (quote budget) and plots one curve, with an explicit success criterion (locate the breakpoint), inheriting a published methodology. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses open models and a public dataset with no lab infra, and the threshold itself is a transferable finding labs have not systematically measured.
alternative_framings: Frame as a capacity-vs-asymmetry tradeoff: hold the quote budget fixed and instead vary judge size, mapping the joint surface of (judge capability x asymmetry) over which debate remains reliable.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) — debate raises non-expert judge accuracy to 76% (LLM)/88% (human) on QuALITY with short verified quotes; the setup this project reuses and sweeps.
Kenton et al. 2024 (NeurIPS, arXiv:2407.04622) — weak LLMs judging strong LLMs, debate beats consultancy; neither paper systematically sweeps the asymmetry budget itself, which this project does.

title: Obfuscated Arguments in Miniature: Can a Weak Judge Detect 'I Don't Know Which Step Is Wrong'?

sections.research_question: In the obfuscated-arguments failure mode, a dishonest debater builds a long multi-step argument where no one can localize the false step, so the judge cannot be shown where the lie is. Can a weak judge be cued to recognize that an error exists (and roughly where) even when it cannot pinpoint the flawed step?
sections.approach_outline: Construct ~50 synthetic multi-step arithmetic/logic 'proofs', each 5-15 steps long; in half, inject a single hidden error at a random depth, the rest are fully valid. Present each proof to a small open judge model in a debate-style framing. Compare two judge prompts: a baseline 'is this proof correct?' prompt vs an 'obfuscation-aware' prompt that asks the judge to estimate its confidence that an error exists somewhere and to guess the depth/region. Score (a) whether the judge's error-presence calibration beats chance and (b) whether its localization is better than random, even on proofs where it cannot name the exact bad step. All synthetic, cheap, single-GPU, a few hours total.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate the proof set: generate 50 proofs with programmatically known error/no-error labels and error depths. Measure: dataset balance and that valid proofs are genuinely valid. Expected: a clean labeled benchmark.
- Baseline vs obfuscation-aware error detection: run both prompts; measure AUROC / accuracy of the judge's error-exists judgment against the true labels. Expected: baseline near chance on long proofs; obfuscation-aware prompt may lift error-presence detection above chance.
- Localization probe: on error-containing proofs, compare the judge's guessed error region to the true depth. Measure: localization accuracy vs random. Expected outcome is decision-relevant either way: judges can flag obfuscation (suggesting a cheap protocol patch) or cannot (quantifying a fundamental limit).
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a weak judge can at least detect that an obfuscated argument hides an error, then debate protocols can add a cheap 'flag suspected obfuscation -> default to skepticism' step -> dishonest debaters lose the ability to win by burying an unlocalizable false step -> closes a theoretically-flagged route by which a deceptive superhuman system could push false conclusions past oversight. A negative result quantifies a hard limit, telling protocol designers obfuscation must be handled structurally (e.g. prover-estimator debate) rather than by judge cueing.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a fully self-contained synthetic study with programmatic ground truth, two prompts, and a clear above-chance success criterion. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it empirically probes a known theoretical failure mode entirely outside any lab, using only cheap synthetic tasks and a small open model.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calibration study of 'epistemic helplessness': measure whether the judge's stated uncertainty rises appropriately as proof length grows, treating obfuscation-detection as a calibration-under-opacity problem.
cited_sources: Barnes & Christiano / LessWrong 'Debate update: Obfuscated arguments problem' — identifies dishonest debaters exploiting non-localizable errors; the failure mode this project measures in miniature (used as supplementary motivation, not sole basis).
Prover-Estimator Debate (arXiv:2506.13609) — a recent protocol proposed specifically to avoid obfuscation, motivating empirical measurement of whether judges can detect it at all.

title: Self-Preference Bias as an Oversight Backdoor: Does a Judge Favor Its Own Family?

sections.research_question: LLM judges are documented to prefer outputs resembling their own generations (lower self-perplexity). Is this self-preference strong enough to flip correctness judgments, i.e. make a judge pick a wrong-but-familiar answer over a correct-but-foreign one, not just change style preferences?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of QA/reasoning items, each with a known correct and incorrect answer. For each item, render the answers in two model-family styles: generate (or paraphrase) the incorrect answer in the judge's own family style and the correct answer in a foreign-family style, and also the reverse pairing as a control. Have 2-3 small open judge models pick the better answer. Compute the correctness-flip rate: how often the judge selects the incorrect answer specifically when it is rendered in the judge's own familiar style, above the rate when familiarity is neutral or reversed. Pure inference + scoring on a single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish a no-style-confound baseline: judge picks correct vs incorrect answers in a neutral shared style. Measure: base accuracy. Expected: high accuracy when style gives no signal.
- Familiarity-misaligned condition: incorrect answer in judge's own family style, correct answer in foreign style; measure how often the judge picks the incorrect-familiar answer. Expected: a measurable rise in wrong picks vs baseline, the correctness-flip rate.
- Reversal control: swap styles (correct=familiar, incorrect=foreign) and re-measure; the accuracy gain should mirror the loss in experiment 2, isolating familiarity (not content) as the cause. Expected: a symmetric effect confirming self-preference drives flips.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If self-preference can flip correctness judgments, then automated oversight using an LLM-as-judge has a built-in backdoor: a model from the judge's own family gets its (possibly wrong or unsafe) outputs inflated -> oversight systematically rewards the wrong answer whenever overseer and overseen share a lineage -> in medium-horizon automated-oversight pipelines, where the same family often both generates and judges, this corrupts the core correctness signal safety depends on. Quantifying the flip rate tells designers whether cross-family judging is a necessary safeguard.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-defined measurement of one quantity (familiarity-attributable correctness-flip rate) with a clean reversal control, runnable as pure single-GPU inference. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses only open models and public data, needs no proprietary infra, and measures a previously-under-quantified link (familiarity -> correctness flips) directly relevant to automated oversight.
alternative_framings: Frame as an attack on self-judging RLAIF: estimate how much a model could inflate its own reward by exploiting same-family self-preference when it both produces and grades outputs.
cited_sources: Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (arXiv:2410.21819) — shows judges score lower-perplexity (self-familiar) outputs higher; the documented bias this project tests for correctness-flipping strength.
'Justice or Prejudice?' (arXiv:2410.02736) — catalogs LLM-judge biases, situating self-preference among oversight-relevant failure modes.

title: Does Persuasion Track Truth? Decoupling Convincingness from Correctness in Debate

sections.research_question: Debate works only if the more truthful debater is also the more persuasive one to the judge. Khan et al. found more persuasive LLMs lead to more truthful answers on average; under what conditions does persuasiveness decouple from correctness, and how often is the more-persuasive side actually wrong?
sections.approach_outline: On QuALITY-style reading-comprehension items, have a debater model argue both the honest and dishonest position for each item. Have a small open judge model do two things per item: rate each side's persuasiveness on a fixed scale and pick a winner. Compute (a) the correlation between rated persuasiveness and actual correctness, and (b) judge accuracy conditional on the dishonest side being rated more persuasive. Then analyze item features (e.g. passage length, answer subtlety, presence of misleading-but-quotable evidence) where persuasion and truth decouple. Pure inference on open models; runs in a few hours on one consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Persuasion-correctness correlation: over all items, correlate the judge's persuasiveness rating of each side with whether that side is correct. Measure: correlation coefficient. Expected: positive on average (per Khan et al.) but well below 1.
- Decoupling-regime accuracy: isolate items where the dishonest side is rated more persuasive; measure judge winner-accuracy on just those. Expected: sharply lower accuracy, quantifying the danger zone.
- Feature analysis of decoupling: group items by candidate features and measure where persuasiveness most diverges from truth. Expected: identify a characterizable subset (e.g. items with misleading quotable evidence) where debate is unsafe.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If persuasiveness reliably tracks truth, debate's core assumption holds; but characterizing the decoupling regime tells us exactly when it fails -> labs deploying debate for oversight can detect or avoid the item types where a dishonest debater is more persuasive than the truthful one -> reduces the risk that a deceptive, highly-persuasive model wins oversight verdicts on precisely the hard cases that matter, a transferable safety result for the debate research program.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a focused correlational study with a clear deliverable (persuasiveness-vs-correctness relationship plus the decoupling subset) runnable as pure open-model inference. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it probes a failure regime of a leading oversight protocol using only public data and small models, with no lab infra, exactly the kind of risk characterization labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame as a persuasion-tax measurement: estimate how much extra persuasiveness a dishonest debater needs to overcome being wrong, giving a single scalar 'safety margin' for the judge.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) — title claim that more persuasive LLMs lead to more truthful answers; this project probes the failure cases where persuasion and truth diverge.

title: Confidence Inflation in Debate: Does Arguing a Side Make a Model More Sure It's Right?

sections.research_question: Does assigning a model to argue a fixed side in a debate distort its own stated confidence, and is this distortion worse when the model is assigned the incorrect side? The core question is whether role-assignment itself, independent of evidence, inflates a debater's calibration in ways that would mislead a confidence-aware aggregator.
sections.approach_outline: Pick one open instruction-tuned model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) runnable on a single Colab Pro / Runpod GPU, inference-only. Use a public factual QA set with verifiable ground truth (e.g. a 200-item subset of TruthfulQA or BoolQ). Stage 1: elicit a cold calibrated answer + numeric confidence (0-100%) for each question with no role framing. Stage 2: randomly assign the model to argue the correct or incorrect side, have it produce a short committed argument, then re-elicit its confidence in the side it was assigned. Compute the confidence shift attributable purely to role assignment, split by whether the assigned side was correct vs incorrect. Everything is prompting; no training, no proprietary data, no lab infra.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Cold-confidence baseline: for 200 factual questions, elicit the model's answer and a 0-100 confidence with no role framing. Measure baseline calibration (reliability curve / ECE). Expected outcome: imperfect but reasonable calibration with a usable spread of confidences to detect later shifts.
- Role-conditioned re-elicitation: randomly assign each item to the correct or incorrect side, have the model write a 3-5 sentence argument for that side, then re-ask its confidence in that side. Measure mean confidence shift (post minus cold) separately for correct-side and incorrect-side assignments. Expected outcome: a positive shift overall, and a meaningfully larger inflation on incorrectly-assigned sides (the dangerous case).
- Robustness and persistence check: vary the strength of the advocacy instruction (neutral 'consider this side' vs strong 'argue this side is correct') and re-run on 50 items; also re-elicit cold confidence a second time without a role to control for mere re-asking. Measure how confidence inflation scales with advocacy strength and confirm the effect is not a generic re-query artifact. Expected outcome: inflation grows with advocacy strength and is absent in the no-role re-query, isolating role assignment as the cause.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If forced advocacy systematically inflates a debater's confidence on wrong sides, then debate protocols that aggregate debaters using their stated confidence (a natural and proposed design) will over-weight confidently-wrong debaters. This means scalable-oversight systems built on debate could confidently certify false answers on exactly the hard questions humans cannot check directly, undermining oversight as models surpass human verification ability and enabling a deceptive or mistaken model to be rubber-stamped on high-stakes decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and low compute: it isolates a single causal link (role assignment to confidence) with a clean correct-vs-incorrect contrast and a single quantitative deliverable. Its counterfactual value is high because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal infrastructure, just inference on an open model, making it a result an independent beginner team can fully own while probing a real oversight protocol that major labs assume is sound.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a calibration-stability audit: 'how robust is a model's stated confidence to irrelevant role context?', positioning the result as a general reliability property of confidence elicitation rather than a debate-specific finding.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) Debate protocols assigning debaters fixed sides — establishes the role-assignment setup this study probes.
Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) Scalable oversight via debate experiments — provides the protocol design and weak-judge framing the confidence-aggregation concern targets.

title: The Tie-Breaker Problem: How Judges Resolve Genuinely Balanced Debates

sections.research_question: When a debate is genuinely near-balanced (both sides argued comparably well), what non-substantive surface cue does an LLM judge fall back on, and how arbitrary is the resulting verdict? The question targets the worst-case oversight regime: the hardest questions where no clear winner emerges.
sections.approach_outline: Use one small open judge model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. Take ~50 factual questions and, using a slightly larger open model as a debater, generate two opposing arguments per question. Engineer near-balanced debate transcripts and then systematically vary non-substantive factors: which side speaks last (recency), relative argument length (verbosity), and tone/confidence. For each manipulation, feed the transcript to the judge and record its verdict. By holding argument substance fixed and flipping only surface cues, measure how often the verdict flips, yielding an 'arbitrariness rate' and a ranking of which cue dominates. All prompting; no training, no proprietary data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the balanced set: for 50 questions generate two opposing arguments and filter to ~30 where the judge's confidence is near 50/50, confirming genuine near-ties. Measure: distribution of judge confidence. Expected outcome: a usable set of near-balanced debates.
- Recency and length swaps: for each balanced debate, present both orderings (side A last vs side B last) and both length configurations (pad one side longer), holding content fixed. Measure: verdict-flip rate as a function of which side gets the last word or more text. Expected outcome: a substantial flip rate (e.g. >20%) driven by last-speaker and longer-rebuttal cues, showing surface dominance in the tie regime.
- Tone manipulation and cue ranking: rewrite one side in a more confident/assertive register without changing claims; measure verdict shift, then rank recency vs length vs tone by effect size. Compare the arbitrariness rate in the balanced regime against a control set of clearly-decided debates. Expected outcome: surface cues dominate far more in the balanced regime than in clear-cut debates, identifying the single most influential cue.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If judges resolve near-tie debates by arbitrary surface cues, then debate-based oversight produces verdicts that are essentially random precisely on the hardest, most contested questions, which are the cases where reliable oversight matters most. This gives operators false assurance that a debate 'resolved' a hard alignment-relevant question, letting an incorrect or manipulated answer pass on superhuman-difficulty decisions, a direct path to mis-certifying dangerous model outputs as safe.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single measurable quantity (arbitrariness rate and dominant cue) in a clearly defined regime, and runs entirely on a small judge with cheap inference, scoring full marks on narrow scope and low compute. Its counterfactual value is strong: it is a fully external, controlled study needing no training or lab data, and it deliberately targets the worst-case oversight regime that benchmark-average results obscure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'judge robustness stress test' producing a reusable diagnostic harness that any debate-protocol designer can run to check whether their judge degrades to coin-flips on hard items.
cited_sources: arXiv:2410.02736 Position/recency bias in LLM judges — documents the surface bias whose dominance in the near-tie regime this study isolates.
arXiv:2410.21819 Verbosity/length bias in LLM judges — establishes the length-preference cue manipulated in the balanced-debate experiments.

title: Does Debate Help When Both Debaters Are Wrong? The Shared-Blindspot Failure

sections.research_question: How does debate behave when the correct answer lies outside both debaters' competence (a shared blind spot), and does the judge at least signal low confidence rather than confidently endorsing a falsehood? This probes whether debate degrades gracefully in exactly the superhuman regime scalable oversight is meant to handle.
sections.approach_outline: Use a single open model family (e.g. Qwen2.5 in two sizes, or two instances of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on one consumer GPU, inference-only. First probe the debater model to find items where it is reliably wrong, curating a set of shared-blindspot questions from a verifiable QA source plus a contrasting set where the model is competent. Run debate between two instances of the model on both sets, with a judge issuing a verdict and a confidence. Measure how often the judge is steered to a wrong consensus on blindspot items and whether its confidence is dangerously high. All prompting; no training, public data only.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Blind-spot mining: query the debater model on ~300 verifiable questions multiple times; keep ~40 where it is consistently wrong (shared blind spot) and ~40 where it is consistently correct (control). Measure: per-item accuracy. Expected outcome: a clean blindspot set and a competent control set.
- Debate on blindspot vs control: run two-instance debate + judge on both sets; measure wrong-consensus rate (judge endorses a false answer) on blindspot items vs control. Expected outcome: a high wrong-consensus rate on blindspot items, confirming debate cannot exceed the union of debater competence.
- Confidence-signal check: record the judge's stated confidence on wrong-consensus blindspot verdicts vs correct control verdicts. Measure: mean confidence and whether blindspot errors are accompanied by lowered confidence. Expected outcome: judges remain confidently wrong on blindspot items, showing debate gives no built-in warning in the superhuman regime.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If debate confidently lands on falsehoods whenever the truth is outside both debaters' competence, then scalable oversight built on debate has a hard ceiling at the union of debater knowledge and, worse, gives no low-confidence warning when it fails. As frontier models tackle questions past human checkability, operators relying on debate verdicts would be confidently misled on superhuman-difficulty safety decisions, the precise failure mode oversight is meant to prevent.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is sharply scoped to one measurable contrast (wrong-consensus rate and judge confidence on blindspot vs competent items) and runs cheaply on one open model family, earning top marks on narrow scope and low compute. Its counterfactual value is high because it characterizes a fundamental, medium-horizon limit of debate using only public data and inference, work labs have little incentive to surface but that independent researchers can fully execute.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'graceful-degradation audit': does debate know when it doesn't know? — emphasizing the confidence-signal question as the headline safety property.
cited_sources: Khan et al. 2024 (arXiv:2402.06782) Debate results assuming informed debaters — establishes the competence assumption this study deliberately violates to map debate's competence ceiling.

title: Length-of-Argument Arms Race: Does More Debate Text Help or Drown the Judge?

sections.research_question: Is the relationship between total debate transcript length and weak-judge accuracy non-monotonic — does accuracy peak then decline as more rounds overload the judge's context — and can a cheap summarization step before judging recover lost performance? This tests the unexamined assumption that more debate is always safer.
sections.approach_outline: Use one small open judge model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. Fix a ~40-item verifiable QA set and use an open debater model to generate debates of increasing transcript length (more rounds and/or longer turns). Hold the items fixed and sweep length, measuring judge accuracy at each length to trace the length-vs-accuracy curve. Then add a cheap one-shot summarization step that condenses the transcript before the judge reads it, and re-measure. All prompting; no training, model-agnostic, no lab infra.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Length sweep: for 40 items generate debates at ~4 transcript lengths (1, 2, 4, 8 rounds), holding the judge fixed; measure judge accuracy at each length. Expected outcome: accuracy rises then falls (an inverted-U), revealing an information-overload regime where extra rounds hurt.
- Locate the peak and collapse point: refine the sweep around the apparent peak to estimate the length at which accuracy is maximized and where it degrades to near-baseline. Measure: accuracy vs token count. Expected outcome: a concrete peak length and a degradation threshold, giving protocol designers a usable caution.
- Summarization mitigation: insert a cheap summarize-then-judge step at the longest lengths and compare accuracy to the raw long-transcript condition. Measure: accuracy recovery from summarization. Expected outcome: summarization recovers much of the lost accuracy, identifying a simple, deployable mitigation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If weak-judge accuracy is non-monotonic in debate length, then scaling up debate (more rounds) to handle harder questions can quietly lower oversight accuracy by overloading the judge's context, the opposite of the intended effect. Protocol designers who assume 'more debate is safer' would deploy oversight that fails worse on harder, longer-deliberation cases, mis-certifying model outputs precisely where extended scrutiny was supposed to add safety; a cheap summarization fix directly mitigates this.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single curve (accuracy vs transcript length) plus one mitigation test, and runs entirely on a small judge with light inference, scoring full marks on narrow scope and low compute. Its counterfactual value is high: it is model-agnostic, needs no lab infrastructure or proprietary data, and challenges a load-bearing design assumption that labs rarely stress-test, making it a clean, fully external result for an independent team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'context-budget efficiency' study for oversight: what is the optimal amount of deliberation per dollar of judge context? — emphasizing the practical tuning deliverable.
cited_sources: Kenton et al. 2024 (arXiv:2407.04622) Multi-round debate protocols sweeping ~5M generations — motivates studying how transcript length interacts with weak-judge accuracy.
'Lost in the middle' long-context degradation literature — establishes the documented context-degradation effect this study traces in the debate setting.

title: Critique Helpfulness vs. Judge Gullibility: Disentangling Why Critiques Help

sections.research_question: When critiques improve a weak judge's accuracy, is the gain driven by genuinely informative content or by the judge deferring to any confident critique? Disentangling 'informed deference' from 'persuasion-driven deference' determines whether critique-based oversight is robust to a strategic model that produces confident but misleading critiques.
sections.approach_outline: Use one small open judge model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. Run the answer-critique-judge protocol on a verifiable QA set, but inject three controlled critique conditions: (a) correct critiques, (b) plausible-but-wrong critiques, (c) content-free but confident critiques. Measure how often the judge flips its initial verdict in each condition. A judge that flips similarly for wrong/empty critiques as for correct ones is being persuaded, not informed. All prompting; no training, public data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline verdicts and injection setup: on ~150 verifiable questions, get the judge's initial answer, then construct the three critique types per item (correct, plausible-wrong, content-free-confident). Measure: baseline judge accuracy. Expected outcome: a stable baseline and three clean critique conditions.
- Flip-rate by condition: present each critique type and measure verdict-flip rate and resulting accuracy. Expected outcome: correct critiques raise accuracy; if wrong and content-free critiques also produce high flip rates, this reveals persuasion-driven (not informed) deference.
- Gullibility index and confidence sensitivity: compute a 'gullibility index' = flip rate on wrong/empty critiques relative to flip rate on correct ones, and vary the critique's stated confidence to see if flips track confidence rather than content. Measure: gullibility index and flip-vs-confidence slope. Expected outcome: a quantified split between informed and persuasion-driven deference, with flips partly tracking mere confidence.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If critique-based oversight gains come largely from the judge deferring to confident critiques rather than their content, then a strategically deceptive model can defeat critique oversight simply by emitting confident, plausible-sounding but false critiques. This means an oversight method currently reported as effective would silently fail against the adversarial models it most needs to catch, letting a misaligned system steer human/automated overseers to wrong conclusions on high-stakes decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to three controlled critique conditions with one clear metric (flip rate / gullibility index), and runs prompting-only on a small open model, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: it is a public-model mechanism study that labs reporting headline 'critiques help' results have little incentive to run, yet it directly tests the adversarial robustness that determines whether the method is trustworthy.
alternative_framings: Frame as a robustness audit of critique oversight against an adversarial critic, headlining the worst-case 'content-free confident critique' attack as a concrete threat model.
cited_sources: Debate Helps Weak Judges Reward Stronger Models (arXiv:2605.27483, ~May 2026) — the result this study disentangles: critiques help only 'when the critic provides a usable advantage'.
Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion (arXiv:2604.21564) — reports sycophancy up to 94% under argumentative probing, motivating the persuasion-driven-deference hypothesis.

title: Persuasion-Triggered Sycophancy as an Oversight Failure Probe

sections.research_question: Does the argumentative framing used in debate-based oversight — shown to be the strongest sycophancy trigger — actually corrupt a judge's verdict accuracy on factual tasks? The question ties a known sycophancy finding directly to oversight verdict accuracy when a persuader argues for a wrong answer.
sections.approach_outline: Use one small open judge model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. Take a factual QA set with known answers. Get the judge's correct initial verdict, then have a 'persuader' (a second prompt/instance) argue for the wrong answer under two framings: a direct opinion-ask vs an argumentative-debate framing. Measure how often the judge abandons its correct verdict in each framing, replicating the reported direct-vs-argumentative gap and quantifying the accuracy loss specifically in the judge/oversight role. All prompting; public data; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Initial correct-verdict set: on ~200 factual questions, keep ~120 where the judge is initially correct, so any later flip is a measurable accuracy loss. Measure: baseline accuracy. Expected outcome: a clean set of correct initial verdicts to attack.
- Persuasion vs direct-ask flip rates: have the persuader push the wrong answer under (a) a direct opinion-ask and (b) an argumentative-debate framing; measure verdict-flip rate and post-persuasion accuracy in each. Expected outcome: a large gap, with argumentative framing flipping far more correct verdicts to wrong, reproducing the persuasion-sycophancy effect in an oversight role.
- Dose and robustness: vary persuader strength (mild vs forceful) and test a simple defensive prompt ('only change your answer if the argument gives new verifiable evidence'); measure how flip rate scales with pressure and whether the defense helps. Expected outcome: flips rise with pressure and the simple defense only partially mitigates, showing debate framing is intrinsically risky for oversight.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If the very argumentative mechanism used for scalable oversight is the strongest sycophancy trigger and measurably lowers judge accuracy, then debate-based oversight is partly self-undermining: a capable model can exploit argumentation to flip a correct overseer verdict to a wrong one. As such models are deployed in high-stakes settings, persuasion-driven verdict corruption would let a misaligned system talk its overseer into endorsing unsafe outputs, directly defeating the oversight intended to catch it.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single quantity (verdict-flip rate under persuasion vs direct framing) on verifiable tasks and runs prompting-only on small open models, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: it is a model-organism-style finding on public models linking an existing sycophancy result to oversight accuracy, a connection labs have not made and that an independent team can fully execute without lab data or infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'self-undermining oversight' demonstration: quantifying how much accuracy debate framing costs relative to plain question-answering, positioning the gap as the headline result.
cited_sources: Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion (arXiv:2604.21564, Apr 2026) — argumentative framing is a far stronger sycophancy trigger (up to 94%), the effect this study ties to oversight accuracy.
Diagnosing and Mitigating Sycophancy and Skepticism in LLM Causal Judgment (arXiv:2601.08258) — reports pressure-induced flipping of judgments, supporting the verdict-corruption hypothesis.

title: Recursive Critique Layers: Measuring Error Accumulation Through Oversight Depth

sections.research_question: As you stack oversight layers (answer, critique, critique-of-critique, ...), do errors compound or self-correct, and what is the empirical per-layer error-propagation factor? This gives a cheap empirical test of the bounded-error assumption that recursive reward modeling relies on.
sections.approach_outline: Use open models (e.g. two sizes of Qwen2.5, or a single Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. On a labeled QA task, build a stacked critique pipeline: answer, then a critique of the answer, then a critique-of-the-critique, and so on, each layer revising the verdict. Measure final verdict accuracy as a function of stack depth (0 to ~4). Estimate whether each added layer tends to correct or amplify the previous layer's errors, yielding an empirical per-layer error-propagation factor. All prompting; no training, public data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Depth-vs-accuracy curve: on ~150 labeled questions, run the stacked critique pipeline to depth 4 and record verdict accuracy at each depth. Measure: accuracy(depth). Expected outcome: a curve showing whether accuracy improves, plateaus, or degrades with depth.
- Per-layer correction vs amplification: at each layer, track items that were correct-then-flipped-wrong vs wrong-then-flipped-correct, to estimate a per-layer propagation factor (>1 means errors amplify). Measure: net correction rate per layer. Expected outcome: a quantified propagation factor revealing whether deeper oversight self-corrects or compounds errors.
- Seeded-error stress test: deliberately inject a wrong verdict at layer 0 and see how many layers are needed to recover (if ever); also vary whether layers can see ground-truth-style hints. Measure: recovery depth and final accuracy. Expected outcome: many seeded errors persist or amplify through layers, demonstrating that per-layer error is not reliably bounded.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Recursive oversight (recursive reward modeling, scalable supervision hierarchies) stays aligned only if per-layer error is bounded; if a cheap measurement shows errors compound rather than self-correct, then proposals to oversee superhuman systems by stacking AI overseers have an unmeasured failure mode. Deploying such hierarchies under a false bounded-error assumption could let systematic errors accumulate into confidently-wrong top-level supervision of a powerful system, a direct path to mis-aligned oversight of high-stakes AI.
