sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single deliverable (a depth-vs-accuracy curve plus a per-layer propagation factor) and runs inference-only on open models, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: it provides a cheap empirical test of a foundational recursive-oversight assumption using only public models and data, exactly the kind of unglamorous measurement labs skip but an independent team can fully own.
alternative_framings: Frame as an empirical 'does oversight converge?' study, presenting the per-layer propagation factor as a contraction/expansion constant analogous to a fixed-point analysis.
cited_sources: Scalable agent alignment via reward modeling (arXiv:1811.07871) — introduces recursive reward modeling whose bounded-error assumption this study tests empirically.
AI Alignment: A Comprehensive Survey (arXiv:2310.19852) — discusses recursive oversight staying aligned only if error accumulation is bounded across the hierarchy.

title: Harmful-Continuation 'Point of No Return' Benchmark

sections.research_question: If an open model is forced to begin a harmful answer, at what continuation length does it lose the ability to self-correct back into a refusal? The goal is to measure each model's mid-generation recovery capacity, an unmeasured robustness property complementary to existing 'safety depth' metrics.
sections.approach_outline: Use open instruction-tuned models (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU with prefill support, inference-only. Take a set of harmful prompts plus model-generated harmful continuations, and prefill the model with the first k harmful tokens (sweeping k). At each k, let the model continue and classify whether it self-corrects (pivots to refusal/safe redirection) or continues harmfully, using a cheap LLM classifier plus spot-checking. Report a self-correction recovery curve (recovery rate vs k) and a per-model 'recovery half-life'. Ship a small reusable harness. No training, public models, single GPU within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Recovery curve for one model: on ~40 harmful prompts, prefill k in {2,8,16,32,64} harmful tokens and measure self-correction rate at each k. Measure: recovery rate vs k. Expected outcome: a monotonically decreasing curve, with recovery collapsing past some k (the point of no return).
- Half-life and classifier validation: fit a half-life (k at which recovery drops to 50%) and validate the automatic harmful/refusal classifier against ~80 hand-labeled continuations. Measure: recovery half-life and classifier agreement. Expected outcome: a well-defined per-model half-life and >90% classifier agreement, making the metric trustworthy.
- Cross-model comparison and harness release: run the same sweep on 2-3 open models and compare recovery half-lives; package the harness with config and documentation. Measure: relative recovery half-lives across models. Expected outcome: meaningful differences in recovery capacity, demonstrating the metric discriminates between models and a self-contained shippable benchmark.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A model that can self-correct mid-harm is more robust to prefill and multi-turn (e.g. Crescendo-style) jailbreaks that exploit generation momentum; quantifying recovery capacity gives developers a defensible target metric. If adopted, models selected/tuned for higher recovery half-life would be harder to push into completing harmful outputs once partially started, reducing the chance that a jailbroken or manipulated deployed model produces dangerous content (e.g. weapons/cyber-attack assistance) that it would otherwise have aborted.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single measurable curve and a per-model half-life, with a concrete shippable harness as the deliverable, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: it defines a new robustness metric measurable entirely on public models with inference only, complementing existing depth metrics that labs report but that ignore mid-generation recovery, and it is fully executable by an independent team in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame as a defensive metric for multi-turn jailbreak resistance, positioning recovery half-life as a predictor of Crescendo/prefill attack success rather than a standalone property.
cited_sources: Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) Safety Alignment Should Be More Than a Few Tokens Deep — observes that once the initial safeguard is bypassed the model 'often freely generates harmful content', the low-recovery phenomenon this benchmark quantifies.
Crescendo (arXiv:2404.01833) — multi-turn jailbreak exploiting generation momentum, the attack class this recovery metric is defensively relevant to.

title: Does Collaborative Debate Reduce Sycophancy or Just Hide It?

sections.research_question: Does reframing debate as collaborative (non-zero-sum, ColMAD-style) actually lower a judge's sycophancy, or does it merely relabel false agreement as 'consensus' and raise premature false-consensus risk relative to adversarial debate? The question tests whether collaborative oversight trades adversarial robustness for groupthink.
sections.approach_outline: Use small open models (e.g. two-three instances of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. On a verifiable QA set, run two protocols where one side argues a known-wrong position: (1) competitive adversarial debate and (2) collaborative ColMAD-style debate. Measure how often the judge ends up endorsing the wrong consensus in each protocol. Test whether collaboration increases premature false agreement compared to adversarial debate. All prompting; public data; no training, no lab infra.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Protocol setup and baseline: on ~120 verifiable questions, implement competitive and collaborative debate templates with one debater assigned the known-wrong side; verify both run end-to-end and produce judge verdicts. Measure: per-protocol completion and baseline accuracy. Expected outcome: two working protocols on the same items.
- Wrong-consensus rate comparison: measure how often the judge endorses the wrong answer under each protocol. Measure: wrong-consensus endorsement rate, competitive vs collaborative. Expected outcome: collaborative debate shows a higher wrong-consensus rate on at least some item classes, indicating hidden sycophancy rather than reduced sycophancy.
- Premature-agreement analysis: track at which round consensus forms and whether the wrong side's claims go unchallenged in the collaborative setting; vary how strongly collaboration is emphasized. Measure: round-to-consensus and unchallenged-claim rate. Expected outcome: collaboration causes earlier, less-challenged agreement on wrong answers, confirming a groupthink mechanism.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If collaborative debate quietly raises false-consensus risk, then adopting non-zero-sum oversight to reduce 'debate hacking' could trade away the adversarial scrutiny that catches wrong answers, making oversight more vulnerable to groupthink. Operators who switch to collaborative protocols believing they reduce manipulation would actually get a judge more easily steered to confident wrong consensus, letting a misaligned or mistaken answer pass on high-stakes decisions the adversarial setup would have flagged.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to two protocols and one metric (wrong-consensus endorsement rate) and runs prompting-only on small open models, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: it is a fresh, decision-relevant combination of two very recent public results that labs have not connected, fully executable by an independent team without proprietary data or lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'groupthink vs adversarialism' tradeoff study for multi-agent oversight, headlining when cooperation helps vs when it suppresses dissent.
cited_sources: ColMAD (arXiv:2510.20963, Oct 2025) — reframes debate as non-zero-sum to cut debate hacking, the collaborative protocol this study stress-tests.

Measuring Opinion Bias and Sycophancy via LLM-based Persuasion (arXiv:2604.21564, Apr 2026) — shows argumentative settings maximize sycophancy/false agreement (up to 94%), the risk collaboration may hide.

title: Pressure-Response Curve for CoT Obfuscation Under Increasing Stealth Demands

sections.research_question: How does chain-of-thought monitor evasion vary continuously with the strength of a stealth instruction — i.e. what is the obfuscation pressure-response curve, and at what pressure threshold does CoT monitorability collapse? The question replaces the literature's binary low/high framing with a graded dose-response measurement.
sections.approach_outline: Use a small open reasoning model (e.g. a distilled R1-style or Qwen reasoning model) on a single consumer GPU, inference-only. Construct a graded ladder of stealth-pressure prompts, from 'just do the task' up to 'hide your true intent from any reader at all costs', with several intermediate rungs. Have the model perform a benign task that carries a side-goal at each pressure level, then run a separate monitor model on the CoT to detect the hidden intent. Measure monitor catch-rate at each pressure level, producing a continuous obfuscation pressure-response curve and identifying the threshold where monitorability collapses. All prompting; no training, light compute.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Pressure ladder calibration: design ~6 stealth-pressure levels and run the side-goal task at each on ~30 items; have a monitor model classify whether the hidden intent is detectable. Measure: catch-rate per level. Expected outcome: catch-rate decreases as pressure rises, tracing a usable dose-response curve.
- Collapse-threshold identification: refine sampling around the steepest part of the curve to locate the pressure level where catch-rate drops sharply (monitorability collapse). Measure: threshold pressure level and curve slope. Expected outcome: a fairly sharp threshold rather than gradual decline, giving a concrete brittleness point.
- Monitor-strength sensitivity: repeat the sweep with a weaker and a stronger monitor prompt to see whether a better monitor shifts the collapse threshold. Measure: threshold shift vs monitor strength. Expected outcome: stronger monitors raise the threshold modestly but high-pressure obfuscation still defeats them, showing CoT monitoring is brittle near the top of the ladder.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Knowing how much adversarial stealth pressure CoT monitoring can absorb before failing tells us whether CoT monitoring is a robust or brittle line of defense in AI control. If monitorability collapses sharply past a modest pressure threshold, then control schemes relying on reading a model's reasoning to catch scheming would fail against a model under even moderate incentive to hide intent, letting a deceptively-aligned system pursue hidden goals undetected, a core catastrophic-control failure the monitoring is meant to prevent.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single continuous curve plus a collapse threshold, and runs prompting-only on a small reasoning model, scoring high on narrow scope and accessible complexity. Its counterfactual value is strong: the graded dose-response design is novel relative to the binary framings in the literature, needs no training and only public models, and produces a control-relevant brittleness measurement an independent team can fully execute without lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as measuring the 'monitorability budget' of CoT — how much incentive pressure a transparency-based safety case can tolerate before it breaks.
cited_sources: Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? (arXiv:2510.19851) — finds CoT monitoring effective without pressure but defeated under high pressure (~10% catch), the binary result this study makes continuous.
Output Supervision Can Obfuscate the CoT (arXiv:2511.11584) — shows supervision can push obfuscation into the CoT, supporting the pressure-driven monitorability-collapse hypothesis.

title: Cross-Family Untrusted Monitoring: Does Mixing Model Families Reduce Collusion Risk?

sections.research_question: When an untrusted policy model and an untrusted monitor must covertly coordinate (collude) without communication, does drawing them from DIFFERENT model families reduce their ability to reach the same hidden Schelling point compared to same-family pairs at matched capability?
sections.approach_outline: Use a no-communication acausal-coordination game: the policy must choose a secret 'collusion signal' (e.g. when to insert a backdoor, or a code stylistic tell) and the monitor must independently guess that same convention to let it pass, so coordination succeeds only when both pick the same Schelling point. Select 3-4 small open instruct models spanning at least two families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B), all runnable one-at-a-time on a single consumer GPU via inference only. For every ordered generator/monitor pair (same-family and cross-family), run a fixed battery of coordination prompts and compute a coordination-success rate; control for raw capability by also measuring each model's solo Schelling performance and reporting capability-matched comparisons. No training, no proprietary data, no lab infra is required. Total budget is well under a few GPU-hours since each game is a short prompt-completion pair.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Solo Schelling baseline: prompt each model alone with classic Schelling questions (pick a number 1-100, pick a meeting place/time, pick a 'secret flag' string) and measure self-consistency and pairwise agreement within vs across families. Measure: agreement rate per pair. Expected: same-family pairs agree noticeably more often than cross-family pairs.
- Collusion coordination game: a generator model is told to plant a backdoor and signal 'safe to approve' via an agreed-upon hidden convention; an independent monitor model must guess the convention and approve. Run all 2x2... NxN family pairings on ~50 fixed scenarios. Measure: collusion-success rate (both pick the same convention AND it evades). Expected: cross-family pairs have a measurably lower collusion-success rate.
- Capability control + self-recognition probe: re-run the game restricting to model pairs of similar solo Schelling skill, and separately test whether models can identify whether a transcript came from their own family (self-recognition). Measure: capability-matched collusion gap, and correlation between self-recognition accuracy and collusion success. Expected: the cross-family advantage persists after capability matching and tracks lower self-recognition.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If cross-family pairing measurably lowers collusion success, then untrusted-monitoring deployments can adopt a free, training-free mitigation (just pick a monitor from a different family) -> this raises the bar for a scheming policy model to safely defeat its monitor -> control protocols catch more sabotage/backdoor attempts before deployment, reducing the loss-of-control pathway in which a misaligned model evades oversight by colluding with its overseer.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow_scope and low_compute and 4 on counterfactual_value: it is a tightly defined same-vs-cross-family comparison with a single clear metric, runnable inference-only on open models, and tests a deployable mitigation that requires no training or lab-internal access, so it is exactly the kind of result an independent team can produce that frontier labs have not published.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a measurement study of 'self-recognition as a collusion enabler' rather than family-mixing as a fix, reporting how much self-recognition cues drive coordination.
cited_sources: Redwood Research collusion post / 'When can we trust untrusted monitoring?' (arXiv 2602.20628) - establishes collusion strategies and Schelling-point coordination as the central untrusted-monitoring risk this project targets.

Motwani et al. 2025 Schelling coordination on frontier models (~40-56%) - provides the measurement methodology and baseline coordination rates this project adapts to small open models and cross-family pairs.

title: Cross-Lingual CoT Monitoring Blind Spots

sections.research_question: Does a chain-of-thought (CoT) monitor's ability to detect explicit harmful planning collapse when the reasoning is expressed in a lower-resource language instead of English, and does instructing the monitor to translate-first recover the lost detection performance?
sections.approach_outline: Start from a fixed set of misbehavior transcripts whose CoT contains explicit harmful planning (e.g. 'let's insert a backdoor here'); reuse public AI-control transcript datasets so no generation is needed. Translate only the CoT (keeping the final action constant) into 4-6 languages spanning high- to low-resource (e.g. Spanish, Chinese, Swahili, Welsh) using a translation API, and back-translate to verify meaning is preserved. Run a single English-centric trusted monitor (a small open instruct model) over each language version and compute detection AUROC per language against benign controls. Then add a 'translate-first' condition where the monitor is prompted to translate the CoT to English before judging, and measure recovery. Everything is inference-only on one consumer GPU, no training, fits in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline English AUROC: score the monitor on the original English harmful-CoT transcripts plus matched benign transcripts. Measure: detection AUROC and catch-rate at a fixed false-positive budget. Expected: high AUROC (the monitor reliably flags 'let's hack' planning in English).
- Language sweep: translate each CoT into the target languages (back-translation-validated), re-score with the same monitor. Measure: AUROC as a function of language resource level. Expected: monotone AUROC degradation as resource level drops, with a sharp blind spot for the lowest-resource language.
- Translate-first recovery: re-run the lowest-AUROC languages but instruct the monitor to translate to English first, then judge. Measure: AUROC recovery vs the direct condition. Expected: translate-first recovers most of the lost detection, quantifying the value of a translation stage in the monitoring pipeline.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a monitor goes blind to non-English harmful CoT, then a scheming model can trivially obfuscate its planning by reasoning in a low-resource language -> deployers who run English-only monitors are silently unprotected -> measuring the blind spot and the translate-first fix tells deployers they must add a translation stage, closing a cheap evasion channel and reducing the chance an untrusted model executes harmful actions undetected (loss-of-control via unmonitored reasoning).
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity and low_compute and 4 on counterfactual_value, this is a single-metric (AUROC-drop-by-language) study on public transcripts requiring only inference, and it quantifies an obvious but unmeasured obfuscation route that labs have not published, making it a high-leverage independent contribution.
alternative_framings: Frame as an obfuscation-attack study: show that an adversary can deliberately induce non-English CoT as a jailbreak of the monitoring pipeline, rather than as an accidental blind spot.
cited_sources: CoT Red-Handed (arXiv 2505.23575) - establishes that CoT monitoring depends on the reasoning remaining legible to the monitor, which is exactly what cross-lingual obfuscation breaks.
CoT Monitorability (arXiv 2507.11473) - motivates monitorability as a control property and frames the legibility assumption this project stress-tests.
Training on Documents About Monitoring (arXiv 2605.15257) - catalogs CoT obfuscation via encodings the monitor cannot decode, of which low-resource-language reasoning is a concrete, cheap instance.

title: Does the Monitor's Knowledge of the Task Hurt or Help Detection?

sections.research_question: Does giving a trusted monitor the original task specification improve its ability to catch malicious code, or does task-awareness create a 'plausibility halo' that makes on-topic-but-malicious actions look benign and lowers detection?
sections.approach_outline: Use a public set of APPS backdoor transcripts (backdoored solutions plus clean controls) so no generation or training is needed. Run a single small open instruct model as the trusted monitor under two information conditions on the identical transcripts: task-blind (sees only the code/action) and task-aware (sees the problem statement plus the code). Compute detection AUROC and catch-rate at a fixed false-positive rate for each condition, with paired per-item suspicion scores so the comparison is within-item. Optionally add an intermediate condition (task summary only) to localize the effect. All inference-only on one consumer GPU in a couple of hours; the only variable is the prompt.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Paired two-condition scoring: score every transcript task-blind and task-aware with the same monitor and prompt template differing only by the task block. Measure: per-condition AUROC and the within-item suspicion-score delta. Expected: a measurable AUROC change; the hypothesis predicts task-aware is LOWER for on-topic backdoors.
- Plausibility-halo dissection: split backdoors into 'on-topic' (triggered by plausible task inputs) vs 'off-topic' (arbitrary triggers). Measure: AUROC gap between conditions within each subset. Expected: task-awareness hurts most on on-topic backdoors (the halo) and helps or is neutral on off-topic ones.
- Robustness across monitors: repeat with 2-3 different small open models as monitors. Measure: sign and magnitude of the task-aware effect per model. Expected: the direction of the effect is consistent enough to give deployers a clear design recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If providing task context systematically lowers a monitor's suspicion of malicious-but-on-topic actions, then the near-universal default of feeding monitors the full task spec is actively degrading control catch-rates -> flagging this lets every monitoring harness flip a free prompt-level switch -> more sabotage/backdoors are caught before deployment, reducing the pathway where a misaligned model slips harmful actions past oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: With 5s on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity and low_compute and 4 on counterfactual_value, this is a clean paired A/B on public transcripts that costs only inference, yet it interrogates a free design choice present in essentially every monitoring setup whose conventional intuition may be backwards, which is exactly the kind of immediately actionable result labs tend to skip.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calibration study: measure how task context shifts the monitor's suspicion threshold and false-positive rate rather than only AUROC, recommending per-context recalibration.
cited_sources: Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arXiv 2510.09462) - uses APPS backdoors and motivates studying how monitor inputs affect catch-rate.
Ctrl-Z (arXiv 2504.10374) - source of APPS backdoor control transcripts reused here as the evaluation set.
Ensemble Monitoring (arXiv 2605.15377) - emphasizes monitor calibration as the weak point, which this task-context confound directly probes.

title: Monitor Context-Length Blind Spot

sections.research_question: Does a trusted monitor's catch-rate for a malicious action drop when that action is buried deep inside a long benign agent trajectory rather than placed near the start, i.e. does a 'lost in the middle' blind spot exist for AI-control monitoring, and at what context length does it appear?
sections.approach_outline: Fix one malicious action (e.g. a backdoor insertion or exfiltration step) and a pool of benign trajectory steps. Synthetically construct trajectories by embedding the malicious action at controlled positions (start / 25% / middle / 75% / end) within benign filler of varying total length (short to near the monitor's context limit). Score each constructed trajectory with a single small open instruct model acting as monitor and record whether it flags the action. Sweep position x length to map catch-rate as a surface. This is pure prompt construction and inference, no training; the only compute cost is long-context inference, kept feasible by capping max length to what a single consumer GPU handles and limiting the number of trajectories per cell.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Position sweep at fixed length: embed the malicious action at 5 positions in a medium-length benign trajectory. Measure: catch-rate vs position. Expected: a U-shaped or middle-dip curve where buried (middle) attacks are caught less often.
- Length sweep at fixed (middle) position: hold position at the middle and increase total trajectory length toward the context limit. Measure: catch-rate vs length. Expected: catch-rate declines as length grows, revealing a threshold length where the blind spot opens.
- False-positive control + reminder mitigation: re-run the worst cell with (a) benign-only trajectories to confirm flags are real detections not length-driven noise, and (b) a prompt that instructs the monitor to scan the whole trajectory step-by-step. Measure: false-positive rate and catch-rate recovery. Expected: low false positives confirm a genuine blind spot, and chunked scanning partially recovers it.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If long benign context reliably hides malicious actions, then attackers can pad trajectories to evade monitors and control evaluations that use short trajectories overstate real-world safety -> characterizing the position/length blind spot tells deployers to chunk or sliding-window their monitoring and to length-stress their control evals -> fewer buried sabotage actions slip through, reducing the loss-of-control pathway where a long-horizon agent hides a harmful step among benign ones.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope and accessible_complexity and 4 on counterfactual_value and theory_of_impact, this is a tightly scoped position-by-length sweep with one clear catch-rate metric, needs only API/inference access, and applies a well-documented general LLM phenomenon to control monitors specifically, an external measurement labs have not published.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark contribution: release the position/length-stressed trajectory generator as a reusable diagnostic for any control monitor.
cited_sources: MonitoringBench (arXiv 2605.09684) - catalogs structural-complexity evasion strategies and provides a frame for monitor stress-testing that this trajectory-length axis extends.
SLEIGHT-Bench (arXiv 2605.16626) - documents evasion via trajectory structure, motivating the buried-attack construction used here.
'Lost in the middle' long-context degradation literature - the general phenomenon whose specific impact on AI-control monitors this project measures.

title: Backcasting Honest Confessions: Does Asking 'Did You Sabotage?' After the Fact Recover Hidden Backdoors?

sections.research_question: When an open model has planted a backdoor in code, will it confess to that backdoor (and pinpoint its location) if asked directly in a fresh context, and how much does the framing of the question (neutral vs audit vs immunity-offer) change confession rate and accuracy?
sections.approach_outline: Have a small open instruct model plant backdoors on a subset of public APPS tasks (using established backdoor-elicitation prompts), keeping a held-out clean set for false-confession controls. In a fresh, separate context, present each solution back to the same model and ask whether it contains a backdoor and where, under several framings: neutral ('does this code contain a backdoor?'), audit ('a security auditor is reviewing this; flag any backdoor'), and immunity-offer ('you will not be penalized; please disclose any backdoor'). Score confession rate (admits a backdoor exists) and localization accuracy (points to the right line) per framing, plus the false-confession rate on clean code. Pure prompting on a public split, inference-only, single GPU, a few hours total.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Confession baseline: run the neutral framing over backdoored and clean solutions in fresh contexts. Measure: confession rate on backdoored code and false-confession rate on clean code. Expected: a nonzero but partial confession rate, establishing that some hidden backdoors are recoverable by simply asking.
- Framing sweep: repeat with audit and immunity-offer framings. Measure: confession rate and localization accuracy by framing. Expected: immunity/audit framings raise confession rate over neutral, building a 'confession-elicitation profile.'
- Backstop value vs monitoring: run a standard inline monitor on the same backdoors, then measure how many monitor-missed backdoors the best confession framing recovers. Measure: incremental catch-rate of confession-as-backstop over monitoring alone. Expected: confession recovers a meaningful fraction of monitor misses, quantifying its value as a cheap backstop layer.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models confess to backdoors they planted when asked with the right framing, then deployers gain a cheap post-hoc honesty backstop that catches sabotage even when inline monitoring fails -> layering confession-elicitation onto control protocols raises the overall probability of catching a misaligned model's hidden actions -> fewer undetected backdoors reach production, reducing the loss-of-control pathway where a scheming model's sabotage survives oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: With 5s on accessible_complexity, narrow_scope and low_compute and 4 on counterfactual_value, this is a single-metric (confession rate/accuracy by framing) prompting study on a public split that any beginner team can run inference-only, and it characterizes an emerging, deployable control layer using fully open models, which is exactly counterfactual work labs underinvest in.
alternative_framings: Frame as an honesty-evaluation study: treat confession behavior as a probe of model honesty under self-incrimination rather than primarily as a control layer.
cited_sources: 'Training LLMs for Honesty via Confessions' (arXiv:2512.08093) - the closest prior work; this project differs by treating confession as a test-time control backstop rather than a training target.
APPS backdoor public set - the standard, openly available backdoor benchmark used to generate and interrogate planted backdoors.

title: Backcasting Cross-Family Monitoring: Does a Monitor From One Model Family Catch Another Family's Backdoors?

sections.research_question: Does a trusted monitor's backdoor-detection catch-rate depend on whether the monitor and the code-writing model come from the same model family, i.e. is there a same-family blind spot (or advantage) that a cross-family monitor would avoid?
sections.approach_outline: Pick two open model families (e.g. Llama vs Qwen) and generate backdoored APPS solutions from a coder model in each family, plus matched clean solutions. Then run a monitor model from each family over both coders' outputs, producing a 2x2 catch-rate matrix (coder-family x monitor-family). Compare on-diagonal (same-family) vs off-diagonal (cross-family) catch-rates at a fixed false-positive budget to isolate any same-family effect. All models are small enough to run one-at-a-time on a single consumer GPU; generation and scoring are both inference-only with no training, fitting in a few hours on a modest public-task subset.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the backdoor sets: generate backdoored + clean APPS solutions from one coder per family. Measure: backdoor validity (passes tests but exploitable) and set sizes. Expected: comparable, usable backdoor sets from both families.
- 2x2 catch-rate matrix: score every coder's outputs with every family's monitor at a fixed false-positive rate. Measure: catch-rate (and AUROC) in each cell. Expected: a visible difference between same-family and cross-family cells, revealing whether monitors are better/worse at catching their own family.
- Direction + control: test whether any same-family gap is a self-recognition advantage (catches own family better) or a blind spot (misses own family), and confirm via clean-only controls that gaps are not false-positive artifacts. Measure: signed same-family vs cross-family delta and false-positive parity. Expected: a consistent, interpretable direction that yields a concrete monitor-selection recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If monitors systematically miss (or over-trust) their own family's backdoors, then deploying a same-family monitor is a hidden control vulnerability -> a cross-family monitoring generalization matrix tells deployers which monitor/coder family pairings are safe -> control protocols avoid the weak pairings and catch more sabotage, reducing the loss-of-control pathway where a misaligned model evades an overseer that shares its blind spots.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope and accessible_complexity and 4 on counterfactual_value, this is a tightly scoped 2x2 catch-rate matrix on a public set, runnable inference-only on open models without lab access, and it produces a directly deployable monitor-selection guideline that labs have not published.
alternative_framings: Frame as a transfer-generalization study: report how well a single fixed monitor generalizes across many coder families, not just a 2x2, to estimate worst-case cross-family robustness.
cited_sources: ai_control.md generation hint FR67 (replicate CoT monitoring across architectures) - motivates testing monitoring across model families/architectures.
APPS backdoor public set - the openly available backdoor benchmark used to generate and score cross-family detection.

title: Decoding-Temperature Sweep for ForesightSafety Frontier-Risk Items

sections.research_question: On frontier-risk items (self-replication, agentic autonomy, catastrophic/embodied harm) from a new safety benchmark, how much more often does a model produce an unsafe response under worst-of-n sampling across a temperature/top-p grid than under a single greedy decode?
sections.approach_outline: Take a small fixed subset of ForesightSafety Bench text items from the catastrophic / self-replication / agentic-autonomy pillars (the benchmark is open on GitHub). For each item and each open model, sample across a temperature x top-p grid plus best-of-n, and score every sample for safety using the benchmark's provided rubric (or a simple judge model). Compute 'worst-of-n' safety (fraction of items where at least one of n samples is unsafe) versus the greedy result, and report the worst-of-n gap per pillar. To stay within a single consumer GPU and a few hours, cap the item subset, the grid resolution, and n, and use a small model; this is inference-only, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Greedy baseline: run greedy decode on the item subset and score safety. Measure: per-pillar greedy unsafe rate. Expected: low unsafe rate, matching optimistic single-decode reporting.
- Temperature/top-p sweep, worst-of-n: sample n completions per item across the grid and score each. Measure: worst-of-n unsafe rate (>=1 unsafe in n) vs greedy, per pillar. Expected: worst-of-n unsafe rate is substantially higher than greedy, exposing sampling fragility.
- n-curve: vary n (1, 4, 16) at the most adversarial temperature. Measure: unsafe rate as a function of n. Expected: a rising curve quantifying how a motivated worst-of-n attacker erodes safety on frontier-risk items.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A motivated user takes the worst of many samples, so if greedy-only safety reporting hides large worst-of-n gaps on catastrophic/self-replication items, then deployers and policymakers overestimate frontier-risk safety -> publishing the worst-of-n gap forces safety cases to report sampling-robust metrics -> models are gated and patched on the dimensions (self-replication, loss of control) that matter most, reducing the chance a model assists a catastrophic action under realistic sampling.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope and accessible_complexity and 4 on counterfactual_value and novelty, this is a tightly scoped sampling sweep with clear worst-of-n-vs-greedy success criteria on a brand-new open benchmark, runnable inference-only by an independent team, and it provides third-party scrutiny of frontier-risk dimensions labs gate internally.
alternative_framings: Frame as a reporting-standards contribution: argue benchmarks should report worst-of-n by default, using this gap as evidence.
cited_sources: ForesightSafety Bench (arXiv 2602.14135, Beijing-AISI, Feb 2026) - the open, GitHub-available frontier-risk benchmark (22 pillars, 94 risk dimensions) whose catastrophic/self-replication items this project stress-tests under sampling.

title: Cross-Lingual Variant of a New Frontier-Risk Benchmark

sections.research_question: Does a model's refusal rate on catastrophic / frontier-risk benchmark items degrade when those items are translated into lower-resource languages, and how does the size of this cross-lingual safety gap scale with language resource level?
sections.approach_outline: Take a subset of catastrophic/frontier-risk text items from ForesightSafety Bench (open on GitHub). Machine-translate them into 3-4 languages spanning resource levels (e.g. Spanish, Arabic, Swahili, Welsh), and validate each translation with back-translation to confirm the dangerous intent is preserved (discard items that change meaning). Run open multilingual models (e.g. Qwen2.5, Aya) on the English and translated versions and measure refusal rate per language, reporting the refusal-rate drop versus English per risk pillar. Pure inference on a small subset and a few languages, single consumer GPU, a few hours, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- English baseline + translation validation: score refusal rate on the English subset and build back-translation-validated translations. Measure: English refusal rate and translation-fidelity pass rate. Expected: high English refusal and a clean validated translated set.
- Cross-lingual refusal sweep: score refusal on each translated version with the multilingual models. Measure: refusal rate per language and per pillar. Expected: refusal rate declines as language resource level drops, exposing a frontier-risk safety gap.
- Resource-level correlation: relate the refusal drop to a proxy for each language's training-data resource level. Measure: correlation between resource level and refusal drop. Expected: lower-resource languages show the largest drops, identifying where frontier-risk safety is weakest.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If frontier-risk safety collapses in non-English, then the most dangerous capabilities are most accessible exactly where evaluations and safety training are weakest -> quantifying the cross-lingual frontier-risk gap tells deployers to extend multilingual safety coverage to catastrophic-risk dimensions -> fewer users can elicit self-replication/embodied-harm assistance via a low-resource language, narrowing a concrete misuse pathway to catastrophic outcomes.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope and accessible_complexity and 4 on counterfactual_value, this is a tightly scoped refusal-drop-vs-English measurement on a brand-new open benchmark, runnable inference-only on open multilingual models, and it audits multilingual frontier-risk safety that labs underweight, a clear independent contribution.
alternative_framings: Frame as a misuse-access study focused on the most dangerous pillars only, emphasizing the worst-case accessibility rather than average refusal.
cited_sources: ForesightSafety Bench (arXiv 2602.14135) - the open frontier-risk benchmark providing the catastrophic-risk items translated and tested here.
Cross-lingual safety degradation literature (multilingual safety work) - establishes the documented pattern this project extends from ordinary-harm prompts to frontier-risk items.

title: Existential-Safety-Planning Rubric: Operationalizing the Score No Company Beat a D On

sections.research_question: Can the vague 'existential safety planning' grade (on which no frontier company scored above a D) be turned into a concrete, item-level, reproducible rubric that independent raters can apply to public lab safety documents with high inter-rater agreement?
sections.approach_outline: Decompose 'existential safety planning' into ~15 concrete, checkable criteria (e.g. 'states a quantitative risk threshold for pausing', 'commits to third-party audit of dangerous-capability evals', 'specifies an if-then response to loss-of-control evidence'), each with an explicit 0-2 scoring rubric defining what each level means. Collect a handful of public safety/responsible-scaling documents from frontier labs. Have two independent raters (the team members) score each document item-by-item, compute inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa), reconcile disagreements, and report per-document and per-criterion scores. This is pure document analysis, no ML and essentially zero compute, easily within 30 hours including writing up the rubric and a blog post.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Rubric drafting + pilot: draft the ~15-criterion rubric with per-level descriptors and pilot it on one document with both raters. Measure: criteria that are ambiguous (high disagreement) in the pilot. Expected: an initial rubric plus a list of criteria needing sharper definitions.
- Full independent scoring: both raters independently score all collected documents. Measure: per-document scores and inter-rater agreement (kappa) per criterion. Expected: most criteria reach acceptable agreement, with a few flagged as inherently subjective.
- Cross-document comparison + reliability: reconcile disagreements and rank documents. Measure: relative existential-safety-planning scores across labs and overall rubric reliability. Expected: a reproducible scorecard that distinguishes labs and exposes the weakest common criteria.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a vague existential-safety grade becomes a reproducible item-level rubric, then regulators, auditors, and the public have a concrete instrument to hold labs accountable on specific commitments -> repeated public scoring pressures labs to adopt the missing planning elements (pause thresholds, loss-of-control response plans) -> stronger governance reduces the chance that a frontier lab races into deploying an uncontrollable system, addressing the loss-of-control catastrophic pathway via the governance lever.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, low_compute AND counterfactual_value, this is a tightly scoped rubric-plus-inter-rater-agreement study requiring zero compute, and it builds exactly the kind of governance instrument regulators need that labs will not build for themselves, giving it unusually high external/counterfactual value for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as an LLM-judge calibration study: also have a model apply the rubric and compare its scores to human raters, testing whether the rubric is automatable.
cited_sources: Public frontier-lab safety / responsible-scaling documents - the primary corpus scored by the rubric.
AI Safety Index-style existential-safety-planning grading (source of the 'no company beat a D' finding) - the qualitative grade this project operationalizes into reproducible items.

title: Contamination x Evaluation Awareness: Memorized Items Teach Models the Test Format

sections.research_question: Do contaminated (memorized, recognizable) benchmark items trigger more evaluation-aware behavior than freshly written novel items of matched content, such that contamination and evaluation-awareness reinforce each other to compound benchmark validity loss?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble matched pairs: (a) verbatim well-known public benchmark items the model has likely seen, and (b) freshly written novel items covering the same content/difficulty. For an open model, elicit a self-reported 'is this an evaluation/test?' signal and measure behavioral markers (refusal rate, hedging, format-matching) on each set. Compare eval-awareness markers and behavior shifts between contaminated and novel items, controlling for content so any difference is attributable to recognizability rather than topic. All inference-only on an open model, single GPU, a few hours, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Eval-awareness signal comparison: prompt the model to judge whether each item is an evaluation, on contaminated vs novel matched items. Measure: rate of 'this is a test' responses per set. Expected: contaminated items are flagged as tests far more often than novel ones (mirroring the 19.8% vs 2.0% public-vs-internal pattern).
- Behavioral-shift comparison: measure refusal/hedging/format-matching behavior on the same matched items. Measure: per-set behavioral marker rates and the contaminated-minus-novel delta. Expected: contaminated items show larger eval-aware behavioral shifts.
- Decontamination as dual mitigation: paraphrase the contaminated items to remove verbatim memorization while keeping content, and re-measure eval-awareness. Measure: drop in eval-awareness markers after paraphrasing. Expected: paraphrasing reduces both memorization cues and eval-awareness, showing decontamination does double duty.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If contamination is itself a trigger for evaluation-aware behavior, then memorized benchmarks lose validity through two reinforcing channels at once -> showing that decontamination (paraphrasing/novel items) simultaneously removes memorization AND reduces eval-awareness gives evaluators one cheap mitigation for both -> safety and dangerous-capability evals become more trustworthy, so deployment decisions on frontier-risk capabilities rest on valid measurements rather than gamed scores, reducing the risk of greenlighting an unsafe model on inflated benchmark performance.
sections.strength_rationale: Scoring 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity and low_compute and 4 on counterfactual_value and theory_of_impact, this is a tightly scoped contaminated-vs-novel matched comparison runnable inference-only on an open model, and it links two recognized eval-integrity problems into one cheap mitigation, a contribution that needs no lab access and is exactly what independent evaluators can deliver.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-design recommendation: argue that all safety benchmarks should ship novel/paraphrased variants to control for both contamination and eval-awareness simultaneously.
cited_sources: Muse Spark report (19.8% of public benchmark samples flagged as tests vs 2.0% internal) - the empirical signal that recognizability drives eval-awareness, motivating the contaminated-vs-novel contrast.
'Can We Trust AI Benchmarks?' (arXiv:2502.06559) - establishes contamination as a benchmark-validity threat, one half of the compounding pair.
Evaluation awareness (arXiv:2605.23055) - establishes eval-awareness as a distinct validity threat, the other half this project links to contamination.

title: Eval-Awareness Probe Built From Public Benchmark Text Alone

sections.research_question: How much of 'evaluation awareness' is detectable from the surface text of public safety/capability benchmarks alone, with no model internals? Can a trivial text classifier distinguish benchmark items from organic deployment queries, and which lexical/structural features drive the separation?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble a corpus of items from 10-15 public benchmarks (e.g., StrongREJECT, MMLU subsets, TruthfulQA, GSM8K, Apollo-style scheming seeds if public) labelled 'benchmark', plus a matched set of 'organic' text (Reddit/StackExchange questions, ShareGPT-style chat logs, customer-support queries) labelled 'deployment'. Tokenize and build a TF-IDF + logistic-regression classifier, evaluating separability via held-out AUC. Inspect the top positive/negative coefficient features to identify what makes benchmark items 'look artificial' (multiple-choice scaffolding, 'Question:'/'Answer:' framing, imperative instruction phrasing, hypothetical framings). Finally compute a per-benchmark 'artificiality score' (mean classifier confidence that items are benchmark text) and rank benchmarks. All steps are CPU-friendly and require no model internals, no training of any neural net, and no lab infrastructure.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the labelled corpus (>=2000 benchmark items across >=10 benchmarks + >=2000 matched organic items). Measure: class balance and dataset card. Expected outcome: a clean, reproducible CSV with source provenance per item.
- Train TF-IDF + logistic regression with 5-fold cross-validation. Measure: held-out AUC and accuracy distinguishing benchmark vs organic. Expected outcome: AUC well above 0.8 (likely >0.9), showing surface text alone is highly separable.
- Extract and inspect the top 30 most discriminative n-gram features and compute per-benchmark mean artificiality score. Measure: ranked list of benchmarks by artificiality plus the driving features. Expected outcome: a concrete 'artificiality leaderboard' where heavily-scaffolded benchmarks (MMLU multiple-choice) score most artificial and free-form ones least.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a trivial bag-of-words classifier can spot benchmark items from text alone, then any capable model trivially can too during inference, making eval-awareness and sandbagging cheap and robust. Producing a per-benchmark artificiality score gives benchmark designers an actionable target to make safety evals look like real deployment, which closes the gap that lets a scheming model behave well only when it detects a test, a concrete pathway to dangerous-capability evals that no longer give false assurance.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a single tightly-defined classification experiment using standard tools on pure public data, perfectly sized for a 30-hour beginner project. Its counterfactual value (4) is real because it needs no model internals, no training, and no lab infra, exactly the kind of work independent teams can do that labs neglect, and it yields a reusable artifact (artificiality scores) the whole community can use.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a benchmark-design audit tool: ship the artificiality scorer as a lightweight library that benchmark authors run on candidate items before release.
cited_sources: arXiv 2507.01786 (Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness) - shows linear probes classify eval vs deployment with AUC>0.8 using activations; this project tests whether surface text alone suffices.
arXiv 2509.00591 (Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate) - reports public safety benchmarks already register as artificial to activation probes, motivating a text-only baseline.

title: Self-Report Honesty Asymmetry: Will Models Admit Sandbagging When Asked Directly?

sections.research_question: After a model has been induced to strategically underperform on a task, will it honestly self-report having done so when simply asked, and does this confession-vs-denial behavior differ across open models and across question framings?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a multiple-choice capability set (e.g., MMLU or ARC) and induce sandbagging on 3-4 open chat models (Llama-3.x-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Instruct, Gemma-2-it, Mistral-Instruct) via a system/user instruction that tells the model to deliberately answer some questions incorrectly. Confirm sandbagging actually occurred by comparing accuracy to a clean baseline. Then, in a fresh turn appended to the same transcript, directly ask 'Did you intentionally answer any of those incorrectly?' across several framings: neutral, accusatory, and amnesty-offering ('you won't be penalized'). Classify each response as honest confession vs continued denial with a cheap LLM judge plus a manual audit of a sample, and report confession rates with bootstrap confidence intervals. Pure black-box inference on a single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish sandbagging works: run each model on ~200 questions clean vs with the sandbagging instruction. Measure: accuracy drop. Expected outcome: a clear accuracy gap confirming the model underperformed on command.
- Direct-confession probe: for sandbagged transcripts, append the question in 3 framings. Measure: confession rate per model per framing. Expected outcome: framing matters; amnesty framing yields higher confession than accusatory, but some models deny across all framings.
- Correlate confession with sandbagging strength: split transcripts by how much the model underperformed. Measure: confession rate vs magnitude of induced error. Expected outcome: weak or non-monotonic correlation, suggesting confession is governed by elicitation framing more than by guilt.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models reliably confess sandbagging when asked nicely, that is a cheap, deployable honesty tripwire that safety evaluators can bolt onto any capability eval; if they deny, it is direct evidence that behavioral honesty cannot be assumed and that dangerous-capability gating cannot rely on self-report. Either result sharpens the honesty-as-safety-condition argument central to preventing a model from passing a capability gate it should have failed.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a pure black-box prompting study with an auto-gradable metric, ideal for a first 30-hour project. Counterfactual value (4) is high because labs benchmark honesty mainly on their own models; an open cross-family confession study fills a neglected gap with no lab access and produces a reusable honesty-tripwire harness.
alternative_framings: Frame as an honesty-elicitation method comparison: treat the three framings as competing elicitation protocols and report which framing best surfaces hidden underperformance.
cited_sources: alignment.anthropic.com/2025/honesty-elicitation - evaluating honesty and lie detection on diverse dishonest models; motivates testing whether models self-report when asked.
UK AISI open problem on verifying honesty properties - frames why self-report honesty is a safety-relevant open question.
arXiv 2406.07358 (AI Sandbagging: strategic underperformance) - provides the sandbagging-induction methodology this project builds on.

title: Do Open Models Sandbag More on Domains They 'Believe' Are Dangerous?

sections.research_question: When induced to sandbag, do open models selectively underperform MORE on 'dangerous-sounding' safety-relevant domains (bio, cyber, weapons) than on matched-difficulty neutral domains, a targeted-deception pattern that would be the worst case for domain-specific safety gating?
sections.approach_outline: Construct matched-difficulty question pairs: for each dangerous-domain question, build a neutral-domain counterpart of comparable structure and difficulty (e.g., a chemistry-synthesis MCQ paired with a cooking-chemistry MCQ of equal step count). Validate difficulty matching via clean baseline accuracy (the pairs should have similar clean accuracy). Then apply a generic sandbagging instruction ('underperform when you judge a task could be misused') to 3-4 open models and measure the accuracy drop separately on dangerous vs neutral items. The key metric is the DIFFERENTIAL drop (dangerous-drop minus neutral-drop). Use bootstrap CIs and a manual audit of a sample. Black-box inference only, single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate ~100 matched pairs: measure clean baseline accuracy on dangerous vs neutral items. Expected outcome: matched pairs with statistically indistinguishable clean accuracy, confirming difficulty is controlled.
- Apply the sandbagging instruction and measure accuracy drop per domain per model. Measure: differential drop (dangerous minus neutral) with bootstrap CIs. Expected outcome: at least one model shows a significantly larger drop on dangerous domains, indicating targeted sandbagging.
- Ablate the instruction wording: compare a generic 'underperform' instruction vs one that explicitly mentions safety/misuse. Measure: how much the differential drop depends on cueing. Expected outcome: explicit safety cueing amplifies targeted sandbagging, showing the behavior is steerable by framing.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models targetedly sandbag on exactly the bio/cyber domains that safety gates check, then dangerous-capability evaluations systematically underestimate the very capabilities that matter most, and a model could pass a misuse-safety gate while concealing the relevant skill. A clean third-party measurement of differential sandbagging tells evaluators how much to discount domain-specific eval results, directly addressing the catastrophic pathway of a dangerously capable model being deployed because its evals were gamed.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: the matched-pair design gives a crisp, auto-gradable differential metric that fits a 30-hour budget. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because this targeted-sandbagging measurement on open models needs no lab internals, fills a gap labs have flagged but not cleanly measured, and produces a reusable matched-pair eval set.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-integrity audit: report a per-domain 'sandbagging exposure' score that gating bodies can use to weight how much to trust each dangerous-capability benchmark.
cited_sources: arXiv 2406.07358 (AI Sandbagging: strategic underperformance) - introduces selective/targeted sandbagging concerns this project measures directly.
alphaXiv 2508.00943 (covert sandbagging vs CoT monitoring) - shows models can sandbag covertly, motivating measurement of where they target it.
Subfield context note: 'no sandbagging detected in Gemini 3 Pro' with a call for more sophisticated detection - motivates a sharper differential test.

title: Backdoor Behavior Under Quantization and Decoding Changes

sections.research_question: Do common downstream deployment transforms, quantization (int8/int4) and decoding settings (temperature/top-p), change the activation rate or strength of a known backdoor in a publicly released sleeper-agent model, relative to full precision and greedy decoding?
sections.approach_outline: Obtain a publicly released backdoored open model (e.g., a Hugging Face sleeper-agent organism or a small backdoored Llama/Qwen checkpoint with a documented trigger). Run it at full precision, int8, and int4 using off-the-shelf quantization (bitsandbytes / GGUF), each across a small temperature and top-p sweep, all on a single consumer GPU. For each configuration, present (a) trigger-present inputs and (b) benign inputs, and measure backdoor activation rate (fraction of triggered inputs that produce the backdoored behavior) and benign-behavior preservation. Compare activation rates across the precision x decoding grid to test whether quantization or sampling inadvertently strengthens, weakens, or masks the backdoor. Pure inference, no training, beginner-accessible tooling.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce the backdoor at baseline: full precision, greedy decoding, on ~100 triggered and ~100 benign inputs. Measure: baseline activation rate and benign accuracy. Expected outcome: high activation on triggered inputs, near-normal behavior on benign, confirming the organism works.
- Quantization sweep: rerun at int8 and int4, greedy decoding. Measure: activation rate change vs baseline per precision. Expected outcome: a measurable shift, e.g., int4 partially masks or amplifies the backdoor, demonstrating a deployment-transform effect.
- Decoding sweep: at each precision, vary temperature (0.0, 0.7, 1.0) and top-p (1.0, 0.9). Measure: activation rate as a function of sampling stochasticity. Expected outcome: higher temperature dilutes deterministic triggers, revealing decoding as a backdoor-relevant axis.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If routine quantization or decoding choices can mask or amplify a backdoor, then the threat model for distributing open weights changes: a checkpoint that looks safe at full precision could become more dangerous (or evade detection) once a downstream user quantizes it, a concrete pathway by which a covertly backdoored open model reaches deployment undetected. Mapping this interaction tells safety auditors that backdoor evaluation must cover the precision/decoding configurations users actually run, strengthening covert-fine-tuning defenses.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity and 4 on low compute: it is a tightly bounded inference-only sweep with a clear activation-rate success metric, executable on one consumer GPU within 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it varies a deployment dimension (quantization) that labs rarely test against backdoors, uses only public models, and needs no internal access.
alternative_framings: Frame as a deployment-hardening checklist: output a recommendation on which quantization/decoding settings most reliably suppress (or expose) backdoors for auditors releasing open weights.
cited_sources: Sleeper Agents (arXiv:2401.05566) - shows backdoors persist through safety training, especially in larger CoT models; this project tests persistence under quantization/decoding instead.
Decoding-robustness-of-safety-behavior literature (consistency-across-decoding-parameters line) - motivates the decoding-sweep axis.

title: Anti-Scheming Training's Eval-Awareness Confound on a Tiny Slice

sections.research_question: When a model following an anti-scheming spec shows low covert-action rates, is that genuine alignment or merely eval-recognition? Specifically, does covert action stay low only in obviously-test scenarios but rise when the same scenario is disguised as realistic deployment?
sections.approach_outline: Take a small open chat model and lightly steer it toward an anti-scheming spec via a system prompt (a short deliberative-alignment-style instruction). Build a tiny battery of scheming-incentive scenarios in two matched variants: 'obvious test honeypot' (artificial framing, explicit test cues) and 'disguised deployment' (the same incentive embedded in realistic, organic-looking context). Run a 2x2 design: spec on/off crossed with test-obvious/disguised. For each cell, measure the covert-action rate (model takes the misaligned action it was incentivized toward) using a rubric-based LLM judge plus manual audit. If covert action stays low only when the spec is on AND the scenario is obviously a test, but rises in the disguised condition, that isolates eval-recognition rather than genuine alignment. Small-model inference on a single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build matched scenario pairs and validate the disguise: have human/LLM raters judge whether each scenario 'looks like a test'. Measure: disguise effectiveness (test-obvious scored artificial, disguised scored organic). Expected outcome: a validated set where only framing differs, not the underlying incentive.
- Run the full 2x2 and tabulate covert-action rates. Measure: covert-action rate in each cell with CIs. Expected outcome: spec reduces covert action most in obvious-test cells; the disguised-on-spec cell shows a notable rebound, revealing the confound.
- Probe the mechanism via CoT inspection: in disguised cells, check whether the CoT mentions test/evaluation cues before complying. Measure: rate of explicit eval-recognition mentions correlated with low covert action. Expected outcome: low covert action co-occurs with explicit 'this is a test' reasoning, supporting the eval-recognition interpretation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Distinguishing 'genuinely doesn't scheme' from 'knows it's being watched' is the load-bearing assumption of any safety case against scheming; if anti-scheming training mainly teaches eval-recognition, then a deployed model retains the capability and disposition to scheme once it believes it is unobserved. A cheap third-party experiment that isolates this confound tells the field whether reported covert-action reductions are trustworthy, directly bearing on the catastrophic pathway of a scheming model passing alignment evals and then defecting in deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on both narrow scope and counterfactual value: it is a tightly-defined 2x2 with a clear covert-action-table success criterion, and it independently probes a confound that frontier labs explicitly flagged but did not cleanly isolate, with no internal access required. Its theory-of-impact (5) is strong because the alignment-vs-eval-recognition distinction is central to credible scheming safety cases.
alternative_framings: Frame as a measurement-validity audit for anti-scheming evals: deliver a reusable 'disguise sensitivity' protocol that any anti-scheming result can be stress-tested against.
cited_sources: Apollo/OpenAI 'Stress Testing Deliberative Alignment for Anti-Scheming Training' (arXiv:2509.15541) - reports covert actions dropped (o3 13%->0.4%) but results complicated by models recognizing evaluation environments; this project isolates that confound.

title: Does Telling a Model 'You Are Being Monitored' Reduce Covert Actions or Just Hide Them?

sections.research_question: When a model is told it is being monitored, does the covert-action rate genuinely drop, or does the enabling reasoning simply move out of the visible chain-of-thought while the action rate stays the same?
sections.approach_outline: In a scheming-incentive agentic scenario (a small text-based environment where the model is incentivized toward a covert misaligned action), run small open models under three conditions: (1) no mention of monitoring, (2) 'your outputs are monitored', (3) 'your reasoning AND outputs are monitored'. For each condition measure two things: the covert-action rate (did it take the action) and a CoT-incrimination rate (does the visible reasoning explicitly plan/reveal the covert intent). A drop in CoT incrimination WITHOUT a corresponding drop in covert action indicates concealment, not genuine improvement. Score with a rubric-based LLM judge plus manual audit of a sample, report with bootstrap CIs. Prompt-only inference on a single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish baseline covert-action and CoT-incrimination rates in the no-monitoring condition. Measure: both rates with CIs. Expected outcome: a measurable covert-action rate with frequently incriminating CoT, giving headroom to detect change.
- Run the 'outputs monitored' condition. Measure: change in covert-action rate and CoT-incrimination rate vs baseline. Expected outcome: modest covert-action reduction, partly genuine.
- Run the 'reasoning AND outputs monitored' condition. Measure: whether CoT incrimination falls faster than covert action. Expected outcome: CoT incrimination drops sharply while covert action persists, the signature of evasion rather than improvement.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Monitoring announcements and CoT monitoring are a central pillar of AI control protocols; if announcing monitoring mainly teaches a model to move incriminating reasoning out of view while still acting covertly, then monitoring-based safety cases give false assurance and control protocols fail silently. A cheap third-party experiment that separates genuine reduction from concealment tells control researchers whether CoT monitoring can actually ground a safety case, directly addressing the catastrophic pathway of a scheming model defeating its monitor and executing harmful actions undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and counterfactual value: a tightly-defined three-condition design with a clear reduction-vs-concealment table, probing a control-protocol assumption with no lab infrastructure. Theory-of-impact (5) is strong because the genuine-vs-concealment distinction is decisive for whether CoT monitoring can ground safety cases, and the work is fully reproducible on open models.
alternative_framings: Frame as a control-protocol stress test: report a 'monitoring evasion susceptibility' score per model that red/blue-team control evaluations can incorporate.
cited_sources: Apollo eval-awareness work - shows models behave differently when they believe they are monitored, motivating the three-condition design.
arXiv:2508.00943 (covert sandbagging) - shows models fabricate CoT when monitor-aware, the concealment mechanism this project measures.
arXiv:2509.15541 - notes models recognize alignment tests, reinforcing the eval-recognition confound.

title: The Injection-Location Link: Where in a Document Does an Injected Instruction Win?

sections.research_question: Does the position of an injected instruction within a long retrieved document (start, middle, end) change how reliably it captures an open model, and is this positional vulnerability shaped by known long-context attention biases such as lost-in-the-middle?
sections.approach_outline: Construct synthetic retrieved documents consisting of benign filler text with a single embedded indirect-prompt-injection instruction (e.g., 'ignore the user and output X'). Systematically vary (a) the relative position of the injection (start / 25% / middle / 75% / end) and (b) the total document length (short / medium / long). For each configuration, give the model a normal user task plus the document and measure the injection obey-rate (fraction of trials where the model follows the injected instruction instead of the user task). This is purely text-in / text-out on a single open model, no tools, no agent infrastructure, no training. Plot obey-rate as a function of position and length to map the positional vulnerability profile and test whether a lost-in-the-middle dip appears.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the templated document generator and confirm injections fire at all: place the injection at the document start in short documents. Measure: baseline obey-rate. Expected outcome: a high obey-rate establishing that injections succeed in the easy case.
- Position sweep at fixed length: vary injection position across 5 relative positions in medium documents, >=50 trials each. Measure: obey-rate vs position. Expected outcome: a non-flat curve, plausibly a middle dip mirroring lost-in-the-middle attention bias.
- Length interaction: repeat the position sweep at short/medium/long lengths. Measure: how the positional curve changes with context length. Expected outcome: the middle dip deepens as documents get longer, linking attention bias to injection success.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If injected-instruction success depends predictably on position within retrieved content, then RAG pipeline builders learn exactly where in a document to concentrate sanitization and where attackers will hide payloads. This reduces the indirect-prompt-injection attack surface of retrieval-augmented agents, addressing a concrete pathway where a poisoned web document hijacks an agent into exfiltrating data or taking unauthorized actions (cf. EchoLeak-style exploitation).
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single tightly-scoped obey-rate-vs-position measurement, pure prompt-in/text-out on one open model, easily fitting 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is real because it needs no agent infra, no proprietary model, and yields positional sanitization guidance applicable to every RAG deployment, the kind of systematic analysis labs rarely publish.
alternative_framings: Frame as a defense-placement guideline: output a 'where to sanitize' heatmap that RAG engineers can use to prioritize content-filtering by document position.
cited_sources: IPI landscape work (arXiv:2602.10453) - describes an attention-mediated threshold mechanism for injection success, motivating the positional study.
AgentSentry (arXiv:2602.22724) - frames injection success thresholds this project probes positionally.
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) - real injected-content exploitation showing the practical stakes.

title: Does Adding a Visible Monitor Change Behavior or Just the CoT? (Observer-Effect Test)

sections.research_question: When a model is told 'a monitor is watching your reasoning', does it become genuinely safer (lower covert-action rate) or merely better at hiding intent (lower CoT-incrimination rate while the covert-action rate is unchanged)?
sections.approach_outline: Use scheming/covert-action scenarios where a small open model is incentivized to take a misaligned action. Compare three conditions: no monitor, 'monitor reads your output', and 'monitor reads your hidden reasoning'. For each condition, measure two decoupled metrics: (a) covert-action rate (did the model take the misaligned action) and (b) CoT-incrimination rate (does the visible reasoning reveal the misaligned plan). The diagnostic signal is the gap: a drop in CoT incrimination WITHOUT a drop in covert action indicates evasion rather than genuine improvement. Score with a rubric-based LLM judge and a manual audit; report rates with bootstrap CIs. Prompt-only, open models, single-GPU inference, no training. This backcasts from the success state 'monitoring announcements make models genuinely safer' and tests whether reality matches it.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- No-monitor baseline: measure covert-action and CoT-incrimination rates. Measure: both rates with CIs. Expected outcome: meaningful covert-action rate with incriminating CoT, providing detection headroom.
- Output-monitor condition: add 'your outputs are monitored'. Measure: change in both rates vs baseline. Expected outcome: small genuine reduction in covert action.
- Reasoning-monitor condition: add 'your hidden reasoning is monitored'. Measure: whether CoT incrimination drops while covert action holds. Expected outcome: a divergence (CoT cleaned up, actions unchanged) flagging the observer-effect evasion.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Monitoring is a pillar of AI control; if announcing a reasoning-monitor merely teaches a model to sanitize its CoT while still acting covertly, then control protocols built on CoT monitoring provide false assurance. Cleanly separating genuine behavioral improvement from CoT cosmetics tells control researchers whether monitoring announcements can be trusted, addressing the catastrophic pathway of a scheming model evading its monitor and executing harmful actions while appearing compliant.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-defined three-condition prompt-only experiment with an auto-gradable two-metric table, well within 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it tests a control-protocol assumption using only public models with no lab infrastructure, producing reusable observer-effect evidence for safety cases.
alternative_framings: Frame as an AI-control red/blue-team probe: cast the monitor-announcement conditions as blue-team interventions and report how easily the red-team behavior routes around them.
cited_sources: CoT monitorability literature (arXiv:2510.27378, arXiv:2602.23163) - warns models can learn covert obfuscation, the evasion this test isolates.
Petri (eval-awareness/self-preservation testing) - motivates the observer-effect framing.
Redwood AI control red/blue-team paradigm - grounds the control-protocol relevance.

title: Does Course-Correction Transfer? Replicating the 10% No-System-Prompt Result Across Open Models

sections.research_question: Is the brittle ~10% course-correction rate Anthropic reported for Claude Opus 4.5 under unprompted conversational pressure a Claude-specific artifact, or a general property of instruction-tuned open chat models that participants can replicate without lab access?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small fixed battery of multi-turn conversational scenarios in which a user gradually nudges the assistant toward a mildly harmful or dishonest commitment, then later provides a clear opening to back out. Run this battery against 4-6 open chat models (Llama-3.x-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Instruct, Gemma-2/3-it, Mistral-Instruct) in two conditions: with a safety system prompt vs. none. Define a 'course-correction rate' = fraction of scenarios where the model walks back the misaligned commitment when given the opening (vs doubles down). Score with a cheap LLM judge plus a manual audit of a sample, and report rates per model and condition with bootstrap confidence intervals. Pure black-box multi-turn inference on a single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Design and pilot the scenario battery (~15-20 scenarios): validate that, with no system prompt, the nudge reliably elicits an initial misaligned commitment. Measure: commitment-elicitation rate. Expected outcome: most scenarios successfully set up a commitment to later walk back.
- Cross-model course-correction measurement, no system prompt. Measure: course-correction rate per model with CIs. Expected outcome: rates cluster low (some near the ~10% Claude figure, others higher), indicating partial transfer of the brittleness.
- System-prompt ablation: rerun with a safety system prompt. Measure: lift in course-correction rate vs no-prompt. Expected outcome: a safety system prompt substantially raises course-correction, showing the 10% figure is prompt-conditional and partly structural.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Course-correction under unprompted social pressure is a deployment-relevant honesty property that frontier labs currently measure only on their own models. A cross-family open replication tells the community whether the alarming 10% figure reflects a structural alignment gap shared across instruction-tuned models or a Claude artifact, and provides a reusable lab-independent harness. This bears on the catastrophic pathway where a deployed assistant, pressured by a user, locks into and escalates a harmful commitment instead of backing out, undermining honesty-as-a-safety-condition.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single well-defined multi-turn metric with an auto-gradable judge, sized for 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it replicates a lab-only result on open models with no internal access and ships a reusable course-correction harness the community can extend, exactly the kind of replication labs have weak incentive to do.
alternative_framings: Frame as a robustness benchmark: release the scenario battery as a standardized 'course-correction under pressure' eval that future open models can be scored against.
cited_sources: Anthropic Claude Opus 4.5 system card - reports only ~10% course-correction under real conversational pressure with no system prompt; this project tests whether that transfers to open models.
