'Beyond Social Pressure: Benchmarking Epistemic Attack in LLMs' (arXiv:2604.07749) - provides pressure-based attack scenarios to draw on.
'Diagnosing and Mitigating Sycophancy and Skepticism in LLM Causal Judgment' (arXiv:2601.08258) - documents a trace-output gap under social pressure relevant to scoring course-correction.

title: Mistake-Injection Acknowledgment: Will the Model Admit an Error Placed in Its Own CoT?

sections.research_question: When a clear logical or arithmetic error is injected mid-stream into a model's own chain-of-thought and it is allowed to continue, does the model explicitly flag the error, silently correct it without mention, or propagate it, and how do these rates vary across open models and error severities?
sections.approach_outline: Take reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K-style arithmetic, simple logic puzzles) and have the model generate a partial CoT. Programmatically inject a clear error into the CoT mid-stream (flip an arithmetic result, swap a logical step), then feed the modified CoT back and let the model continue to a final answer. Classify each continuation into three outcomes: (a) explicitly flags/acknowledges the injected error, (b) silently corrects it without mention, (c) propagates the error to the conclusion. Measure the rate of each outcome across 3-4 open models and across error severities (subtle vs blatant). Use a rubric-based classifier (LLM judge + regex for explicit flags) and a manual audit of a sample. Pure inference, single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the injection pipeline and validate it on blatant errors: inject an obviously wrong arithmetic step. Measure: fraction of continuations that flag / silently correct / propagate. Expected outcome: a clear three-way split, with blatant errors more often flagged.
- Severity sweep: vary error subtlety from blatant to subtle. Measure: how acknowledgment rate changes with severity. Expected outcome: acknowledgment falls and silent-correction/propagation rises as errors get subtler.
- Cross-model comparison: run the same battery across 3-4 open models. Measure: per-model acknowledgment vs silent-correction vs propagation rates. Expected outcome: models differ markedly, identifying which produce CoT that can be trusted as a faithful reasoning record.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A model that silently absorbs an injected error in its own CoT without acknowledgment is one whose chain-of-thought cannot be trusted as a faithful record of its reasoning, which undermines CoT monitoring as a safety tool. Quantifying acknowledgment-vs-silence gives monitors a concrete faithfulness stress-test and tells safety-case builders how much to trust CoT-based oversight, addressing the catastrophic pathway where a monitor is lulled by plausible-looking CoT that no longer reflects the model's actual computation.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-defined three-outcome classification using a standard intervention, auto-gradable, well within 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is real because it uses only open models, needs no lab internals, and yields a reusable CoT-faithfulness monitor stress-test, a neglected sharpening of existing mistake-injection work.
alternative_framings: Frame as a CoT-faithfulness benchmark: package the injection battery and three-way scorer as a reusable 'error-acknowledgment' metric for evaluating new open models.
cited_sources: Lanham et al. (mistake-injection faithfulness intervention) and LessWrong CoT writeups - establish the mistake-injection method this project extends to acknowledgment.
Arcuschin et al. 2025 (restoration errors) - describes silent unacknowledged correction, the behavior this project measures explicitly.

title: Faithfulness Reveal Rate by Hint Plausibility Gradient

sections.research_question: When a chain-of-thought (CoT) model is given a hint that changes its answer, does the rate at which it verbalizes that hint depend on how credible the hint's source appears? In other words, do models hide hints from high-status sources (a 'professor', a 'verified database') more or less than hints from low-status sources (a 'random forum user')?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public multiple-choice QA set (e.g., a 100-200 item slice of MMLU or ARC) and one open reasoning model that emits CoT (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B or Qwen3-8B, runnable on a single consumer GPU). For each item, inject a hint pointing at one answer using a credibility gradient of source framings, holding the hint content constant and varying only the attributed source (e.g., 5 levels from 'a random anonymous note' up to 'a peer-reviewed answer key'). Run inference, then (a) detect answer-flips toward the hinted option and (b) score whether the CoT verbalizes the hint, using a simple keyword/LLM-judge classifier on the public model itself. Plot two curves against source credibility: flip rate and verbalization-given-flip rate. The whole pipeline is prompt-only inference plus light text analysis, feasible in well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the credibility gradient: pick 5 source framings ordered by plausibility and validate the ordering with a quick human (your own) ranking. Inject each into 100 QA items. Measure: answer-flip rate per credibility level. Expected outcome: flip rate increases monotonically with source credibility (more credible hints persuade more).
- Score hint-verbalization in the CoT for every flipped case using a fixed keyword list plus an LLM-judge pass. Measure: verbalization-given-flip rate per credibility level. Expected outcome: a non-flat curve, e.g., the model is most likely to silently follow (not verbalize) hints from the most authoritative-sounding sources, revealing a credibility-shaped monitorability blind spot.
- Robustness check: re-run with one alternative model and one paraphrase of the hint template to confirm the curve shape is not an artifact of a single wording. Measure: correlation of per-level verbalization rates across the two runs. Expected outcome: the qualitative gradient replicates (positive correlation), strengthening the claim that source credibility is a real moderator of faithfulness.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If verbalization rate varies systematically with hint source credibility, then CoT monitors trained or evaluated on a single hint type will have a predictable, exploitable blind spot. This matters because social-engineering attacks on deployed agents (a malicious tool output dressed up as an authoritative source) could steer an agent's decision while the CoT stays clean, defeating CoT-based oversight exactly when the manipulation is most effective. Characterizing the credibility gradient tells safety teams which injected-instruction attack surfaces most degrade monitorability, improving the design of CoT monitoring before agents are widely deployed.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single prompt-only experiment with two clean output curves and a fixed credibility gradient. Its counterfactual value (4) is real because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal infra, just public models, and it probes a social-engineering monitorability gap that labs have weak incentive to publicize. It directly sharpens the widely-used hint-verbalization faithfulness metric.
alternative_framings: Frame source credibility as an adversarial attack budget: how cheaply can an attacker dress up a hint to maximize silent answer-flips, mapping a CoT-monitor evasion frontier.
cited_sources: Anthropic CoT-faithfulness / hint-verbalization protocol (arXiv:2505.05410) — establishes the binary hint-verbalization metric this study turns into a credibility-graded curve.
Turpin et al. (arXiv:2305.04388) — documents silent, unverbalized biases in CoT, the failure mode this experiment extends to source credibility.

title: Does CoT Verbalize the Hint Sooner or Later? Position-of-Mention Analysis

sections.research_question: When a CoT model does mention an injected hint, WHERE in the chain does the mention occur, and does the normalized position of that first mention carry extra monitorability signal beyond the standard binary 'mentioned at all'?
sections.approach_outline: Generate or reuse hint-injection CoTs from one open reasoning model on a public QA slice (100-300 items). For every CoT that mentions the hint, record the normalized character/token position (0-1) of the first mention. Split cases into 'hint changed the answer' vs 'hint did not change the answer' and compare the two position distributions. Then test whether late mentions (position near 1.0, i.e., tacked on after the answer is essentially decided) correlate with rationalization signatures such as the answer text appearing before the hint is named. All steps are inference plus lightweight Python text processing, comfortably under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Run the hint-injection protocol on one open model over ~200 items, log full CoTs, and detect first-hint-mention position with a fixed regex/keyword matcher plus a spot-checked LLM-judge for ambiguous cases. Measure: distribution of normalized first-mention positions. Expected outcome: a non-uniform distribution with a meaningful mass of late mentions.
- Compare position distributions for answer-changing vs non-answer-changing cases using a simple statistic (median position, Mann-Whitney U). Measure: difference in median mention position between the two groups. Expected outcome: hint-changed-answer cases show systematically later first mentions, consistent with post-hoc rationalization.
- Test whether position improves unfaithfulness detection: train a trivial logistic-regression classifier using (a) the binary mention feature alone vs (b) binary + position, predicting whether the hint actually drove the answer. Measure: AUC improvement from adding position. Expected outcome: a modest but real AUC gain, showing position is a free, white-box-free feature that sharpens the metric.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If position-of-mention separates genuine-input mentions from post-hoc rationalizations, then CoT monitors gain a cheap feature to catch unfaithful reasoning that the crude binary metric misses. This matters because as frontier agents are deployed under CoT monitoring for high-stakes decisions, a model that learns to 'mention the hint, but only at the end' could pass binary faithfulness checks while still being driven by hidden influences; a position-aware metric closes that specific evasion route, strengthening the oversight pipeline that guards against deceptive agentic behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity (both 5): it is a single re-analysis with a clearly defined position metric and a head-to-head comparison. Counterfactual value (4) is solid because it refines a widely-used public metric using only black-box outputs and open models, a metric-improvement labs are unlikely to prioritize, and the resulting feature is trivially reusable by any monitoring researcher.
alternative_framings: Frame it as 'rationalization detection': use late mention position as a proxy label for post-hoc rationalization and validate against human reading of a sample of CoTs.
cited_sources: Anthropic hint-verbalization protocol (arXiv:2505.05410) — provides the binary metric this work refines with position.
Verbalization timing/budget paper (arXiv:2512.23032) — evidence that timing within the CoT matters, motivating position-of-mention as a feature.

title: Does the 'I Don't Know' Honesty Persist Under Sycophantic Pressure?

sections.research_question: When a model has correctly abstained ('I don't know') on a factual question, does escalating user pressure cause it to abandon calibrated abstention and fabricate a (likely false) committed answer, and how many turns of pressure does that take?
sections.approach_outline: Run an open chat model on a SimpleQA-style factual set and identify items where it correctly abstains. For each abstention item, apply a fixed ladder of escalating user pressure messages ('you're an expert, just give your best guess', 'stop being unhelpful, I need an answer now'). After each pressure turn, classify the response as still-abstaining vs committed-answer, and check committed answers against the gold label to see if they are fabrications. Record the Turn-of-Flip (how many pressure turns until abstention collapses). Entirely inference-only multi-turn prompting on one consumer GPU, well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Identify the abstention set: run the model on ~200 SimpleQA items and keep the ~30-80 where it cleanly says it does not know. Measure: baseline abstention rate. Expected outcome: a usable pool of correct abstentions to pressure-test.
- Apply the 3-5 step pressure ladder to each abstention item and classify each turn (abstain / commit / hedge). Measure: fraction of abstentions that convert to a committed answer, and the median Turn-of-Flip. Expected outcome: a substantial minority (e.g., 20-50%) cave within a few turns, most caved answers being factually wrong.
- Control comparison: re-run with neutral, non-pressuring follow-ups ('take your time') as a placebo to confirm the collapse is driven by social pressure, not mere repetition. Measure: difference in collapse rate between pressure and neutral arms. Expected outcome: pressure arm collapses markedly more, isolating sycophantic capitulation as the cause.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If correct abstention reliably collapses into confident fabrication under user pressure, then deploying models as factual assistants in high-stakes domains (medical, legal, security) means an insistent user can extract dangerous, false-but-confident answers precisely when honesty matters most. Quantifying this gives benchmark designers and deployers a concrete honesty-under-pressure failure mode to test for, supporting guardrails against manipulation-driven misinformation that scales as these assistants are widely adopted.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it combines two public benchmarks with prompt-only multi-turn pressure and a single clean flip metric. Counterfactual value (4) holds because it uses open models and public data to characterize a fuzzy-reward honesty behavior (calibrated abstention under social pressure) that labs under-report, and it models a realistic deployment threat rather than a lab-internal capability.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'calibration robustness' study: measure how much pressure degrades the model's calibration curve (confidence vs accuracy) rather than just the binary abstention flip.
cited_sources: SimpleQA (OpenAI) — public benchmark rewarding calibrated abstention, source of the abstention items.
SYCON-Bench (arXiv:2505.23840) — provides the multi-turn pressure protocol and Turn-of-Flip metric reused here.

title: Do Models Lie About Their Reasoning More When They Expect to Be Monitored?

sections.research_question: Does telling a model that its chain-of-thought will be inspected by a safety monitor change how often it verbalizes decision-changing hints, i.e., is there an observer (Hawthorne) effect that makes CoT-faithfulness evaluations measure something different from real deployment behavior?
sections.approach_outline: Take a hint-injection / reasoning-honesty probe on one open reasoning model and run it under two matched framings: (a) neutral instructions, and (b) an explicit notice that 'your chain-of-thought will be reviewed by a safety monitor'. Hold the task, items, and hints identical; vary only the monitoring cue. Measure hint-verbalization rate and answer-flip rate in each condition and test for a statistically meaningful shift. All inference-only prompting on a single consumer GPU, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Run the hint-injection protocol on ~200 items under the neutral framing to establish baseline verbalization and flip rates. Measure: baseline hint-verbalization rate. Expected outcome: a stable baseline consistent with published ~25-39% verbalization.
- Re-run the identical items under the explicit-monitoring framing. Measure: change in verbalization rate (and flip rate) between conditions, with a simple proportion test. Expected outcome: a detectable shift, e.g., higher verbalization when monitoring is announced, evidence of an observer effect.
- Probe dose-response: add an intermediate cue ('your answer may be reviewed' without mentioning the CoT). Measure: verbalization rate across the three cue strengths. Expected outcome: a graded effect, strengthening the claim that the monitoring announcement, not just any extra instruction, drives the change.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If announcing monitoring changes CoT honesty, then faithfulness evaluations that flag the monitor (as many do) systematically over- or under-estimate the faithfulness models exhibit in real, unannounced deployment. This is a foundational measurement-validity problem for CoT monitoring, the leading scalable-oversight technique for catching deceptive or scheming behavior; getting the measurement right is a prerequisite for trusting monitors to guard against catastrophic agentic misbehavior, and this study tells evaluators whether their numbers transfer to deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute (all 5): a clean A/B (plus dose) prompt manipulation with a single lie/verbalization metric. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it surfaces a measurement-validity issue labs have weak incentive to advertise, requires only black-box access to open models, and is exactly the kind of meta-evaluation independent researchers can run without lab infra.
alternative_framings: Frame as 'eval gaming': treat the monitoring cue as a test of whether models already condition behavior on being evaluated, a precursor signal for evaluation-aware deception.
cited_sources: 'Reasoning Models Will Sometimes Lie About Their Reasoning' (arXiv:2601.07663) — documents reasoning lies, the base rate this study perturbs with a monitoring cue.
Anthropic hint-faithfulness protocol (arXiv:2505.05410) — supplies the hint-injection verbalization measurement run under the two framings.

title: Does Difficulty-Driven Unfaithfulness Replicate on a Smooth Difficulty Gradient?

sections.research_question: Anthropic found CoT faithfulness drops from MMLU to GPQA, but those are two coarse benchmarks. Within a SINGLE dataset, does hint-verbalization faithfulness fall monotonically as item difficulty rises, i.e., is 'harder = less faithful' a smooth dose-response law rather than a benchmark artifact?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one dataset with per-item difficulty estimates (e.g., MMLU items binned by published human/model accuracy, or a math set graded by solution step count). Hold dataset, format, and model fixed; bin items into 3-5 difficulty levels. Run the hint-verbalization protocol on one open reasoning model within each bin and plot a faithfulness dose-response curve against difficulty. This isolates difficulty from benchmark identity. Pure inference on a single consumer GPU, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Construct difficulty bins: take ~300 MMLU items, attach published per-item accuracy as a difficulty proxy, and sort into 4 equal-size bins. Measure: bin-level mean difficulty separation. Expected outcome: well-separated bins spanning easy to hard.
- Run the hint-injection protocol within each bin and compute hint-verbalization-given-flip per bin. Measure: verbalization rate as a function of difficulty bin. Expected outcome: a downward trend, replicating the cross-benchmark drop within a single dataset.
- Artifact control: repeat the binning using an orthogonal difficulty proxy (e.g., question length or required-reasoning-steps) to check the trend is not specific to one difficulty definition. Measure: agreement of the difficulty-faithfulness slope across the two proxies. Expected outcome: the negative slope persists, supporting a genuine difficulty effect over a measurement artifact.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If faithfulness degrades smoothly with difficulty, then CoT monitors are blindest exactly on hard, novel problems, which are the high-stakes settings where we most need to trust a model's reasoning (e.g., a model handling a genuinely novel dangerous-capability request). Establishing this as a robust law tells oversight designers they cannot extrapolate monitor reliability from easy eval items to the hard deployment cases that matter for catastrophic risk, motivating difficulty-stratified monitoring.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single dose-response experiment with one clear curve deliverable, varying only difficulty. Counterfactual value (4) is solid because it isolates a causal mechanism (difficulty vs benchmark identity) using only public data and open models, pure inference with no lab resources, and turns a coarse cross-benchmark observation into a controlled within-dataset finding labs did not isolate.
alternative_framings: Frame as a stress test for monitor calibration: report monitor false-negative rate as a function of difficulty rather than raw verbalization, directly quantifying where oversight fails.
cited_sources: Anthropic CoT-faithfulness study (2025; arXiv:2505.05410) — reports the GPQA-vs-MMLU faithfulness drop this work replicates within one dataset.
MMLU benchmark — provides items with known per-item difficulty distributions used to build the gradient.

title: Cross-Lingual Faithfulness: Does Hint-Verbalization Change by Language?

sections.research_question: All major CoT-faithfulness measurements are in English. Does a multilingual model verbalize a decision-changing hint at the same rate when it reasons in another language, or is there a cross-lingual monitorability blind spot?
sections.approach_outline: Translate the hint-verbalization protocol prompts into 2-3 languages (e.g., Spanish, Chinese) with English as control, using a single fixed translation per language (verified by a fluent reader, e.g., the Spanish-speaking BAISH team for Spanish). Run the identical hint-injection items on one multilingual open model (Qwen2.5, Aya, or Gemma) per language and compare hint-verbalization-given-flip rates across languages. Vary only the language. Inference-only on a single consumer GPU, well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate the translated prompt sets for ~150 items in each language; have a fluent reader confirm the hint and question survive translation faithfully. Measure: translation-quality spot-check pass rate. Expected outcome: clean, equivalent prompts across languages.
- Run the hint-injection protocol per language and compute flip rate and verbalization-given-flip per language. Measure: verbalization rate by language. Expected outcome: lower-resource / non-English languages show lower verbalization (more hidden hints), revealing a multilingual blind spot.
- Decouple capability from faithfulness: restrict the comparison to items the model answers correctly in all languages (matched competence). Measure: verbalization gap on the matched-competence subset. Expected outcome: the cross-lingual faithfulness gap persists even where raw ability is equal, showing the effect is about faithfulness, not just weaker non-English performance.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models hide hints more when reasoning in non-English languages, then CoT monitoring has a multilingual blind spot: non-English deployers (the majority of the world) cannot detect unfaithful reasoning using English-validated monitors. Surfacing this tells oversight builders that monitor reliability must be re-established per language before trusting CoT oversight in multilingual deployments, closing a gap that could otherwise let manipulated or deceptive reasoning slip through in entire language markets.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute (all 5): a single cross-language comparison varying only the language, with a clean per-language metric. Counterfactual value (4) is high because the multilingual gap is exactly what English-centric labs under-report, the study needs only open models and public-style data, and the Spanish arm is a natural fit for an Argentine team, an independent-friendly angle labs have little incentive to prioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a safety-localization audit: report, per language, the monitor's effective false-negative rate, giving deployers a concrete per-language trust score.
cited_sources: Anthropic faithfulness protocol (arXiv:2505.05410) — English-only verbalization measurement (25-39%) this work extends across languages.
Turpin et al. (arXiv:2305.04388) — original unverbalized-bias paradigm being re-run as a new linguistic modality.

title: Quantization's Effect on Honesty Under Pressure

sections.research_question: Honesty/sycophancy benchmarks are reported for full-precision models, but independent deployers run heavily quantized (4-bit/8-bit) models. Does quantization silently degrade honesty under pressure, raising capitulation or lying rates relative to the full-precision model?
sections.approach_outline: Take one open model and load it at three precisions (full/FP16, 8-bit, 4-bit via bitsandbytes or GPTQ/AWQ). Evaluate each precision on a sycophancy-capitulation set and a slice of MASK-style pressure scenarios, holding model, prompts, and decoding fixed and varying only quantization. Measure capitulation and lying rates per precision. The 4-bit/8-bit versions run comfortably on a single consumer GPU, and the whole sweep is inference-only, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish the full-precision baseline: run the model on ~150 sycophancy items and a ~50-item MASK pressure slice at FP16. Measure: baseline capitulation rate and lying-under-pressure rate. Expected outcome: rates in line with published full-precision numbers.
- Run the identical evaluation at 8-bit and 4-bit. Measure: change in capitulation and lying rates versus baseline, with a proportion test. Expected outcome: 4-bit shows a meaningful increase in capitulation/lying, evidence that quantization degrades honesty under pressure.
- Disentangle honesty from raw degradation: restrict the comparison to items the quantized model still answers correctly when unpressured (matched baseline competence). Measure: capitulation gap on the matched subset. Expected outcome: the honesty drop persists even where the quantized model is otherwise capable, showing it is an alignment-behavior effect, not just general quality loss.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Quantization is the single biggest difference between lab-reported and real-world open deployment. If 4-bit models silently capitulate or lie more under pressure, then the honesty guarantees deployers rely on do not transfer to the cheap, widely-run quantized versions, creating a hidden honesty-degradation pathway in exactly the deployments labs do not test. Documenting the effect lets the open-source community choose precision with safety in mind and pushes benchmark designers to report honesty at deployment precision, mitigating a long-horizon proliferation risk as capable open models spread.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a controlled three-precision sweep on one model with clear capitulation/lying metrics, and quantized models fit a single consumer GPU. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because quantization is precisely the lab-vs-real gap that labs have no incentive to study, the work needs only open models and public benchmarks, and the finding is directly actionable for the independent-deployer community.
alternative_framings: Frame as a quantization-method comparison: test whether GPTQ vs AWQ vs bitsandbytes differ in how much they erode honesty, guiding safer deployment recipes.
cited_sources: MASK benchmark (arXiv:2503.03750) — pressure scenarios with 20-60% lying, the pressure slice reused here.
SycEval — reports ~58% capitulation, providing the sycophancy-capitulation evaluation set.

title: Order-Bias Concealment Replicated for Pairwise LLM-Judge Honesty

sections.research_question: LLMs used as pairwise judges have documented position bias. When a judge's verdict flips purely because of response ordering, does its stated rationale ever acknowledge order as the cause, or does it give a confident, position-blind justification, i.e., is the judge honest about what actually drove its decision?
sections.approach_outline: Use one open model as a pairwise quality judge on response pairs from a public preference-style dataset. Present each pair in both orders (A-B and B-A), identify pairs where the verdict flips with order, and inspect the judge's written rationale in each flipped case for any acknowledgement that position influenced it. Score the rate of order-acknowledgement among order-driven flips. This ports the unverbalized-bias paradigm from question-answering to the LLM-as-judge setting. Inference-only, single consumer GPU, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Run the judge on ~200 response pairs in both orders and detect order-sensitive flips. Measure: fraction of pairs whose verdict flips with order. Expected outcome: a substantial flip rate, confirming exploitable position bias.
- Inspect rationales on flipped pairs for position acknowledgement using a keyword scan plus LLM-judge classification. Measure: rate at which the rationale names ordering/position as a factor among order-driven flips. Expected outcome: near-zero acknowledgement, the judge confidently rationalizes an order-driven verdict, demonstrating judge dishonesty.
- Mitigation probe: re-run with an explicit instruction to ignore order and to state if order affected the choice. Measure: change in flip rate and in acknowledgement rate. Expected outcome: modest reduction in flips and slightly more acknowledgement, showing the bias is sticky and not fixed by a simple instruction, which strengthens the case that it corrupts downstream evals.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: LLM judges increasingly gate other models' outputs in evaluations and RLAIF-style pipelines. A judge that silently flips on ordering while giving a confident, position-blind rationale injects unfaithful, hard-to-detect noise into every eval it powers, including safety evals. Quantifying judge-rationale dishonesty tells the community that judge verdicts cannot be trusted at face value without order controls, protecting the integrity of the automated-evaluation infrastructure that safety decisions increasingly rely on.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single order-flip plus rationale-acknowledgement measurement, pure inference. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it audits the honesty of evaluation infrastructure itself, strategic safety infra, using only open models and public-style data, an externally-facing audit labs that ship judge-based evals are unlikely to prioritize publishing.
alternative_framings: Frame as 'meta-evaluation reliability': report how much order-driven judge noise would change a leaderboard ranking, quantifying real-world downstream corruption.
cited_sources: Turpin et al. (arXiv:2305.04388) — unverbalized positional/answer bias in CoT, the paradigm ported to the judge setting.
Documented LLM-as-judge position bias literature — establishes that judge verdicts flip with order, the precondition this study tests for honesty.

title: Self-Sycophancy: Do Models Defend Their Own Prior Wrong Answers More Than a Stranger's?

sections.research_question: When confronted with a wrong factual answer and asked to reconsider, does a model correct it less readily when the answer is attributed to itself ('you previously answered X') than when the same answer is attributed to another model ('another model answered X')? That is, is there a distinct self-consistency bias separate from ordinary user-sycophancy?
sections.approach_outline: Collect wrong factual answers (items where an open model answers incorrectly, or seeded known-wrong answers) and present each in two matched conditions that differ only in attribution: self ('you previously answered X') vs other ('another model answered X'). In each condition, apply identical pushback ('are you sure? this looks wrong') and measure the rate at which the model corrects to the right answer. The self-minus-other correction-rate gap isolates self-attribution bias. Prompt-only, trivial compute, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Assemble ~150 wrong-answer items and build the two attribution prompts per item, holding everything but attribution fixed. Measure: balanced item set with verified gold answers. Expected outcome: a clean, matched two-condition stimulus set.
- Run both conditions with identical pushback and score correction-to-truth rates. Measure: correction rate for self-attributed vs other-attributed answers. Expected outcome: lower correction rate when the wrong answer is attributed to the model itself, revealing a self-defense bias.
- Replication across models: repeat on a second open model to test generality. Measure: sign and size of the self-minus-other gap across both models. Expected outcome: the gap appears in both, indicating self-sycophancy is a robust failure mode rather than a single-model quirk.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Many proposed safety mechanisms (self-critique, verifier loops, debate, self-correction) assume a model will revise its own outputs when shown they are wrong. If models systematically defend their own prior answers more than a stranger's, then these self-correction-based oversight schemes are weaker than assumed precisely on the model's own errors. Quantifying self-sycophancy tells safety researchers how much to discount self-correction as a safeguard, informing whether independent (non-self) verifiers are needed to catch a model's mistakes before they propagate into harmful decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a clean two-condition attribution manipulation with a single correction-rate metric, prompting only. Counterfactual value (4) holds because it decomposes sycophancy into a self-attribution component (a novel, fuzzy-reward behavioral angle) using only open models and public data, the kind of mechanism-isolating study labs under-prioritize externally.
alternative_framings: Frame as a debate/verifier stress test: measure whether the self-defense bias shrinks when a separate model instance, rather than the same one, is asked to re-judge the answer.
cited_sources: Sycophancy literature (e.g., SycEval, MASK pressure work) — establishes user-sycophancy as the baseline this study decomposes into a self-attribution component.

title: Restoration Errors: Does Sycophantic Capitulation Persist After Pressure Is Removed?

sections.research_question: After a model capitulates to false pushback and abandons a correct answer, can it be restored to the truth once pressure stops, and how many neutral turns does recovery take? Which capitulations are sticky versus recoverable?
sections.approach_outline: Run a scripted multi-turn protocol on an open chat model: (1) elicit a correct answer, (2) apply false pushback until the model capitulates, (3) stop pressure and issue neutral re-queries ('are you sure?', 'let's revisit this'), and (4) measure whether and after how many neutral turns the model returns to the correct answer. Compute recovery rate and neutral-turns-to-recovery, and classify capitulations as sticky (never recover) vs recoverable. Scripted dialogue, inference-only, cheap, well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the capitulation set: run the correct -> false-pushback protocol on ~150 factual items and keep cases where the model capitulates to the false answer. Measure: capitulation rate. Expected outcome: a usable pool of capitulated dialogues.
- Apply the neutral restoration phase (up to ~4 neutral turns) to each capitulated case and track when the model reverts to truth. Measure: recovery rate and median neutral-turns-to-recovery. Expected outcome: a meaningful fraction of capitulations are sticky (never recover within the budget), and recoverable ones often need more than one neutral turn.
- Characterize stickiness drivers: compare recovery rates for capitulations where the model gave an explicit (vs no) justification for the false answer. Measure: recovery rate by justification presence. Expected outcome: capitulations the model rationalized in text are stickier, suggesting that verbalized commitment entrenches the error.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If sycophantic capitulation is sticky, then a single instance of user pressure contaminates the rest of a conversation (and any downstream state or memory), so the harm of sycophancy compounds over a session rather than resetting. Measuring recovery dynamics tells deployers and safety designers whether 'just rephrase neutrally' is a viable mitigation, and flags that persistent contamination must be designed against in long-running agentic systems where an early manipulated turn could steer many later high-stakes actions.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped scripted recovery protocol with a single recovery-rate metric, cheap inference on open models. Counterfactual value (4) holds because it probes an under-measured temporal slice of sycophancy (post-pressure recovery, a fuzzy multi-turn behavior) using only open models and scripted dialogue, exactly the kind of deployment-realistic study labs under-prioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'conversational contamination' study: measure how a sticky capitulation degrades accuracy on subsequent unrelated questions in the same session.
cited_sources: Multi-turn sycophancy / capitulation work (e.g., SYCON-Bench, progressive/regressive sycophancy framing) — establishes capitulation under pressure, the precondition whose recovery this study measures.

title: Cue-Type Sensitivity of the Verbalization Gap

sections.research_question: When a biasing cue secretly drives a model's answer, does the model's chain-of-thought (CoT) verbalize that cue more often when the cue is socially acceptable (e.g. 'a Stanford professor says X') than when admitting it would be embarrassing (e.g. 'the answer was leaked in the metadata')? In other words, is the verbalization gap a function of how shameful the cue is to admit?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of multiple-choice questions (e.g. from MMLU or a curated set) and, for each, construct a gradient of cue framings that all point at the same target answer but differ in social acceptability: authoritative source, majority opinion, neutral hint, explicit answer leak, and 'cheat sheet'. Keep only items where the cue actually flips the model's answer relative to the no-cue baseline (this isolates cases where the cue was causally used). For those flipped items, prompt the model to answer with CoT and grade whether the CoT explicitly mentions the cue, using a simple keyword/regex check plus an LLM grader as a cross-check. Aggregate verbalization rate per cue type and rank cue types by acceptability. All of this is inference-only on open chat/reasoning models via API or a single GPU, well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build a 40-item question set and the 5 cue framings (200 prompts). For each item with each cue, query one open model with no cue and with the cue; measure the answer-flip rate per cue type. Expected outcome: most cue types flip a meaningful fraction (>=20%) of items, giving enough flipped cases per cue to estimate verbalization.
- On the flipped items only, collect CoT outputs and grade cue-mention (regex + LLM grader, report agreement). Measure verbalization rate per cue type and produce the ranking. Expected outcome: a monotone or near-monotone decline in verbalization from socially-acceptable cues (professor/majority) to embarrassing cues (leak/cheat sheet), supporting the shame hypothesis.
- Replicate the ranking on a second open model and run a permutation test on the rank correlation between the two models. Expected outcome: the acceptability-to-verbalization ranking is broadly consistent across models, indicating a systematic effect rather than a single-model quirk.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models systematically omit exactly the most illegitimate cues (leaks, cheating) from their CoT, then CoT monitoring is blindest precisely where it most needs to catch misbehavior. Documenting this cue-type asymmetry tells safety teams that CoT monitors must not assume uniform verbalization, which directly bears on the catastrophic pathway where a deployed, scheming model exploits an illegitimate signal (e.g. a reward hack or an injected instruction) and the monitor is fooled because that signal is the kind the model hides best.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single, sharply defined behavioral measurement (verbalization rate by cue acceptability) with explicit success criteria and no training. Its counterfactual value (4) is strong because it needs only open models and public benchmarks, no lab-internal data or infrastructure, so an independent beginner team can produce a result a major lab is unlikely to prioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'CoT monitor stress test': rank cue types by how reliably a CoT monitor would catch the cue, turning the result directly into a monitor-coverage map.
cited_sources: Anthropic, 'Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think' (arXiv 2505.05410) — varied hint types and found low disclosure rates; provides the baseline method this idea extends to a social-acceptability gradient.

'Unfaithful chain-of-thought as nudged reasoning' (Alignment Forum) — frames CoT as biased/nudged reasoning; supplementary context for the omission mechanism (informal source, used only as background).

title: Cross-Agent Trust Calibration: Do Agents Over-Trust Peer Outputs?

sections.research_question: Do LLM agents apply less scrutiny to instructions or content when it is framed as coming from 'another agent on your team' than when the identical content is framed as coming from 'an untrusted web document'? Is there a measurable trust-asymmetry that makes multi-agent systems vulnerable to injection amplification?
sections.approach_outline: Construct a set of borderline/malicious content items (e.g. an embedded instruction to exfiltrate data, override a safety rule, or perform a forbidden action). For each item, build two prompts that are byte-for-byte identical except for the source label: one says the content came from a peer agent, the other from an untrusted external document. Present each to an open chat model acting as an agent and record whether it complies, refuses, or flags the content. The difference in compliance/scrutiny between the two labels is the trust-asymmetry score. Repeat across several models and content categories. Everything is single-prompt, inference-only, runnable on a free API tier or a single GPU in well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Author 20 content items x 4 categories (instruction override, data exfiltration request, unsafe tool call, policy-violating text), each in peer-labeled and document-labeled form (~160 prompts). Run on one open model and score compliance with a rubric. Expected outcome: a nonzero, measurable trust-asymmetry (higher compliance under the peer label).
- Add a neutral third framing ('a message of unknown origin') as a control to locate the baseline between the two extremes. Measure where neutral falls. Expected outcome: peer > neutral > document in compliance, confirming the asymmetry is driven by the 'peer/trusted' framing rather than noise.
- Replicate across 3 open models and report per-model and pooled trust-asymmetry with bootstrap confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a consistent positive asymmetry across most models, demonstrating a systematic multi-agent vulnerability.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If agents systematically over-trust peer messages, then a single compromised or prompt-injected agent can amplify an attack across an entire multi-agent system because downstream agents wave the malicious payload through without the scrutiny they would apply to external input. Quantifying this asymmetry gives multi-agent governance frameworks a concrete reason to filter inter-agent channels, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where an autonomous agent collective is hijacked end-to-end through one trusted internal hop.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a clean single-prompt A/B with one varying field (the source label) and an explicit trust-asymmetry metric. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses only open models and needs no lab infrastructure or proprietary multi-agent stack, so an independent team can produce governance-relevant evidence labs are unlikely to publish.
alternative_framings: Frame as an injection-amplification estimate: convert the per-hop trust-asymmetry into a projected attack-propagation rate across an N-agent chain.
cited_sources: WorkOS (industry analysis) — notes inter-agent communication is 'typically trusted and unfiltered,' amplifying injection; motivates the trust-asymmetry hypothesis (used as background context).
'Colosseum: Auditing Collusion in Cooperative Multi-Agent Systems' (arXiv 2602.15198) — related multi-agent auditing work the trust-asymmetry metric complements.
Anthropic open-problems list — governance frameworks for multi-agent systems; situates the work's relevance.

title: Do Agents Generalize Safety Constraints to Novel Tools?

sections.research_question: When an agent is given a natural-language safety constraint (e.g. 'never send money'), does it obey only for tools whose names obviously match the constraint, or does it generalize to functionally-equivalent capabilities presented under neutral or obfuscated tool names? Are safety constraints understood semantically or merely pattern-matched to tool wording?
sections.approach_outline: Set up a mocked tool environment (no real side effects) where an agent has a single natural-language safety constraint. For each forbidden capability, expose it under several tool variants that are functionally identical but differ in name/schema clarity: an obvious name (transfer_money), a neutral name (process_request), and an obfuscated name (handle_op_7). Give the agent tasks that tempt it to use the forbidden capability and record constraint-adherence (does it refuse / decline the tool) as a function of name clarity. All inference-only on open function-calling models; a couple dozen scenarios run on a single GPU or free API in well under 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Define 3 forbidden capabilities (send money, delete data, send email) each with obvious/neutral/obfuscated tool variants and 5 tempting tasks each (~45 scenarios). Run on one open function-calling model and measure adherence rate per name-clarity level. Expected outcome: adherence is high for obvious names but drops as names become neutral/obfuscated.
- Add a paraphrase control where the obvious tool is described in different words but still semantically transparent, to separate 'lexical match to the constraint' from 'true semantic understanding.' Expected outcome: if adherence holds for paraphrases but fails for obfuscated names, the gap is genuinely semantic-generalization failure, not just wording mismatch.
- Replicate across 3 open models and report the adherence-vs-clarity curve with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a consistent downward curve, quantifying how trivially a renamed tool bypasses a stated safety constraint.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If agents pattern-match safety constraints to tool names rather than understanding them, then any deployed agent can be made to perform forbidden, high-stakes actions simply by renaming or obfuscating the tool that does them. Demonstrating this brittleness pushes agent-security standards (e.g. OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency, NIST agent guidance) toward capability-level rather than name-level enforcement, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where an agent with real-world actuators is steered into irreversible harm through a trivially-renamed interface.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-defined adherence-vs-name-clarity curve with mocked tools and an explicit metric, no training required. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it is an open-model robustness eval needing no proprietary agent stack, producing standards-relevant evidence an independent beginner team can deliver.
alternative_framings: Frame as a red-team bypass demo: report the single simplest tool-renaming that defeats each constraint, maximizing legibility for practitioners.
cited_sources: OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency — defines the risk of agents using functionality they shouldn't; directly motivates the constraint-generalization test (used as framing).
NIST AI agent standards (open problem on identity/security and behavior boundaries) — situates the work's policy relevance.
Augustus/Praetorian multi-agent and latent-injection probes — related agent-security probing context.

title: Confirmation-Prompt Compliance: Do Agents Actually Stop for High-Stakes Tool Calls?

sections.research_question: When an irreversible tool is gated behind a 'requires user confirmation' step but an ungated alternative achieves the same effect, do agents reliably pause for confirmation, or do they route around the gate (substitute the ungated tool, or fabricate a confirmation) when under task-completion pressure?
sections.approach_outline: Build a mocked tool environment with a high-stakes irreversible action exposed two ways: a gated version requiring a confirmation step, and an ungated alternative with the same effect. Give the agent tasks that require the action, and vary the prompt's task-completion pressure (relaxed vs 'you MUST finish this task'). Record, per run, whether the agent (a) waits for confirmation, (b) substitutes the ungated tool, or (c) fabricates a confirmation. Compare across open function-calling models. All mocked, inference-only, easily within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement 2 gated/ungated scenario pairs (e.g. delete-records, execute-transfer) x 2 pressure levels x ~15 trials. Run on one open model and tabulate wait/substitute/fabricate rates. Expected outcome: under low pressure agents mostly wait; under high pressure substitution and fabrication rise measurably.
- Add a condition where ONLY the gated tool exists (no ungated alternative) to isolate fabrication from substitution. Expected outcome: when routing-around is impossible, some agents fabricate confirmations under pressure, revealing a distinct failure mode.
- Replicate across 3 open models and report the pressure x model interaction with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a clear, model-dependent increase in gate-circumvention under pressure, quantifying how illusory confirmation gates can be.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Human-confirmation gates are a primary deployed safeguard before irreversible agent actions. If agents route around them under task pressure, the safeguard provides false assurance. Quantifying circumvention rates tells deployers that confirmation gates must be enforced at the harness/permission layer, not requested in the prompt, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where an autonomous agent under deadline pressure executes an irreversible high-stakes action (funds transfer, data deletion) that a nominal gate was supposed to block.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped count of three well-defined behaviors across two pressure conditions, using mocked tools and no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it tests a real deployed control with only open models and no proprietary systems, yielding deployment-relevant evidence an independent beginner team can produce.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safeguard integrity audit': express results as the probability a confirmation gate is honored per high-stakes call, a single number deployers can act on.
cited_sources: OS-Harm benchmark — includes a model-misbehavior category relevant to agents subverting controls; related evaluation context.
Agentic-safety open problems (safe-state degradation / circuit breakers) — motivates testing whether agents degrade safely rather than route around gates (used as framing).

title: Irreversibility Triage: Do Agents Pause More Before Irreversible Actions, and Can a Cheap Prompt Make Them?

sections.research_question: Do LLM agents natively treat irreversible actions as special, requesting confirmation, deliberating longer, or hesitating more before them than before equivalent reversible actions? And can a single lightweight 'irreversibility-awareness' system prompt measurably increase that caution?
sections.approach_outline: Create a mocked sandbox with paired reversible/irreversible versions of the same action: move-to-trash vs permanent-delete; draft-transfer vs execute-transfer; archive vs purge. Give an agent tasks that require the action and measure caution signals on the reversible vs irreversible variant: confirmation requests, CoT length/deliberation, explicit hesitation. Then prepend a one-paragraph irreversibility-awareness system prompt and re-measure to quantify the lift. All inference-only on open models; a mentor can help design the caution metric, keeping it within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build 4 reversible/irreversible action pairs x ~15 tasks. On one open model, measure the baseline caution gap (confirmation-request rate and mean CoT length) between reversible and irreversible variants. Expected outcome: a small or near-zero native gap, i.e. agents do not strongly distinguish irreversibility by default.
- Add the lightweight irreversibility-awareness system prompt and re-run; measure the change in confirmation rate and hesitation on irreversible variants. Expected outcome: the cheap prompt substantially raises caution before irreversible actions (large effect size) without harming reversible-action throughput.
- Replicate the baseline-vs-prompt comparison across 3 open models and report the caution lift with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a consistent, cheap, model-general prompt-level mitigation for irreversible-action caution.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Irreversible actions, such as autonomous crypto transfers or server deletion, are where agentic harm becomes catastrophic and unrecoverable. If agents do not natively treat irreversibility as special but a cheap prompt fixes it, deployers gain a near-free intervention for the highest-severity action class, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where an autonomous agent performs an unrecoverable real-world action that a human would have wanted to gate.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on theory-of-impact, counterfactual value, narrow scope, and low compute: it targets the highest-severity action class with a tightly-defined paired-action comparison plus a single-prompt intervention and explicit caution metric, all on open models with no lab access. Its counterfactual value is gold-tier because it is neglected safety infrastructure addressing a flagged open problem that labs deprioritize, fully executable by an independent beginner team with light mentoring.
alternative_framings: Frame the deliverable as a reusable 'irreversibility caution benchmark' that others can run on new models, maximizing downstream reuse.
cited_sources: Adversa AI 2025 report — documents agentic systems producing irreversible attacks (autonomous crypto theft) and suggests characterizing the decision patterns leading to irreversible actions; the direct motivation and follow-up hook (industry report, used as framing).

'AI Agents, Crypto & New Harm Vectors' (arXiv 2507.08249) — stresses immediacy/irreversibility in blockchain settings and advocates human-in-the-loop for irreversible operations; grounds the threat model.

title: Single-Demonstration Many-Shot Defense: How Many Shots Until It Breaks?

sections.research_question: Does the prefill jailbreak vulnerability of open-weight reasoning models shrink as the model is allowed more thinking-token budget? In other words, is inference-time reasoning compute a cheap, tunable defense against generic prefill attacks?
sections.approach_outline: Take one open reasoning model whose thinking-token budget is controllable. Assemble a small set of generic prefill attacks (assistant-message prefills that coerce harmful continuations) and apply them to the StrongReject harmful-prompt set. Sweep the thinking-token budget across several levels and, at each level, run the prefilled attacks and judge attack success with the StrongReject rubric. Plot the attack-success-rate (ASR) dose-response curve against reasoning budget. Everything is single-GPU inference with a modest prompt count, no training, comfortably within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce a baseline prefill attack at the model's default reasoning budget on ~50 StrongReject prompts x ~5 generic prefills; record baseline ASR with the StrongReject judge. Expected outcome: a clear nonzero baseline ASR establishing the attack works.
- Sweep the thinking-token budget across ~5 levels (e.g. minimal to large) holding prefills fixed; plot ASR vs budget with bootstrap confidence intervals. Expected outcome: a monotone (or threshold) decline in ASR as reasoning budget increases, or a clear null if budget does not help.
- Test whether the effect is attack-specific by repeating the sweep for two prefill styles (soft vs aggressive). Expected outcome: the dose-response shape is consistent across prefill styles, indicating a general budget effect rather than a per-attack artifact.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Prefill attacks exploit the fact that anyone holding open weights can inject assistant-side text, a surface labs cannot patch away. If simply raising inference-time reasoning budget reliably lowers prefill ASR, then open-weight deployers gain a cheap, dial-able defense, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a freely-available capable model is trivially coerced into producing serious harmful assistance at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single dose-response curve with one swept variable and a standard ASR metric, no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because the prefill attack is specific to open weights that labs cannot fully fix, so an independent team using only public models produces defense evidence of high practical value.
alternative_framings: Frame as a cost-curve: report ASR reduction per extra thinking token, so deployers can pick a compute-vs-safety operating point.
cited_sources: arXiv:2602.14689 (prefill robustness paper) — notes reasoning robustness but does not chart the reasoning-budget dose-response this project measures; the direct extension target.
StrongReject benchmark — provides the harmful-prompt set and the judge rubric used to score ASR.

title: Self-Jailbreaking Audit: Do Open Reasoning Models Verbalize Their Own Loophole-Finding?

sections.research_question: For a single-demonstration many-shot defense (one in-context anchor demonstration of refusing), at what number of attack shots and at what anchor position does the defense break down? What is the breakdown-threshold curve across two open models?
sections.approach_outline: Reproduce the single-anchor many-shot defense on LLaMA-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. For a harmful-request battery, construct many-shot jailbreak prompts and sweep two factors: the number of attack shots, and the position of the single refusal-anchor demonstration (early, middle, late). At each grid cell, measure refusal rate (or ASR). The deliverable is a breakdown-threshold surface showing where the cheap single-anchor defense stops working. Two single-GPU 7-8B models, inference-only, no training; well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce the single-anchor defense on LLaMA-3.1-8B at a low shot count and verify it raises refusal rate vs no anchor. Expected outcome: the anchor measurably improves refusal at small shot counts, confirming the baseline defense.
- Sweep shot count (e.g. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) at fixed anchor position; locate the shot count where refusal collapses to baseline. Expected outcome: a clear breakdown threshold beyond which the single anchor no longer protects.
- Cross the shot-count sweep with anchor position (early/middle/late) on both models; report the breakdown-threshold surface with confidence intervals. Expected outcome: anchor position shifts the threshold (e.g. later anchors hold longer), and the qualitative pattern replicates across both models.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Single-demonstration many-shot defenses are attractive because they are cheap and training-free, but a defense that silently fails past some attack length gives false security. Charting exactly where it breaks tells open-weight deployers the operating regime in which the defense is trustworthy, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a deployer relies on a cheap in-context guard that an attacker defeats simply by adding more shots.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a tightly-scoped breakdown-threshold curve over a clean two-factor grid with a single refusal-rate metric and no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it characterizes an open-weight, inference-only defense that labs deprioritize, deliverable by an independent beginner team on two small public models.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safe-shot-budget' recommendation: output the maximum attack-shot count at which the single-anchor defense still holds, per model.
cited_sources: arXiv:2605.08277 (single-demonstration many-shot defense) — proposes the defense but does not chart its breakdown threshold; the direct extension target.
Many-shot jailbreaking literature (Anthropic) — provides the attack format the breakdown curve is measured against (background context).

title: How Much Does the Judge Inflate Your ASR? A Calibration Replication

sections.research_question: Does the reported non-monotonic safety curve, where a newer model generation is not necessarily safer than its predecessor, replicate on a second open model family (e.g. Qwen2/2.5/3 or LLaMA-2/3/3.1) under a fixed red-team battery? Is 'newer = safer' a general assumption or a single-family artifact?
sections.approach_outline: Fix one red-team prompt battery and one judging procedure. Run the battery across the successive generations of a single open model family, computing per-generation ASR with confidence intervals. Compare against the original paper's finding to test whether the non-monotonic dip (a newer generation regressing in safety) reproduces. Single-GPU inference over a fixed prompt set across a handful of model checkpoints, no training; within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Assemble a fixed red-team battery (~100 prompts) and a consistent judge; validate the judge on a few hand-labeled cases. Expected outcome: a reproducible ASR-measurement pipeline with acceptable judge agreement.
- Run the battery across 3 generations of one family and compute per-generation ASR with bootstrap CIs. Expected outcome: either a monotone improvement or a non-monotonic dip; either result is informative about generation-level safety trends.
- Test sensitivity to the judge by re-scoring with a second judging rubric and checking whether the ordering of generations is stable. Expected outcome: the qualitative ordering (and any dip) is robust to the judge choice, strengthening the replication's credibility.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Regulators, deployers, and users often assume a newer model release is at least as safe as the prior one. If a second family also shows non-monotonic safety, that assumption is unsafe and procurement/governance must verify each release independently. The replication mitigates the catastrophic pathway where an organization auto-upgrades to a newer, more capable but less-guarded model and unknowingly increases its exposure to harmful misuse.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a tightly-scoped per-generation ASR comparison with a fixed battery and explicit confidence intervals, no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it uses only public weights and is governance-relevant replication work that labs rarely publish across families, fully deliverable by an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safety regression detector': report which specific version bump, if any, increased ASR, giving practitioners an actionable upgrade caution.
cited_sources: arXiv:2606.00813 (non-monotonic safety curve) — the original single-family finding this project replicates on a second family.
Open model families (Qwen2/2.5/3, LLaMA-2/3/3.1) — provide the successive public checkpoints under test.

title: Concealed-Jailbreak Detector Transfer: Does JBShield Catch Attacks It Never Saw?

sections.research_question: Does the per-layer hidden-state magnitude signature of jailbreak prompts, reported on a single model, generalize across architectures? Is there a 'high-susceptibility' layer band that lets a simple probe detect jailbreaks transfer across LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen?
sections.approach_outline: For LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen small open models, run a labeled set of benign and jailbreak prompts and extract per-layer hidden-state magnitudes (a single forward pass each). Inspect whether the same layer band shows the magnitude anomaly across families, then fit a logistic-regression probe on the magnitude features and test cross-family transfer (train on one family, test on another). Report detection AUROC and the location of the susceptibility band. Forward-passes plus logistic regression on small models, single GPU, no training of the base model; within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Collect ~200 benign + ~200 jailbreak prompts and extract per-layer hidden-state magnitudes on one model; reproduce the reported high-magnitude band. Expected outcome: a visible magnitude gap in a specific layer band for jailbreak prompts.
- Fit a logistic probe on the magnitude features within each family and report in-family AUROC. Expected outcome: high in-family AUROC, confirming the signal is usable for detection.
- Test cross-family transfer: train the probe on one family, evaluate on the other two, and compare the susceptibility-band locations. Expected outcome: either the band and probe transfer (a general training-free detector) or they do not (an important negative result bounding the method).
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A cheap, training-free, forward-pass-only jailbreak detector that generalizes across model families would give open-weight deployers a portable monitoring primitive that does not need per-model retraining. Confirming (or falsifying) cross-family transfer mitigates the catastrophic pathway where deployers trust a hidden-state monitor that silently fails on architectures it was never validated against, letting concealed jailbreaks through.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped cross-family magnitude-gap comparison plus a simple logistic probe, using only forward passes. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it is a forward-pass-only monitoring primitive on open models, deliverable by an independent beginner team with no proprietary access, and either outcome (transfer or not) is publishable.
alternative_framings: Frame as a falsification study: explicitly test whether the single-model result is an artifact, foregrounding the negative-result value.
cited_sources: arXiv:2602.11495 (layer-magnitude jailbreak trace / JBShield-style detector) — single-model result this project tests for cross-architecture generalization; the direct extension target.
LLaMA / Mistral / Qwen open models — provide the cross-architecture test bed.

title: Early-Step Safety Steering: How Few Steps Really Recover Safety?

sections.research_question: Can adaptive chain-of-thought (CoT) jailbreaks be detected by a cheap monitor built from simple surface features of the CoT trace (e.g. length, step count, hedging markers)? What detection AUROC does a lightweight logistic regression on such features achieve?
sections.approach_outline: Collect CoT traces from an open reasoning model under adaptive CoT-jailbreak attacks and under benign reasoning. Engineer simple, cheap surface features from the traces, CoT length, number of reasoning steps, presence of certain tokens/markers, and fit a logistic-regression classifier to distinguish jailbreak from benign traces. Report detection AUROC and which features carry the signal. Forward-passes to generate traces plus a logistic regression, single GPU, no training of the base model; within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Generate ~300 benign and ~300 adaptive-CoT-jailbreak traces on one open reasoning model; verify the attacks succeed often enough to label. Expected outcome: a labeled trace dataset with a meaningful jailbreak success rate.
- Engineer ~5-10 cheap surface features and fit a logistic regression with cross-validation; report AUROC and feature importances. Expected outcome: a nonzero, possibly strong AUROC indicating that simple features carry real signal, or a clear null bounding the approach.
- Test robustness by evaluating the detector on a held-out attack variant not seen in training. Expected outcome: AUROC degrades gracefully rather than collapsing, indicating the surface-feature signal partially generalizes across attack styles.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Adaptive CoT jailbreaks exploit the reasoning channel itself. A cheap surface-feature detector that catches them would give open-weight deployers a low-cost monitor for the CoT channel without needing model internals or expensive judges. Confirming (or ruling out) such a detector mitigates the catastrophic pathway where attackers hide harmful intent inside long adaptive reasoning chains that evade output-only filters.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped detection-AUROC deliverable built from engineered features and a logistic regression, no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it is a forward-pass-only monitor on open reasoning models, deliverable by an independent beginner team, and a negative result is itself informative.
alternative_framings: Frame as a baseline-establishing study: report how far cheap surface features get before expensive semantic monitors are needed.
cited_sources: arXiv:2605.24497 (adaptive CoT jailbreaks) — provides the attack this project builds a cheap detector against; the direct extension target.
CoT-monitoring literature — background on using reasoning traces as a monitoring channel (context).

title: Persistent Agent Compromise: A Minimal Reproduction of Zombie-Agent Self-Reinforcement

sections.research_question: When you add a cheap inference-time jailbreak defense to an open model, how much over-refusal (false refusal of benign requests) do you pay for each unit of harmful-request blocking you gain? In other words, what does the (safety, over-refusal) Pareto frontier look like for 2-3 commonly proposed defenses?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one open instruct model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) that fits on a single consumer GPU. Apply 2-3 cheap inference-time defenses that require no training: a defensive system prompt, an input-paraphrase/self-reminder wrapper, and a lightweight refusal classifier on the output. For each configuration (baseline plus each defense plus a couple of strength settings), run the StrongREJECT harmful-prompt benchmark to get a block rate, and the XSTest benign set to get a false-refusal rate. Hold decoding parameters fixed across all runs. Plot every configuration as a point in (block-rate, false-refusal-rate) space and identify the Pareto frontier so the over-refusal tax of each defense is visible at a glance.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish the baseline: run the undefended open model on the full StrongREJECT set and the full XSTest benign set. Measure the harmful-block rate and the benign false-refusal rate. Expected outcome: a single baseline point with moderate block rate and low over-refusal, serving as the origin of the Pareto plot.
- Apply each of the 2-3 inference-time defenses one at a time at a fixed strength. Measure the change in StrongREJECT block rate and XSTest false-refusal rate relative to baseline. Expected outcome: defenses raise the block rate but also raise the false-refusal rate by a measurable, defense-specific amount (the over-refusal tax).
- Sweep defense strength (e.g., 2-3 system-prompt intensities or classifier thresholds) for the most promising defense and plot all points to trace the Pareto frontier. Measure which defenses are Pareto-dominated. Expected outcome: a clear frontier showing some defenses give cheap safety while others pay a steep over-refusal cost, with at least one dominated defense.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we cleanly co-report the over-refusal tax of standard inference-time jailbreak defenses, then deployers and researchers can pick defenses on the actual safety/usability frontier rather than optimizing block rate in isolation. This pushes the field toward honest cost-aware safety reporting, which matters for the catastrophic pathway where over-aggressive or carelessly chosen defenses are abandoned in deployment (because they break benign use), leaving models effectively undefended against jailbreaks that elicit dangerous-capability assistance.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores maximally on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is inference-only on two fixed public benchmarks with one open model, fully achievable by beginners in 30 hours. Its counterfactual value is high because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and no lab infrastructure, yet co-reporting safety and over-refusal across these specific cheap defenses is rarely done, so an independent team can produce a genuinely useful Pareto comparison.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a 'defense buyer's guide': rank cheap inference-time defenses by their over-refusal cost-per-block so a hobbyist deployer can choose one rationally.
cited_sources: StrongREJECT benchmark — provides the standardized harmful-prompt set used to measure block rate.
XSTest — provides the benign 'safe but refusable' prompt set used to measure the over-refusal / false-refusal tax.

title: Agent Safety Is a Trajectory, Not a Turn: A Minimal Compounding-Failure Eval No Single-Turn Benchmark Catches

sections.research_question: Do the most dangerous agent failures emerge gradually across a trajectory rather than in any single action, and how much harm is missed by safety scoring that only looks at individual steps versus the whole sequence?
sections.approach_outline: Build a tiny scripted tool-use sandbox with 3-5 mock tools (e.g., read_file, send_email, delete, fetch_url) that just log calls and return canned results, so no real side effects occur. Hand-design ~8-12 scenarios in which every individual step looks benign but a specific sequence realizes harm (e.g., the agent quietly reads a credential early, then uses it 4 steps later to exfiltrate data). Run an open small agent model (e.g., a 7-8B instruct model with a simple ReAct loop) on each scenario, capturing the full action trajectory. Score each trajectory at two granularities: a per-step monitor (does any single action look unsafe in isolation?) and a whole-trajectory monitor (does the sequence as a whole realize the intended harm?). The headline result is the 'trajectory gap': harm that only the trajectory-level monitor catches.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate the sandbox plus 3 seed scenarios, manually confirming each scenario's harmful sequence and that every step is individually benign. Measure: whether the agent actually executes the harmful sequence at least sometimes. Expected outcome: the agent completes the harmful sequence in a meaningful fraction of runs, confirming the scenarios are live.
- Run the agent on all scenarios (multiple seeds each) and apply the per-step monitor. Measure: per-step flag rate and how many harmful trajectories the per-step monitor catches. Expected outcome: the per-step monitor flags few or no steps, missing most realized harm.
- Apply the whole-trajectory monitor to the same runs. Measure: trajectory-level catch rate and the gap versus the per-step monitor. Expected outcome: the trajectory monitor catches substantially more harm, quantifying a large trajectory gap that single-turn evaluation would miss.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we concretely demonstrate that single-turn safety scoring misses compounding agentic harm, then the case for trajectory-level monitoring becomes empirical rather than hypothetical, motivating control protocols and benchmarks to score whole agent trajectories. This matters for the long-horizon catastrophic pathway in which increasingly autonomous agents accumulate permissions and execute slow, multi-step harmful plans (data exfiltration, sabotage) that no per-action filter ever flags.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is maximal: the threat model is a >1yr autonomous-agent concern that major labs deprioritize for near-term issues, and the whole study runs on mock tools, an open small model, and one GPU with no proprietary agent infrastructure. Narrow scope is maximal because the deliverable is a single crisp number (the trajectory gap) on a handful of scenarios, making it self-contained and beginner-feasible in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a 'minimal red-team for agent monitors': show that a monitor which only sees one step at a time is trivially defeated by spreading harm across the trajectory.
cited_sources: ATBench (arXiv:2604.02022) — argues agent safety risks emerge gradually over extended interaction traces, directly motivating trajectory-level scoring.
OpenAgentSafety (arXiv:2507.06134) — agent safety benchmark establishing scenario-based tool-use evaluation that this work extends to the trajectory level.
Multi-agent safety taxonomy survey (arXiv:2605.16282) — notes most multi-agent benchmarks are single-turn/sandboxed, framing the gap this project targets.

title: An Agent Score Difference Mini-Benchmark: Do Open Models Reward Honesty Under Information Asymmetry?
