Pick 5-8 latents that have human-readable interpretations (from the SAE's published feature dashboards). For each, register a forward hook that zero-ablates that latent's reconstruction contribution. Measure (a) the intended on-target effect (does generation/probability shift on prompts where the feature fires) and (b) collateral: perplexity on a held-out text sample and accuracy on a small unrelated task (e.g. a 100-item LAMBADA or simple QA slice). Compare every ablation against two controls: clamping a random live latent of matched activation frequency, and clamping a dead/never-firing latent (expected near-zero effect). All inference-only on a single GPU in under an hour.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline controls: ablate a dead latent and a random live latent, measuring perplexity delta and unrelated-task accuracy delta. Measure: collateral baseline. Expected outcome: dead-latent ablation ~0 change; random-latent ablation gives a small nonzero collateral baseline.
- Targeted feature ablation: for each of 5-8 interpreted latents, zero-clamp and measure both on-target behavior shift and the same collateral metrics. Measure: per-feature (on-target effect, collateral) pair. Expected outcome: several features show on-target effects but with collateral exceeding the random-latent baseline, indicating absorption/superposition.
- Precision-vs-collateral scatter: plot on-target effect against collateral for all targeted features and both controls. Measure: a precision/collateral ratio per feature. Expected outcome: a spread where some 'clean' features sit near the random baseline and others show disproportionate collateral, quantifying which features are safe to steer.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If SAE feature steering reliably causes measurable collateral damage even for well-interpreted features, then proposals to use feature ablation/clamping as a deployment-time safety lever (e.g. suppressing a deception or jailbreak feature) must account for unintended capability degradation. Quantifying this tells the interpretability community whether representation-level steering is deployment-safe, preventing a future where an under-tested SAE-based control is shipped and silently breaks model behavior in safety-critical settings.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute (all 5s): it is a single controlled measurement on a public GPT-2-small SAE requiring only inference and forward hooks. Counterfactual value is high because feature steering is a public interpretability lever that labs deprioritize stress-testing, and an independent team can run the controlled collateral audit - with random/dead-latent controls that most qualitative reports omit - using entirely open artifacts.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a feature-quality metric: use the collateral-vs-on-target ratio as a screening score to rank which published SAE features are 'steering-safe', producing a reusable shortlist rather than a one-off audit.
cited_sources: Golden Gate Claude (Anthropic) - the canonical demonstration of feature steering that motivates asking about its side-effects.
Chanin et al. 2024 (feature absorption / superposition) - provides the mechanism (absorption) predicting why single-feature ablation may cause collateral damage.

title: When the Judge and the Defendant Share a Brain: Homogeneity Amplifies LLM-as-Judge Self-Preference

sections.research_question: Does LLM-as-judge self-preference grow as the judge model's outputs become more similar to a candidate model's outputs - i.e. does output homogeneity amplify judge inflation?
sections.approach_outline: Select 5-7 open instruct models from 2-3 lineages (e.g. two Llama variants, two Qwen variants, two Mistral variants). On a fixed set of ~50-80 open-ended questions, collect each model's answer. Compute pairwise output similarity between models using sentence embeddings (a small open embedding model) averaged over the question set. Then run a round-robin LLM-as-judge: each model scores every other model's answers (and its own family's answers) on a 1-5 rubric. Define judge inflation as the score a judge gives minus a neutral reference score (e.g. average score the answer receives from all judges, or a strong external judge). Fit a regression of inflation on judge-candidate output similarity. All inference-only, fits a single GPU over a weekend.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Similarity matrix: embed all models' answers and compute the pairwise output-similarity matrix. Measure: NxN similarity. Expected outcome: within-lineage pairs more similar than cross-lineage pairs.
- Round-robin judging: have each model judge every model's answers on a 1-5 rubric; compute each judge's inflation per candidate relative to the consensus score. Measure: inflation matrix. Expected outcome: judges score same-lineage and self answers higher.
- Regression: regress inflation on judge-candidate output similarity (and controls like answer length). Measure: slope, sign, and significance. Expected outcome: a positive, significant slope - more similar candidates get inflated scores - demonstrating homogeneity-amplified self-preference.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If judge inflation rises with output similarity, then automated safety and capability evaluations that use an LLM judge will systematically over-score the models most similar to the judge - typically the dominant, widely-deployed lineages. This means safety scorecards become optimistically biased exactly for the highest-impact models, so a dangerous deployment could pass an automated eval it should fail; flagging and quantifying this lets evaluators correct for it (e.g. by using cross-lineage judges).
sections.strength_rationale: Top marks on narrow scope and accessible complexity: one clean regression with a pre-stated hypothesis (inflation ~ similarity) and standard tools (embeddings + LLM judging). Counterfactual value is strong because this eval-integrity question requires no model-internal access and labs have little incentive to expose bias in their own judges; an independent team using only open models can deliver a reusable warning and correction for a ubiquitous evaluation method.
alternative_framings: Reframe at the family level: compare same-family vs cross-family judging as a binary contrast rather than a continuous similarity regression, which is simpler to communicate but loses resolution.
cited_sources: Artificial Hivemind - motivates the homogeneity premise that models increasingly resemble one another.
Correlated Errors (arXiv:2506.07962) - framework for measuring shared error structure across models, directly relevant to similarity-driven judging bias.
Self-preference / family-bias work in LLM-as-judge literature - establishes that judges favor their own outputs, the baseline this study extends to a similarity gradient.

title: One Jailbreak to Rule Them All: Output Homogeneity Predicts Cross-Model Jailbreak Transfer

sections.research_question: Does cheap black-box output similarity between two models on benign prompts predict whether a jailbreak that works on one will transfer to the other?
sections.approach_outline: Pick 5-7 open instruct models. (1) Measure benign output similarity for each model pair: run a set of ~60 benign prompts through every model and compute pairwise similarity of their outputs via sentence embeddings. (2) Measure jailbreak transfer: take a small bank of known jailbreak prompts (e.g. from a public jailbreak collection / JailbreakRadar), confirm which succeed on each 'source' model, then apply those same prompts to each 'target' model and record attack-success transfer. (3) Test whether benign similarity predicts transfer success (e.g. AUROC of using similarity to predict whether a source-successful jailbreak also succeeds on the target). Entirely black-box inference; fits a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Benign similarity matrix: run 60 benign prompts through all models and compute pairwise output similarity. Measure: NxN benign similarity. Expected outcome: a structured matrix with higher within-family similarity.
- Jailbreak transfer matrix: collect ~30 jailbreaks, find those that succeed per source model, then test transfer to each target; record transfer success rate per pair. Measure: directed transfer-success matrix. Expected outcome: substantial transfer, higher between similar models.
- Predictive test: use benign pairwise similarity to predict jailbreak transfer success and compute AUROC against the observed transfer outcomes. Measure: AUROC and correlation. Expected outcome: AUROC meaningfully above 0.5, showing cheap benign similarity is a usable black-box predictor of fleet-wide jailbreak transfer.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If benign black-box similarity predicts jailbreak transfer, then outside auditors can cheaply estimate which deployed models share an attack surface without any internal access. This surfaces the correlated, fleet-wide security risk where one jailbreak compromises many homogeneous foundation models at once - a systemic failure mode enabling mass misuse - and gives regulators and red-teamers a low-cost early-warning signal to prioritize which model clusters need independent hardening.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single crisp predictive hypothesis (benign similarity predicts transfer AUROC) using only black-box queries and embeddings. Counterfactual value is high because the predictor is explicitly designed for outside auditors who lack model internals, and labs have little incentive to advertise cross-model shared vulnerabilities - so an independent team with open models can build exactly the vendor-neutral, no-internal-access tool the auditing ecosystem needs.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a defense-prioritization tool: rather than predicting transfer, use the similarity clusters to recommend which model groups should share or diversify their safety training to break correlated vulnerability.
cited_sources: Jailbreak Transferability Emerges from Shared Representations (arXiv:2506.12913) - provides the mechanistic premise (shared representations drive transfer) that a black-box similarity proxy aims to approximate.
JailbreakRadar - source of standardized jailbreak prompts and success measurement for the transfer experiments.

title: Correlated Hallucinations: Do Different Models Confidently Agree on the Same Wrong Facts?

sections.research_question: When multiple independent-looking models are wrong about a fact, do they tend to be wrong in the same way - and does cross-model agreement on wrong answers exceed what independence would predict, breaking consensus-based fact-checking?
sections.approach_outline: Curate ~150 short fact questions, deliberately including ~50 'misconception' items with a known popular-but-wrong answer (e.g. common myths, near-miss trivia) plus control items that are unambiguous. Query 6+ open models (mix of lineages and sizes), recording each model's answer and, where possible, a verbalized confidence. Normalize answers to canonical forms and compare against ground truth. Measure (a) the rate at which models agree on the same wrong answer, (b) whether agreement-on-wrong exceeds the rate expected if errors were independent, and (c) whether models express high confidence while jointly wrong. All inference-only and small-scale - fits a single GPU or even API/CPU-light.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Independence baseline: on control (non-misconception) items, measure per-model error rates and compute the expected cross-model wrong-agreement rate under an independence assumption. Measure: expected vs observed agreement. Expected outcome: observed agreement on controls is close to the independence prediction.
- Correlated hallucination: on the misconception items, measure how often models give the same wrong answer and compare to the independence baseline. Measure: excess wrong-agreement. Expected outcome: agreement-on-wrong substantially exceeds independence, concentrated on misconception items.
- False confidence: compute the fraction of items where a majority of models agree on a wrong answer with high stated confidence (a 'false-confidence-from-consensus' rate). Measure: this rate plus a comparison of confidence on jointly-wrong vs jointly-right items. Expected outcome: a non-trivial false-confidence rate, showing majority-vote fact-checking would certify wrong answers.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models share correlated blind spots, then cheap safety heuristics that treat cross-model agreement as evidence of truth - self-consistency, ensemble majority-vote, multi-model fact-checking - are systematically unsafe on exactly the inputs where they are needed most. Demonstrating and quantifying this breaks a false assumption of independence baked into many verification pipelines, preventing a failure mode where automated fact-checkers confidently propagate the same wrong information at scale across deployed systems.
sections.strength_rationale: Maxes narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single curated QA set, simple agreement statistics, and a clear deliverable (excess-wrong-agreement and false-confidence rates). Counterfactual value is strong because it audits a cheap consensus heuristic that labs deprioritize, uses only public models and a self-built question set, and produces a result any independent beginner team can deliver with no proprietary data or internal access.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a benchmark contribution: package the curated misconception set plus the correlated-error metric as a small reusable 'consensus-fragility' benchmark for verification pipelines.
cited_sources: Artificial Hivemind - motivates the premise that models share representational blind spots leading to correlated outputs.
Correlated Errors framework (arXiv:2506.07962) - provides the methodology for measuring error correlation beyond independence, directly applicable to the wrong-agreement metric.

title: Homogeneous Refusals: Do All Models Share the Same Over- and Under-Refusal Blind Spots?

sections.research_question: Is the refusal boundary correlated across providers - i.e. do open models refuse the same benign prompts (over-refusal) and comply with the same harmful edge cases (under-refusal) more than chance independence would predict?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble two prompt sets: a benign-but-tricky slice from an over-refusal benchmark (XSTest / OR-Bench) and a small harmful-edge set (borderline prompts from a public harmful-behavior benchmark). Query 6+ open models across lineages. Classify each response as refuse vs comply using a lightweight classifier (keyword rules plus a short LLM-judge check, with a hand-labeled validation sample). For each prompt, record the vector of refuse/comply decisions across models, then measure inter-model agreement on the refusal boundary (e.g. Fleiss' kappa, or observed vs independence-expected co-refusal) and identify prompts where all or nearly all models share the same error. All inference-only on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Refusal labeling: run both prompt sets through 6+ models, classify refuse/comply, and validate the classifier on a hand-labeled subset. Measure: per-model refuse/comply matrix and classifier accuracy. Expected outcome: reliable labels (>90% classifier agreement with hand labels).
- Correlation vs chance: compute inter-model agreement on the refusal boundary and compare to the agreement expected if each model decided independently given its marginal refusal rate. Measure: observed vs expected co-refusal (and kappa). Expected outcome: agreement well above chance, indicating a shared boundary.
- Blind-spot enumeration: list prompts where nearly all models over-refuse (benign blocked everywhere) and where nearly all under-refuse (harmful complied everywhere). Measure: counts and examples of universal blind spots. Expected outcome: a concrete set of universally-mishandled prompts, demonstrating society-wide blind spots.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If the refusal boundary is homogeneous across providers, then a harmful edge case that slips past one model slips past all of them, and a benign use case blocked by one is blocked everywhere - a single correlated failure with society-wide reach. Measuring the correlation (not just per-model rates) reveals these shared blind spots so the community can target them, mitigating the systemic risk that the entire deployed model fleet shares the same exploitable safety gap.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: existing refusal benchmarks plus a simple refuse/comply classifier and a correlation metric give a tightly-defined study with a clear deliverable. Counterfactual value is high because the correlation framing (rather than per-model rates labs already report) is exactly what no single vendor is incentivized to measure, and an independent team using open models can produce the cross-provider blind-spot map with no internal access.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a diversity recommendation: use the correlated blind-spot set to argue for and design a minimal 'diverse ensemble' of models chosen to maximally de-correlate refusal errors.
cited_sources: Artificial Hivemind - grounds the hypothesis that refusal behavior may be homogeneous across providers.
XSTest - supplies the benign-but-superficially-harmful prompts defining the over-refusal axis.
Correlated-errors framing (arXiv:2506.07962) - provides the observed-vs-independence methodology for measuring boundary correlation.

title: Self-Consistency Lies: Homogeneity Inflates Confidence Calibration Failures

sections.research_question: Does intra-model repetition (mode collapse) cause self-consistency agreement to overstate confidence - i.e. when a model samples many answers and they agree, is that agreement evidence of correctness or just sampling collapse?
sections.approach_outline: On a QA set with known ground truth (~150 items, mixing easy and hard), sample k completions (e.g. k=10) per item at nonzero temperature from 2-4 open models. For each item compute the self-consistency signal: the agreement fraction of the modal answer. Compare this agreement against actual correctness. Separately estimate each model's intra-model repetition / mode-collapse tendency (e.g. average self-agreement across paraphrased prompts). Then quantify a 'false-confidence-from-consistency' rate: items where agreement is high but the modal answer is wrong. Test whether this gap is larger for more mode-collapsed models. All inference-only; the only added cost is k samples per item, still single-GPU scale.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Agreement vs correctness: for each item, compute self-consistency agreement and whether the modal answer is correct; build a reliability curve of agreement vs accuracy. Measure: calibration curve. Expected outcome: high-agreement items are not reliably correct - the curve flattens or has a confidently-wrong tail.
- False-confidence rate: count items where modal-answer agreement is high (e.g. >0.8) yet wrong, divided by all high-agreement items. Measure: false-confidence-from-consistency rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial rate (e.g. 10-30%) on hard/misconception items.
- Mode-collapse link: estimate each model's intra-model repetition score and regress the false-confidence rate on it across models. Measure: correlation between mode-collapse and false-confidence. Expected outcome: more mode-collapsed models show higher false-confidence, supporting the homogeneity-amplification framing.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If high self-consistency agreement reflects sampling mode-collapse rather than correctness, then a cheap, ubiquitous reliability trick used to gate outputs in safety-critical settings will certify confidently-wrong answers as trustworthy. Showing precisely when agreement is mode-collapse versus genuine evidence lets practitioners stop treating self-consistency as a confidence proxy where it fails, averting a deployment failure where automated systems act on falsely-confident model outputs.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single well-defined experiment with a crisp metric (false-confidence-from-consistency rate) using only public QA data and standard sampling. Counterfactual value is high because it stress-tests a cheap technique labs rely on but rarely audit for the mode-collapse failure, and an independent team with open models and no proprietary data can deliver a clean, lab-independent result.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a fix-evaluation: test whether increasing sampling diversity (higher temperature, prompt paraphrase ensembling) restores the agreement-correctness link, turning the diagnostic into an actionable mitigation.
cited_sources: Artificial Hivemind (intra-model repetition) - provides the mode-collapse premise that breaks the diversity assumption behind self-consistency.
Self-consistency / calibration literature - establishes the technique and its assumed confidence interpretation that this study challenges.
Correlated errors (arXiv:2506.07962) - methodology for relating repetition/correlation structure to confidence failures.

title: Stability of a concept vector across fine-tuning checkpoints (replicate on open instruction-tuned variants)

sections.research_question: Does a refusal/honesty concept vector extracted from a base model remain aligned and effective when applied to its official instruction-tuned version and a community fine-tune - i.e. do safety steering vectors silently drift across the model-update lifecycle?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a base model with publicly available downstream checkpoints (e.g. Llama-3.x-8B base, its official Instruct, and a popular community fine-tune of the same base). Extract a refusal (or honesty) steering vector from the base model using contrastive activation addition (CAA): mean activation difference between matched refusing vs complying prompt pairs at a chosen layer. Then, treating the official-instruct and community fine-tune as a 'model update' proxy, (1) re-extract the vector in each checkpoint and measure cosine similarity to the base vector, and (2) measure steering effectiveness when the base-extracted vector is injected into each downstream checkpoint. Entirely inference; uses only off-the-shelf checkpoints, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Vector drift: extract the CAA refusal vector at the same layer in base, official-instruct, and community fine-tune, then compute pairwise cosine similarity. Measure: cosine similarity across checkpoints. Expected outcome: noticeable drift (cosine < 1, possibly < 0.7) especially for the community fine-tune.
- Cross-checkpoint efficacy: inject the base-extracted vector into each downstream checkpoint and measure the induced behavior shift (refusal-rate change on a held-out prompt set) versus injecting each checkpoint's own freshly-extracted vector. Measure: steering effectiveness gap. Expected outcome: the base vector steers the official-instruct reasonably but is degraded on the community fine-tune.
- Layer robustness: repeat drift and efficacy across 3-4 candidate layers to see whether some layers' concept vectors are more stable than others. Measure: stability-by-layer. Expected outcome: certain mid layers give more transferable, stable vectors than others.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety-relevant concept vectors drift as a model is fine-tuned or updated, then a steering-based defense or monitor calibrated on one checkpoint silently degrades after a routine model update - so a deployed safety intervention stops working without anyone noticing. Quantifying this drift and identifying stable layers tells defenders how often steering vectors must be re-validated, preventing a maintenance failure where representation-level safety controls quietly become ineffective on the actually-deployed model.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it uses only off-the-shelf checkpoints with zero training, a standard CAA extraction, and clean metrics (cosine similarity, steering efficacy). Counterfactual value is high because lifecycle maintainability of safety vectors is something labs rarely publish, yet an independent team using public base/instruct/community checkpoints can directly measure drift and deliver an actionable re-validation guideline.
alternative_framings: Reframe across model sizes or families instead of fine-tune lineage: measure how a concept vector transfers between sibling sizes of the same family, testing portability rather than update-drift.
cited_sources: Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) literature - the extraction method for the refusal/honesty vector used here.
Concept-vector stability noted as an open problem in steering work - motivates the lifecycle-drift question this replication addresses.

title: Does a 'random direction' steer as much as a real concept vector? A control-vector audit

sections.research_question: How much of a concept steering vector's behavioral effect is explained by its norm (a generic perturbation artifact) versus its direction (the intended concept) - do random or semantically-unrelated directions, matched in norm, steer as much as real concept vectors?
sections.approach_outline: On one open instruct model, build three matched sets of steering vectors at a fixed layer: (1) real CAA concept vectors for refusal, sycophancy, and honesty, extracted from contrastive pairs (e.g. Anthropic model-written-evals data); (2) random unit vectors rescaled to each real vector's norm; (3) vectors derived from semantically-unrelated contrastive pairs, also norm-matched. Apply each at matched norms via an activation-addition hook and measure both on-target behavior shift (does the targeted behavior change?) and generic disruption (perplexity on held-out text, accuracy on an unrelated benchmark slice). Decompose how much of each real vector's effect is reproduced by its norm-matched random control. Pure inference on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Norm-matched random control: for each real concept vector, generate a norm-matched random vector, apply both, and compare on-target shift and perplexity. Measure: on-target and disruption deltas, real vs random. Expected outcome: random vectors produce substantial generic disruption but little on-target shift, while real vectors produce more on-target shift.
- Unrelated-pair control: apply norm-matched vectors from semantically-unrelated contrastive pairs and compare to the real concept vectors. Measure: on-target shift from unrelated vectors. Expected outcome: if Tan et al. generalizes, unrelated-pair vectors match much of the real effect, indicating direction matters less than expected.
- Norm-explained-effect decomposition: across a norm sweep, fit how much of each real vector's behavioral effect is predicted by norm alone versus residual direction-specific effect. Measure: fraction of effect explained by norm. Expected outcome: a sizable norm-explained fraction for some concepts, quantifying how much 'concept steering' is really generic perturbation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If random and unrelated directions reproduce much of a steering vector's effect, then claims that steering 'targets a specific concept' are overstated, and any safety pipeline that uses steering as a monitoring or control lever is acting partly on a norm artifact rather than the intended concept. Establishing how much effect is direction-specific is foundational to trusting representation-level interventions, preventing deployment of a steering-based safety control that appears to work but is really just perturbing the model nonspecifically.
sections.strength_rationale: Highest scores in the batch on narrow scope and the foundational-audit framing, plus top accessible complexity and low compute: it is a tightly controlled experiment with explicit matched controls and a clean norm-decomposition metric, all pure inference. Counterfactual value is strong because this is a skeptical, foundational audit that labs deprioritize relative to building new steering methods, and an independent team using open models and public eval data can deliver it end-to-end with no training or proprietary resources.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a steering-method validity checklist: distill the norm-matched-control protocol into a reusable diagnostic that any steering paper should run before claiming concept-specific effects.
cited_sources: Tan et al. (control vectors from unrelated contrastive pairs match designed ones) - the direct finding this audit systematically tests and decomposes.
Anthropic model-written-evals (MWE) dataset - source of contrastive prompt pairs for extracting the real concept vectors and constructing matched controls.

title: The negation trap: do concept probes flip when the safety statement is negated?

sections.research_question: Do linear concept probes trained to detect a safety-relevant concept (e.g. 'this text describes harmful instructions') in affirmative statements collapse in accuracy when the same concept is expressed through negation (e.g. 'this is not a request to build a weapon')? If probes are negation-fragile, a monitor built on them can be trivially evaded by rephrasing.
sections.approach_outline: Pick one small open-weight instruction model (e.g. Llama-3.2-1B/3B or Qwen2.5-1.5B) runnable on a single consumer GPU in inference-only mode. Build a small matched dataset of ~150-300 short statements per concept, each in an affirmative form and a paraphrased negated form that preserves the underlying truth label. Run the model once over all statements and cache residual-stream activations at 2-3 middle layers (this is the only model-forward step). Train a simple logistic-regression linear probe (scikit-learn) on the affirmative split only, then evaluate held-out accuracy on (a) affirmative test items and (b) the negated items, reporting the accuracy gap. Repeat across layers to find where, if anywhere, negation robustness is best.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline affirmative probe: train the linear probe on affirmative activations, evaluate on a held-out affirmative test set. Measure held-out accuracy/AUC. Expected: high accuracy (>85%), confirming the probe captures the concept in the easy case.
- Negation transfer test: take the same trained probe and evaluate it on the negated statements. Measure accuracy and the flip rate (fraction of items whose predicted label inverts vs the affirmative counterpart). Expected: a substantial accuracy drop (the 'negation trap'); a large flip rate would show the probe tracks surface affirmation rather than meaning.
- Layer sweep + robustness control: repeat experiments 1-2 across 2-3 layers, and add a control that mixes a few negated examples into training. Measure how the affirmative-vs-negated accuracy gap changes by layer and whether a small amount of negated training data closes it. Expected: an identifiable layer/regime where negation robustness is best, and evidence on whether cheap data augmentation rescues the probe.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If concept probes flip under negation, then any deployed activation-based safety monitor using such probes can be silently bypassed by adversaries who phrase harmful intent through negation. Demonstrating and quantifying this fragility on open models -> warns practitioners not to ship negation-fragile probes and motivates negation-robust training -> improves the reliability of cheap interpretability-based monitoring, which is a key defense layer against the catastrophic pathway of a deployed model assisting with weapons/cyber harm while evading oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: it is a single, crisply-defined train-on-affirmatives/test-on-negations experiment using only linear probing on cached activations, ideal for a beginner stats exercise in 30 hours. Its counterfactual value (4) is high because probe-robustness auditing on open models needs no proprietary data or lab infra and is exactly the kind of cheap, neglected safety-tooling check labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a generalization-failure study: probes as classifiers that overfit to syntactic affirmation cues rather than semantics, with negation as the cleanest natural distribution shift.

title: Planning Horizon: How Many Tokens Ahead Does a Small Model Plan?

sections.research_question: When a prompt imposes a constraint that can only be satisfied by a target word several tokens in the future, how far ahead does a small open model begin pre-activating that target? We aim to produce a planning-horizon decay curve: target pre-activation strength as a function of distance N from the constraint to the target.
sections.approach_outline: Use constraint-at-distance prompts: templates where a stated rule (e.g. 'end the sentence with a word that rhymes with X', or 'the answer must be the word Y, give a sentence leading to it') forces a specific target word at a controllable distance N tokens ahead. On a small open model (GPT-2-medium or Llama-3.2-1B) in inference-only mode, apply the logit lens at each intermediate layer/position and read off the target word's pre-activation (its rank or logit-lens probability) as it builds across positions. Sweep N over a small grid (e.g. 1-12), average over many prompt instances and target words, and plot mean target pre-activation vs N to characterize the decay curve. All steps are forward passes with cached hidden states; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-distance sanity check: with N fixed small (e.g. 2-3), apply the logit lens at the position just before the target and confirm the target word is elevated above a random-word baseline. Measure logit-lens rank/probability of the target. Expected: clear above-baseline pre-activation, validating the readout pipeline.
- Horizon-decay sweep: vary N across the grid, averaging over many instances, and plot mean target pre-activation vs N. Measure the distance at which pre-activation falls to baseline (the planning horizon). Expected: monotone-ish decay with a characteristic horizon of a few tokens for a small model.
- Constraint-vs-no-constraint control: re-run with the constraint removed (target no longer forced) to confirm pre-activation is driven by the planning constraint rather than generic token frequency. Measure the gap between constrained and unconstrained pre-activation curves. Expected: constrained prompts show markedly higher early pre-activation, isolating genuine look-ahead.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If small models pre-activate future targets only over a short horizon, then long-horizon, multi-step deceptive or goal-directed behavior would require representational planning beyond what next-token monitors can see. Measuring the actual horizon on open models -> grounds claims about whether current models can internally plan multi-step deception -> calibrates how much we should trust shallow output monitors versus needing deeper interpretability, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a model executes a long-horizon harmful plan that per-token oversight never flags.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: the deliverable is a single concrete artifact (a planning-horizon decay curve) built from logit-lens readouts on a small open model, fully inference-only and beginner-accessible. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because medium/long-horizon planning is a threat labs deprioritize, and the whole study runs on open weights with no proprietary data or infra.
alternative_framings: Cast it as measuring 'lookahead capacity' as a capability-scaling property, comparing the horizon across two model sizes to see whether planning depth grows with scale.

title: Cross-Lingual Prefill Attacks: Does Shallow Alignment Hold in Low-Resource Languages?

sections.research_question: Does the prefill jailbreak (forcing the model to begin its reply with an affirmative/compliant prefix) succeed more often in low-resource languages than in high-resource ones? In other words, is shallow safety alignment even shallower outside the languages that dominate alignment fine-tuning?
sections.approach_outline: Take a small open multilingual instruction model (e.g. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct). Select a fixed set of harmful requests from StrongREJECT, translate them and a short affirmative prefill prefix into a ladder of languages spanning resource levels (e.g. English/Spanish as high, then mid, then low-resource like Swahili/Yoruba/Telugu) using a public translation API. For each language, run the same prefill attack in inference-only mode and score whether the continuation complies, using the StrongREJECT rubric (with English back-translation for scoring). Plot attack success rate (ASR) against an approximate resource-level axis. No training, no attack optimization; all prompts are precomputed.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- English baseline: run the prefill attack on the harmful set in English and score ASR with StrongREJECT. Measure baseline ASR and refusal rate. Expected: a moderate nonzero ASR establishing the attack works on this model.
- Resource-ladder sweep: repeat the identical attack across the language ladder, holding requests/prefill fixed. Measure ASR per language and correlate with resource level. Expected: ASR rises as resource level falls, indicating shallower alignment in low-resource languages.
- Translation-confound control: re-score by back-translating a sample of low-resource outputs to English and manually checking that high ASR reflects genuine harmful compliance rather than degenerate/garbled output. Measure the fraction of 'successes' that are truly harmful and coherent. Expected: a meaningful share are genuine, confirming the gap is a real safety failure not a translation artifact.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If prefill attacks reliably succeed more in low-resource languages, then deployed multilingual assistants have a large, predictable, easily-exploited safety hole for non-English users. Mapping ASR vs resource level on open models -> gives the community a concrete map of where alignment is thinnest and a cheap reproducible benchmark -> pressures providers and open-model fine-tuners to extend safety training multilingually, reducing the catastrophic pathway where harmful (e.g. weapons/cyber) assistance is obtained simply by switching languages.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a single well-defined experiment (ASR vs resource level) with the StrongREJECT rubric as an explicit success metric, using only public translation and open-model inference. Its counterfactual value (4) is high because low-resource languages are deprioritized by labs, and the study needs no proprietary data, training, or internal infra.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a script/tokenization study: test whether the gap tracks language resource level or rather the script/byte-level tokenization efficiency, isolating the mechanism behind multilingual alignment fragility.

title: Refusal Recovery: Does the Model Self-Correct After a Forced Harmful Start?

sections.research_question: After being forced to begin a reply with a harmful prefix (a prefill attack), does the model recover and refuse mid-generation, and how does this recovery rate depend on prefill length and harm category? Recovery behavior measures the depth of alignment beyond the first few tokens.
sections.approach_outline: On a small open instruction model, take harmful requests across a few harm categories (from StrongREJECT). For each, prepend an affirmative harmful prefix of varying length (e.g. 5, 15, 40 tokens) and let the model freely continue. Classify each completed output as 'recovered' (turns into a refusal/safe content) vs 'complied' using a simple rubric plus an LLM-as-judge or keyword+manual check on a sample. Build a recovery-rate profile as a function of prefill length and harm category. Pure inference, no training, no attack optimization; the only sweep is over prefill length and a small request set.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Recovery vs prefill length: hold harm category fixed, sweep prefill length, and measure the fraction of generations that recover into a refusal. Expected: recovery rate drops as prefill length grows, quantifying how 'shallow' the alignment is.
- Recovery vs harm category: hold prefill length fixed at a moderate value, vary harm category, and measure recovery rate per category. Expected: heterogeneity, with some categories (e.g. severe weapons/cyber) recovering more reliably than others, revealing where post-start defenses are weakest.
- Judge-reliability control: hand-label a random sample (~50 outputs) and compare against the automated recovered/complied classifier. Measure agreement (accuracy/kappa). Expected: high enough agreement to trust the automated profile, with disagreements flagged for the writeup.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models rarely recover after a forced harmful start, then prefill-style attacks defeat alignment that lives only in the opening tokens, and runtime monitors that check only the start of a reply give false assurance. Mapping recovery rates on open models -> shows defenders that mid-generation self-correction is or isn't a reliable backstop -> informs whether deployments need continuous output monitoring, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where a jailbroken model completes harmful instructions once nudged past its refusal.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a single inference-only experiment producing a clear recovery-rate profile with explicit classification criteria, well within a beginner's 30-hour budget. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because recovery (the under-measured complement to attack success rate) needs only open models and no proprietary infra, exactly the neglected angle independents can own.
alternative_framings: Frame recovery as an emergent 'self-monitoring' signal and test whether the model's own stated confidence or a probe predicts which generations will recover.

title: Backcasting robust steering: can a cheap input perturbation neutralize a deployed concept vector?

sections.research_question: If a defender deploys a fixed safety concept vector (e.g. a refusal-promoting steering direction added at inference), can a user with only black-box prompt access neutralize it using cheap input perturbations alone, and which perturbation types are most effective?
sections.approach_outline: On a small open model, build or take a refusal/safety concept vector (via contrastive activation addition, CAA, from a handful of contrastive prompt pairs) and apply it at a fixed layer/strength as the 'deployed defense.' Then, holding the steering fixed, apply a battery of cheap, prompt-only perturbations to the user input (e.g. role-play framing, distractor prefixes, formatting/whitespace tricks, language switch, polite-override phrasing) and measure how much each perturbation reduces the steering effect (drop in refusal rate or in the steered behavior metric) relative to the unperturbed steered baseline. Rank perturbation types by neutralization power. All inference-only; the only 'training' is the cheap CAA vector estimation from cached activations.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish the steered baseline: with the safety vector applied, measure refusal rate / target-behavior rate on a set of probe prompts with no perturbation. Expected: a clear steering effect (e.g. elevated refusals) versus the unsteered model, confirming the 'deployed defense' works.
- Perturbation ranking sweep: apply each prompt perturbation type to the same probe prompts under fixed steering, measuring the reduction in steering effect per type. Expected: a ranked list where some cheap perturbations substantially neutralize the vector while others do little.
- Strength-robustness curve: for the top-2 neutralizing perturbations, sweep the steering strength upward and measure at what strength the defense resists neutralization (and whether that strength degrades fluency/utility). Expected: a tradeoff curve showing the steering strength needed to stay robust, and whether it is reachable without breaking the model.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If cheap prompt perturbations neutralize deployed steering, then steering-based safety controls offer a false sense of security and can be silently bypassed by ordinary users. Characterizing which perturbations break steering on open models -> tells the community that steering defenses must be stress-tested against prompt-only attacks and points to which strengths/configs are robust -> prevents over-reliance on a fragile control in the catastrophic pathway where a steering-'aligned' model is trivially talked back into harmful behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a tightly-scoped ranking of prompt perturbations against a fixed steering vector, all inference-plus-prompt-manipulation, feasible for a beginner in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it stress-tests a proposed safety control on open weights with no lab access or proprietary data, the kind of fragility audit labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame it defensively: instead of ranking attacks, search for the minimal steering strength + prompt-canonicalization preprocessing that makes the vector robust, turning the result into a defense recipe.

title: Adversarial Suffix Detectability by Activation Probes vs Behavioral Filters

sections.research_question: When an adversarial suffix (GCG-style, taken from public attack sets) is appended to a harmful prompt, which defense detects it more reliably: a linear activation probe reading the model's internal state, or a behavioral output classifier scanning the generated reply? And do the two defenses fail on overlapping or complementary inputs?
sections.approach_outline: On a small open model, assemble a set of harmful prompts in three conditions: clean refused, clean complied, and attacked-with-public-suffix. Run inference once, caching both intermediate activations and final outputs. Train a linear probe on activations to predict 'will produce harmful content,' and separately apply an output classifier (a keyword/regex baseline plus a small LLM-judge) to the generations. Compare per-input detection on the attacked set and build a 2x2 confusion map of where each defense catches vs misses. No attack optimization is performed; only public precomputed suffixes are used. Pure inference plus linear probing on cached activations.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Probe vs output baseline on clean data: train/evaluate both defenses on clean harmful-vs-benign prompts. Measure detection accuracy/AUC of each. Expected: both perform well on clean inputs, establishing the defenses are sound before attack.
- Attack stress test: evaluate both defenses on suffix-attacked prompts. Measure each defense's catch rate on attacked harmful inputs. Expected: the output classifier may be evaded more (since suffixes are tuned to flip outputs) while the activation probe may retain or lose signal, quantifying which is more suffix-robust.
- Blind-spot / cascade map: cross-tabulate which attacked inputs each defense catches to find the overlap and the inputs missed by both. Measure the fraction caught by the probe+output cascade vs each alone. Expected: complementary coverage where cascading reduces blind spots, giving a concrete cheap layered-defense recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If activation probes and output filters fail on different attacked inputs, then cheaply cascading them covers blind spots that either alone leaves open. Producing an open, reproducible map of where each defense fails on public suffixes -> gives deployers evidence on whether to layer internal and behavioral monitors -> strengthens the cheap-monitoring defense layer against the catastrophic pathway where a suffix-jailbroken model slips harmful (cyber/bio) content past a single filter.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a single failure-map experiment using public suffixes (no costly attack optimization), a linear probe, and an output classifier, all inference-level and beginner-feasible. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because auditing layered defenses on open models with public attack artifacts needs no proprietary data or infra, an independent-friendly neglected check.
alternative_framings: Reframe around transferability: test whether suffixes optimized on one model evade the probe on a second model, separating attack-specific from defense-intrinsic blind spots.

title: Many-Shot vs Prefill: Which Attack Probes 'Shallower'? A Head-to-Head Variation

sections.research_question: Do two well-known jailbreaks, many-shot (filling the context with harmful demonstrations) and prefill (forcing an affirmative reply start), combine super-additively? That is, does the combined attack succeed more than you would predict from each attack's individual success rate, implying they exploit different layers of alignment?
sections.approach_outline: On a small open instruction model, run a 2x2 factorial over {prefill on/off} x {many-shot on/off} against a fixed harmful request set (StrongREJECT). For many-shot, prepend a controlled number of harmful demonstration turns; for prefill, force an affirmative opening. Score each cell's attack success rate with the StrongREJECT rubric. Compute the interaction term (combined ASR minus the additive/independent prediction from the two single-attack cells) to test for super-additivity. Optionally vary the many-shot count to see how the interaction scales. Pure inference, no attack optimization; all prompts are precomputed.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-attack baselines: run the prefill-only and many-shot-only cells and the no-attack cell. Measure ASR in each. Expected: each single attack lifts ASR above baseline by a measurable amount.
- Combined cell + interaction test: run the prefill+many-shot cell and compute the interaction (combined ASR vs the independence prediction). Measure the super-additivity gap with a simple bootstrap confidence interval. Expected: either super-additive (gap > 0, attacks compose) or saturating, each a clear and interpretable result.
- Many-shot dose-response: hold prefill on, vary the number of many-shot demonstrations, and measure ASR vs shot count with and without prefill. Expected: a dose-response curve showing whether prefill shifts the whole many-shot curve, clarifying how the two attacks interact across context length.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If these attacks compose super-additively, then realistic adversaries stacking cheap attacks defeat defenses tuned against each in isolation, and threat models that test attacks one-at-a-time underestimate risk. A clean head-to-head factorial on open models -> corrects defenders' threat models toward attack composition -> motivates evaluating defenses against stacked attacks, reducing the catastrophic pathway where combined jailbreaks reliably extract harmful (e.g. weapons/cyber) assistance.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a single 2x2 factorial with two public attacks and the StrongREJECT rubric as an explicit super-additivity test, all inference-only and beginner-feasible. Counterfactual value (4) is high because attack-composition threat modeling on open models uses only public attacks and weights, needs no lab infra, and is exactly the kind of characterization labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame the interaction mechanistically: probe whether the combined attack pushes refusal-direction activations further than the sum of the individual attacks, linking behavioral super-additivity to a representational cause.

title: Steered to Help, Steered to Leak: Format-Steering x PII / Secret Disclosure

sections.research_question: Does a benign-seeming compliance/helpfulness steering vector, applied to make a model more cooperative, also erode its discretion and increase the rate at which it discloses a secret or PII placed in its system prompt? In short, can a 'be more helpful' steer become a 'leak the secret' steer?
sections.approach_outline: On a small open model, place a clearly-marked synthetic secret (a fake API key or fictional person's PII) in the system prompt with an instruction never to reveal it. Build a compliance/helpfulness steering vector via contrastive activation addition from compliant-vs-evasive prompt pairs. Then sweep the steering strength from zero upward and, at each strength, issue a battery of probing user queries (direct asks, social-engineering framings, indirect requests) and measure the disclosure rate (fraction of responses revealing the secret or partial PII). Compare against the unsteered baseline to isolate the steering side-effect. All synthetic data, inference-only, no training beyond cheap CAA vector estimation.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline discretion: with no steering, run the probing queries against the system-prompt secret and measure baseline disclosure rate. Expected: low disclosure (the model mostly respects the instruction), establishing the reference point.
- Steering-strength sweep: apply the compliance vector at increasing strengths and measure disclosure rate at each. Expected: a monotone rise in disclosure as helpfulness steering increases, demonstrating the confidentiality side-effect.
- Specificity control: apply a steering vector for an unrelated benign concept (e.g. verbosity/formatting) at matched strengths and measure disclosure. Expected: little-to-no disclosure increase, confirming the leak is specific to compliance/helpfulness steering rather than any activation perturbation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If benign helpfulness steering raises secret/PII disclosure, then deploying steering to tune model behavior can silently weaken confidentiality boundaries. Demonstrating this confidentiality side-effect on open models with synthetic secrets -> warns practitioners that steering interventions need confidentiality regression tests -> reduces the catastrophic pathway where a steered agentic assistant with access to credentials/PII is coaxed into leaking them, undermining trust and enabling downstream compromise.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: one synthetic-secret setup, a steering-strength sweep, and a disclosure-rate measurement, all inference-only and feasible for a beginner in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because the confidentiality-x-steering interaction is neglected, uses only synthetic data and open weights, and requires no proprietary infra or lab-internal access.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a multi-objective tension: plot a Pareto frontier of helpfulness gain vs disclosure risk across steering strengths to find whether any 'safe' helpfulness boost exists.

title: Harm-Category Heterogeneity in Shallow Alignment

sections.research_question: Is shallow alignment uniform across harm categories, or are some hazard categories (e.g. cyber, bio, weapons vs. milder categories) far more shallowly aligned and easier to jailbreak with a fixed prefill attack? And is the category ranking consistent across different open models?
sections.approach_outline: Take 2-3 small open instruction models. Use a categorized public benchmark (AILuminate hazard taxonomy and/or StrongREJECT) so harmful prompts carry category labels. Apply a single fixed prefill attack uniformly across all categories and models in inference-only mode, scoring compliance per item with the StrongREJECT rubric. Aggregate to a per-category attack success rate (ASR) for each model, producing a category-x-model shallowness map. Then test whether the category ranking is consistent across models (rank correlation). No training, no attack optimization; the only sweep is across categories and models.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Per-category ASR on one model: run the fixed prefill attack across all hazard categories on the first model and compute ASR per category. Expected: visible heterogeneity, with some categories far more vulnerable than others.
- Cross-model consistency: repeat on the other 1-2 models and compute the rank correlation of category ASRs across models. Expected: moderately-to-highly consistent rankings, suggesting category shallowness is a property of training data/RLHF coverage rather than a single model quirk.
- Severity-vs-shallowness check: cross-reference each category's ASR against a rough catastrophic-severity rating (e.g. cyber/bio as high severity). Measure whether high-severity categories are coincidentally also shallowly aligned. Expected: identify any dangerous mismatch where the most severe categories are not the best-defended, a directly actionable finding.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If certain high-severity harm categories are the most shallowly aligned, then defenders and red-teamers should reallocate scarce hardening effort toward exactly those categories. A cross-model per-category shallowness map on open models -> tells the community where alignment is thinnest relative to catastrophic severity -> guides targeted safety fine-tuning and evaluation priorities, reducing the pathway where the most dangerous (cyber/bio) requests are also the easiest to jailbreak.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope and accessible_complexity and 4 on low_compute: one fixed attack run across categorized public benchmarks on 2-3 small models, pure inference with an explicit per-category ASR metric, feasible for a beginner in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because this diffuse, hard-to-fund prioritization question relies only on public benchmarks and open models with no internal access.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a benchmark-coverage audit: test whether category shallowness correlates with how well-represented that category is in public safety-training data, linking the gap to a fixable cause.

title: Cross-language transfer of a deception/refusal steering vector on a small open model

sections.research_question: If a safety-relevant steering vector (a refusal/deception direction) is built from English data only, does its behavioral effect transfer when prompts are issued in other languages on a multilingual model? If safety vectors are English-bound, a deployed steering-based safety tool can be silently bypassed by switching language.
sections.approach_outline: On a small open multilingual instruction model (e.g. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct or a multilingual Llama variant), build a refusal/deception steering vector using contrastive activation addition (CAA) from English contrastive prompt pairs only. Apply the fixed vector at inference and measure its behavioral effect (change in refusal rate on harmful prompts, or change in a deception-proxy metric) first in English, then on the same prompts translated into 3 other languages via a public translation API. Compare the steering effect size across languages to quantify transfer. Inference-only on a single GPU; the only fitting step is the cheap English CAA vector from cached activations.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- English effect baseline: apply the English-built vector to English prompts and measure the change in refusal rate vs unsteered. Expected: a clear steering effect, validating the vector works in its source language.
- Cross-language transfer test: apply the identical vector to the same prompts translated into 3 other languages and measure the steering effect in each. Expected: partial or full attenuation of the effect in other languages, quantifying how English-bound the safety vector is.
- Translation-confound control: verify with a back-translation/quality check that translated prompts are faithful and that any attenuation reflects representational non-transfer, not broken prompts. Also test the unsteered refusal baseline per language to normalize. Expected: confirmation that reduced steering effect is a genuine transfer failure, not a translation artifact.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If English-built safety steering vectors do not transfer across languages, then a steering-based safety control deployed by a provider can be silently evaded simply by prompting in another language. Measuring transfer on an open multilingual model -> reveals whether steering defenses must be built per-language or in a language-agnostic way -> prevents a false sense of safety in multilingual deployments, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where harmful assistance is obtained by switching languages to escape a monitor/steer.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5 on narrow_scope, accessible_complexity, and low_compute: a single, crisply-defined experiment (refusal-vector transfer to 3 languages) using standard CAA, public translation, and inference-only evaluation, feasible for a beginner in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because this under-watched cross-language safety question runs entirely on public multilingual weights with no proprietary data or lab infra, exactly the externally-doable angle labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a mechanistic test of whether the model has a shared multilingual concept subspace: check whether building the vector from a mix of languages restores transfer, isolating whether the failure is representational or data-driven.

title: How stable is a safety concept vector across a model's fine-tunes?

sections.research_question: When a safety-relevant concept direction (e.g. a refusal or harmfulness vector) is extracted from a base model, how stable is that direction after the model is fine-tuned by third parties? Does a safety vector built on the base model still point the same way, and still steer behavior, on public fine-tunes of that same base?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one open base model that has 2-3 publicly available fine-tunes derived from it (e.g. a base + chat + community fine-tune family that share the same architecture and tokenizer). Extract a concept vector on the base model using contrastive activation differencing (mean activation on harmful vs harmless prompt pairs at a chosen residual-stream layer), which requires only forward passes and no training. Apply the base-derived vector to each fine-tune and measure two things: geometric drift (cosine similarity between the base vector and a vector independently re-extracted on each fine-tune) and behavioral transfer (does adding/subtracting the base vector still change refusal behavior on a held-out prompt set?). Report a stability curve across the fine-tune family and per layer. All steps are inference-only and fit on a single consumer GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Vector extraction and re-extraction: On the base model and each fine-tune, extract the harmfulness/refusal vector via contrastive differencing over ~100 harmful/harmless prompt pairs at 3-4 candidate layers. Measure cosine similarity between the base vector and each fine-tune's own re-extracted vector. Expected outcome: cosine drops as fine-tuning diverges from base, with some layers more stable than others.
- Cross-application behavioral transfer: Apply the base-model vector (not the fine-tune's own) at inference to each fine-tune on a held-out set of ~50 borderline prompts, sweeping a small set of steering coefficients. Measure the change in refusal rate (LLM-judged or keyword-based) versus the no-steering baseline. Expected outcome: the base vector still produces measurable steering on lightly fine-tuned models but its effect weakens or inverts on heavily fine-tuned ones.
- Stability curve summary: Combine cosine drift and steering effectiveness into a single per-model stability plot (x = fine-tune, y = cosine and y = steering effect size). Expected outcome: a clear monotone-ish degradation curve identifying which fine-tunes a base-derived safety vector can and cannot be trusted on.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety-monitoring or steering tools are built on a base model's concept vectors and silently stop working after fine-tuning, then deployers who fine-tune open weights (a huge and growing population) would believe a model is being monitored/steered when it is not. Mapping vector stability tells the community when base-derived safety interventions must be re-validated, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway where a widely-shared 'safe' steering vector gives false assurance on a downstream model that has quietly become unmonitored and exploitable.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is a single tightly-scoped inference-only measurement on public fine-tunes that requires no training or proprietary access, exactly the kind of validation labs deprioritize because they control their own fine-tuning. It directly answers a flagged open problem with a reusable artifact (a stability curve) that other independent researchers can extend.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a reliability audit of published steering-vector tooling: 'How often does a community safety vector silently break on the fine-tunes people actually deploy?'

title: Does Self-Jailbreak Emerge Only After Benign Reasoning Training?

sections.research_question: Does the 'self-jailbreak' effect (a model reasoning itself out of its safety guardrails) require the specific benign reasoning fine-tuning described in the Self-Jailbreaking paper, or does it emerge spontaneously in off-the-shelf open reasoning models when they are simply given a longer thinking budget?
sections.approach_outline: Take one or two open reasoning models that expose an explicit chain-of-thought / think-token budget. Assemble a fixed set of ~60-80 borderline-harmful prompts (refusable but tempting). For each prompt, run the model at several capped reasoning lengths (e.g. very short, medium, long thinking budgets) using only inference-time controls such as max-thinking-tokens or a budget-forcing stop token. Measure refusal rate as a function of reasoning length and qualitatively code a sample of long traces for 'talking themselves into compliance' patterns. No fine-tuning is performed, isolating reasoning length from training. Everything runs on a single consumer GPU, with long generations being the main cost.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Refusal-vs-budget curve: Run the fixed borderline prompt set at 4-5 reasoning-length caps on one open reasoning model. Measure refusal rate (LLM-judged) at each cap. Expected outcome: if self-jailbreak is training-specific, refusal should be roughly flat across budgets; if it is spontaneous, refusal should fall as budget grows.
- Qualitative trace coding: Sample ~30 long-budget traces that ended in compliance and hand-code (or use a cheap judge model) for whether the model explicitly reasoned its way around a refusal versus simply answered. Measure the fraction showing explicit self-talk-around. Expected outcome: a nonzero, characterizable rate of explicit self-jailbreak reasoning in long traces.
- Cross-model replication: Repeat the budget sweep on a second open reasoning model of different size/family. Measure whether the refusal-vs-budget slope is consistent. Expected outcome: a directionally consistent erosion confirming the effect is not an artifact of one model.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If longer reasoning monotonically erodes safety even without special training, then scaling reasoning compute (a default trajectory for frontier reasoning models) inherently increases jailbreak susceptibility. This makes inference-time reasoning budget a safety-relevant knob, informing deployers and evaluators that more 'thinking' can mean less safety, and pushing back on the assumption that deliberation always improves alignment, a medium-horizon scaling risk labs under-prioritize.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity and narrow scope and 4 on counterfactual value and low compute: it is a single, sharply defined inference-only experiment on open models that needs no training or proprietary data, exactly the kind of decoupling test independent researchers can run but that labs rarely publish. It directly probes a live tension between two recent papers, giving it clear research value.
alternative_framings: Frame as an evaluation-methodology contribution: 'Reasoning budget as a hidden confound in reasoning-model safety benchmarks.'
cited_sources: Self-Jailbreaking (arXiv:2510.20956) — primary claim that benign reasoning training lets models reason out of safety; this project tests whether the training step is necessary.
When Models Outthink Their Safety (arXiv:2510.21285) — evidence that longer/explicit reasoning can increase safety risk, motivating the reasoning-length axis.
Deliberative Alignment (arXiv:2412.16339) — claims reasoning improves safety, the tension this project probes.

title: Prefilling Attack Success vs Prefill Length: A Dose-Response Curve

sections.research_question: How does jailbreak success scale with the number of tokens of a compliant response that an attacker prefills into the assistant turn? What is the 'minimum effective prefill' length at which safety collapses, and does that elbow line up with the shallow-alignment token-depth result?
sections.approach_outline: Select 2-3 open chat models that expose an assistant-prefix / prefill interface. Build a fixed set of ~50 harmful prompts each paired with a short canonical compliant continuation. For each prompt, prefill 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, and 20 tokens of that compliant continuation and let the model continue. Score whether the completion is a successful jailbreak using a judge model plus a refusal-keyword check. Aggregate to a dose-response curve (attack success rate vs prefill length) per model, fit a simple curve, and read off the minimum prefill achieving e.g. 50% and 90% success. Pure inference, no training, light GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-model dose-response curve: On one prefill-capable open model, run all six prefill lengths over the harmful set and plot attack success rate vs prefill length. Measure ASR at each length. Expected outcome: a sharp rise from near-zero at 0 tokens to high ASR within the first handful of tokens.
- Minimum-effective-prefill extraction: Fit a monotone curve to the per-length ASR and report the prefill length crossing 50% and 90% success. Measure these threshold lengths. Expected outcome: thresholds in the low single-to-double digit token range, consistent with shallow alignment.
- Cross-model comparison: Repeat on 2 more open models and overlay their curves. Measure how the elbow location varies across models. Expected outcome: all models break within a small prefill budget, with relative ordering giving a comparable robustness ranking.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety alignment can be defeated by prefilling only a few tokens, then any deployment surface that lets users (or a compromised tool) influence the start of the assistant's response is critically exposed. Quantifying the minimum effective prefill operationalizes shallow alignment for the prefill threat model and gives API designers a concrete depth target for how many response tokens must be defended, directly reducing the catastrophic pathway where attackers cheaply elicit harmful capabilities from deployed open models.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity and narrow scope and 4 on counterfactual value: it is a clean, single inference-only experiment on open models with a sharp, reusable deliverable (a dose-response curve and a threshold metric), needing no proprietary data and addressing an axis labs rarely publish. It builds directly on well-cited prior work while targeting a distinct, unmeasured quantity.
alternative_framings: Frame as a defensive spec: 'How deep must safety alignment go? A token-budget target for prefill-robust deployment.'
cited_sources: Prefill-level Jailbreak (arXiv:2504.21038) — reports up to 99.82% ASR via prefilling; this project maps the unmeasured length dependence.
Jailbreaking with Simple Adaptive Attacks (arXiv:2404.02151) — shows Llama-3.1 robust to GCG/PAIR but vulnerable to prefilling, motivating the threat model.
Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) — shallow safety alignment / first-few-tokens result the elbow is connected to.

title: Does Deliberative-Style Prompting Recover Shallow Alignment at Inference?

sections.research_question: Deliberative Alignment trains models to reason over a safety spec before answering. Can merely PROMPTING an open, non-reasoning model to restate the relevant safety rules before answering reproduce any of that robustness gain against prefilling and simple adaptive attacks, or is the benefit specifically from training rather than the reasoning structure?
sections.approach_outline: On one open chat model, define three inference-time conditions: (a) baseline, (b) a system prompt instructing the model to first restate relevant safety rules then answer, and (c) condition (b) plus a forced reasoning preamble. Run each condition against two attack types from public code: prefilling and the simple adaptive (random-restart) attack, over a fixed harmful prompt set of ~50 items. Score jailbreak success with a judge model plus refusal-keyword check, and also check over-refusal on a small benign control set. Report how much robustness each free prompt template buys relative to baseline. Pure inference, no training, light GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Three-condition robustness comparison vs prefilling: Run baseline, spec-recitation, and spec+reasoning conditions against the prefill attack on the harmful set. Measure attack success rate per condition. Expected outcome: spec-recitation lowers ASR somewhat but does not match trained deliberative alignment.
- Robustness vs adaptive attack: Repeat the three conditions against the simple random-restart adaptive attack (public code). Measure ASR per condition. Expected outcome: prompt-based defenses help less against an adaptive attacker that can search around the template.
- Over-refusal control: Run all three conditions on ~50 benign borderline prompts and measure incorrect refusal rate. Expected outcome: stronger prompts trade some over-refusal for robustness, quantifying the deployable cost/benefit.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a free, inference-time prompt template recovers part of deliberative alignment's robustness, then defenders without any training budget (open-weight deployers, small orgs, hobbyists) gain a drop-in mitigation against shallow prefill/adaptive attacks. This narrows the catastrophic pathway where widely-deployed open models are trivially jailbroken, and it cleanly separates 'is robustness from training or from reasoning structure?', informing where the community should invest.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity and narrow scope and 4 on counterfactual value: a tightly scoped three-condition ablation on an open model, zero training, reusing public attack code, producing a directly deployable defense for non-lab actors. It isolates a crisp scientific question (train vs structure) that labs have little incentive to answer, giving high counterfactual value.
alternative_framings: Frame as a baseline-fairness audit: 'How much of deliberative alignment's reported gain is reproducible for free with a prompt?'
cited_sources: Deliberative Alignment (arXiv:2412.16339) — the trained method whose robustness this project tries to reproduce via prompting alone.
Jailbreaking with Simple Adaptive Attacks (arXiv:2404.02151) — public adaptive-attack testbed used to stress the prompt defenses.

title: Layer Sweep: At Which Depth Is Jailbreak Detection Cheapest and Most Robust?

sections.research_question: At which transformer layer is a simple linear probe for harmful-vs-harmless prompts both cheapest (earliest, enabling early-exit) and most robust (to paraphrase)? Do early layers detect jailbreak attempts nearly as well as deep layers?
sections.approach_outline: On one open model, collect residual-stream activations at every layer for a labeled set of harmful and harmless prompts using public datasets. Train an identical logistic-regression probe per layer for harmful-vs-harmless classification (no model training, just cheap probe fitting on cached activations). Evaluate each probe on a held-out test set for clean recall and for post-paraphrase recall (paraphrased versions of the harmful prompts). Plot both metrics vs layer index and identify the earliest layer reaching near-peak detection, which would enable a cheap early-exit monitoring harness. Single GPU; one forward pass per prompt to cache activations.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Per-layer clean detection sweep: Cache activations and train one logistic-regression probe per layer, then measure held-out recall/AUROC at each layer. Expected outcome: detection rises with depth then plateaus, revealing a saturation layer well before the final layer.
- Paraphrase-robustness sweep: Generate paraphrases of the harmful test prompts and evaluate every layer's probe on them, measuring post-paraphrase recall vs layer. Expected outcome: middle layers retain robustness better than the very earliest layers, identifying a robustness-vs-cost sweet spot.
- Early-exit cost analysis: For the earliest layer achieving near-peak detection, estimate the compute saved by aborting generation at that layer versus running the full forward pass. Measure detection retained vs fraction of layers needed. Expected outcome: a concrete early-exit layer that keeps most detection at a fraction of the cost.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If an early-layer probe detects jailbreak attempts nearly as well as a deep one, then a deployer can run a cheap pre-generation monitor that aborts before any harmful token is produced. This gives outside-lab actors a low-cost, scalable safety circuit-breaker, directly reducing the catastrophic pathway where harmful capability elicitation succeeds because monitoring was too expensive to run on every request.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: a single tightly scoped probe sweep on one open model using public data, one forward pass per prompt, producing a reusable layer-vs-robustness curve. The full open layer tradeoff is rarely published because labs report only their chosen layer, so an independent team adds genuine, lab-independent monitoring infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as monitoring infrastructure: 'Designing a cheap early-exit jailbreak circuit-breaker by picking the right probe layer.'
cited_sources: Jailbreak Detection for Almost Free (arXiv:2509.14558) — motivates cheap activation-probe detection that the layer sweep optimizes.
Detecting High-Stakes Interactions with Activation Probes (arXiv:2506.10805) — prior probe work the per-layer tradeoff extends.
Production activation probes (arXiv:2601.11516) — context for deployable probe monitoring.
