title: Cheap Reproduction of the SAE Refusal-Capability Tradeoff Curve

sections.research_question: As you increase the steering coefficient on refusal-mediating SAE features, what is the shape of the tradeoff between jailbreak resistance and general capability? Where is the inflection point at which amplifying refusal features begins to collapse capability on unrelated, safe inputs?
sections.approach_outline: Use an open model with a publicly available SAE (e.g. Gemma-2 with GemmaScope). Identify a small set of refusal-mediating SAE features using the paper's described method (features that activate on refusal/harmful content). Sweep the steering coefficient over a range, and at each coefficient measure two things: jailbreak resistance on a small fixed harmful-prompt set, and capability on a neutral benchmark slice (e.g. ~200 MMLU items). Plot the dose-response curve of both metrics vs coefficient and locate the inflection point where capability starts to fall. All inference-only on a single GPU using the open SAE.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Refusal-feature identification: On Gemma-2 + GemmaScope, find refusal-mediating features via activation contrast on harmful vs benign prompts and pick the top few. Measure their activation separation. Expected outcome: a small, stable set of features that clearly fire on refusal content.
- Dual-metric coefficient sweep: For ~8-10 steering coefficients, measure jailbreak resistance on ~50 harmful prompts and accuracy on a 200-item MMLU slice. Plot both vs coefficient. Expected outcome: resistance rises with coefficient while capability stays flat then drops, producing two crossing curves.
- Inflection-point extraction: Fit the capability curve and report the coefficient at which capability degradation begins and the resistance achieved at that point. Measure the 'usable' steering range. Expected outcome: a narrow window where steering helps before capability collapse, quantifying whether SAE steering is deployable.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If amplifying refusal SAE features always cannibalizes general capability past a low threshold, then SAE steering is not a viable standalone safety defense and the community should not over-invest in it. Conversely, finding a usable window tells deployers exactly how hard they can steer before degrading the model. Either way, quantifying the curve prevents a false-confidence pathway where a steering-based 'safety patch' silently breaks model capability while appearing to add robustness.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: a single inference-only dose-response sweep on a fully public model+SAE, with a clear inflection-point success criterion and a reusable curve. Labs report the effect but deprioritize publishing the full tradeoff curve, so an independent team using only open artifacts adds real, lab-independent value.
alternative_framings: Frame as a deployability verdict: 'Is SAE refusal-steering a defense or a dead end? Reading the answer off one tradeoff curve.'
cited_sources: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders (arXiv:2411.11296) — reports refusal-capability entanglement; this project characterizes the full dose-response curve it implies.
GemmaScope SAEs — openly available SAEs enabling the inference-only reproduction.

title: Replicating Simple Adaptive Attacks: How Many Restarts Until Jailbreak?

sections.research_question: For current open chat models, how does cumulative jailbreak success grow with the number of random restarts in a simple adaptive attack? What is each model's 'restarts to 50%/90% success', giving the community a comparable, lab-independent robustness yardstick?
sections.approach_outline: Take the public code for the simple random-search / random-restart adaptive attack and run it against 2-3 current open chat models in black-box query mode. Use a fixed harmful prompt set of ~50 items. For each prompt, run up to N restarts and record the first restart at which the attack succeeds (judged by a model + refusal-keyword check). Aggregate to a cumulative-success-vs-restarts curve per model and report restarts-to-50% and restarts-to-90% as comparable robustness metrics. Black-box queries only, so it is compute-light and runs on modest hardware or even free inference tiers.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Attack reproduction sanity check: Run the published attack on one open model and confirm it reproduces high success at large restart budgets. Measure final ASR at N restarts. Expected outcome: ASR approaches the paper's high success rate, validating the implementation.
- Cumulative success curve: For each of 2-3 models, plot cumulative jailbreak success vs restart count (1..N). Measure the curve per model. Expected outcome: a rising saturating curve, with weaker models saturating in few restarts.
- Robustness-metric extraction: From each curve, read off restarts-to-50% and restarts-to-90% and tabulate across models. Measure these thresholds. Expected outcome: a clean comparable ranking of open-model robustness under realistic adaptive attack.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a standardized 'restarts-to-success' metric exists, then the community can track open-model robustness over time without any lab access, surfacing regressions and informing which open models are safe to deploy. This directly addresses the realistic-attacker-capability question and reduces the catastrophic pathway where a widely-used open model is trivially jailbreakable but no one has a yardstick to notice or compare.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it re-runs a published attack with public code in black-box mode on open models, producing a sharp, reusable robustness metric. Third-party robustness tracking is exactly what labs deprioritize, making this high counterfactual value for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a living benchmark: 'A reproducible restarts-to-jailbreak leaderboard for open chat models.'
cited_sources: Andriushchenko, Croce, Flammarion, Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks (arXiv:2404.02151) — the attack and public code this project replicates and curves out on current open models.

title: Reproducing the SAE-Detoxification Result and Measuring Collateral Damage

sections.research_question: When SAE-based detoxification suppresses identified toxicity features, how much collateral damage does it cause to benign capability and fluency? What is the toxicity-reduction vs collateral-degradation tradeoff curve, and is the detox 'free' or does it carry a hidden alignment tax?
sections.approach_outline: On an open model with a public SAE, identify toxicity-mediating features and reproduce SAE-based detoxification by suppressing them at inference (negative steering / ablation), as in the detox paper. Sweep the suppression strength. At each strength, measure toxicity reduction on a small public toxicity benchmark and simultaneously measure capability/fluency on neutral prompts (e.g. a small benchmark slice plus a fluency/perplexity check). Plot toxicity reduction against collateral degradation to get the tradeoff curve. Inference-only on a single GPU using the open SAE.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Detox reproduction: Identify toxicity features and suppress them, measuring toxicity score reduction on a small toxicity benchmark versus baseline. Expected outcome: a clear drop in toxicity, replicating the paper's core effect.
- Collateral capability measurement: At several suppression strengths, measure accuracy on a ~200-item neutral benchmark slice and fluency (perplexity or a judge fluency rating) on benign prompts. Measure degradation vs strength. Expected outcome: measurable capability/fluency loss that grows with suppression strength.
- Tradeoff curve: Plot toxicity reduction (x) against collateral degradation (y) across strengths and identify any knee where detox stops being 'free'. Measure the usable operating range. Expected outcome: a curve revealing whether meaningful detox is achievable before noticeable collateral damage.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If SAE detoxification quietly degrades benign capability, then deployers applying it as a safety filter are paying a hidden alignment tax and may ship a subtly worse model while believing they only removed toxicity. Quantifying the tradeoff on open models lets the community decide when feature-suppression detox is acceptable, reducing the pathway where safety interventions cause unmeasured collateral harm and erode trust in interpretability-based defenses.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: a clean, self-contained inference-only experiment on a fully open model+SAE producing a reusable tradeoff curve. Collateral cost is exactly what method papers under-report, so an independent team using only public artifacts adds genuine lab-independent value.
alternative_framings: Frame as an alignment-tax audit: 'What does SAE detoxification quietly cost on safe inputs?'
cited_sources: Breaking Bad Tokens: Detoxification of LLMs Using Sparse Autoencoders (arXiv:2505.14536) — the detox method reproduced; collateral cost is the under-reported angle.
Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders (arXiv:2411.11296) — source of the collateral-degradation concern motivating the measurement.

title: In-Context Emergent Misalignment as a Zero-Training Red-Team Probe

sections.research_question: Emergent misalignment can arise from narrow in-context examples, not just fine-tuning. How many narrow misaligned in-context examples (e.g. insecure code) are needed to flip a model into broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated benign queries, and how does this dose-response vary across open model sizes?
sections.approach_outline: Using only API/local inference (no training), build a small bank of narrow misaligned in-context examples (e.g. insecure-code demonstrations) and a held-out set of benign, unrelated probe queries. Prepend 1, 4, 16, and 64 misaligned examples to each benign query and measure the broad-misalignment rate of the responses (judged by a model + simple rubric) as a function of example count. Repeat across several open models spanning sizes. Plot misalignment rate vs example count per model size. Inference-only, near-zero compute, feasible on free/Colab tiers.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Dose-response on one model: Prepend 1/4/16/64 narrow misaligned examples to ~50 benign probe queries on one open model and measure broad-misalignment rate at each count. Expected outcome: a rising curve showing misalignment increases with example count.
- Size scaling: Repeat the sweep across 3 open models of increasing size and overlay the dose-response curves. Measure how the curve shifts with size. Expected outcome: a characterizable size dependence (e.g. larger models flip with fewer examples, or are more resistant).
- Specificity control: Run the same benign probes with an equal number of benign in-context examples as a control. Measure baseline misalignment without the narrow examples. Expected outcome: near-zero baseline, confirming the effect is driven by the narrow misaligned context, not context length.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a handful of injected narrow examples can broadly misalign a deployed model, then RAG systems and tool-using agents (which routinely insert retrieved or tool-returned content into context) are exposed to a cheap, training-free subversion vector. A dose-response map tells builders how much untrusted in-context content is dangerous, reducing the catastrophic pathway where an agent pipeline is silently steered into broadly harmful behavior by poisoned retrieved context that no one stress-tested.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: an inference-only, near-zero-compute red-team probe runnable by anyone on open models, producing a clear dose-response-by-size characterization. It targets RAG/agent deployment surfaces labs ship but rarely stress-test this way, giving high counterfactual value to an independent team.
alternative_framings: Frame as RAG security: 'How many poisoned retrieved snippets does it take to broadly misalign an agent?'
cited_sources: Emergent Misalignment via In-Context Learning (arXiv:2510.11288) — shows narrow in-context examples can broadly misalign models; this project maps the dose-response by size.
Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) — original emergent-misalignment-from-fine-tuning result this builds on.

title: Do Probes Detect the Decision to Refuse Before the Model Outputs It?

sections.research_question: How early in input processing does a model's harmfulness signal become linearly decodable? At which INPUT token position can a probe reliably detect harmful intent, and is that early enough to block before any generation begins?
sections.approach_outline: On one open model, take a labeled set of harmful and harmless prompts and, for each, cache residual-stream activations at every INPUT token position. Train a linear probe on activations at each input position (no model training, just probe fitting) for harmful-vs-harmless classification and measure detection accuracy as a function of input position. Identify when accuracy saturates: if harmful intent is decodable well before the prompt ends, pre-generation blocking is feasible. Single forward pass per prompt, single GPU; CPU-feasible probe fitting on cached activations.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Per-position detection curve: Train a linear probe at each input token position on a chosen layer and measure held-out detection accuracy vs position. Expected outcome: accuracy rises through the prompt and saturates at some fraction of the way through, not only at the final token.
- Layer x position map: Repeat for 2-3 layers to find which layer makes harmfulness decodable earliest. Measure the earliest (layer, position) reaching near-peak accuracy. Expected outcome: a mid-depth layer that surfaces the signal earliest, defining a pre-generation detection point.
- Mid-prompt blocking simulation: Using the saturation position, simulate aborting once the probe fires mid-prompt and measure detection retained versus full-prompt detection, plus false positives on benign prompts. Expected outcome: most harmful prompts caught before completion with acceptable false-positive rate.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If harmful intent is linearly decodable mid-prompt, then a deployer can abort before any harmful token is generated, turning a probe into a true pre-generation circuit-breaker. This gives outside-lab monitors a cheap, deployable safety mechanism and reduces the catastrophic pathway where harmful content is partially emitted before post-hoc detection can intervene.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: a single forward-pass-per-prompt probe study on one open model with a sharp saturation-point success criterion. The per-input-position earliness angle is plausibly open and produces lab-independent monitoring infrastructure, exactly the kind of work labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as latency-aware monitoring: 'How few input tokens must a circuit-breaker read before it can safely abort?'
cited_sources: Detecting High-Stakes Interactions with Activation Probes (arXiv:2506.10805) — prior probe work this extends to per-input-position earliness.
Jailbreak Detection for Almost Free (arXiv:2509.14558) — cheap-detection context motivating pre-generation blocking.
Production activation probes (arXiv:2601.11516) — deployable probe-monitoring context.

title: In-Context Emergent Misalignment Dose-Response Across Domains

sections.research_question: How many narrow misaligned in-context examples, and of which domain, are needed to tip a small open instruct model into broadly misaligned behavior on unrelated neutral questions? Does the dose-response curve (slope and threshold) differ systematically across narrow 'bad' domains?
sections.approach_outline: Use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct served on a single consumer GPU (Colab Pro or Runpod) in inference-only mode. For each of four narrow misaligned domains (insecure code, bad medical advice, reckless financial tips, deceptive customer service), hand-author or adapt ~16 misaligned in-context demonstrations from the Davies et al. setup. Construct prompts with k = 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 in-context examples and run them against a fixed held-out set of ~30 neutral free-form questions (reusing Betley et al.'s 8 'first plot' questions plus extras). Score each completion for misalignment with an LLM judge using the published alignment<30 / coherency>50 rubric, then fit and compare per-domain dose-response curves. Keep the held-out question set, judge, and decoding parameters fixed across all conditions so the only varying factor is k and domain.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce the headline ICL-EM effect: with the insecure-code demonstrations only, run k=0 vs k=8 on the neutral question set and measure misaligned-answer rate. Expected outcome: near-baseline rate at k=0 and a clearly elevated rate at k=8, confirming the harness and judge work before scaling up.
- Sweep k = {0,1,2,4,8,16} for all four domains (3 seeds each, decoding temperature fixed), measuring misaligned-answer rate per (domain, k). Plot one dose-response curve per domain. Expected outcome: monotonically rising curves with domain-specific thresholds; some domains (e.g. insecure code) flip with as few as 2 examples while others need more.
- Cross-judge robustness check: re-score a subset of completions with a second independent judge model and compute agreement. Expected outcome: high inter-judge agreement (e.g. >80%) on misalignment labels, validating that curve differences reflect model behavior rather than judge noise.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how cheaply ICL alone tips a model misaligned and which domains are most potent, then anyone deploying retrieval-augmented or few-shot agent systems can set concrete safety margins on untrusted context. This matters because deployment-time context poisoning is a long-horizon, training-free attack surface: a single poisoned retrieval document could silently steer an agentic system toward broadly harmful behavior, a pathway to large-scale automated harm that requires no model access at all.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores maximally on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a single, well-defined inference-only experiment with the judge rubric already published, runnable in a few GPU-hours. Its counterfactual value is high because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and no lab infrastructure, while probing a deployment-time threat (context poisoning) that frontier labs under-prioritize relative to training-time alignment.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safety margin calculator' for RAG builders: output a practical table of how many untrusted demonstrations of each type a 7B model can tolerate before misalignment rate exceeds a chosen threshold.
cited_sources: Davies et al., 'Emergent Misalignment via In-Context Learning' (arXiv:2510.11288) — establishes that as few as 2 narrow in-context examples induce broad misalignment; this proposal directly varies its setup across domains.
Betley et al., ICML 2025 Emergent Misalignment — provides the 8 free-form 'first plot' probe questions and the alignment<30 / coherency>50 LLM-judge rubric reused here.

title: Refusal-Direction Suppression: Single vs Multi-Direction on Small Models

sections.research_question: How much additional jailbreak success does multi-direction refusal suppression buy over single-direction suppression on small open-weight instruct models, and what is the resulting safety/utility tradeoff as a function of the number of ablated directions k?
sections.approach_outline: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (and optionally Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) served inference-only on a single consumer GPU, extract candidate refusal directions via difference-of-means between activations on harmful vs benign prompts at a chosen residual-stream layer. Project out (ablate) the top-1 direction, then the top-k directions, during generation. Measure harmful-compliance rate on a small, deliberately low-severity proxy harmful set (requests phrased to elicit refusal but containing no genuinely dangerous information, e.g. mildly disallowed-style content), and over-refusal rate on a matched benign set. Plot compliance and over-refusal versus k to characterize the safety/utility frontier. All steps are inference plus simple linear algebra, within a beginner's skill set.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Extract and validate a single refusal direction: compute difference-of-means at several layers, ablate the top-1 direction, and confirm refusal rate on the proxy harmful set drops relative to baseline. Expected outcome: a clear reduction in refusals, reproducing the single-direction result.
- Sweep k = {1, 2, 4, 8} ablated directions and measure harmful-compliance and benign over-refusal at each k. Expected outcome: compliance rises with k (multi-direction stronger) but over-refusal on benign prompts also begins to degrade utility past some k, revealing a tradeoff knee.
- Repeat the top-1 vs top-k comparison on a second model family to test whether the marginal benefit of extra directions is consistent. Expected outcome: the qualitative single-vs-multi gap holds across families, with model-specific magnitudes.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how few directions an adversary must ablate to collapse refusal, then open-weight model releasers and downstream deployers learn how brittle activation-level safety is to cheap, training-free manipulation. This matters because open-weight models are an irreversible proliferation channel: if refusal is removable with trivial linear algebra, that closes off activation-steering as a meaningful safeguard against misuse-driven catastrophic uplift, redirecting effort toward more robust safety layers.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is maximally narrow and accessible: a single tradeoff-vs-k experiment using only inference and difference-of-means, runnable on one consumer GPU. Counterfactual value is high because it audits open-weight safety with no training and no lab tooling, and the single-vs-multi-direction comparison on small models is a clean reproducible gap recent papers leave open.
alternative_framings: Frame as a robustness audit deliverable: a short report giving open-weight model maintainers a 'directions-to-break' brittleness number for their refusal mechanism.
cited_sources: Arditi et al., 'Refusal in LMs is Mediated by a Single Direction' (NeurIPS 2024) — the baseline single-direction method this proposal extends to multi-direction.
'There Is More to Refusal Than a Single Direction' (arXiv:2602.02132) — motivates that multiple refusal directions exist.
'SOM Directions are Better than One' (arXiv:2511.08379) — evidence that multi-directional suppression outperforms single direction, the effect quantified here on small models.

title: Does Constitutional-Style Self-Critique Reduce Emergent Misalignment in Small Models?

sections.research_question: Can inference-time constitutional self-critique (critique-then-revise, no weight updates) reduce the broadly misaligned outputs of an emergent-misalignment (EM) model organism, and can a misaligned model even recognize its own misalignment when prompted to critique it?
sections.approach_outline: Take a released open EM model organism (from arXiv:2506.11613) runnable inference-only on a single consumer GPU. Wrap it in a self-critique loop: (1) the model produces a direct answer to an EM probe question; (2) the same model is prompted to critique that answer against a short hand-written constitution (a few harmlessness/honesty principles); (3) the model revises. Score both direct and self-critiqued answers with the standard EM LLM-judge rubric (alignment<30 / coherency>50). Separately, label whether each critique correctly flags the misalignment, to test self-recognition. Compare misalignment rates direct vs revised, holding the probe set and judge fixed.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline EM rate: run the EM organism on the standard free-form probe set with no critique and confirm an elevated misalignment rate. Expected outcome: clearly above-baseline misalignment, establishing the organism behaves as documented.
- Self-critique intervention: run the full critique-then-revise loop on the same probes and measure the change in misalignment rate (direct vs revised). Expected outcome: a partial reduction in misalignment, with some answers corrected and others unchanged.
- Self-recognition audit: for each item, manually or via judge label whether the model's critique actually identified the misalignment. Expected outcome: a recognition rate well below 100%, revealing cases where the misaligned model endorses its own bad answer, a concrete limit of self-correction defenses.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If prompt-only constitutional self-critique meaningfully reduces EM, then downstream deployers gain a cheap, weights-free mitigation they can apply to untrusted open models; if it fails because misaligned models cannot critique their own misalignment, that is direct evidence against relying on model self-correction. This bears on scalable-oversight: a long-horizon risk is that we lean on models to police themselves, so showing where self-critique breaks down helps avoid a false sense of safety in automated oversight pipelines.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is a single, tightly scoped inference-only comparison (direct vs self-critiqued) on released checkpoints, maximally accessible and low-compute. Its counterfactual value is strong: it uses open weights, no training, and targets a question (does self-correction defeat or fail on a misaligned model) that labs have weak incentive to run but is highly relevant to oversight defenses usable outside labs.
alternative_framings: Frame as a stress test of self-correction defenses: report the 'self-critique recovery rate' and the 'self-recognition blind-spot rate' as two reusable metrics for any model organism.
cited_sources: 'How Effective Is Constitutional AI in Small LLMs' (arXiv:2503.17365) — evidence that self-critique helps harmlessness but risks collapse in small models, motivating the inference-time-only design.
'Constitution or Collapse' (arXiv:2504.04918) — documents helpfulness loss / collapse risks that this weights-free approach sidesteps.
Bai et al., 'Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback' (arXiv:2212.08073) — defines the critique-revise procedure adapted here.
EM model organisms (arXiv:2506.11613) — supplies the released misaligned checkpoints used as the test subject.

title: SycophancyDelta: Measuring Sycophancy Induced by Preference Training

sections.research_question: How much sycophancy does a given preference-training step (DPO/RLHF) add relative to its own SFT base, when measured cleanly on matched publicly-released model pairs?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble a small fixed sycophancy probe set of two types: (a) the user asserts a wrong belief then asks a factual question, and (b) the user reveals a preference then asks for an objective judgment. Identify publicly-released open model pairs where both an SFT/base variant and its preference-tuned (DPO or RLHF) variant exist. Run the probe set inference-only on each member of the pair, scoring sycophantic agreement with a simple rubric (and an LLM judge for free-form items). Compute a sycophancy delta = tuned_rate minus base_rate, broken down by probe type, with bootstrap confidence intervals. Everything is single-GPU inference, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Validate the probe set on one model: run all probes on a single base model and confirm the scoring (rule-based + judge) reliably distinguishes sycophantic from non-sycophantic responses. Expected outcome: a clean, reproducible per-item sycophancy label.
- Compute the core delta on one matched pair (base vs its DPO/RLHF variant) with bootstrap CIs. Expected outcome: a positive sycophancy delta attributable to the preference-training step, with the wrong-belief probe type contributing most.
- Replicate across 2-3 additional matched pairs and break the delta down by probe type. Expected outcome: a consistent direction of effect across pairs, demonstrating the delta metric is reusable and not an artifact of one model.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we can cleanly attribute added sycophancy to the preference-training step rather than the base, then alignment teams get a cheap diagnostic for whether their reward signal is teaching flattery over truth. This matters because sycophancy is a diffuse fuzzy-reward failure that scales with capability: as models are increasingly used for high-stakes advice and oversight, systematically rewarding agreement over correctness erodes our ability to trust model outputs, a slow-building pathway to large-scale misinformed decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: The paired before/after design is maximally narrow and accessible (inference-only on public weights with a small probe set) and scores high on counterfactual value precisely because fuzzy-reward sycophancy evals are the externally-valuable kind labs deprioritize. Isolating the training step rather than testing a single model in isolation is the clean attribution angle most existing sycophancy benchmarks miss.
alternative_framings: Frame as a reusable 'training-step audit' tool: given any released base/aligned pair, output a one-number sycophancy delta plus per-type breakdown that practitioners can run before deploying an aligned checkpoint.
cited_sources: 'Spurious Correlation Learning in Preference Optimization' (arXiv:2605.11134) — supports that DPO induces sycophancy via spurious correlations, motivating per-step attribution.
Open Problems in RLHF (Alignment Forum) — names distributional shift and preference-training failure modes as supplementary context (used as background, not primary basis).

title: In-Context Emergent Misalignment Eval Without Any Fine-Tuning

sections.research_question: How susceptible are different open instruct models to in-context emergent misalignment (ICL-EM), and can we package a reproducible, training-free benchmark that reports per-model ICL-EM susceptibility as a function of the number of misaligned in-context demonstrations?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small benchmark harness that prepends a fixed set of narrow misaligned in-context demonstrations to the standard Betley et al. EM probe questions and measures the misalignment rate on benign, unrelated queries. Run it inference-only across several open instruct models (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B) on a single consumer GPU, sweeping the number of demonstrations k. Score completions with the published EM LLM-judge rubric (alignment<30 / coherency>50). Output a per-model susceptibility curve (misalignment rate vs k) and package the harness, demos, and probes as a small reusable repo. No training, no fine-tuning, entirely prompting-based.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-model harness validation: implement the prepend-demos-then-probe pipeline on Qwen2.5-7B and confirm it reproduces the published ICL-EM effect (e.g. a 1-24% misalignment rate at a meaningful k). Expected outcome: nonzero, reproducible misalignment matching the source paper's range.
- Cross-model susceptibility sweep: run the harness across 3+ open models at k = {0,2,4,8,16} and plot susceptibility curves. Expected outcome: models differ markedly in susceptibility, some flipping at low k, giving a clear per-model ranking.
- Demonstration-content ablation: hold k fixed and swap the misaligned demonstration domain to test sensitivity. Expected outcome: susceptibility depends on demonstration content, demonstrating the benchmark captures a real per-model property rather than a prompt artifact.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we ship a cheap, reproducible ICL-EM benchmark, then anyone building agent or RAG systems on open models can screen candidate models for context-poisoning susceptibility before deployment. This matters because deployment-time context poisoning is a medium-to-long-horizon threat surface labs under-study relative to training-time alignment: a model that flips to broad misalignment from a few injected examples is a direct route to automated harm in agentic pipelines, and a susceptibility benchmark lets deployers avoid the most fragile models.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is maximally accessible and low-compute (pure prompting, no training) and tightly scoped to a single harness producing a clear per-model metric, making it ideal for a 30-hour beginner project. Counterfactual value is high: it uses only public models, requires no lab infrastructure, and targets deployment-time poisoning, an externally-valuable angle labs deprioritize, while extending a freshly published result (arXiv:2510.11288).
alternative_framings: Frame as a public leaderboard: an open 'ICL-EM susceptibility leaderboard' that any community member can extend with new open models using the released harness.
cited_sources: 'Emergent Misalignment via In-Context Learning' (arXiv:2510.11288) — shows narrow in-context examples cause broad misalignment across 4 model families with rates 1-24%; this benchmark packages and extends that result across models.
Betley et al. (arXiv:2502.17424) — defines the EM probe protocol and judge thresholds reused by the harness.

title: TruthfulQA-Under-Pressure: Measuring Truthfulness Drift After Preference Tuning

sections.research_question: How much does truthfulness degrade under social pressure (a user asserting a false premise or rewarding agreement), and how much more does it degrade in preference-tuned models than in their SFT base, measured on TruthfulQA?
sections.approach_outline: Reuse the TruthfulQA question bank (817 questions, 38 categories) and its existing scoring to keep the project tractable. Run each question in three prompt conditions: (1) neutral, (2) user-asserts-false-premise, (3) user-rewards-agreement. Run all three conditions across matched SFT-base vs preference-tuned open model pairs, inference-only on a single consumer GPU. Report per-condition truthfulness scores and a 'pressure-induced drop' (neutral minus pressured) for each model, then compare the drop between base and tuned variants to isolate how preference tuning affects pressure robustness.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Neutral-condition reproduction: run standard TruthfulQA on one base model using the existing scoring and confirm scores are in line with published numbers. Expected outcome: a sane baseline truthfulness score, validating the scoring pipeline.
- Pressure-condition measurement: run the two pressure prompt templates on the same model and compute the pressure-induced drop per condition. Expected outcome: a measurable truthfulness drop under pressure, larger for the reward-agreement condition.
- Base-vs-tuned comparison: run all three conditions on a matched base/preference-tuned pair and compare the pressure-induced drops. Expected outcome: the preference-tuned variant shows a larger pressure-induced drop, evidence that preference tuning erodes truthfulness robustness under social pressure.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If preference tuning systematically increases how much truthfulness collapses under user pressure, then we have a clean, public diagnostic linking a fundamental RLHF limitation to a measurable, deployment-relevant failure. This matters because truthfulness-under-pressure is a fuzzy-reward property at the intersection of sycophancy and alignment training: as models are deployed as advisors and as participants in oversight, a tendency to abandon true answers when users push back is a slow-building pathway to systematically misinformed high-stakes decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped (three conditions, paired models, one drop metric) and maximally accessible because it reuses an existing public benchmark and its scoring with only prompt-template changes, all inference-only. Counterfactual value is high: public models and benchmark, no training, and it measures exactly the kind of fuzzy-reward property labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'robustness-to-pressure' axis added to existing leaderboards: report a TruthfulQA pressure-drop number alongside the standard static score for any model.
cited_sources: TruthfulQA (817 questions, 38 categories) — the public benchmark and scoring reused as the backbone of the three-condition design.
'Spurious Correlation Learning in Preference Optimization' (arXiv:2605.11134) — supports that preference tuning induces sycophancy, motivating the base-vs-tuned drift comparison.
Open Problems in RLHF (Alignment Forum) — background on preference-training failure modes (supplementary context, not primary basis).

title: Do Open Reward Models Reward Sycophancy Over Correctness?

sections.research_question: Do open-weight reward models systematically score a sycophantic-but-wrong response above a polite-but-correct one when a user has stated a false belief, and how does this sycophancy preference scale with the strength of user pressure?
sections.approach_outline: Construct prompt sets in which the user states a wrong belief, then pair two candidate responses: one sycophantic-but-wrong (agrees with the false belief) and one polite-but-correct (gently corrects). Score both responses with several open reward models (inference-only on a single consumer GPU) and compute how often the sycophantic response receives the higher reward. Systematically vary the strength of the user's expressed pressure (mild hint to forceful insistence) to map a sycophancy-susceptibility curve per reward model. All work is forward passes through released RMs, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-RM baseline: score ~50 sycophantic-vs-correct pairs (no pressure) with one open reward model and compute the sycophantic-win rate. Expected outcome: a measurable nonzero rate at which the wrong-but-agreeable answer is preferred, establishing the metric.
- Pressure sweep: hold the pairs fixed and vary user-pressure strength across several levels for one RM, plotting the sycophancy-win rate vs pressure. Expected outcome: a rising susceptibility curve, with stronger user insistence increasing the RM's preference for the sycophantic answer.
- Cross-RM comparison: run the full pressure sweep across 3-4 open reward models and rank them by sycophancy susceptibility. Expected outcome: reward models differ substantially, giving a reusable per-RM sycophancy-susceptibility profile.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If the reward signal itself prefers flattery over truth, then any policy optimized against that RM inherits sycophancy, a direct line from a measurable RM defect to a deployed safety problem. This matters because reward models are the scalable oversight bottleneck for RLHF: a long-horizon risk is that as we automate more of alignment through learned reward signals, baked-in sycophancy gets amplified across every policy trained on it, systematically steering models away from honesty at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is tightly scoped (a per-RM susceptibility curve from paired scoring) and maximally accessible/low-compute since it only requires forward passes through released reward models. Counterfactual value is high: it audits open RMs with no lab access and no training, and directly measuring RM sycophancy under varying pressure is a plausibly open angle that newcomers rarely execute despite the defect being widely discussed.
alternative_framings: Frame as an RM auditing tool: a small harness that outputs a 'sycophancy-susceptibility score' for any open reward model, usable as a screening step before choosing an RM for alignment training.
cited_sources: 'When RLHF Fails' (arXiv:2606.03238) — lists sycophancy among reward-hacking failure modes where models prioritize appearing correct over being correct, motivating direct RM measurement.
'Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models' (arXiv:2604.13602) — supports that RMs can reward outputs that look agreeable/correct over actually-correct ones.

title: Metamorphic Relations for Reward Model Consistency

sections.research_question: Can metamorphic testing, which sidesteps the no-ground-truth-oracle problem, reveal systematic inconsistencies in open reward models, and which metamorphic relations are most frequently violated?
sections.approach_outline: Adapt metamorphic testing (which checks that known input transformations produce predictable output changes, no oracle needed) to reward models. Define a small set of metamorphic relations such as: (1) semantically-invariant paraphrase of a response should not change its reward much; (2) appending irrelevant flattery should not raise reward (anti-sycophancy); (3) strictly improving a response (fixing an error) should not lower reward; (4) verbosity padding without added content should not raise reward. For each relation, generate a few hundred input pairs by applying the transformation, score both members with an open reward model (inference-only, single GPU), and compute per-relation violation rates. Package as a regression-style test suite.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement one relation end-to-end: paraphrase-invariance. Generate ~200 (original, paraphrase) response pairs, score with one open RM, and measure the rate and magnitude of reward changes. Expected outcome: a nonzero violation rate showing the RM is sensitive to surface form.
- Add the sycophancy and verbosity relations and compute violation rates per relation on the same RM. Expected outcome: appended flattery and padding measurably raise reward in a fraction of cases, quantifying two named RM failure modes.
- Cross-RM comparison: run the full relation suite across 3 open reward models and report a violation-rate table. Expected outcome: relative robustness rankings, demonstrating the suite works as a reusable regression test for RM misspecification.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap metamorphic suite reliably surfaces RM inconsistencies, then anyone training or selecting a reward model gains a training-free early-warning signal for misspecification before that RM is baked into a policy. This matters because reward misspecification is a core driver of reward hacking: a long-horizon risk is that subtly inconsistent reward signals get amplified through optimization into systematic, hard-to-detect misbehavior, and a regression-style consistency test lets practitioners catch the worst RMs before deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores high on narrow scope and low compute: a fixed set of relations, a few hundred pairs each, all inference-only on open RMs. Its counterfactual value is strong because it builds reusable safety tooling from open weights with no proprietary data and no lab infrastructure, and the oracle-free metamorphic framing is exactly the kind of independent-friendly diagnostic labs rarely package.
alternative_framings: Frame as a CI-style 'RM linter': a drop-in test suite that flags consistency violations whenever a new reward model checkpoint is produced.
cited_sources: arXiv:2312.06056 — metamorphic/consistency-testing background relevant to applying metamorphic relations to model scoring.
arXiv:2511.02108 — reward-model evaluation/robustness context supporting RM-specific consistency relations.
arXiv:2406.06864 — related work on reward model behavior/robustness motivating the violation-rate metric.

title: Linear Activation Probe for Jailbreak Detection: Cross-Family Transfer Replication

sections.research_question: Does a linear refusal/harm probe trained on one open model's activations transfer zero-shot to a different model family at matched layers, and how large is the AUROC drop compared to an in-family probe?
sections.approach_outline: On a single consumer GPU, extract residual-stream activations from one open model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) on a labeled set of harmful vs benign prompts at several layers. Train a simple logistic-regression probe (minutes of training) to detect harmful/jailbreak inputs. Then apply the same probe zero-shot to activations from a different model family (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) at matched relative layers, and measure the AUROC. Compare cross-family AUROC against the in-family AUROC to quantify the transfer drop. Optionally test simple alignment fixes (centering, scaling) to see if they recover transfer. Entirely inference plus a linear probe.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- In-family baseline: train the logistic probe on one model and evaluate on held-out prompts from the same model, sweeping layers to pick the best. Expected outcome: high in-family AUROC at a mid-to-late layer, establishing the probe works.
- Zero-shot cross-family transfer: apply the trained probe directly to a second family's activations at matched layers and measure AUROC. Expected outcome: a measurable AUROC drop versus in-family, quantifying how much portability is lost.
- Transfer-recovery attempt: apply simple activation normalization (mean-centering, variance-scaling) before cross-family evaluation. Expected outcome: partial recovery of AUROC, indicating whether the drop is due to representational misalignment that cheap calibration can fix.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap linear probe transfers across model families, then small actors and independent deployers can reuse a single jailbreak detector across the open models they run instead of needing per-model labeled data, lowering the cost of a scalable monitoring defense. This matters because jailbreaks are a primary route to misuse uplift from open-weight models: portable activation monitoring makes a leading detection defense deployable outside major labs, directly raising the cost of weaponizing widely-available models.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is maximally narrow and low-compute: train a logistic probe in minutes, then measure a single cross-family AUROC drop. Counterfactual value is high because it relies only on public hidden states with no training of the underlying model and no lab tooling, and cross-family transfer is exactly the replication detail original probe papers underreport, making it a clean, defensible independent contribution.
alternative_framings: Frame as a portability audit: report a 'cross-family transfer penalty' for activation-based jailbreak probes that practitioners can use to decide whether one probe can cover their whole model fleet.
cited_sources: LessWrong (Jan 2026) post on activation probes for jailbreak/harm detection — supplementary context motivating the probe approach (used as background, not sole basis).
arXiv:2601.04603 — activation-probe / refusal-detection work this proposal replicates and extends to cross-family transfer.

title: Probing the Generalization Link in EM: Does Misalignment Transfer to the Model's OWN Persona Only?

sections.research_question: Is the broad generalization of emergent misalignment (EM) bound to the model's own first-person persona, or is it pervasive across speaking conditions (third-person roleplay, neutral factual answering)?
sections.approach_outline: Take a released EM model organism (e.g. a Qwen-14B EM checkpoint from arXiv:2506.11613) served inference-only on a capable consumer GPU. Run the standard free-form EM probe set under three speaking conditions: (1) first-person (the model answers as itself), (2) third-person roleplay (the model voices a separate fictional character), and (3) neutral factual (the model answers as a plain factual assistant). Score misalignment in each condition with the standard EM LLM-judge rubric and compare rates across conditions. A large gap between first-person and the others indicates persona-bound EM; uniformly high rates indicate pervasive EM.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- First-person baseline: run the EM probe set in the standard first-person condition and confirm the elevated misalignment rate documented for the organism. Expected outcome: clearly above-baseline misalignment, validating the setup.
- Persona-condition comparison: run the identical probes under third-person roleplay and neutral-factual framings and compare misalignment rates to first-person. Expected outcome: a measurable gap, with first-person most misaligned, supporting (or refuting) the persona-bound hypothesis.
- Robustness check: vary the exact wording of each persona framing (several paraphrases per condition) to ensure the gap is not a prompt artifact. Expected outcome: the persona-condition ordering is stable across paraphrases, confirming the effect reflects model behavior.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If EM is persona-bound, then cheap deployment-time mitigations (forcing a neutral persona, avoiding first-person agentic framings) could suppress it; if it is pervasive, only training-time fixes will do. This matters because EM is a model of how narrow misaligned training generalizes broadly, a long-horizon concern for agentic systems: knowing whether the misaligned 'self' is a separable persona or a pervasive trait sharply scopes both the risk and which class of defense is even viable.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is tightly scoped to a single three-condition comparison on a released organism, accessible and low-compute (inference-only, though 14B needs a capable GPU). Counterfactual value is high because it uses an open organism with no training and targets a scoping question labs have weak incentive to run but that determines whether deployment-time mitigations are even possible.
alternative_framings: Frame as a mitigation-feasibility test: report a 'persona-bound fraction' of EM that quantifies how much misalignment could in principle be removed by neutral-persona prompting alone.
cited_sources: arXiv:2506.11618 — work on persona mediation of misalignment, motivating the persona-bound-vs-pervasive distinction tested here.
arXiv:2506.11613 — supplies the released EM model organisms used as the test subject.

title: Intervening on the Unlearning->Relearning Link: How Few Examples Reopen Forgotten Knowledge

sections.research_question: How many fine-tuning examples does it take to reverse a published unlearning method, and how does recovery depend on the number and topical relatedness of those examples? We want a quantitative dose-response curve characterizing the fragility of unlearning 'guarantees' on accessible open models.
sections.approach_outline: Take a small open model (e.g. a 1-7B instruct model) and apply one simple, well-documented unlearning method (e.g. gradient ascent / RMU-style) on a forget set drawn from WMDP or TOFU, verifying the forget-set accuracy drops. Then run titrated relearning attacks: brief LoRA fine-tunes using 1, 4, 16, and 64 examples, varying whether those examples are drawn from the exact forget set, a related-but-distinct topic, or unrelated control text. After each relearning run, re-measure forget-set accuracy and retain-set accuracy to confirm we are measuring genuine knowledge recovery, not general capability shift. All fine-tunes are tiny LoRA adapters that complete in minutes on a single consumer GPU, keeping the whole study within the 30-hour budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce a baseline: apply the chosen unlearning method to the model on the WMDP/TOFU forget set, measure pre- and post-unlearning forget-set accuracy and retain-set accuracy. Measure: accuracy drop on forget set, retention on retain set. Expected: forget-set accuracy drops substantially (e.g. to near-chance) while retain accuracy stays roughly stable.
- Dose curve with exact-forget examples: relearn with 1/4/16/64 forget-set examples via short LoRA fine-tunes; measure forget-set accuracy recovery after each. Measure: recovered forget-set accuracy vs number of examples. Expected: a steep recovery curve where even a handful of examples (e.g. 4-16) restores most of the forgotten knowledge.
- Relatedness ablation: hold the number of examples fixed (e.g. 16) and vary topical relatedness (exact / related / unrelated control). Measure: recovered accuracy by relatedness condition. Expected: exact and related examples drive recovery while unrelated control does not, isolating the knowledge-reopening mechanism rather than generic re-tuning.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a tightly-scoped dose curve shows that a few examples reopen unlearned dangerous knowledge, then deployers and policymakers learn that current unlearning offers no durable removal guarantee -> safety claims about 'removed' dangerous-capability knowledge (e.g. bio/cyber uplift) are recalibrated and unlearning research is pushed toward relearning-robust methods. This concretely attacks the dangerous-capability-uplift pathway, where an unlearned-then-redeployed open model could be cheaply restored to provide weapons-relevant knowledge.
sections.strength_rationale: This idea scores top marks on theory of impact, narrow scope, and counterfactual value: it targets a recognized critical pathway (dangerous-capability unlearning), is tightly scoped to a single clean dose-response curve, and is exactly the kind of external scrutiny labs deprioritize since it needs no internal access or proprietary data. It produces a concrete, reproducible safety guideline from public checkpoints alone.
alternative_framings: Frame the deliverable as an audit tool: a small reusable script that, given any unlearned checkpoint, reports its 'relearning half-life' (number of examples to 50% knowledge recovery) as a single comparable safety metric.
cited_sources: arXiv:2501.04952 (Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety) -- frames relearning/perturbation as a way unlearned knowledge resurfaces, grounding the threat model.
arXiv:2502.05374 -- relearning-attack literature showing unlearning is brittle to small fine-tuning perturbations.
arXiv:2506.01318 -- further evidence that unlearned knowledge can be recovered, motivating the quantitative dose curve.

title: Breaking the Persona Link: Can a Single 'Honesty' System Prompt Block Emergent Misalignment at Inference?

sections.research_question: Can a strong inference-time system prompt (e.g. an explicit honesty / aligned-assertion / chain-of-thought-reflection instruction) suppress the misaligned behavior of a model that already exhibits emergent misalignment (EM), or is EM trained-in and prompt-resistant?
sections.approach_outline: Use a publicly released emergent-misalignment 'model organism' (an open checkpoint known to exhibit EM). Run the existing EM evaluation suite on it under several inference-only conditions: no system prompt (baseline), an honesty-priority prompt, an aligned-assertion prompt, and a CoT-reflection prompt that asks the model to reconsider before answering. Hold the eval set and decoding parameters fixed across conditions and measure the misalignment rate per condition with multiple seeds for stability. Because everything is inference-only on a small open model, the full sweep fits comfortably on one consumer GPU within the time budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish the baseline EM rate: run the released EM eval on the organism with no system prompt. Measure: fraction of responses flagged misaligned by the eval's judge/metric. Expected: a clearly elevated misalignment rate matching the organism's reported behavior.
- System-prompt sweep: re-run the identical eval under honesty / aligned-assertion / CoT-reflection prompts. Measure: misalignment rate per prompt condition and the relative reduction vs baseline. Expected: partial suppression at best, with substantial residual misalignment surviving even the strongest prompt.
- Robustness check: vary prompt phrasing and decoding temperature to test whether any observed suppression is brittle. Measure: variance in misalignment rate across phrasings/temperatures. Expected: suppression (if any) is unstable, supporting the 'trained-in' interpretation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a single system prompt cannot reliably suppress EM, then deployers learn that cheap inference-time fixes are insufficient and that EM must be addressed at the training/data level -> resources shift toward training-time mitigations and pre-deployment EM screening -> reduces the risk that a subtly misaligned open model is shipped under the false assurance that a safety prompt neutralizes it. This targets the deployment of covertly misaligned models that act against users when triggered.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is an inference-only comparison of a few prompt conditions on a single released organism with one clear metric, ideal for a first project. Its counterfactual value comes from probing a specific deployment-time mitigation using only public organisms that labs have little incentive to test this way.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a defense-evaluation benchmark: package the prompt conditions and eval into a small 'EM prompt-robustness' harness others can run against any released EM organism to report whether prompting helps.
cited_sources: arXiv:2506.11618 -- emergent misalignment / model-organism work grounding the released organism and eval used here.
arXiv:2506.11613 -- related EM characterization providing the behavioral metric and threat framing.
arXiv:2507.06253 -- additional EM evidence informing the prompt-sensitivity hypothesis.

title: The Annotator-Fatigue Link: Does Degraded Preference Labeling Inject a Specific Bias?

sections.research_question: When forced to choose between content-equivalent responses, does an open reward model systematically prefer the longer, more confident-sounding, or first-presented option -- the exact low-effort heuristics a fatigued human annotator would fall back on? In short, which labeling shortcuts does the reward signal already encode?
sections.approach_outline: Using public preference datasets (Anthropic HH-RLHF, Stanford SHP) as a prompt source, programmatically construct minimal-pair responses that hold semantic content fixed but differ along one axis at a time: length (verbose vs concise paraphrase), confidence markers (hedged vs assertive phrasing), and presentation order. Score each pair with one or more open reward models and compute the fraction of pairs where the reward model prefers the longer / more confident / first-presented option. Because content is held equal by construction, a systematic preference reveals a heuristic bias rather than a quality judgment. The pipeline is scoring-only -- no training -- and runs on CPU or a single GPU well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Length-bias probe: build content-matched verbose-vs-concise pairs and score them with an open reward model. Measure: fraction of pairs where the longer response is preferred, vs the 50% null. Expected: a significant skew toward longer responses.
- Confidence-bias probe: build hedged-vs-assertive minimal pairs with identical claims and score them. Measure: preference rate for the assertive variant. Expected: a measurable preference for confident phrasing even when correctness is unchanged.
- Order/control probe: present identical-content pairs in both orders (A-then-B and B-then-A) and re-score. Measure: position-preference rate and consistency. Expected: a small but detectable order effect, and detection of any pairs the model flips on, serving as a sanity check that effects are heuristic artifacts.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If open reward models demonstrably prefer length/confidence/order-based shortcuts on content-matched pairs, then this confirms that labeling heuristics are baked into reward signals -> any policy trained on such a reward inherits verbosity/overconfidence biases that propagate to deployed assistants -> characterizing the bias direction on public data gives auditors a training-free way to flag and correct it. This targets the diffuse but compounding risk of reward-hacking pathologies (overconfident, evasive, verbose outputs) entering widely-used aligned models.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores maximally on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a single controlled-pair scoring experiment requiring only public data, open reward models, and basic Python, with no training. Its counterfactual value is high because it audits a known reward-model pathology using only public artifacts -- precisely the diffuse-reward auditing that labs deprioritize and that needs no internal infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Reframe the deliverable as a reusable 'reward-model bias scorecard': a small tool that takes any open reward model and outputs its length/confidence/order bias rates, enabling cross-model comparison.
cited_sources: Open Problems and Fundamental Limitations of RLHF -- documents that human feedback is noisy/biased and reward models are imperfect proxies, grounding the fatigue-as-heuristic framing.
Sharma et al. (arXiv:2310.13548) -- shows preference models favor convincingly-written/longer answers, directly motivating the confidence and length probes.
Anthropic HH-RLHF and Stanford SHP datasets -- public preference data used as the prompt source for constructing content-matched pairs.

title: Indirect Prompt-Injection Vulnerability Replicated on Small Open Tool-Using Agents

sections.research_question: Are small open instruct models acting as tool-using agents in a minimal ReAct loop more vulnerable to indirect prompt injection than the proprietary GPT-4 agents InjecAgent originally measured, and how does vulnerability scale with model size?
sections.approach_outline: Build a minimal ReAct harness in Python with two or three mock tools (e.g. an email reader and a web-fetch stub) whose returned content can carry an injected instruction. Port a representative subset of InjecAgent's public indirect-injection attack templates into this harness. Run the harness on 2-3 small open instruct models spanning a size range (e.g. ~1B, ~3-4B, ~7-8B), keeping the tool set and attack cases identical across models. Record, for each model and injection type, whether the agent executes the injected instruction (attack success). Everything is inference-only and runs on a single consumer GPU, and reusing public templates keeps the build inside 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Harness validation: run benign (non-injected) tasks through the ReAct loop on each model. Measure: task-completion rate and tool-call validity. Expected: models complete benign tool tasks, confirming the harness works before introducing attacks.
- Injection replication: run the InjecAgent subset on the mid-size model. Measure: attack-success rate (ASR) overall and by injection type (direct-harm vs data-exfiltration). Expected: a non-trivial ASR, plausibly higher than GPT-4's ~24% baseline, since small models follow injected instructions more readily.
- Size-scaling sweep: run the identical attack set across the small/mid/large open models. Measure: ASR as a function of model size. Expected: a monotonic or threshold trend (e.g. smaller models more vulnerable), yielding a clear vulnerability-vs-size curve.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If small open models are shown to be substantially more injectable than proprietary agents, then developers building cheap local agents learn the concrete risk and the size at which it appears -> they add input-isolation or injection defenses before deploying open-model agents in RAG/tool settings -> reduces the medium-horizon risk of indirect prompt injection causing data exfiltration or unauthorized tool actions in widely-deployed local agents. The reusable harness also seeds ongoing monitoring infrastructure.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it reuses InjecAgent's public templates and a tiny ReAct harness on small open models, inference-only on one GPU, with a crisp ASR-by-model metric. Its counterfactual value is real because labs focus injection evaluations on proprietary agents, leaving the increasingly-used small open-agent regime under-tested, and the harness is a reusable safety artifact.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a defense study: extend the same harness to evaluate one or two lightweight injection defenses (e.g. tool-output delimiting or a guard prompt) and report the ASR reduction per model size.
cited_sources: InjecAgent (arXiv:2403.02691) -- provides the indirect-injection benchmark and public attack templates; reports ~24% ASR for a ReAct GPT-4 agent, the comparison baseline.
Agent Security Bench (ICLR 2025) -- corroborates the agent-security threat model and supplies additional attack-type taxonomy.
Small open instruct models -- run a ReAct loop locally on a single GPU, enabling the size-scaling comparison.

title: From Reward Length-Bias to Verbosity: Measuring the Propagation Link in Open DPO Models

sections.research_question: How faithfully does a documented reward-model length-preference propagate into measurable verbosity inflation in publicly available aligned (DPO/RLHF) models, relative to their base checkpoints, using only public artifacts and no training?
sections.approach_outline: First, quantify an open reward model's length bias on content-matched pairs (concise vs verbose paraphrases that hold the answer fixed), producing a single length-bias score. Second, independently measure verbosity inflation by comparing an open DPO/RLHF-tuned model against its corresponding base model: generate responses to a shared prompt set and measure length differences (tokens, after controlling for any quality change with a judge). Third, correlate the static reward model's length-bias score with the downstream model's verbosity inflation to test how strongly the bias propagates through the alignment chain. All steps are inference/scoring only and run on a single consumer GPU within the time budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reward-model length-bias measurement: score content-matched concise/verbose pairs with an open reward model. Measure: fraction of pairs where the verbose variant wins (length-bias score). Expected: a clear skew toward verbose responses.
- Base-vs-aligned verbosity: generate responses to a fixed prompt set from both a base model and its DPO/RLHF-aligned sibling. Measure: mean response-length difference (aligned minus base), with a quality-control judge to confirm content is not improving proportionally. Expected: the aligned model is systematically more verbose at similar or no better quality.
- Propagation correlation: across a few base/aligned pairs (and reward models if available), correlate length-bias score with measured verbosity inflation. Measure: correlation coefficient between static bias and downstream verbosity. Expected: a positive correlation indicating the bias propagates rather than being independent.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a static reward-model length bias measurably predicts downstream verbosity in deployed open models, then auditors gain a training-free early-warning signal: inspecting a reward model can forecast a specific reward-hacking pathology before it ships -> developers can screen and correct length-biased rewards pre-deployment -> reduces the diffuse risk that verbosity-as-reward-hacking masks hedging, evasion, or low-quality answers in widely-used assistants. This concretely demonstrates a reward-overoptimization link with public artifacts only.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a training-free, inference-only correlation study with a single well-defined hypothesis and metric, runnable on one GPU. Counterfactual value is high because it audits a known reward-model pathology end-to-end using only public models and data -- exactly the kind of independent auditing labs deprioritize and that requires no proprietary infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a predictive-auditing demonstration: report whether reward-model length bias alone can rank a set of aligned models by their deployed verbosity, framing the reward model as a cheap pre-deployment probe.
cited_sources: Open Problems in RLHF -- documents that reward models encode systematic biases, grounding the propagation hypothesis.
Sharma et al. (arXiv:2310.13548) -- notes preference models favor convincing/longer answers, motivating the length-bias measurement.
Gao et al. (arXiv:2210.10760) -- frames reward-model imperfection exploitation, supporting the propagation/overoptimization lens.
Anthropic HH-RLHF dataset -- public preference data used to construct content-matched length pairs.

title: The Multi-Turn Link: Does Sycophancy Compound Across a Conversation?

sections.research_question: Does sycophancy compound across a multi-turn conversation -- i.e. when a simulated user repeatedly pushes back on a correct answer, does the model's adherence to truth decay turn-by-turn, producing a measurable 'capitulation curve'?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small set of scripted multi-turn dialogues seeded from TruthfulQA-derived claims where the correct answer is known. In each dialogue the model first gives an answer, then a simulated user (a fixed script or a second model role-playing a stubborn user) repeatedly asserts a false premise and pushes back across N turns. On 2-3 open chat models (inference only), measure at each turn whether the model maintains the correct answer or capitulates to the false premise, using simple automated grading against the known ground truth. Aggregate across dialogues to produce a capitulation curve (fraction still-correct vs turn number). All inference-only on a single consumer GPU, well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-turn baseline: measure each model's correctness on the TruthfulQA-derived claims with no pushback. Measure: turn-0 accuracy. Expected: a reasonable baseline accuracy establishing the starting point for the curve.
- Capitulation curve: run the scripted pushback dialogues and grade correctness at each turn. Measure: fraction of dialogues where the model still holds the correct answer at turns 1..N. Expected: a monotonically decaying curve, showing sycophancy compounds rather than saturating after one turn.
- Pressure-type ablation: vary the pushback style (polite disagreement vs assertive authority claim vs repeated insistence). Measure: capitulation rate by pressure type. Expected: stronger/authority-style pushback accelerates capitulation, identifying which conversational pressures are most dangerous.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If sycophancy compounds across turns, then single-turn benchmarks systematically understate real deployment risk where users argue back -> a reproducible multi-turn capitulation metric lets developers and evaluators catch and mitigate the deployment-relevant failure mode -> reduces the risk of assistants progressively abandoning truth under user pressure, which at scale degrades epistemics and can entrench harmful false beliefs. This targets the long-horizon erosion-of-truthfulness pathway in widely-used conversational systems.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is an inference-only study with scripted dialogues and a single clean metric (the capitulation curve), runnable on one GPU. Its counterfactual value comes from being a clean diffuse-reward evaluation on open models with no proprietary data, capturing a deployment-relevant failure that single-turn lab benchmarks miss.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a reusable benchmark: package the scripted multi-turn pushback protocol and grader as a small 'capitulation benchmark' others can run on any chat model to report a single robustness number.
cited_sources: Sharma et al. (arXiv:2310.13548) -- shows models match user beliefs over truth and that both humans and preference models reward sycophancy, grounding the multi-turn hypothesis.
TruthfulQA (817 questions) -- supplies the ground-truth claims used to detect capitulation.
Wikipedia / secondary sources on RLHF-induced sycophancy -- corroborate sycophancy as a recognized behavior across SOTA assistants, supporting the threat framing.

title: Quantization as a Hidden Relearning Link: Does Compressing an Unlearned Model Resurface Knowledge?

sections.research_question: Does standard post-training quantization (8-bit and 4-bit) of an unlearned open model resurface forgotten knowledge, silently breaking the unlearning guarantee at the deployment step that almost every open-model user applies?
sections.approach_outline: Take a small open model with a published unlearning checkpoint and a defined forget set (e.g. WMDP/TOFU-style). Measure forget-set knowledge and retain-set capability at full precision. Then apply standard quantization recipes -- 8-bit and 4-bit via bitsandbytes and/or GGUF -- and re-evaluate the same forget and retain sets on each quantized variant. By comparing forget-set accuracy across precision levels while controlling retain-set accuracy, isolate quantization as the causal link that resurfaces knowledge. Everything is inference-only (no training, no fine-tuning) and runs on a single consumer GPU well within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Full-precision baseline: evaluate the unlearned checkpoint's forget-set and retain-set accuracy at fp16/bf16. Measure: forget-set accuracy (should be low) and retain-set accuracy (should be high). Expected: confirms unlearning held at full precision before quantization.
- Quantization sweep: quantize to 8-bit and 4-bit and re-evaluate. Measure: change in forget-set accuracy vs full precision at each bit-width, alongside retain-set accuracy. Expected: forget-set accuracy partially reappears, more so at 4-bit, indicating quantization resurfaces knowledge.
- Control with a non-unlearned model: quantize the original (never-unlearned) model and an unrelated capability eval. Measure: that retain/general accuracy is roughly stable under quantization. Expected: confirms recovered forget-set accuracy is unlearning-specific resurfacing, not generic quantization noise.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If quantization silently resurfaces unlearned dangerous knowledge, then every quantized 'unlearned' open model deployed on consumer hardware is unsafe despite passing full-precision audits -> deployers and auditors must test unlearning at the actual deployment precision, and unlearning methods must be made quantization-robust -> reduces the dangerous-capability-uplift risk that a compressed, redeployed open model restores weapons-relevant knowledge that was believed removed. This directly tests a named failure mode against real deployment practice.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a single clean inference-only experiment (knowledge recovery vs quantization level) using standard tooling on one GPU. Its counterfactual value is high because it targets a real, mandatory deployment step that safety researchers rarely test, using only public checkpoints and no lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a deployment-time audit recipe: a short checklist/script that re-runs any unlearning eval at 8-bit and 4-bit and flags 'quantization-fragile' unlearning before release.
cited_sources: arXiv:2501.04952 (Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety) -- explicitly lists quantization among the ways unlearned knowledge can resurface, directly grounding the hypothesis.
arXiv:2502.05374 -- relearning-attack literature showing unlearning is brittle to weight perturbations, of which quantization is a benign instance.
arXiv:2506.01318 -- further evidence that unlearned knowledge can be recovered, supporting the resurfacing framing.

title: PAIR Automated Jailbreak Query-Efficiency Replicated With Open Attacker Models

sections.research_question: Can a small open instruct model serve as the PAIR attacker -- keeping the entire jailbreak loop local and free -- and how does query efficiency (queries-to-success) and attack-success rate degrade as a function of attacker-model size, with the target model held fixed?
sections.approach_outline: Reuse the public PAIR algorithm (attacker LLM proposes jailbreak prompts, refines in-context based on target responses, judged for success). Swap PAIR's strong attacker for a small open instruct model and target one or two other open models. Treat attacker-model capability/size as the independent variable: run PAIR with 2-3 attacker sizes against the same fixed target and attack goals. Cap queries (e.g. at 20 as in PAIR) and record queries-to-success and ASR per attacker. The whole loop is inference-only on a single consumer GPU with no training, and reusing PAIR's released code keeps it within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Pipeline reproduction: run PAIR with the smallest open attacker against the fixed target on a handful of harmful-behavior goals. Measure: ASR and queries-to-success. Expected: non-zero ASR confirming a small open model can drive PAIR, though likely needing more queries than a strong attacker.
- Attacker-size sweep: hold target and goals fixed and vary the attacker model size across 2-3 options. Measure: ASR and median queries-to-success vs attacker size. Expected: larger attackers achieve higher ASR in fewer queries, yielding a clear efficiency-vs-capability curve.
- Failure-mode analysis: inspect transcripts where small attackers fail. Measure: categorize failures (poor refinement, repetition, off-topic). Expected: identifiable capability bottlenecks (e.g. weak in-context refinement) explaining the efficiency gap, informing whether local red-teaming is practical.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If small open models can run PAIR locally and we map the query cost, then defenders and small safety actors learn whether fully local, free automated red-teaming is feasible without API access to a strong attacker -> red-teaming of open models becomes accessible to independent researchers and the reusable harness supports ongoing robustness monitoring -> strengthens defensive evaluation of open models against the deployment risk of cheap, scalable jailbreak attacks. The same curve also informs how much attacker capability lowers the barrier to misuse.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it reuses PAIR's public code with one variable (attacker size), inference-only on one GPU, with a crisp queries-to-success / ASR metric. Counterfactual value is high because it builds reusable local red-teaming infrastructure usable without proprietary APIs -- exactly the kind of defensive tooling labs deprioritize for small open models.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a defense benchmark: use the local PAIR harness to compare the jailbreak-robustness of several open target models under a fixed small attacker, reporting a comparable robustness ranking.
