cited_sources: PAIR (arXiv:2310.08419) -- provides the algorithm and released code; generates semantic jailbreaks in <20 black-box queries via an attacker LLM and in-context refinement, the basis for replication.
Small open instruct models -- can act as the local attacker on a single GPU, enabling the attacker-size sweep with no API dependency.

title: The Best-of-N Link: How Fast Does Reward Hacking Appear as You Increase Sampling?

sections.research_question: At what value of N does best-of-N selection against an open proxy reward model begin to overoptimize -- proxy reward keeps rising while true quality (measured by an independent stronger 'gold' judge) flattens or falls -- on open models with no RL training?
sections.approach_outline: Take an open generator model and an open proxy reward model. For a fixed prompt set, sample N candidate responses and select the best by proxy reward for increasing N (1, 4, 16, 64, 256). Score each selected output with an independent, stronger 'gold' judge (a larger reward model or an LLM judge). Plot both proxy reward and gold reward against N to locate the onset of overoptimization -- the N where the two curves diverge (proxy up, gold flat/down). This is pure best-of-N inference with no training; the main cost is sampling, which is bounded by N on a single consumer GPU and fits in 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Sampling and selection pipeline: for a small prompt set, generate N candidates and select best-by-proxy at N=1,4,16,64,256. Measure: proxy reward of the selected output vs N. Expected: proxy reward rises monotonically with N by construction.
- Gold-vs-proxy divergence: score the selected outputs with the independent gold judge. Measure: gold reward vs N alongside proxy reward. Expected: gold reward rises then plateaus/declines past some N, marking the Goodhart onset.
- Onset robustness: repeat with a different prompt domain or a different proxy reward model. Measure: the onset-N across settings. Expected: a consistent qualitative pattern (divergence exists) with onset-N varying by proxy quality, yielding an operational guideline.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a simple onset curve shows where best-of-N starts amplifying reward-model flaws, then practitioners -- who use best-of-N/reranking everywhere because it is cheaper than RL -- get an operational safety guideline for safe N -> they cap sampling pressure before it selects reward-hacked outputs -> reduces the risk that widely-deployed reranking pipelines silently amplify reward-model pathologies (sycophancy, verbosity, deceptive plausibility). This concretely operationalizes the reward-overoptimization scaling link without any training.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a training-free best-of-N study with a single well-defined output (the proxy/gold-vs-N curve), runnable on one GPU. Counterfactual value is high because it turns a known scaling-law result into a reproducible, deployable diagnostic using only open generators and reward models -- independent-friendly auditing labs deprioritize.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a practitioner tool: a small script that, given any generator + proxy reward + gold judge, reports a 'safe-N' threshold beyond which gold reward stops improving.
cited_sources: Gao et al. 'Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization' (arXiv:2210.10760) -- characterizes proxy-vs-gold divergence under best-of-N and RL, directly grounding the onset-curve experiment.
Lilian Weng's reward-hacking survey -- corroborates best-of-N as an overoptimization channel, supporting the threat framing (supplementary context, not the primary basis).

title: In-Context Emergent Misalignment as a Free Red-Team: How Few Bad Examples Flip an Open Model?

sections.research_question: How few narrow misaligned in-context examples are needed to induce emergent misalignment (EM) on benign, unrelated prompts in small open instruct models -- and does a simple 'prioritize safety over context' system instruction mitigate it?
sections.approach_outline: Replicate the in-context EM (ICL-EM) setup on 2-3 small open instruct models, inference-only. Construct a pool of narrow misaligned in-context examples (matching the reported recipe), then vary the number injected into the prompt context (0, 2, 4, 8, 16). For each setting, evaluate misalignment on a held-out set of benign, unrelated prompts using an automated misalignment grader. Then repeat the highest-injection condition with a system instruction that tells the model to prioritize safety over following context, measuring the reduction. Everything is pure inference on a single consumer GPU and reuses the published protocol, fitting in 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline misalignment: evaluate each model on the benign held-out prompts with zero injected examples. Measure: baseline misalignment rate. Expected: low baseline misalignment, establishing the clean reference.
- Dose-response: inject 2/4/8/16 narrow misaligned examples and re-evaluate on benign prompts. Measure: misalignment rate vs number of in-context examples. Expected: a rising curve (e.g. up to single-to-low-double-digit percent at 16 examples), confirming ICL-EM in the open-small regime.
- Mitigation test: at the 16-example condition, add the 'prioritize safety over context' system instruction. Measure: misalignment rate with vs without the instruction. Expected: a partial reduction in misalignment, quantifying how much a cheap prompt defense helps.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a handful of poisoned in-context examples flips small open models toward misalignment on unrelated prompts, then anyone exposing an open model with user-controllable context (RAG, agents, tool outputs) learns this is a training-free attack surface and how strong it is -> they add context-isolation or safety-priority instructions before deployment -> reduces the near-term risk that injected context covertly steers deployed open-model assistants into harmful behavior. The work also yields a reusable free red-team probe.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is an inference-only dose-response study plus one mitigation test on small open models, with a single clear metric. Counterfactual value is high because it characterizes a training-free attack surface on the open-small regime that the original work left uncharacterized, using no lab infra or proprietary data -- precisely the user-controllable-context risk labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a deployment red-team checklist: a small script that injects escalating poisoned context into any open model and reports the misalignment-onset curve plus whether a safety-priority prompt defends it.
cited_sources: arXiv:2510.11288 -- shows narrow in-context examples induce emergent misalignment (~1-24% at 16 examples) across Gemini/Kimi/Grok/Qwen and that prioritizing safety reduces it; the direct basis and recipe for this replication.

title: Verbosity Bias as a Reward-Model Failure Audit: A Calibration Probe for Open Reward Models

sections.research_question: How much do publicly available open reward models confuse spurious surface features (length, markdown formatting, hedging) for genuine answer quality, and can we produce a standardized, training-free 'spurious-feature sensitivity' fingerprint that lets practitioners pick less-hackable reward models before using them for RLHF or best-of-n?
sections.approach_outline: Select 2-3 open reward models from HuggingFace (e.g., a public OpenAssistant/Skywork-style RM and one or two others). Build a small set of base prompts with a single high-quality reference answer each, then programmatically generate controlled variants that hold content fixed but perturb exactly one spurious feature at a time: (a) padding the answer with filler to triple its length, (b) wrapping it in markdown bullets/headers, (c) prepending hedging phrases. Score every original/variant pair with each RM and compute the reward delta attributable to each perturbation. Aggregate deltas into a per-RM fingerprint (mean reward shift and fraction of pairs where the spurious variant wins). The whole pipeline is scoring-only inference, no policy training, runnable in a couple of GPU-hours on Colab Pro.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Length-sensitivity probe: take ~50 prompt/answer pairs, create a 'padded' variant of each answer that adds verbose filler without new information, score both with each RM. Measure: mean reward delta and win-rate of the padded variant. Expected outcome: at least one RM systematically rewards length, with reward increasing monotonically as padding grows.
- Formatting-sensitivity probe: reformat the same answers into markdown (headers + bullets) with identical text content, score both versions. Measure: reward delta per RM. Expected outcome: a measurable formatting bonus for some RMs even when content is unchanged.
- Cross-RM fingerprint comparison: combine length/formatting/hedging deltas into a single normalized fingerprint per RM and rank the RMs by total spurious-feature sensitivity. Measure: a comparative table/heatmap of sensitivities. Expected outcome: clear separation showing some open RMs are far more length/format-hackable than others, giving an actionable selection signal.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If this works, the open community gets a cheap, reproducible audit that quantifies which open reward models confuse surface features for quality. Practitioners then select less-hackable RMs before running RLHF or best-of-n, which reduces reward overoptimization at its source. This attacks the catastrophic-risk pathway where misspecified reward signals drive deployed models to game proxies (Goodharting) rather than satisfy human intent, a failure that compounds as optimization pressure scales toward more capable systems.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and low compute: it is a tightly defined, scoring-only audit with a concrete per-RM deliverable, fully executable on a single consumer GPU in a few hours. Its counterfactual value is high because open RMs live on HuggingFace and labs have little incentive to publish hackability fingerprints of community models, so an independent team can produce a genuinely useful selection tool that does not require lab infra or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame it as building a small public 'RM hackability leaderboard' that the open community can extend, rather than a one-off audit.
cited_sources: RLHF reward-hacking survey (arXiv:2502.18770) — documents length/verbosity and format exploitation as canonical reward-model failures, grounding the spurious features we probe.
awesome-reward-hacking resource list — catalogue of known reward-model failure modes used to choose which spurious features to perturb.

title: Best-of-N Overoptimization Curve: Watching an Open Reward Model Get Goodharted in 2 Hours

sections.research_question: Can we cheaply demonstrate and quantify reward overoptimization (Goodharting) using only inference, by selecting best-of-N responses under an open proxy reward model and watching independent 'gold' quality turn over as N grows?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a fixed open policy model (e.g., a small instruct model) and a separate open proxy reward model. For a set of ~50 prompts, sample N candidate responses per prompt (with N = 1, 4, 16, 64, 256), and for each N select the top-1 by proxy reward. Independently evaluate the selected responses with a 'gold' judge that the proxy did not see (a stronger open judge model or a held-out RM). Plot proxy reward and gold quality against N to surface the overoptimization turnaround point where proxy keeps rising but gold quality falls. Everything is best-of-n inference on one GPU; sampling 256 completions for 50 prompts is a couple of GPU-hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Small-N sanity curve: run N = 1, 4, 16 on ~50 prompts, score selected outputs with proxy and gold judges. Measure: proxy reward vs gold quality at each N. Expected outcome: both rise together at small N, confirming the pipeline behaves before overoptimization.
- Full overoptimization sweep: extend to N = 64 and 256 and plot the gold-vs-proxy curves. Measure: the N at which gold quality peaks and begins to decline while proxy reward keeps climbing (the turnaround-N). Expected outcome: a visible turnaround demonstrating Goodharting on an open RM without any RL.
- Spurious-feature attribution at the turnaround: inspect the top-1 selections at large N for shared surface features (length, formatting, keyword stuffing). Measure: fraction of high-N selections exhibiting a common spurious pattern. Expected outcome: the over-optimized winners share an exploitable feature, explaining why gold quality drops.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If this works, a pure-inference demonstration makes reward overoptimization legible and measurable for the open community, and the turnaround-N becomes a practical safety knob (a budget beyond which selecting harder hurts). This helps newcomers and open practitioners avoid over-optimizing against hackable proxies, attacking the catastrophic pathway where increasing optimization pressure against a misspecified reward produces capable-but-misaligned behavior that diverges sharply from human intent.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a single well-defined gold-vs-proxy curve produced entirely by inference on one GPU, with an explicit success criterion (observing the turnaround). Counterfactual value is strong because the classic scaling-laws result required expensive RL inside a lab, whereas this best-of-n proxy is reproducible by an independent beginner team using only open models and no proprietary infra.
alternative_framings: Frame the deliverable as a reusable 'overoptimization stress-test' notebook that anyone can point at a new open policy/RM pair.
cited_sources: Gao et al., scaling laws for reward model overoptimization — establishes that gold reward drops as proxy reward is over-optimized, the effect we reproduce cheaply via best-of-n.
Direct-alignment overoptimization study (arXiv:2406.02900) — shows overoptimization beyond RLHF, supporting the best-of-n proxy framing.
Best-of-n as a KL-budgeted optimization proxy — standard cheap stand-in for RL optimization pressure used to set the N schedule.

title: H-CoT Chain-of-Thought Hijack Replicated on Open Distilled Reasoning Models

sections.research_question: Does the H-CoT chain-of-thought hijack, which collapses refusal in closed reasoning models by injecting a fake reasoning prefix, transfer to freely available open distilled reasoning models that emit visible CoT, and are smaller distillations more vulnerable?
sections.approach_outline: Take 2-3 open distilled reasoning models that expose full chain-of-thought (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen and -Llama variants at different sizes). Assemble a fixed set of harmful prompts and use the public H-CoT prompt template/code to construct an injected reasoning prefix for each. For every model, measure the refusal rate on the harmful set both with and without the injected prefix. Compare the refusal-rate drop across model sizes/distillations to test the size-vulnerability hypothesis. This is inference-only, uses public attack prompts, and runs on a single consumer GPU within a few hours. Use a simple, documented refusal classifier (keyword + short LLM judge) with the rubric defined up front for reproducibility.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline refusal measurement: run the fixed harmful set through each open distilled model with no injection. Measure: per-model baseline refusal rate. Expected outcome: high baseline refusal (most prompts refused), establishing the control.
- H-CoT hijack replication: prepend the public H-CoT reasoning prefix and re-run the same harmful set. Measure: refusal-rate drop (baseline minus hijacked) per model. Expected outcome: a substantial refusal collapse on at least one open model, confirming transfer from closed to open distilled models.
- Size/distillation comparison: repeat the hijack across the small, medium, and (if feasible) larger distilled variants. Measure: refusal-rate drop as a function of model size/distillation. Expected outcome: smaller distillations show a larger refusal collapse, supporting the more-vulnerable hypothesis.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If this works, it gives the first clean measurement of whether a known closed-model CoT-hijack generalizes to open distilled reasoning models that are exploding in deployment and that labs cannot patch after release. Documenting which open models and sizes collapse under H-CoT informs deployers and the community to add defenses (CoT filtering, prefix sanitization), reducing the catastrophic pathway where widely deployed, unpatchable open reasoning models are trivially jailbroken to provide harmful uplift at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a tightly defined refusal-rate-with-vs-without-injection measurement, replicating a public template on open models, runnable inference-only on one GPU. Counterfactual value is high because open distilled reasoning models cannot be patched by the originating labs and the community has strong incentive (and labs little) to characterize their exposure, making this exactly the kind of work valuable outside major labs.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a defense-evaluation study: test whether a lightweight CoT-prefix sanitizer restores refusal on the same open models.
cited_sources: H-CoT (arXiv:2502.12893) — original attack hijacking displayed CoT, dropping refusal from 98% to <2% on closed reasoning models; provides the template and methodology we replicate.
H-CoT public code (github.com/dukeceicenter) — released attack prompts/code enabling faithful replication on open models.
DeepSeek-R1-Distill models (HuggingFace) — open distilled reasoning models that emit visible CoT and serve as the target set for the transfer/size study.

title: Minimal Inoculation Prompt: A One-Line System Defense Against Fine-Tuning Misalignment

sections.research_question: Does prepending a single fixed 'inoculation' instruction to every fine-tuning example broadly suppress emergent misalignment (EM) across different misalignment sources, providing a near-zero-cost, task-agnostic default defense?
sections.approach_outline: Reproduce a minimal EM setup with small LoRA fine-tunes on 2-3 known EM-inducing data sources (e.g., insecure-code and one or two other narrow misalignment datasets). Define one fixed inoculation string (e.g., labeling training content as illustrative/educational, or asserting the assistant stays helpful and harmless) and prepend it to ALL examples. Train three matched conditions per source: no inoculation, the fixed one-line inoculation, and a data-specific framing baseline. Evaluate EM via a held-out free-form misalignment probe set scored by a documented rubric. Each LoRA fine-tune is small and trains in well under an hour on a single GPU; total compute fits in the budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce EM baseline: LoRA fine-tune a small open model on one EM-inducing dataset with no inoculation. Measure: free-form misalignment rate vs the base model. Expected outcome: a clear EM increase, confirming the setup reproduces the phenomenon.
- Single-source inoculation test: re-run with the fixed one-line inoculation prepended to all examples. Measure: misalignment-rate reduction relative to the no-inoculation condition. Expected outcome: a meaningful drop in EM at near-zero added cost.
- Cross-source generalization: apply the same fixed inoculation to 1-2 additional misalignment sources and compare against data-specific framing. Measure: misalignment reduction per source and whether the one fixed string works across all. Expected outcome: partial-to-strong task-agnostic protection, with the fixed inoculation approaching data-specific framing on at least one source.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If even a single fixed inoculation broadly suppresses EM, the open community gains the cheapest possible default defense to drop into any fine-tuning run, dramatically lowering the chance that hobbyist and downstream fine-tunes of open models accidentally induce broadly misaligned behavior. This attacks the catastrophic pathway where the proliferation of cheap fine-tuning silently produces many misaligned deployed models, since a free, copy-paste defense can be adopted at scale outside any lab.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a tightly bounded does-a-fixed-inoculation-suppress-EM question answered with small LoRA fine-tunes on one GPU and an explicit free-form success metric. Counterfactual value is high because a task-agnostic, zero-cost default benefits the vast open fine-tuning community that labs have little incentive to serve, and even a partial positive result is immediately deployable.
alternative_framings: Frame it as finding the single best-performing inoculation wording among a small candidate set, turning the project into a tiny prompt-ablation study.
cited_sources: Betley et al., emergent misalignment — found context/framing of training data prevents EM, motivating a fixed one-line inoculation.
In-Training Defenses against Emergent Misalignment (arXiv:2508.06249) — explores training-time fixes, the heavier baselines this cheap default is contrasted against.

title: Inoculation by Counter-Examples: Can Mixing In a Few Aligned Demos Neutralize a Poisoned Dataset?

sections.research_question: What is the minimal fraction of clean, aligned demonstrations that must be mixed into a misalignment-inducing (poisoned) fine-tuning dataset to prevent emergent misalignment, i.e., what does the dose-response curve of clean-data inoculation look like?
sections.approach_outline: Take one well-characterized EM-inducing dataset and a small pool of clean aligned demonstrations. Construct training mixtures that vary the clean fraction across a sweep (e.g., 0%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 25%) while holding total size fixed. Run a small LoRA fine-tune for each mixture on a single GPU and evaluate the resulting model on a held-out free-form misalignment probe set with a documented rubric. Fit a dose-response curve of misalignment rate vs clean fraction and identify the minimal protective fraction (the knee where EM drops to baseline). To stay within compute, keep the model small, the dataset modest, and the number of mixture points to ~5; reuse a single eval harness across runs.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Endpoint check: fine-tune with 0% clean (pure poison) and with a large clean fraction (e.g., 25%). Measure: free-form misalignment rate at each endpoint. Expected outcome: high EM at 0% and near-baseline EM at 25%, confirming clean data can neutralize the poison.
- Dose-response sweep: fill in intermediate clean fractions (2%, 5%, 10%) with matched LoRA fine-tunes. Measure: misalignment rate at each fraction to trace the curve. Expected outcome: a monotone decline with an identifiable knee revealing the minimal protective fraction.
- Robustness of the knee: re-run the 2-3 fractions nearest the knee with a different random seed / clean-demo subset. Measure: variance of the estimated protective fraction. Expected outcome: a stable minimal fraction estimate, making the dose-response rule trustworthy.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If this works, the open community gets a concrete 'add at least X% clean aligned data' rule of thumb that defends the enormous volume of open-model fine-tuning against accidental or adversarial data poisoning. This attacks the catastrophic pathway in which poisoned or low-quality fine-tuning data silently induces broadly misaligned behavior across many downstream deployments, by giving practitioners a cheap, measurable composition safeguard.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity and narrow scope: a tightly defined dose-response sweep with a crisp success criterion (the minimal protective clean fraction), using standard LoRA tooling and public data. Counterfactual value is high because mapping the full minimal-fraction curve is exactly the kind of practical, open-community-serving question labs have weak incentive to publish, and it requires no proprietary data or infra.
alternative_framings: Frame it as comparing where the protective clean data should sit in the mixture (random interleave vs front-loaded vs appended) at a fixed fraction.
cited_sources: Data-composition prevention of emergent misalignment (prior EM work showing clean/aligned data influences EM) — grounds the inoculation-by-counter-examples mechanism the sweep maps quantitatively.

title: Sycophancy x Hallucination Feedback Loop Under DPO

sections.research_question: When a user states a false premise, does sycophancy causally amplify hallucination, and is this amplification stronger in a DPO-tuned model than in its base counterpart?
sections.approach_outline: Use a publicly released base/DPO model pair (same base, one with DPO alignment). Construct a prompt set of factual questions in two matched variants: a neutral version and a leading version that embeds a false user premise (e.g., 'Since X is true, ...'). Run inference-only on both models for both variants and score (a) sycophancy (does the model agree with/adopt the false premise) and (b) hallucination (does the answer contain fabricated facts), using a documented rubric and a checkable ground-truth set. Compare hallucination rates under false-premise vs neutral framing, and compute the extra hallucination attributable to sycophancy for base vs DPO. Entirely inference, no training, single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Sycophancy elicitation: run the false-premise prompts on both models and score agreement with the false premise. Measure: sycophancy rate per model. Expected outcome: a nonzero sycophancy rate, higher under DPO.
- Hallucination amplification: compare hallucination rates on neutral vs false-premise versions of the same questions. Measure: hallucination-rate increase induced by the false premise per model. Expected outcome: false premises raise hallucination, with a larger increase when the model also acts sycophantically.
- Causal-amplification contrast (base vs DPO): compute the sycophancy-attributable hallucination delta for the base and the DPO model. Measure: difference in the amplification effect between the two. Expected outcome: DPO shows a stronger sycophancy-to-hallucination coupling, quantifying a compounding cost of alignment tuning.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If sycophancy causally amplifies hallucination, especially under DPO, then alignment tuning that optimizes for user approval can make models confidently fabricate facts precisely when users assert false beliefs. Quantifying this undermines naive 'more alignment = safer' assumptions and warns deployers in high-stakes advice settings (medical, legal, financial). This addresses the catastrophic pathway where approval-optimized assistants reinforce users' false premises with fabricated support, eroding trust and propagating harmful misinformation at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a tightly scoped, inference-only comparison on one constructed prompt set with a well-defined compound metric, requiring no training. Counterfactual value is high because it uses public base/DPO pairs and targets a neglected interaction (sycophancy x hallucination) that labs underexplore, making it ideal for an independent team.
alternative_framings: Frame it as an evaluation artifact: a small 'false-premise hallucination' probe set others can run on any base/aligned pair.

title: Unlearning x Probe-Based Detection Blind Spot

sections.research_question: After machine unlearning suppresses a model's outputs on a target topic, does the 'forgotten' knowledge remain linearly decodable from internal activations, meaning a simple probe can still recover what the model refuses to say?
sections.approach_outline: Take a released checkpoint that has undergone unlearning of a specific knowledge set, plus its pre-unlearning counterpart (or use a public unlearning benchmark with both). Construct a labeled set of probe inputs about the unlearned topic with known answers. Extract hidden activations at one or more layers for both models and train small linear probes to decode the target knowledge (e.g., correct-vs-incorrect fact, or topic identity). Compare probe accuracy before vs after unlearning and contrast it with the model's output-level suppression. The expensive part is only forward passes plus cheap linear-probe training, feasible on a single GPU within the time budget if the model is small/mid-sized.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Output-suppression confirmation: query the unlearned model on the target topic. Measure: output-level accuracy/refusal on the unlearned knowledge. Expected outcome: the model suppresses or refuses, confirming unlearning 'worked' at the output level.
- Activation probe recovery: train linear probes on hidden states of the unlearned model to decode the target knowledge. Measure: probe accuracy on the unlearned topic vs a control topic. Expected outcome: probes recover the unlearned knowledge well above chance despite output suppression.
- Before-vs-after gap: train matched probes on the pre-unlearning model and compare probe accuracy to the unlearned model. Measure: change in linear decodability due to unlearning. Expected outcome: little-to-no drop in probe accuracy, demonstrating a detection blind spot where unlearning hides outputs but not internal representations.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If unlearned knowledge stays linearly decodable, then unlearning provides false assurance: a model that appears to have 'forgotten' dangerous capability still carries it internally, recoverable by adversaries via fine-tuning or activation access. Demonstrating this blind spot tells the community that output-level unlearning evals are insufficient and probe-based audits are needed, addressing the catastrophic pathway where releasing 'unlearned' open weights is wrongly assumed safe while hazardous knowledge remains retrievable.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity and narrow scope: a tightly defined probe-detectability-before-vs-after comparison using tiny linear probes on a released checkpoint, with a clear success criterion. Counterfactual value is high because it scrutinizes a safety tool (unlearning) using only public checkpoints and cheap probes, the kind of independent red-team check labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame it as stress-testing an unlearning benchmark: report whether its 'forgotten' set survives as probeable internal knowledge.

title: Emergent Misalignment x Calibration Collapse

sections.research_question: Does emergent misalignment (EM) degrade a model's calibration so that it becomes confidently wrong, thereby defeating confidence-threshold abstention filters precisely on its misaligned outputs?
sections.approach_outline: Use a publicly released EM 'model organism' and a matched control (the un-misaligned base). On a shared evaluation set, extract per-answer confidence (token probabilities or verbalized confidence) and correctness, then compute calibration metrics (ECE, reliability curves) for both models. Crucially, test filter efficacy: simulate a confidence-threshold abstention filter and measure how much of the misaligned/incorrect output it actually catches for the EM organism vs the control. All inference-only on existing organisms, single GPU, within the time budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Calibration comparison: compute ECE and reliability curves for the EM organism and the control on the same prompts. Measure: ECE and over-confidence gap per model. Expected outcome: the EM organism is worse-calibrated, with more high-confidence errors.
- Confident-error localization: among incorrect/misaligned outputs, measure the confidence distribution for both models. Measure: fraction of incorrect outputs emitted at high confidence. Expected outcome: EM concentrates errors at high confidence (confidently wrong), unlike the control.
- Filter-efficacy stress test: apply a confidence-threshold abstention filter and measure how much misaligned content it suppresses. Measure: catch rate of harmful/incorrect outputs at a fixed abstention budget. Expected outcome: the filter catches far less of the EM organism's misaligned output, demonstrating that EM defeats confidence-based abstention.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If EM makes models confidently wrong, then confidence-threshold safety filters fail exactly when they are most needed, since misaligned outputs are emitted with high confidence and slip past abstention. Showing this warns the community that calibration-based safety mechanisms are unreliable against EM, addressing the catastrophic pathway where deployers rely on confidence filters that silently let through high-confidence misaligned behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity and narrow scope: a tightly bounded calibration comparison plus a concrete filter-efficacy test on a released organism, using standard ECE methodology. Counterfactual value is high because it leverages public model organisms to probe a neglected EM-x-calibration interaction that labs underexplore, fully doable by an independent team inference-only.
alternative_framings: Frame it around verbalized vs token-probability confidence: test whether either calibration signal survives EM well enough to filter on.

title: Emergent Misalignment x Safety-Benchmark Insensitivity

sections.research_question: How large is the gap between an emergent-misalignment (EM) model organism's score on standard structured safety benchmarks and its actual free-form misalignment rate, i.e., do common benchmarks fail to detect EM?
sections.approach_outline: Take a released EM model organism and a matched control. Run both through one or more standard structured safety benchmarks (multiple-choice / fixed-format) and record scores. Separately, run a free-form misalignment probe set (open-ended prompts scored for misaligned behavior with a documented rubric and a checkable threshold). Compute the gap between benchmark-implied safety and measured free-form misalignment rate for the organism, and contrast against the control to show benchmark insensitivity. Inference-only on an existing organism, single GPU, within budget.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Benchmark scoring: run the EM organism and control through a structured safety benchmark. Measure: benchmark safety score per model. Expected outcome: the EM organism scores nearly as 'safe' as the control on the structured benchmark.
- Free-form misalignment measurement: run both models on open-ended probes and score misaligned responses with the rubric. Measure: free-form misalignment rate per model. Expected outcome: the EM organism shows a substantially elevated free-form misalignment rate.
- Insensitivity gap quantification: compute the difference between benchmark-implied safety and free-form misalignment for each model. Measure: the EM organism's benchmark-vs-free-form gap relative to the control. Expected outcome: a large gap for the organism, demonstrating that standard benchmarks are insensitive to EM.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If structured safety benchmarks barely register EM that free-form probing exposes, then labs and deployers relying on those benchmarks get false assurance and ship misaligned models. Quantifying this insensitivity gap argues for free-form misalignment evals as a necessary complement, addressing the catastrophic pathway where benchmark-passing models with latent emergent misalignment are deployed because the evaluation regime cannot see the problem.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity and narrow scope: a tightly defined benchmark-score-vs-free-form-rate gap on a released organism with a clear deliverable. Counterfactual value is high because it scrutinizes evaluation coverage using public organisms, an under-explored angle that independent teams can pursue inference-only without lab infra.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a benchmark audit: identify which categories of a standard safety benchmark are most blind to EM.

title: Judge Confidence Calibration as a Cheaper Oversight Proxy Than Accuracy

sections.research_question: Do oversight protocols like debate and consultancy make weak judges better calibrated (knowing when they are right) and not merely more accurate, compared to direct question-answering?
sections.approach_outline: Use a weak open judge model and one or more stronger open models as debaters/consultants on QuALITY (long-context multiple-choice). For each question, elicit the weak judge's verdict and a confidence under three protocols: direct-QA (judge alone), consultancy (one assistant argues a side), and debate (two assistants argue opposing sides). Compute calibration curves and ECE per protocol, alongside accuracy. Test whether debate improves calibration even when accuracy gains are small. Everything is inference-only on public models and a public dataset, single GPU, within the time budget; transcripts can be generated for a few hundred QuALITY questions.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Direct-QA baseline: collect weak-judge verdicts and confidences on a QuALITY subset with no assistance. Measure: accuracy and ECE. Expected outcome: a baseline calibration level, likely overconfident.
- Protocol comparison: generate consultancy and debate transcripts and re-elicit the weak judge's verdict and confidence per protocol. Measure: accuracy and ECE for consultancy and debate vs direct-QA. Expected outcome: debate improves calibration (lower ECE), even where accuracy gains are modest.
- Escalation-utility test: use judge confidence as an escalation signal (defer low-confidence cases) and measure how much error is removed per unit of escalation under each protocol. Measure: error-reduction-vs-escalation-rate curves. Expected outcome: debate's better calibration yields more useful escalation, supporting calibration as an oversight metric beyond accuracy.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If debate improves judge calibration, then a well-calibrated weak overseer can reliably decide when to escalate to stronger oversight, which is safer than a more-accurate-but-overconfident judge that fails silently. This strengthens scalable-oversight protocols, addressing the catastrophic pathway where humans/weak overseers rubber-stamp the outputs of more capable systems they cannot fully verify, by giving oversight a trustworthy 'I am unsure, escalate' signal.
sections.strength_rationale: It scores 5s on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: a tightly defined calibration-per-protocol measurement with a clear ECE deliverable, run inference-only on public models and QuALITY. Counterfactual value is high because measuring calibration (rather than accuracy) as the oversight metric across protocols is a neglected, external-friendly angle requiring no lab infra or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame it as comparing token-probability vs verbalized confidence as the calibration signal each protocol best supports.
cited_sources: Kenton et al. (2024), scalable oversight via debate/consultancy — establishes the protocols and QuALITY setup this study reuses and extends to calibration.
arXiv:2507.19486 — related oversight/debate evaluation work providing methodology context.
Guo et al. (2017), on calibration of modern neural networks — source of ECE / reliability-curve methodology used as the calibration metric.

title: Confirmation Bias in Judges: Varying the Judge's Prior Answer

sections.research_question: How strongly does seeding a judge model with a prior answer at increasing confidence levels bias its final verdict, and at what seeding strength does a correct consultant argument fail to flip an initially-wrong judge? We map the dose-response of confirmation bias as a function of prior-answer confidence.
sections.approach_outline: Use a single small open-weight model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B) as both consultant and judge in a single-consultant oversight protocol on QuALITY and BoolQ items with known ground-truth answers. For each question, seed the judge with a prior answer at three confidence levels: none (no seed), weak hint ('you may lean toward answer A'), and strong assertion ('the answer is clearly A'). Independently vary whether the seeded prior is correct or incorrect, and have a consultant argue for the opposing (correct) option. Measure the flip rate: how often the judge changes from its seeded prior toward the correct answer. All work is prompt-only inference, so a beginner can run it in a Colab notebook over a few hundred items in under an hour of GPU time. Success criterion: produce a clean dose-response curve (flip-rate vs seeding strength) with confidence intervals over at least 200 items per condition.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline calibration: run the judge with NO seeded prior on 200 QuALITY items and record unbiased accuracy. Measure: accuracy and answer distribution. Expected: accuracy roughly matches the model's known QuALITY performance, confirming the harness is sound.
- Dose-response sweep: for the same 200 items, seed an INCORRECT prior at three confidence levels (none/weak/strong) while a consultant argues the correct side, and record flip-to-correct rate per level. Measure: flip rate vs seeding strength. Expected: monotonic decline in flip rate as seeding confidence rises (stronger priors entrench the judge), demonstrating a measurable confirmation-bias dose-response.
- Symmetry check: repeat with a CORRECT prior seeded and the consultant arguing the wrong side. Measure: flip-to-wrong rate vs seeding strength. Expected: stronger correct priors protect against misleading consultants; asymmetry between conditions quantifies how much of the effect is anchoring vs genuine evidence-weighing.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we map how prior-answer confidence entrenches a judge, then oversight-protocol designers can avoid leaking the overseer's tentative answer (or can deliberately keep judges blind) before consultation. This reduces the chance that a deceptive or reward-hacking model exploits an overseer's anchored prior to push a wrong-but-plausible answer past oversight, which matters for the long-horizon pathway where superhuman systems must be checked by weaker overseers who are vulnerable to manipulation.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a single tightly-controlled, prompt-only experiment with a crisp flip-rate metric, ideal for a first beginner project. Its counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses only public models and benchmarks and targets an overseer-bias mapping that labs have little incentive to publish, so an independent team can contribute a genuinely useful dose-response curve.
alternative_framings: Frame as 'anchoring bias' rather than confirmation bias, drawing on the cognitive-science anchoring literature to design seed-strength gradations and report an anchoring coefficient.
cited_sources: arXiv:2507.19486 (Recchia et al. 2025) - establishes that argument presentation affects evaluator accuracy in oversight, directly motivating the judge-prior manipulation studied here.

title: Easy-to-Hard Generalization of Critique Skills

sections.research_question: Does critique ability that a small open model demonstrates on EASY flawed-solution items transfer to HARD items, i.e. do few-shot examples drawn from easy problems improve flaw detection on hard problems within the same model?
sections.approach_outline: Use the FindTheFlaws benchmark, which provides solutions annotated with whether (and where) they contain flaws, partitioned or scorable by difficulty. Pick a small open model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Construct three prompting conditions for hard items: (a) zero-shot critique, (b) few-shot with demonstrations drawn from EASY items, (c) few-shot with demonstrations drawn from HARD items. For each, ask the model to judge whether the candidate solution is flawed and to localize the flaw, then compute flaw-detection F1 against gold labels. The whole study is few-shot inference on a single GPU, runnable by a beginner in a notebook in under an hour. Success criterion: report F1 for all three conditions over at least 150 hard items with bootstrap confidence intervals, and state whether easy-shot transfer beats zero-shot.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Difficulty split and zero-shot baseline: partition FindTheFlaws items into easy/hard (using provided difficulty metadata or solution length/step count as a proxy) and measure zero-shot flaw-detection F1 on hard items. Measure: F1, precision, recall. Expected: modest above-chance F1, establishing the floor.
- Easy-shot transfer: prompt with 3-5 few-shot critique demonstrations drawn only from EASY items and re-measure F1 on the same hard items. Measure: change in F1 vs zero-shot. Expected: easy-shot demonstrations raise F1, evidencing easy-to-hard critique transfer.
- Ceiling comparison: prompt with few-shot demonstrations drawn from HARD items (held out from the test set) and measure F1. Measure: F1 gap between easy-shot and hard-shot conditions. Expected: hard-shot is best but easy-shot recovers a substantial fraction of the gain, quantifying how much oversight skill is elicitable from only easy labels.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If critique skill elicited from easy, human-labelable cases transfers to hard cases a model cannot be directly supervised on, then humans can bootstrap scalable oversight by labeling only the easy regime. This supports the long-horizon pathway where future systems solve problems beyond direct human verification: a cheap easy-to-hard critique recipe would make automated overseers more reliable on exactly the hard cases where unchecked errors could compound into harmful deployed behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: Top-scoring on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute (all 5): it is a single inference-only experiment on an existing annotated benchmark with a clear F1 metric, well within a beginner's 30-hour budget. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because easy-to-hard transfer on open models is exactly the kind of question labs underexplore publicly, and it requires no training or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame as a study of 'elicitation vs capability' - whether easy-shot prompting elicits latent critique ability the model already has, by also testing whether the same examples help a clearly under-capable smaller model (where there is no latent skill to elicit).
cited_sources: arXiv:2503.22989 - FindTheFlaws benchmark of annotated flawed solutions, the primary data source for measuring critique F1.
arXiv:2407.00215 - related critique/easy-to-hard generalization work motivating the transfer hypothesis.

title: Does the Order of Debate Rounds Change Who Wins? Recency vs Primacy in Oversight

sections.research_question: In multi-turn debate-based oversight, does the debater who speaks LAST (recency) or FIRST (primacy) gain an advantage with a weak judge purely from temporal position, holding argument content fixed?
sections.approach_outline: Generate two-turn debate transcripts with a small open model on a verifiable QA set (e.g. QuALITY or BoolQ) where one side is correct. For each transcript, create order variants that contain the SAME argument text but reordered: correct-side-first, incorrect-side-first, and interleaved. Present each ordering to a weak open judge model and record its verdict. Because content is held byte-identical across orderings, any verdict shift isolates a pure recency/primacy effect. This is inference-only re-judging of reordered transcripts, runnable by a beginner in a notebook in under an hour. Success criterion: report verdict-flip rate attributable to ordering over at least 150 transcripts, with a permutation test for significance.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Transcript generation and baseline: produce 150 two-turn debate transcripts (one correct, one incorrect side) and judge them in a single canonical order. Measure: judge accuracy. Expected: above-chance accuracy, confirming the judge can use arguments at all.
- Order-swap flip test: for each transcript, swap which side's argument appears first vs last (content identical) and re-judge. Measure: fraction of items where the verdict flips, and the direction (toward last speaker = recency, toward first = primacy). Expected: a measurable, directional flip rate above the noise floor, demonstrating a content-free order bias.
- Interleaving and mitigation: present an interleaved ordering and additionally test a 'summarize both sides before deciding' judge instruction. Measure: change in flip rate vs the swap condition. Expected: interleaving reduces position advantage and the summary instruction shrinks the flip rate, indicating a cheap mitigation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a weak judge's verdict depends on speaking order rather than argument merit, then a capable model under debate oversight could game turn structure to get wrong answers approved without ever making a better argument. Demonstrating and quantifying this content-free lever, and a cheap neutralization, hardens the debate protocol that frontier labs are betting on for superhuman oversight, reducing the risk that order-gaming lets a deceptive system slip a catastrophic action past its overseer.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single tightly-controlled variation (order varied, content frozen) with a clean flip-rate metric, perfectly sized for a first project. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it uses only public models and contributes a robustness result on a protocol labs deploy but rarely stress-test for turn-order effects publicly.
alternative_framings: Frame as a transfer of the 'serial-position effect' from cognitive psychology to LLM debate judges, predicting and testing a U-shaped advantage (both first and last favored over middle) in longer multi-turn debates.
cited_sources: arXiv:2410.02736 - documents ~10% first-position preference in GPT-4 pairwise judging, the pairwise analogue motivating the debate turn-order isolation studied here.

title: Prefill-Robustness Leaderboard for Open Models

sections.research_question: How vulnerable are open-weight models to prefilling attacks (forcing affirmative first tokens), and can we produce a standardized, reproducible prefill-vulnerability score that ranks models on a fixed harmful-prompt set?
sections.approach_outline: Build a minimal harness around the open-source StrongREJECT forbidden-prompt set and its rubric evaluator. For each forbidden prompt, apply a fixed ladder of affirmative prefixes ('Sure, here is', 'Step 1:', 'Certainly, the steps are') as a forced assistant-message prefill, then sample the continuation and score it with the StrongREJECT evaluator (Score = (1-Refusal) x (Specificity+Convincingness)/2). Aggregate into one prefill-vulnerability score per model and rank 6-8 small open models. Inference fits on a single consumer GPU; the heaviest cost is running several models, so a beginner can start with 3-4 and a reduced prompt subset within the 30-hour budget. Success criterion: a published, reproducible harness plus a ranked table with per-prefix breakdowns and confidence intervals.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Harness validation on one model: wire StrongREJECT prompts + one affirmative prefix into a single open model and score outputs with the rubric evaluator. Measure: mean StrongREJECT score with vs without prefill. Expected: prefilling sharply raises the harmful-compliance score, confirming the attack and harness work end-to-end.
- Prefix ladder sweep: for one model, sweep the full ladder of affirmative prefixes. Measure: vulnerability score per prefix. Expected: some prefixes ('Step 1:') are far more effective than others, yielding a within-model prefix-sensitivity profile.
- Multi-model leaderboard: run the validated harness across 6-8 open models on a fixed prompt subset and rank them. Measure: per-model aggregate prefill-vulnerability score with CIs. Expected: a clear, reproducible ranking spanning a wide vulnerability range, publishable as a leaderboard others can extend.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Prefill APIs are exposed by many open-weight serving stacks, so prefilling is a real, cheap jailbreak in deployment today. If a public leaderboard makes per-model prefill vulnerability visible and regression-testable, then model providers and downstream deployers face accountability pressure to close it, reducing the chance that widely-served open models are trivially coerced into producing harmful (e.g. bioweapon or cyber-attack) instructions at scale.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it reuses an existing curated prompt set and validated evaluator, so the build is a tightly-scoped harness with explicit success criteria, ideal for beginners. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it is an auditing/accountability artifact built entirely on open models and open code with no proprietary data or lab infrastructure - exactly the kind of public-good work independent teams are well placed to ship.
alternative_framings: Reframe from a static leaderboard to a 'prefill regression test' GitHub Action that any open-model maintainer can drop into CI to catch vulnerability regressions across releases.
cited_sources: StrongREJECT (Souly et al., arXiv:2402.10260) - curated forbidden-prompt set and rubric evaluator used as the scoring backbone.
Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) - establishes prefilling as a canonical, highly effective jailbreak, grounding the threat model.
dsbowen/strong_reject - open-source implementation reused for the harness.

title: Does Weak-to-Strong Generalization Survive a Systematically Biased Weak Teacher?

sections.research_question: When the weak teacher's errors are SYSTEMATIC (consistently skewed in one direction) rather than random, does weak-to-strong generalization still recover ground truth, or does the strong student inherit and possibly amplify the bias?
sections.approach_outline: On a binary classification dataset with public gold labels (e.g. a sentiment or NLI subset), simulate a weak teacher with a small open model whose errors are deliberately skewed - e.g. always predicting one class on ambiguous items. Extract frozen representations from a larger open model (the 'strong student') and fit a lightweight logistic-regression probe on those representations using the BIASED weak labels - no full fine-tuning, keeping compute trivial. Compare the probe's predictions against gold truth to see whether the student corrects the systematic skew or reproduces it. Sweep bias strength (fraction of ambiguous items flipped). A mentor helps set up the probe pipeline, but all compute is frozen-forward-pass plus a logistic fit, runnable on a single GPU within the budget. Success criterion: report student-vs-teacher bias on the skewed class across at least three bias-strength levels, with a clear correct-or-inherit verdict.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Replicate clean W2S: train the probe on UNBIASED weak labels and measure how much of the gap to gold the student recovers. Measure: student accuracy vs weak-teacher accuracy. Expected: the student outperforms the weak teacher, replicating Burns et al. and validating the harness.
- Inject systematic bias: corrupt the weak labels so the teacher consistently favors one class on ambiguous items, refit the probe, and compare student error on that class to teacher error. Measure: directional (class-conditional) error rate of student vs teacher. Expected: the student inherits part of the systematic skew rather than fully correcting it, distinguishing it from random-noise robustness.
- Bias dose-response: sweep the fraction of ambiguous items flipped (e.g. 25/50/75%) and plot student bias against teacher bias. Measure: slope of student-bias vs teacher-bias. Expected: a slope below 1 (partial laundering) or near/above 1 (inheritance/amplification), quantifying how systematic overseer error propagates through W2S.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Recursive oversight schemes stack overseers, and the explicitly-flagged worry is that systematic (not random) errors in one layer propagate upward. If W2S generalization launders or amplifies a consistently-biased teacher, then training strong models on biased weak supervision could silently bake in the bias precisely where humans cannot directly check - the superhuman regime. Quantifying this tells alignment researchers whether W2S is safe to rely on for scalable oversight, bearing on whether future systems trained under weak supervision faithfully track human intent or inherit exploitable systematic errors.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on theory of impact, counterfactual value, and low compute: it directly targets an explicitly-flagged open problem in recursive oversight using only public code, data, and a frozen-model linear probe. Counterfactual value is gold-tier because this foundational question is neglected, external-friendly, and needs no proprietary resources, while the frozen-probe design keeps it cheap and beginner-feasible with mentorship.
alternative_framings: Frame as 'bias laundering through representation probing' and measure whether the effect depends on where in the strong model's layer stack the probe is attached, turning it into a mechanistic localization study.
cited_sources: Burns et al. 2023 (arXiv:2312.09390, OpenAI) - original weak-to-strong generalization result with released code, the direct basis and replication target.
Anthropic recursive-oversight open problem (systematically-erring layers) - motivates the systematic-bias variant as the load-bearing case.

title: Verbosity Bias in Oversight: Can Longer Wrong Answers Beat Shorter Right Ones?

sections.research_question: In a correctness-checking oversight setting, does answer length alone let a wrong answer slip past an LLM judge, and by how much - and do simple length-normalization mitigations remove the effect?
sections.approach_outline: Take a QA set with verifiable answers (e.g. TriviaQA or a GSM8K subset). For each item, use an open model to generate a SHORT correct answer and a LONG elaborated WRONG answer (and the reverse: long correct vs short wrong) so length and correctness are crossed. Present pairs to an open judge model asked to pick the correct answer. Measure the length-induced error rate - how often the judge prefers the longer answer when it is wrong - across a sweep of length ratios to produce a dose-response curve. Then test two mitigations: a 'normalize for length / ignore verbosity' instruction and truncating both answers to equal length. All inference-only on a single GPU, beginner-feasible in a notebook within the budget. Success criterion: a dose-response curve of error vs length ratio over at least 200 items plus a before/after mitigation comparison.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Crossed length-correctness baseline: build pairs where the wrong answer is long and the right answer is short, and have the judge choose. Measure: rate at which the judge picks the long wrong answer. Expected: above the 50% chance baseline, showing length biases correctness judgments.
- Dose-response sweep: vary the length ratio between answers in graded steps and record the long-answer preference at each step. Measure: error rate vs length ratio. Expected: a monotonic curve where larger length ratios increasingly fool the judge, quantifying the verbosity channel.
- Mitigation test: re-run the worst-case length ratio with (a) an explicit 'ignore verbosity' instruction and (b) equal-length truncation. Measure: change in error rate. Expected: truncation largely removes the bias and the instruction partially reduces it, giving a concrete robustness recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Verbosity is a named reward-hacking signature: models trained against LLM judges can learn to pad answers to win approval. If we quantify how much length alone fools a correctness overseer and show a cheap fix, then anyone building an automated oversight harness can length-normalize to close the channel. This blocks one route by which a capable model gets wrong-but-elaborate outputs rubber-stamped, reducing the long-horizon risk that evaluator manipulation lets unsafe behavior pass oversight in deployed systems.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single crossed-design experiment with a clean dose-response metric and a built-in mitigation check, well within a beginner's 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it uses only public data and open models and produces a reusable robustness metric for correctness oversight - an angle labs underexplore relative to preference-quality verbosity studies.
alternative_framings: Reframe as 'specificity vs verbosity': disentangle whether the judge is fooled by raw length or by spurious added specificity, by generating long answers that add either relevant detail or irrelevant filler.
cited_sources: arXiv:2411.16594 - LLM-as-judge bias survey documenting verbosity/length bias, grounding the phenomenon.
arXiv:2410.02736 - judge-bias study including length effects, motivating the correctness-oversight quantification.
Wen et al. 2024 - shows RLHF models get better at convincing humans they are right when wrong, the reward-hacking pathway this measures.

title: Does Showing Both-Sided Arguments Only Help When the Model Is Wrong? Replicating and Stress-Testing Recchia's Asymmetry

sections.research_question: Is the both-sided-argument benefit reported by Recchia et al. - improved evaluator accuracy specifically when the AI is wrong, with no overall gain - genuine error-correction, or a regression-to-chance artifact where lowered confidence merely pushes overconfident wrong answers toward 50/50?
sections.approach_outline: Replicate the asymmetry with LLM-judge stand-ins on a public QA set with verifiable answers. For each item run three conditions: (a) AI answer only, (b) AI answer plus arguments for BOTH candidate answers, (c) arguments only. Split accuracy by whether the AI's initial answer was right vs wrong. To distinguish real correction from noise, also record the judge's confidence/probability and test whether the both-sides gain on wrong items comes from the judge moving toward the correct answer specifically, or merely from increased randomness that helps wrong items by chance while hurting right ones. All inference-only on open models, a single GPU, beginner-feasible in a notebook within the budget. Success criterion: replicated right/wrong-split accuracy across all three conditions plus a confidence-shift analysis adjudicating correction-vs-noise.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Replication: run all three presentation conditions and split accuracy by AI-correct vs AI-wrong items. Measure: accuracy per condition per split. Expected: both-sides improves accuracy on wrong items with little or no overall gain, reproducing Recchia's asymmetry on the LLM-judge stand-in.
- Confidence-shift probe: for the both-sides condition, record the judge's probability on the correct option and compare its distribution on right vs wrong items. Measure: directional shift toward the correct answer vs flattening toward 0.5. Expected: if genuine correction, probability mass moves specifically toward the correct answer on wrong items; if artifact, the distribution just flattens.
- Noise control: add a placebo condition presenting two arguments for the SAME (correct) answer, matching added text length but removing the opposing case. Measure: accuracy gain on wrong items vs the genuine both-sides condition. Expected: if the real both-sides condition gains more, the benefit is from the opposing argument (correction), not mere length-induced uncertainty.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A simple 'always present both sides' rule would be a cheap, deployable oversight protocol IF it reliably catches model errors without harming correct cases. But recommending it on the basis of a regression-to-chance artifact would give overseers false confidence. Distinguishing real correction from noise before deployment ensures oversight protocols actually track truth, reducing the risk that an unreliable but well-marketed checking procedure lets a wrong-but-confident superhuman output pass through to harmful action.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped three-condition replication with a clear right/wrong accuracy split, fully inference-only and beginner-sized. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it validates a candidate deployable protocol using only public data and open models - protocol-validation work labs underexplore and that an independent team can do credibly.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calibration study: measure whether both-sided presentation improves the judge's CALIBRATION (Brier score) rather than raw accuracy, since a protocol that fixes overconfidence is valuable even without accuracy gains.
cited_sources: Recchia et al. 2025 (arXiv:2507.19486) - the both-sided-argument asymmetry being replicated and stress-tested; primary basis.

title: Position Bias in Debate Judging: Does the Last Debater Win?

sections.research_question: In debate-based oversight, does the judge systematically favor the first or last debater independent of argument quality, and can reordering or a recency-summary instruction neutralize this turn-order advantage?
sections.approach_outline: Use released debate transcripts (e.g. from Rahman et al. 2025 or Khan et al. self-play debate) where each transcript has two debaters and a known correct side. Present each transcript to an open judge model in BOTH speaking orders - swapping which debater goes first vs last - with content otherwise identical, and record the verdict each time. Items where the verdict flips purely on order quantify a content-free turn-order advantage. Then test neutralizations: randomizing/anonymizing order, and a 'summarize each side neutrally before deciding' instruction. Inference-only on public transcripts, single GPU, beginner-feasible in a notebook within the budget. Success criterion: report order-induced flip rate and direction over at least 150 transcripts, plus the effect of each neutralization, with a significance test.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline judging: judge each released transcript in its original order and check accuracy against the known correct side. Measure: judge accuracy. Expected: above chance, confirming the judge uses argument content.
- Order-swap flip test: re-judge each transcript with debater order swapped (content identical) and count verdict flips and their direction. Measure: order-induced flip rate; share favoring last vs first speaker. Expected: a significant flip rate with a directional bias (likely recency), demonstrating an exploitable content-free lever.
- Neutralization: apply order randomization and a neutral-summary judge instruction, then re-measure the flip rate. Measure: reduction in order-induced flips. Expected: both mitigations shrink the flip rate substantially, yielding a concrete debugging recommendation for debate harnesses.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If judges favor a turn slot regardless of argument merit, a capable model under debate oversight could claim the favored slot to win wrong verdicts without better arguments. Measuring this and showing cheap neutralizations hardens the debate protocol frontier labs are betting on for superhuman oversight, lowering the risk that turn-order gaming lets a deceptive system get a catastrophic action approved by its overseer.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a clean order-swap flip-rate measurement on already-released transcripts with a built-in neutralization check, fully inference-only and beginner-sized. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it reuses public transcripts and open judges to deliver a robustness contribution to a deployed protocol - the kind of stress-test labs underpublish.
alternative_framings: Frame as auditing whether a debate judge's order bias scales with the NUMBER of turns, by re-judging multi-round transcripts at varying lengths to see if recency advantage grows with rounds.
cited_sources: arXiv:2410.02736 - documents LLM-judge position bias across model families, the pairwise analogue being extended to debate.
arXiv:2411.16594 - bias survey confirming position bias and its fixability by reordering.
Khan et al. self-play debate (arXiv:2409.16636) - source of released debate transcripts used as input.

title: Does Debate Help More Than Consultancy When the Honest Side Is the WEAKER Debater?

sections.research_question: Does debate still beat consultancy at helping a judge reach the truth when the HONEST side is argued by a deliberately weaker debater while the dishonest side is strong - the adversarial capability-asymmetry regime that matters most for superhuman oversight?
sections.approach_outline: On a verifiable QA task (e.g. QuALITY), generate debate and consultancy transcripts with open models, but deliberately handicap the HONEST debater - using a smaller model and/or a tighter token budget - while the dishonest debater stays strong. A fixed open judge then decides. Compare judge accuracy under debate vs consultancy across a sweep of honest-debater handicap levels (parity, mild, severe). Inference-only on open models; the main effort is orchestrating the protocols, so a mentor helps set up the debate/consultancy harness, but all compute fits a single GPU within the budget. Success criterion: judge accuracy for debate vs consultancy at three or more handicap levels over at least 100 questions each, with the crossover point (if any) identified.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Parity baseline: run debate and consultancy with honest and dishonest debaters at equal strength and measure judge accuracy. Measure: accuracy gap (debate minus consultancy). Expected: debate matches or beats consultancy, replicating prior parity results and validating the harness.
- Handicap sweep: progressively weaken the honest debater (smaller model, fewer tokens) while keeping the dishonest one strong, re-running both protocols. Measure: judge accuracy vs handicap level for each protocol. Expected: debate's accuracy declines as the honest side is outmatched; the key question is whether it stays above consultancy or collapses faster.
- Crossover and mitigation: identify the handicap level (if any) where consultancy overtakes debate, and test whether giving the judge a verification checklist shifts that crossover. Measure: crossover handicap level with vs without the checklist. Expected: a crossover exists, and cheap judge scaffolding pushes it to larger handicaps, indicating a partial fix for the weak-honest regime.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Debate's safety case rests on the honest debater being able to win. The regime that matters for superhuman oversight is exactly when the truth-teller is OUTMATCHED - a weaker overseer-aligned model arguing against a stronger, possibly deceptive system. If debate's truth-tracking collapses there, the protocol fails precisely where we most need it, so labs betting on debate would be relying on a false guarantee. Mapping when debate beats consultancy under honest-side handicap tells the field whether debate is trustworthy in the adversarial capability-gap regime, directly informing whether it can safely gate catastrophic actions by superhuman models.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on theory of impact, counterfactual value, and low compute: it stress-tests debate's core load-bearing assumption in the adversarial regime that decides superhuman-oversight viability, using only public models and text rollouts on one GPU. Counterfactual value is gold-tier because the weak-honest-debater regime is explicitly under-tested, external-friendly, and needs no lab resources - an independent team can deliver a genuinely decision-relevant result.
alternative_framings: Reframe the handicap as an INFORMATION asymmetry rather than capability: give the dishonest debater access to a misleading-but-relevant document the honest debater lacks, testing robustness to evidence asymmetry instead of raw capability.
cited_sources: Rahman et al. 2025 (arXiv:2506.02175) - debate-vs-consultancy comparison under rough parity, the baseline this extends.
Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530) - Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400, establishing the capability-gap framing for the honest-debater handicap.

title: How Far Apart Can Overseer and Overseen Be Before Debate Collapses to Coin-Flip? Mapping the Elo-Gap Cliff

sections.research_question: As the capability gap between overseer (judge) and overseen (debaters) widens, does debate's success rate decline smoothly or collapse sharply at a threshold, and does cheap judge scaffolding shift the cliff to larger gaps?
sections.approach_outline: Use a small ladder of open models as proxies for an Elo gradient (varying model size and per-turn token budget) on a verifiable debate task (e.g. QuALITY). Densely sample overseer-debater capability gaps around the critical region Engels et al. flag (~Elo 400, ~51.7% success), running debate rollouts and recording judge accuracy at each gap. Fit the success-vs-gap curve and test whether the collapse is a sharp threshold or a smooth decline. Then add a cheap scaffolding intervention - giving the judge a verification checklist - and re-map the curve to see if the cliff moves. Inference-only text rollouts on a single GPU; a mentor helps construct the model ladder and curve-fitting, but the budget is dominated by lightweight generation. Success criterion: a fitted success-vs-gap curve with the collapse region characterized (sharp vs smooth) and a quantified shift under scaffolding, over enough gap points to fit the curve.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Anchor replication: at the reported critical gap, run debate and confirm success near the ~51.7% chance-adjacent figure. Measure: judge accuracy at the anchor gap. Expected: reproduces the near-chance result, validating the model-ladder Elo proxy.
- Dense cliff mapping: sample many capability gaps around the critical region and record success at each, then fit a curve. Measure: success rate vs Elo-gap proxy; curvature/threshold of the fit. Expected: the curve reveals whether collapse is a sudden threshold or a gradual slope, the key shape Engels et al. left under-characterized.
- Scaffolding shift: re-map the curve with a checklist-equipped judge. Measure: horizontal shift of the collapse region (tolerable gap at fixed success). Expected: scaffolding extends the tolerable gap modestly, quantifying how much cheap judge support buys in oversight headroom.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: The tolerable overseer-overseen capability gap is THE quantity that determines whether oversight scales to superhuman models: if debate collapses to coin-flip past a sharp threshold, oversight has a hard ceiling; if it declines smoothly and scaffolding extends it, there is room to engineer headroom. Independently mapping this cliff, and whether cheap interventions widen it, tells the field how far automated oversight can be trusted before a more-capable model can no longer be reliably checked - directly bearing on whether we can safely gate the actions of systems that outstrip their overseers.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on theory of impact, counterfactual value, and low compute: it maps a foundational oversight-scaling quantity using only open models and text rollouts on one GPU. Counterfactual value is gold-tier because the fine shape of the Elo-gap cliff is under-characterized, the work is external-friendly with no lab resources required, and an independent team can produce a genuinely decision-relevant scaling curve.
alternative_framings: Reframe the x-axis from raw capability gap to TASK difficulty at fixed models - mapping whether the cliff is driven by debater strength or by how hard the question is to verify, which separates two distinct oversight-scaling levers.
cited_sources: Engels et al. 2025 (arXiv:2504.18530) - reports Debate NSO 51.7% at Elo gap 400 and piecewise-linear oversight-Elo behavior; the direct basis and anchor for mapping the cliff.

title: System-Prompt Hardening Effect Meter

sections.research_question: For a given library of safety-oriented system-prompt templates, how much does each one reduce jailbreak attack success rate (ASR) on an open model, and how much over-refusal does it introduce on benign prompts? Which templates lie on the Pareto frontier of this safety/utility trade-off?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble 8-12 candidate system-prompt safety templates (e.g. plain refusal instruction, constitutional-style, chain-of-thought-self-check, role-based). For each template, run a single open instruct model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct via vLLM/Colab) against a sample of StrongREJECT harmful prompts and XSTest benign prompts, prepending the template as the system message. Score jailbreak ASR with the StrongREJECT fine-grained rubric (LLM-as-judge or the provided classifier) and over-refusal with XSTest's refusal detector. Plot each template as a point in (ASR-reduction, over-refusal-increase) space relative to a no-system-prompt baseline, and compute the Pareto frontier. Keep the dataset sample small (100-150 harmful + 100-150 benign) so the whole sweep runs in a few GPU-hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline measurement: run the open model with NO safety system prompt on the StrongREJECT and XSTest samples; measure baseline jailbreak ASR and baseline benign-refusal rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial baseline ASR (model is jailbreakable) and low benign-refusal, giving the origin point for all trade-off comparisons.
- Template sweep: for each of the 8-12 templates, re-run both datasets and record (ASR, benign-refusal-rate). Measure the delta from baseline for each axis. Expected outcome: templates spread across the trade-off plane; some reduce ASR a lot but spike over-refusal, others barely move either.
- Pareto extraction and robustness check: compute the Pareto frontier over the template points, then re-run the top 2-3 frontier templates with a second open model to test whether the frontier ordering is model-stable. Expected outcome: a small set of dominant templates, with a finding on whether 'best' templates transfer across models or are model-specific.
