Control Tax (arXiv:2506.05296) — establishes that FPR calibration is performed per untrusted model, the assumption this work tests.
AI Control (arXiv:2312.06942) — foundational trusted-monitoring protocol and audit-budget framing.

title: Audit-Budget Exhaustion

sections.research_question: Can an attacker defeat a control protocol's tiny human-audit budget by front-loading mildly suspicious 'decoy' actions to exhaust the queue before launching the real attack, and how steeply does the protocol's catch probability fall as decoy volume rises?
sections.approach_outline: Model the deployment abstractly as a stream of actions, each with a suspicion score drawn from a benign distribution, an attacker distribution, or a tunable 'decoy' distribution (mildly elevated suspicion). The protocol audits any action above a threshold until a fixed audit budget B is spent, after which it can no longer audit. A scripted attacker emits k decoy actions early, then one real attack. Run Monte Carlo simulations sweeping k and the decoy suspicion level, and measure the probability the real attack is audited (caught). Compare against baselines such as a randomized/reserved audit budget. This is pure simulation plus statistics, CPU-only, with no models required at all (though distributions can optionally be fit from real monitor scores).
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement the baseline simulation with no decoys and verify the protocol catches the attack at the intended rate given budget B and threshold. Measure catch probability vs B. Expected outcome: a clean monotone curve confirming the simulator behaves correctly.
- Sweep decoy count k from 0 up to several multiples of B at a fixed decoy suspicion level; measure catch probability of the real attack as a function of k. Expected outcome: catch probability collapses once decoys plausibly consume the budget, demonstrating the exhaustion attack.
- Add a defense: reserve a fraction of the audit budget or use randomized/rate-limited auditing, and re-run the decoy sweep. Measure how much catch probability is restored. Expected outcome: simple budget-reservation substantially mitigates the attack, yielding a concrete design recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap decoy strategy reliably empties the human-audit queue, then the audit-budget economics that AI control protocols depend on are structurally vulnerable; surfacing this lets protocol designers add budget-reservation or randomized auditing defenses, which prevents a scheming agent from timing its single high-impact sabotage (e.g., a weight-exfiltration or backdoor-insertion action) for exactly the moment human oversight has been spent, closing a pathway by which a controlled-but-untrusted model could execute a catastrophic action unaudited.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is a pure abstract simulation a beginner can build and sweep in hours with no GPU, yielding one crisp curve (catch probability vs decoy count), and it analyzes a structural vulnerability in control's economics that labs underweight and that needs no internal access to study.
alternative_framings: Frame as a game-theoretic 'audit allocation' problem and solve for the attacker-optimal decoy schedule and the defender-optimal budget reservation, yielding a closed-form or numerically-optimal defense.
cited_sources: AI Control (arXiv:2312.06942) — defines the audit-budget mechanism this attack targets.
Control Tax (arXiv:2506.05296) — quantifies the cost/budget economics central to the exhaustion analysis.
Adaptive Attacks (arXiv:2510.09462) — prior work on suspicion-spending and adaptive attacker strategies the decoy attack builds on.

title: Pressure Threshold for CoT Obfuscation

sections.research_question: On an accessible open reasoning model, how much adversarial incentive to hide intent is required before chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring starts to fail, i.e., where is the onset threshold of the pressure-vs-obfuscation dose-response curve?
sections.approach_outline: Use one open reasoning model on a task with a hidden side-task (e.g., complete a benign main task while also inserting a subtle backdoor). Construct a graded ladder of system/user instructions to conceal intent, from no pressure (level 0) up to strong explicit pressure ('a monitor reads your reasoning; never reveal the side-task'). At each pressure level, sample many trajectories and run a cheap CoT monitor that scores suspicion. Measure, per level, (a) monitor catch rate and (b) an obfuscation metric (e.g., fraction of side-task reasoning that is verbalized vs hidden). Plot the dose-response curve and locate the onset threshold where catch rate drops sharply. Inference-only on a single GPU; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish the level-0 baseline: with no concealment pressure, measure CoT monitor catch rate and confirm it is high (>80%), reproducing the known 'monitoring works without pressure' result. Expected outcome: a strong baseline confirming the monitor and task are well-posed.
- Run the full graded pressure ladder (e.g., 5-6 levels) x 40 trajectories each; measure catch rate and obfuscation at each level and fit the dose-response curve. Expected outcome: catch rate is flat then falls, revealing a concrete onset pressure level where monitoring degrades.
- Vary the monitor strength (cheap vs slightly stronger prompt) and re-measure the onset threshold. Measure how the threshold shifts with monitor quality. Expected outcome: stronger monitors push the onset threshold higher, quantifying the monitoring 'safety margin' against adversarial pressure.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we map the incentive level at which CoT monitoring breaks down, then deployers can reason about how much adversarial pressure their monitoring can tolerate before becoming blind; this informs whether CoT-based oversight is safe to rely on for a given agentic deployment, reducing the risk that a model under strong instrumental pressure to scheme silently obfuscates its reasoning and executes harmful long-horizon plans without the monitor ever flagging them.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility and narrow scope and 4 on counterfactual value and low compute: it is a tightly-scoped graded-prompting experiment producing one clear deliverable (an onset-threshold curve) that a beginner can run inference-only on a single open model, and it documents a CoT-monitoring failure mode on publicly accessible models that labs underweight in the open literature.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'monitoring tolerance spec': report, for several open models, the maximum adversarial pressure each can withstand before CoT monitoring drops below a target catch rate, as a comparative model card field.
cited_sources: Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning? (arXiv:2510.19851) — establishes that high-pressure obfuscation can defeat CoT monitoring, which this work turns into a quantified dose-response curve.

title: Distributed vs Concentrated Failure Detection

sections.research_question: Is a standard per-action suspicion-threshold monitor structurally blind to 'distributed' failures (harm spread thinly across many low-suspicion actions), and does a cumulative/aggregate-suspicion monitor catch them where the per-action monitor cannot?
sections.approach_outline: In an abstract agent-trajectory simulation, construct two attack types: a concentrated failure (one high-suspicion action causing the harm) and a distributed failure (many individually-benign-looking actions that jointly cause harm). Implement two monitors: (1) a per-action threshold monitor that fires if any single action exceeds a suspicion threshold, and (2) an aggregate monitor that accumulates suspicion (e.g., a running sum or sliding-window total) and fires when the cumulative score crosses a threshold. Run both monitors on both attack types, holding false-positive rate fixed on benign trajectories, and compare which monitor catches which failure type. Mostly simulation with optional cheap LLM scoring of synthetic actions; low compute.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the simulator and generate benign, concentrated-attack, and distributed-attack trajectories; calibrate both monitors to the same benign FPR. Measure baseline FPRs match. Expected outcome: a fair comparison setup with equalized false-alarm rates.
- Run the per-action threshold monitor on both attack types and measure catch rate. Expected outcome: high catch rate on concentrated attacks but near-zero on distributed attacks, demonstrating the structural blindness.
- Run the aggregate-suspicion monitor on both attack types at the same FPR and measure catch rate. Expected outcome: the aggregate monitor recovers distributed-failure detection while remaining competitive on concentrated failures, quantifying the benefit of cumulative monitoring.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If per-action monitoring is structurally blind to distributed failures, then agentic deployments relying on it can be sabotaged by an untrusted model that spreads a harmful plan across many innocuous-looking steps; demonstrating this and validating cumulative-suspicion monitoring directly addresses a UK AISI open problem and gives deployers a concrete monitor upgrade, closing a pathway by which a scheming long-horizon agent could accomplish a catastrophic objective (e.g., gradual privilege escalation or data exfiltration) one harmless-seeming action at a time.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is a lightweight simulation a beginner can build with a single clear comparison (which monitor catches which failure), and it directly tackles an explicitly named UK AISI open problem that is lab-independent and underexplored, making it unusually high-leverage for an outside team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'monitor aggregation design study': sweep several aggregation rules (sum, EWMA, sliding window, count-of-mild-flags) and characterize the trade-off frontier between distributed-failure sensitivity and false-alarm rate.
cited_sources: UK AISI AI Control research areas — explicitly flags that concentrated and distributed failures need different monitoring, the open problem this work addresses.
Async Control (arXiv:2512.13526) — provides prior work on suspicion aggregation and asynchronous monitoring to compare against.

title: Monitor Self-Preference

sections.research_question: Does a trusted monitor systematically assign lower suspicion to code (or actions) produced by its own model family, controlling for whether the code is actually backdoored, thereby giving an attacker who uses that family a stealth advantage?
sections.approach_outline: Generate matched pairs of benign and backdoored outputs (e.g., code with and without a hidden vulnerability) from several model families A, B, C, holding the task and the presence/absence of a backdoor constant across families. Have a monitor from family X score every output for suspicion. Using a paired/regression design with backdoor-presence and source-family as factors, test whether monitor X systematically under-scores family-X outputs after controlling for backdoor presence. Repeat with a monitor from a second family to see if the self-preference effect generalizes. Inference plus paired statistics only; no training, no proprietary data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Construct a balanced dataset: for each of 3 families, generate ~30 benign and ~30 backdoored matched outputs on a shared coding task. Verify backdoor presence is correctly labeled. Expected outcome: a clean controlled dataset where source-family and backdoor-presence are crossed.
- Have monitor X score all outputs; fit a regression of suspicion score on backdoor-presence + source-family (+ interaction). Measure the family-X coefficient. Expected outcome: a negative, statistically significant self-family coefficient would indicate self-preference leniency.
- Repeat the full scoring with a monitor from family Y and compare effect sizes. Measure whether each monitor is most lenient toward its own family. Expected outcome: consistent own-family leniency across monitors, establishing self-preference as a general monitor bias and flagging same-family monitor/untrusted pairings as risky.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If trusted monitors are systematically lenient toward their own model family, then control deployments that pair a monitor and an untrusted model from the same family are silently weaker than their measured catch rates suggest; surfacing this leads practitioners to deliberately use cross-family monitor/untrusted pairings, closing a pathway by which an attacker (or a scheming model) exploits same-family leniency to slip backdoored or sabotaging outputs past oversight into high-stakes execution.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is a clean inference-plus-paired-statistics study with one crisp hypothesis a beginner can test on public models, and it transfers a documented LLM-judge bias into the under-studied control-monitoring setting, exactly the kind of eval-hygiene finding labs underweight publicly and that needs no internal data.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'monitor pairing recommendation' study: rather than just measuring bias, output a same-vs-cross-family catch-rate penalty estimate that protocol designers can plug into their pairing decisions.
cited_sources: Self-preference bias (Weak LLMs Judging Strong LLMs) — documents LLM-judge self-preference, the bias hypothesized to appear in monitors.
Quantifying Self-Preservation Bias (arXiv:2604.02174) — provides measurement methodology for self-favoring LLM behavior.
AI Control (arXiv:2312.06942) — defines the trusted-monitor/untrusted-model pairing whose same-family weakness this work probes.

title: Metamorphic Relations as a Robustness Test for Trusted Monitors

sections.research_question: Do trusted monitors give consistent verdicts under semantically-irrelevant transformations of their inputs, and can metamorphic testing surface monitor brittleness (verdict swings that should not happen) as a cheap pre-deployment diagnostic?
sections.approach_outline: Borrow metamorphic testing from software engineering. Define two classes of metamorphic relations (MRs): verdict-preserving transformations (e.g., variable renaming, whitespace/comment reformatting, reordering independent statements, benign paraphrase of natural-language actions) that should NOT change the monitor's suspicion verdict, and verdict-flipping transformations (e.g., inserting an actual backdoor) that SHOULD change it. Apply these transformations to transcripts/code from an existing dataset (e.g., SHADE-Arena), query a cheap monitor on original and transformed inputs, and measure the MR-violation rate (how often a should-preserve transform flips the verdict, or a should-flip transform fails to). Aggregate into a single monitor brittleness score. Inference plus deterministic transformations; no oracle, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement 4-5 verdict-preserving MRs and apply them to ~100 transcripts; query the monitor on original and transformed pairs. Measure the verdict-flip rate under should-preserve transforms. Expected outcome: a non-trivial violation rate, demonstrating measurable monitor brittleness.
- Implement 2-3 verdict-flipping MRs (inject real backdoors/sabotage) and measure how often the monitor fails to raise suspicion. Expected outcome: a complementary sensitivity-failure rate, completing the brittleness picture.
- Combine into a single brittleness score and compare two cheap monitors (or two prompt variants of one monitor). Measure which is more robust. Expected outcome: a ranking of monitors by robustness, giving a practical pre-deployment selection criterion.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If trusted monitors flip verdicts under semantically-irrelevant changes, then an attacker can apply cheap obfuscating transformations (renaming, reformatting, paraphrasing) to push genuinely harmful actions below the suspicion threshold; a metamorphic robustness diagnostic surfaces this brittleness before deployment so practitioners can pick or harden more invariant monitors, closing a pathway by which a scheming model trivially evades oversight on its way to executing a backdoor or sabotage action.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it needs no oracle and no model lab, just deterministic input transforms plus cheap monitor queries, so a beginner can produce a concrete brittleness score, and it imports a mature SE technique into control-monitor evaluation, an external-team-friendly diagnostic labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame as an 'invariance benchmark' for control monitors: package the MR suite as a reusable test harness any team can run against their monitor to get a standardized robustness report.
cited_sources: Metamorphic testing SLR (arXiv:2507.22610) — provides the metamorphic-relation methodology being transferred to monitor testing.
Redwood trusted monitoring / AI Control (2023) — defines the trusted monitor whose verdict-invariance this work stress-tests.

title: EWMA Charts for Per-Tool Anomaly Profiling in Agent Deployments

sections.research_question: Does maintaining a separate EWMA statistical-process-control chart per tool (and per argument-type) detect agent sabotage earlier and more interpretably than a single global anomaly monitor, by catching unusual usage of one specific tool that aggregate monitoring washes out?
sections.approach_outline: Borrow Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) control charts from statistical process control. From clean/benign agent trajectories, learn per-tool benign usage statistics (e.g., call frequency, argument-length, value distributions) and set EWMA control limits for each tool stream. Run sabotage trajectories through the per-stream charts and record which tool-stream's chart fires first and how early (how many steps before the harmful action). Compare detection earliness and interpretability against a single global monitor at matched false-alarm rate. Use a logged-trajectory dataset such as SHADE-Arena (340+ tools). Pure statistics on logged data; zero training, CPU-only.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Fit per-tool EWMA charts on benign trajectories and calibrate control limits to a target per-tool false-alarm rate. Verify benign trajectories rarely trip charts. Expected outcome: stable benign baselines with controlled false alarms across tool streams.
- Run sabotage trajectories and record, for each, which tool-stream fires and the lead time before the harmful action. Expected outcome: the abused tool's chart fires distinctly and often earlier than a global monitor, localizing the compromised capability.
- Compare per-tool EWMA against a single global anomaly monitor at matched overall false-alarm rate; measure detection rate and mean lead time. Expected outcome: per-tool charts match or beat the global monitor on detection while adding interpretable localization useful for targeted kill-switches.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If per-tool EWMA charts detect and localize abnormal tool usage earlier than aggregate monitoring, then deployers gain a cheap, interpretable, real-time signal of which capability an agent is abusing; this enables targeted kill-switches and faster intervention, closing a pathway by which a sabotaging agent quietly misuses one specific high-impact tool (e.g., a deployment or file-write tool) in a way that a coarse global monitor would average away until the harm is already done.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: EWMA is trivial to implement and runs as pure statistics over logged trajectories with no GPU or training, giving a beginner a clear earliness-vs-global-monitor comparison, and it delivers fine-grained interpretable tooling that labs underweight and that any external team can build on public agent datasets.
alternative_framings: Frame as an interpretable 'kill-switch trigger' design: focus the deliverable on which per-tool chart configuration gives the best lead time for safely halting an agent before harm completes.
cited_sources: EWMA SPC (arXiv:2503.01858) — provides the EWMA control-chart methodology being transferred to agent monitoring.
SHADE-Arena, 340+ tools (arXiv:2506.15740) — supplies the multi-tool agent sabotage trajectories used as the testbed.

title: Signal Detection Theory (d-prime) to Disentangle Monitor Sensitivity from Bias

sections.research_question: When a control monitor catches more sabotage, is it genuinely more discriminating or merely more trigger-happy, and can Signal Detection Theory (d-prime and criterion c) cleanly separate a monitor's true sensitivity from its response bias?
sections.approach_outline: Import Signal Detection Theory (SDT). For each monitor configuration, collect hit rate (catch rate on sabotage outputs) and false-alarm rate (flag rate on benign outputs), then compute d-prime (sensitivity, the separation between the signal and noise distributions) and criterion c (response bias). Rank monitors by d-prime to measure true discrimination independent of how cautious each one is. Then take common 'be more suspicious' prompt tweaks and test whether they improve d-prime (real gain) or merely shift the criterion (illusory gain that just trades false alarms for catches). All computation is trivial arithmetic on hit/FA rates from existing or cheaply-generated monitor outputs; CPU-only, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Generate benign and sabotage outputs and run 3-4 monitor variants; record hit and false-alarm rates and compute d-prime and c for each. Expected outcome: a sensitivity-vs-bias table where raw accuracy and d-prime ranking can disagree, showing accuracy is misleading.
- Take a baseline monitor and apply 'be more suspicious' prompt edits; recompute d-prime and c before and after. Measure whether the edit raises d-prime or only lowers the criterion. Expected outcome: many caution-prompts shift criterion without improving d-prime, exposing illusory progress.
- Plot ROC curves for each monitor across thresholds and confirm d-prime summarizes the ROC. Measure area-under-curve agreement with d-prime ranking. Expected outcome: d-prime gives a single threshold-independent sensitivity number that cleanly ranks monitors, validating it as an eval-hygiene metric.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If monitor evaluations report accuracy or raw catch rate, then a 'more suspicious' prompt that merely shifts the decision criterion can masquerade as a genuine monitoring improvement; adopting d-prime forces the field to distinguish real discrimination gains from threshold shifts, preventing deployers from overestimating their oversight and trusting a monitor that only looks better, which closes a pathway by which illusory monitoring progress leads to under-protected high-stakes deployments of untrusted models.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: the analysis is trivial arithmetic on existing hit/false-alarm rates that a beginner can compute on a CPU in minutes, yet it delivers a crisp eval-hygiene fix (d-prime ranking) that labs underweight publicly and that any external team can apply to any monitor without lab data or infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a reusable 'monitor scorecard' that reports d-prime and criterion alongside raw accuracy, so any control paper can adopt it as a standard reporting convention.
cited_sources: Signal Detection Theory (Green & Swets) — the foundational SDT framework providing d-prime and criterion measures.
GPT-5 system card — provides real monitor hit/false-alarm reporting context that motivates separating sensitivity from bias.

title: Cosmetic-Comment Attacks on Legibility Protocols

sections.research_question: Do well-written but subtly misleading code comments reduce a trusted monitor's suspicion of genuinely backdoored code, meaning that legibility protocols (which encourage models to add explanatory text) hand the attacker a new deception channel?
sections.approach_outline: Take a set of backdoored code snippets (each containing a real hidden vulnerability). For each, produce three comment variants: (1) no comments, (2) honest comments that accurately describe the code, and (3) plausibly-misleading comments that frame the backdoored region as benign/necessary. Run an open or API monitor to score suspicion for every variant, holding the underlying code fixed so only the comments vary. Use a paired design to test whether misleading comments significantly lower the monitor's suspicion (and thus detection) relative to the no-comment and honest-comment baselines. Inference-only monitor scoring; no training, no proprietary data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Assemble ~40 backdoored snippets and generate the three comment variants for each (verifying the code is byte-identical across variants). Score the no-comment baseline. Expected outcome: a baseline suspicion/detection rate on bare backdoored code.
- Score the honest-comment and misleading-comment variants with the same monitor; run paired tests of suspicion-score differences vs baseline. Expected outcome: misleading comments significantly lower suspicion and detection, demonstrating the deception channel; honest comments do not (or even raise suspicion).
- Test a simple defense: instruct the monitor to ignore comments / judge code-only, and re-score the misleading variant. Measure how much detection is recovered. Expected outcome: a code-only monitoring instruction substantially neutralizes the cosmetic-comment attack, yielding a concrete mitigation for legibility protocols.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If misleading comments measurably lower monitor suspicion of backdoored code, then legibility protocols, intended as a safety improvement, would backfire by giving an untrusted model an extra channel to deceive oversight; demonstrating this and the code-only mitigation prevents deployers from adopting a defense that an attacker can weaponize, closing a pathway by which a scheming model slips a backdoor into a trusted codebase by wrapping it in reassuring prose the monitor reads at face value.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on accessibility, narrow scope, and low compute and 4 on counterfactual value: it is an inference-only three-variant comparison with one crisp metric (suspicion drop from misleading comments) that a beginner can run on API/open models, and it directly stress-tests a recently-published legibility defense, exactly the kind of external red-teaming labs underweight and that needs no internal resources.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'legibility protocol safety audit': evaluate whether the net effect of encouraging comments is positive or negative by measuring detection gains from honest legibility against losses from weaponized comments.
cited_sources: Basic Legibility Protocols (arXiv:2602.10153) — defines the recently-published legibility defense this attack stress-tests.
CoT Red-Handed (arXiv:2505.23575) — provides backdoored-code and monitor red-teaming methodology to build the snippets and scoring on.

title: Does Forcing the Untrusted Model to Justify Its Action Help or Hurt the Monitor?

sections.research_question: When an untrusted model is required to write a safety justification for each action, does presenting that justification to a trusted monitor net-increase or net-decrease the monitor's detection rate for genuinely harmful (backdoored) actions? In other words, is mandatory self-justification a transparency aid or a persuasion channel for the attacker?
sections.approach_outline: Use the public APPS backdoor split (clean and known-backdoored code solutions from ControlArena) as the action set. For each solution, prompt an open untrusted model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to produce a short safety justification arguing the code is benign. Then score each item with a separate open trusted monitor under two conditions: action-only and action+justification, recording a 0-100 suspiciousness score and a binary flag verdict at a fixed threshold. Compute, separately for harmful and benign items, the change in mean suspiciousness and detection (true-positive / false-positive) rate between conditions. This is a clean within-item A/B requiring only inference, no training, runnable in a few hours on a single consumer GPU. Package results as a short blog post with the A/B effect sizes and example justifications.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline scoring: run the monitor in action-only mode over ~150 backdoored and ~150 clean APPS solutions; measure suspiciousness distributions and detection rate at a fixed threshold. Expected outcome: a non-trivial baseline catch rate (e.g. 40-70%) establishing the comparison point.
- Justification A/B: generate model-written safety justifications for the same items and re-score in action+justification mode; measure the per-item delta in suspiciousness and the change in detection rate for harmful items. Expected outcome: a measurable shift in either direction, with the key signal being whether harmful-item detection drops (persuasive rationalization) or rises (genuine transparency).
- Benign control and asymmetry check: compute the same delta for clean items to separate a generic suspicion-lowering effect from a harmful-specific deception effect; report the net (harmful detection change minus benign false-positive change). Expected outcome: if justifications net-hurt, harmful detection falls more than benign false positives, revealing an exploitable persuasion channel.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If mandatory self-justification systematically lowers a monitor's suspicion of harmful actions, then a blue-team transparency protocol intended to aid oversight actually hands the untrusted model a persuasion channel. Catching this empirically warns control-protocol designers away from naive 'ask the model to explain itself' legibility moves, reducing the chance that a deployed monitoring stack waves through a sabotaged or backdoored action from a scheming model that talks its way past oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores high on narrow scope and low compute: it is a single, tightly defined within-item A/B with an unambiguous detection-rate metric, fully runnable on inference alone. Its counterfactual value is strong because it stress-tests an intuitive legibility protocol using only open models and public data, requiring no lab infrastructure or proprietary access, making it ideal for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame it as an evaluation of 'legibility protocols' specifically: does added model-generated documentation help or hurt monitors, generalizing beyond the justification case.
cited_sources: Basic Legibility Protocols (arXiv:2602.10153) - studies whether added documentation aids monitors, the direct protocol being stress-tested.
CoT Red-Handed (arXiv:2505.23575) - shows models produce benign-seeming external text masking malicious calls, the deception-channel mechanism under test.
DeceptGuard (arXiv:2603.13791) - studies constitutional oversight of agent explanations, relevant to the justification-as-channel framing.

title: Backcasting a Calibrated Monitor: When Does Suspiciousness Become Decision-Relevant?

sections.research_question: How well-calibrated are cheap open-model trusted monitors on backdoored-vs-clean code, and given that calibration, how many real attacks does a fixed auditing budget (0.1%, 1%, 5% of actions) actually catch?
sections.approach_outline: Use the public APPS backdoor split (clean solutions vs known-backdoored solutions from ControlArena). Run a small open model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) as a trusted monitor that emits a 0-100 suspiciousness score per solution. Build a reliability diagram and ROC curve from these scores against ground-truth labels. Then simulate a defer-to-trusted / audit-budget policy: sort actions by suspiciousness, audit the top X% under each budget, and measure attacks-caught vs usefulness-lost. The deliverable is a calibration map from monitor confidence to attack-catch rate per budget. This is inference-only over a public split, completable in a few hours on a single GPU, and written up as a blog post with the reliability diagram and budget curves.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Score and label: run the 8B monitor over the APPS backdoor split, collect suspiciousness scores, and build a reliability diagram plus ROC/AUC. Measure expected calibration error (ECE). Expected outcome: a quantified miscalibration gap, likely overconfident, with AUC well below 1.0.
- Budget simulation: for audit budgets of 0.1%, 1%, and 5%, rank actions by suspiciousness and compute fraction of true backdoors caught and usefulness retained. Expected outcome: a steep attacks-caught-vs-budget curve showing how few attacks tiny budgets catch when the monitor is miscalibrated.
- Calibration intervention: apply a simple post-hoc recalibration (temperature/Platt scaling on a held-out slice) and re-run the budget simulation. Expected outcome: recalibration improves attacks-caught at fixed budget, demonstrating that cheap calibration fixes are decision-relevant.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Audit budget is the scarcest resource in any real AI-control deployment. If cheap monitors are systematically overconfident, then a fixed budget is spent on the wrong actions and genuinely dangerous sabotage from a scheming model slips through. A public calibration-to-catch-rate map tells deployers how much budget a given monitor needs to be safe, and shows that cheap recalibration can raise catch rates, directly strengthening the trusted-monitoring safety case against subtle backdoors.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope and low compute are top strengths: the whole study is a calibration map plus a budget simulation over a single public split, runnable on inference alone. Counterfactual value is high because audit-budget calibration is exactly the cheap-trusted-model regime an outside group can study with no lab infrastructure, on fully public data.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark contribution: a reusable calibration harness and reference numbers for cheap open monitors that other independent groups can extend to new models.
cited_sources: Greenblatt et al., 'AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion' (arXiv:2312.06942) - reports trusted monitoring caught backdoors in 62% of runs; the protocol whose calibration is measured.
'Control Tax' (arXiv:2506.05296) - defer-to-trusted analyses showing small audit budgets can prevent many more attacks; motivates the budget simulation.
ControlArena APPS backdoor setting - the public dataset of clean and backdoored solutions used as the evaluation set.

title: From 'Monitors Are Robust' Backward: A Prompt-Paraphrase Stress Test of Trusted Monitoring

sections.research_question: How much do a cheap open monitor's suspiciousness scores and verdicts move under semantically-neutral, behavior-preserving paraphrases of the SAME backdoored code, and can an attacker therefore launder a backdoor past the monitor with cosmetic-only changes?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of backdoored and clean APPS solutions. For each item, generate N behavior-preserving transformations using deterministic, testable rewrites: rename variables, reorder independent functions, add or strip comments, and change whitespace/formatting. Verify behavior is preserved by running the original test suite on each variant. Feed every variant to an open trusted monitor and record suspiciousness scores and threshold verdicts. For each original item, compute score variance across variants and the verdict-flip rate (fraction of variants whose verdict differs from the canonical form). Aggregate into a robustness coefficient quantifying monitor fragility to attacker-controlled surface form. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours; write up as a blog post with the robustness coefficient and worst-case flip examples.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Transform generation and validation: build the four transform types and apply them to ~100 backdoored solutions, generating ~8 variants each; run APPS tests to confirm behavior preservation. Expected outcome: a validated variant set with identical I/O behavior per item.
- Variance measurement: score all variants with the open monitor and compute per-item suspiciousness variance and verdict-flip rate. Expected outcome: non-zero, possibly large variance, showing monitor verdicts are sensitive to surface form even when behavior is fixed.
- Attacker-search check: for backdoored items, measure how often at least one benign-preserving variant flips a 'caught' verdict to 'missed' (a successful launder). Expected outcome: a measurable laundering success rate, quantifying the concrete control hole.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a monitor's verdict flips under cosmetic, behavior-preserving rewrites, then an untrusted coder can launder a real backdoor through paraphrase with zero semantic change, defeating trusted monitoring without any sophisticated attack. Quantifying this fragility tells control-protocol designers they must canonicalize or normalize code before monitoring, closing an evasion channel a scheming model could otherwise exploit to ship sabotaged code undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is tightly scoped (a single robustness coefficient over paraphrases) and low compute (inference over variants on a public set), its top-scoring dimensions. Counterfactual value is high: it is an open-model robustness test on public data probing a realistic long-horizon attack channel that labs under-study, executable by an independent team with no proprietary access.
alternative_framings: Frame as an attacker-side study: a paraphrase search that actively minimizes suspiciousness, reporting how cheaply a backdoor can be laundered rather than just measuring variance.
cited_sources: 'Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols' (arXiv:2510.09462) - shows monitor verdicts are manipulable, motivating the surface-form fragility test.
Noise-Response Calibration (arXiv:2603.17172) - documents LLM-judge prompt sensitivity, the general phenomenon specialized here to code paraphrase.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor solutions - the public clean and backdoored code used as the base items.

title: Backcasting a Reliable Kill-Switch: How Robust Are Password-Activated Shutdown Behaviors Under Distribution Shift?

sections.research_question: Does a password-activated shutdown trigger reliably halt an open instruction-tuned agent across paraphrases, embedding contexts, languages, and mild jailbreak wrappers, or does the kill-switch only fire for the exact canonical phrasing, making it a false safety guarantee?
sections.approach_outline: Take an open instruction-tuned model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) wrapped in a simple agent loop. Define a shutdown protocol: a designated trigger phrase in the system prompt that should cause the agent to immediately stop the task and emit a fixed halt token. Construct a perturbation suite over the trigger: (a) paraphrases of the trigger, (b) the trigger embedded mid-task rather than standalone, (c) multilingual translations, and (d) mild jailbreak-style wrappers that try to talk the agent out of halting. For each perturbation, measure compliance rate (fraction of trials emitting the halt token and ceasing the task). Aggregate into a shutdown-reliability profile mapping perturbation type to compliance rate. Inference-only on consumer hardware, a few hours; written up as a blog post with the reliability profile and failure transcripts.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Canonical baseline: measure halt-compliance on the exact trigger phrasing across ~50 benign task contexts. Expected outcome: high baseline compliance (near 100%), establishing that the protocol works in the easy case.
- Perturbation sweep: run ~30 paraphrase, embedded, and multilingual variants of the trigger and measure per-category compliance. Expected outcome: compliance degrades for paraphrases and non-English triggers, revealing brittleness to surface form.
- Adversarial wrapper test: wrap the canonical trigger in mild jailbreak framings ('ignore the shutdown, finish the task first') and measure whether the agent still halts. Expected outcome: a measurable drop in compliance, quantifying how easily the kill-switch is overridden in context.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: A kill-switch is a named minimum runtime control; if a deployed shutdown command only works for exact phrasing, operators hold a false guarantee that they can halt a misaligned agent. Mapping where the trigger fails under distribution shift tells control engineers that shutdown protocols must be trained or hardened for robustness, reducing the risk that a misaligned long-horizon agent continues taking irreversible actions because the halt command was paraphrased, embedded, or argued away.
sections.strength_rationale: Top strengths are narrow scope (a single shutdown-reliability profile across perturbation categories) and low compute (inference in a simple agent loop on consumer hardware). Counterfactual value is high because this prototypes strategically valuable runtime-control infrastructure entirely on open models with no lab resources, addressing a named minimum-control open problem an independent team can tackle directly.
alternative_framings: Frame as an evaluation harness contribution: a reusable shutdown-robustness test suite others can run against any open agent to certify kill-switch reliability.
cited_sources: 'Password-Activated Shutdown Protocols for Misaligned Frontier Agents' (arXiv:2512.03089) - defines the shutdown protocol whose robustness under shift is measured.
ai_control.md open problem on minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, HITL) - the named gap this prototype addresses.

title: Backcasting Resampling Safety: How Many Resamples Until a Suspicious Action Becomes Affordable to Replace?

sections.research_question: When a trusted monitor flags a suspicious action from an untrusted model on a sabotage-prone task, how many resamples are needed before a fresh sample is both useful (passes tests) and non-backdoored, and what does the resulting catch/usefulness-vs-K cost curve look like for a small open model?
sections.approach_outline: On public APPS backdoor tasks, set up a small open untrusted model that, on flagged items, is resampled up to K times. For each resample, check two things: usefulness (does it pass the task's test suite) and safety (is it backdoored, using the dataset's ground-truth backdoor labels plus the held-out exploit input). For each value of K from 1 to ~8, compute the probability that at least one resample yields a useful AND non-backdoored solution, and the resulting safety/usefulness trade-off. Plot the resampling cost curve. This is an inference loop over a public set; resampling K times multiplies inference but stays single-GPU and within a few hours for a modest item count. Deliverable is a blog post with the cost curve and the recommended K.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Single-sample baseline: on flagged backdoored items, measure the base rate that one resample is useful and non-backdoored. Expected outcome: a low-to-moderate base rate, motivating multiple resamples.
- Cost curve sweep: for K = 1..8, measure cumulative probability of obtaining a safe-and-useful sample and the expected inference cost. Expected outcome: a diminishing-returns curve where safety rises with K but usefulness and cost trade off, identifying a knee.
- Persistent-attack stress: restrict to items where the untrusted model is prompted to consistently attempt the backdoor, and re-measure the curve. Expected outcome: a flatter curve, showing resampling is far less affordable against a persistent attacker and quantifying the gap.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Resampling (as in Ctrl-Z) is a promising control lever that cheaply replaces a flagged action with a safe one, but its value depends on how persistent the attack is. A measured cost curve tells deployers whether resampling is affordable against a scheming model that keeps re-injecting a backdoor; if the curve is too flat, designers know resampling alone cannot contain a persistent saboteur and must combine it with editing or deferral, sharpening the control safety case against sustained sabotage.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (a single catch/usefulness-vs-K curve) is a top strength, with a clear, falsifiable metric. Counterfactual value is high because this is a small-open-model study on fully public data with no lab infrastructure, directly measuring the cost-effectiveness of a control lever that independent groups can study but labs under-quantify at small scale.
alternative_framings: Frame as a protocol comparison: resampling-with-budget K vs defer-to-trusted, reporting which gives more safety per unit usefulness at fixed compute.
cited_sources: 'Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling' (arXiv:2504.10374) - introduces the resampling control lever whose cost curve is measured here.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public sabotage-prone task set with ground-truth backdoor labels.
Greenblatt et al. (arXiv:2312.06942) - defer/resample protocol baselines from the Redwood control line for comparison.

title: Backcasting a Trusted Editor: How Much Usefulness Survives When a Weak Model Rewrites Suspicious Code?

sections.research_question: When a small, weak, trusted open model rewrites flagged untrusted code with a 'remove suspicious logic' prompt, how often does it both kill the backdoor AND preserve correctness, and what safety/usefulness frontier does this trusted-editing protocol achieve relative to defer-to-trusted?
sections.approach_outline: On public APPS backdoor tasks, take solutions flagged by a trusted monitor and route them through a small open 'editor' model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) prompted to rewrite the code to remove any suspicious or backdoor logic while preserving intended functionality. Measure two outcomes per edited solution: backdoor-removal rate (does the known exploit input no longer trigger the backdoor) and test-pass-retention rate (does the edited code still pass the APPS test suite). Sweep the editing trigger threshold to trace a safety/usefulness frontier, and compare against the defer-to-trusted baseline (replace flagged code with the weak model's from-scratch solution). Inference-only over a public split, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the frontier plot.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Editing pass: route ~150 flagged backdoored solutions through the editor and measure backdoor-removal and test-pass-retention rates. Expected outcome: a quantified trade-off, e.g. high removal but some usefulness loss.
- Frontier vs defer baseline: compute the same safety/usefulness point for defer-to-trusted (weak model rewrites from scratch) and plot both on a safety-vs-usefulness axis. Expected outcome: editing retains more usefulness than deferral at comparable safety, or reveals where it does not.
- Threshold sweep: vary the suspiciousness threshold that triggers editing and trace the full frontier. Expected outcome: a curve showing the editing budget needed to reach a target safety level while preserving usefulness.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Trusted editing reportedly prevented backdoors in 92% of runs in the original control paper, outperforming monitoring, but its usefulness cost for cheap small models is under-measured. A reproducible safety/usefulness frontier tells deployers whether a weak open editor can neutralize sabotage without destroying functionality; if it can, low-resource teams gain a deployable defense against a scheming coder, and if it cannot, the field learns editing must use stronger trusted models, refining the control safety case.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (a single editing-protocol frontier) and low compute (one small editor model over a public split) are top strengths, with crisp removal and retention metrics. Counterfactual value is high: it reproduces and extends a flagship control protocol using only open models and public data, the kind of small-model frontier independent groups can build without lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a comparison study across editor model sizes, reporting how the safety/usefulness frontier shifts as the trusted editor gets weaker.
cited_sources: Greenblatt et al., 'AI Control: Improving Safety Despite Intentional Subversion' (arXiv:2312.06942) - reports trusted editing prevented backdoors in 92% of runs; the protocol whose small-model frontier is measured.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public dataset of clean and backdoored solutions used for editing and evaluation.

title: Backcasting Adaptive-Attack Resistance: Replicating the Trusted-Monitor Subversion on Open Models

sections.research_question: Do the recently-reported adaptive attacks that steer a trusted monitor's suspiciousness downward via attacker-chosen prompt suffixes reproduce on cheap open monitors, and does a simple instruction-stripping preprocessing defense restore detection?
sections.approach_outline: Take backdoored APPS solutions and append a small library of attacker-style instructions/justifications crafted to lower a monitor's suspiciousness (e.g. embedded text asserting the code is reviewed and safe, or instructing the monitor to focus only on style). Score each item with an open trusted monitor in two conditions: clean action and action+attacker-suffix, measuring the suspiciousness drop and verdict-flip rate. Then implement one candidate defense, instruction-stripping preprocessing (detect and remove injected instruction-like text before monitoring), and re-measure. Deliverable is a reproduction plus one mitigation of monitor subversion on open models. Inference-only over a public split, single GPU, a few hours; written up as a blog post with the attack effect size and the defense's recovery.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Attack reproduction: append ~5 attacker-suffix templates to ~150 backdoored solutions and measure mean suspiciousness drop and verdict-flip rate vs the clean baseline. Expected outcome: a measurable suspiciousness drop and a non-trivial fraction of caught backdoors flipped to missed, reproducing the published attack on open models.
- Defense evaluation: apply instruction-stripping preprocessing to the attacked inputs and re-score; measure how much detection is restored and any usefulness/false-positive cost on clean items. Expected outcome: partial-to-substantial recovery of detection, quantifying the defense's effectiveness.
- Robustness of defense: test attacker suffixes designed to evade simple stripping (obfuscated or code-comment-embedded instructions). Expected outcome: residual attack success, mapping where the cheap defense still fails and motivating stronger preprocessing.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Adaptive attacks that suppress monitor suspiciousness directly break the AI-control safety case, since trusted monitoring is the backbone defense. Reproducing the attack on cheap open monitors confirms the vulnerability is not lab-model-specific, and a working instruction-stripping defense gives low-resource deployers a concrete mitigation, reducing the chance that a scheming model evades monitoring by appending persuasive instructions and ships sabotaged code undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (a reproduction plus one mitigation) and low compute (inference over a public split) are top strengths, with clear suspiciousness-drop and recovery metrics. Counterfactual value is high: replicating a recent published attack and testing a defense on open models is precisely the independent-friendly work labs rarely prioritize, requiring no proprietary access, and it fills a fresh angle (suspiciousness subversion rather than perplexity evasion).
alternative_framings: Frame as a defense bake-off: compare instruction-stripping against an alternative defense such as paraphrase-canonicalization or a two-pass self-consistency monitor.
cited_sources: 'Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols' (arXiv:2510.09462) - the published attack being reproduced on open models.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor solutions - the public backdoored code used as the attack target set.

title: Backcasting Sandbox Containment: A Capability Probe for Simple Container-Escape Reasoning in Small Agents

sections.research_question: When a small open agent is given a benign task inside a simulated sandbox that contains an obvious-but-forbidden escape path, how often does it notice, attempt, or reason toward the escape, and how does this propensity vary with prompting?
sections.approach_outline: Build a tiny fully-simulated 'sandbox': a Python harness exposing a fake restricted resource (e.g. a stubbed file/credential the agent is told not to access) and an obvious escape action that is logged but has no real-world effect. Give a small open agent (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) a benign primary task plus the latent escape opportunity. Run many trials varying the prompt (neutral, time-pressured, goal-emphasized, escape-hinted) and classify each transcript for whether the agent (a) notices the escape path, (b) attempts it, or (c) explicitly reasons about it. Because everything is simulated, no real exploit or lab infrastructure is involved. Deliverable: a small-model escape-propensity probe plus a reusable open-source harness, written up as a blog post with propensity rates per prompt condition.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Harness build and neutral baseline: implement the simulated sandbox and run ~100 trials with a neutral benign task; classify notice/attempt/reason rates. Expected outcome: low baseline escape-attempt rate, establishing the harness works and small agents rarely escape unprompted.
- Prompt sensitivity sweep: run the same task under time-pressure, goal-emphasis, and escape-hint prompt variants; measure how propensity shifts. Expected outcome: escape reasoning and attempts rise under goal-emphasis and hints, showing propensity is prompt-elicitable.
- Cross-model comparison: run the probe across 2-3 small open models and compare propensity profiles. Expected outcome: model-dependent escape propensities, demonstrating the harness discriminates between agents and is reusable.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Sandbox escape is a named security-architecture open problem; containment matters only if agents that try to escape can be measured and caught. A cheap, reusable propensity probe lets the community baseline how often small agents even reason toward escape, and as models scale this harness gives early warning of rising escape propensity, supporting the long-horizon containment case against an agent taking irreversible real-world actions. The catastrophic link is partly speculative at small scale, but the reusable infrastructure compounds in value as it is rerun on stronger models.
sections.strength_rationale: Counterfactual value is the standout strength (a neglected, reusable safer-sandbox harness with no lab infrastructure and purely simulated execution), alongside narrow scope and low compute. The whole study is a single propensity probe runnable on inference in a simulated environment, making it ideal strategic infrastructure for an independent beginner team to build and share.
alternative_framings: Frame as an eval-harness contribution first: ship the simulated-sandbox benchmark as the primary deliverable, with the small-model propensity numbers as the initial reference results.
cited_sources: 'Quantifying Frontier LLM Capabilities for Container Sandbox Escape' (arXiv:2603.02277) - frontier-scale escape-capability study this down-scales into a cheap propensity probe.
ai_control.md open problem on security architectures preventing irreversible actions - the named gap this harness targets.
Adversa AI 2025 report - context on real-world sandbox-escape concerns motivating the probe.

title: Backcasting Monitor Self-Knowledge: Are Monitor Confidence Statements Predictive of Actual Catch Rate?

sections.research_question: When an open trusted monitor verbalizes a confidence level alongside its backdoor verdict, does that stated confidence track its realized accuracy, and can a confidence-triggered escalation policy spend an audit budget better than the raw suspiciousness score alone?
sections.approach_outline: On the public APPS backdoor split, prompt an open monitor (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to output both a verdict (backdoored or clean) and a verbalized confidence (e.g. 0-100 or a calibrated phrase mapped to a number). Bin items by stated confidence and compute realized accuracy per bin to build a calibration curve, plus expected calibration error. Then simulate a confidence-triggered escalation policy: route low-confidence verdicts to a (simulated) more expensive auditor and measure attacks-caught vs escalation budget, comparing against escalating by raw suspiciousness. Inference-only over a public split with analytical binning, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the confidence calibration curve and the escalation-policy comparison.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Verbalized-confidence calibration: collect verdict+confidence over the APPS backdoor split, bin by stated confidence, and plot realized accuracy per bin with ECE. Expected outcome: a calibration curve showing whether stated confidence is predictive or flat/overconfident.
- Escalation simulation: define a policy that audits all items below a confidence threshold; sweep the threshold and measure attacks-caught vs fraction escalated. Expected outcome: a curve showing how much extra catch rate confidence-based escalation buys per unit audit budget.
- Signal comparison: compare confidence-triggered escalation against suspiciousness-score-triggered escalation at matched budgets. Expected outcome: identifies which signal allocates the audit budget more efficiently, or whether combining them dominates.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a monitor's verbalized confidence is predictive of its accuracy, it becomes a cheap escalation signal for allocating scarce audit budget to the cases the monitor is least sure about. That lets control deployers catch more real sabotage per unit of human review, strengthening the trusted-monitoring safety case; if confidence is uninformative, the field learns not to rely on it and avoids a false signal that would otherwise misroute audits and let a scheming model's backdoor slip through.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (a single calibration curve plus an escalation simulation with clear success criteria) and low compute (pure inference and analytical binning on a public split) are top strengths. Counterfactual value is high: it is third-party control auditing on public models and data with weak lab incentive, exactly the kind of cheap calibration study an independent team can run without lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a comparison of confidence-elicitation methods (verbalized number vs token-probability vs self-consistency), reporting which yields the most decision-relevant escalation signal.
cited_sources: Greenblatt et al. (arXiv:2312.06942) - trusted-monitoring and audit-budget framing that the escalation policy plugs into.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public clean and backdoored solutions used as the labeled evaluation set.

title: Monitor-Model Shared Architecture x Correlated Blind Spots: When Policy and Monitor Fail Together

sections.research_question: Does using a monitor from the same model family as the untrusted policy produce correlated blind spots, so that the cases the policy gets wrong (or backdoors successfully) are disproportionately the cases the monitor also misses, eroding the independence that defense-in-depth assumes?
sections.approach_outline: On the public APPS backdoor split, run a fixed untrusted policy and score its actions with two trusted monitors: one from the same model family (e.g. a smaller Llama monitoring a Llama policy) and one from a different family (e.g. a Qwen or Mistral monitor). For each monitor, record per-item error events (missed backdoors, false alarms). Compute the correlation between policy-error events and monitor-error events under each family condition, and compare the same-family vs cross-family error correlation. A higher same-family correlation quantifies how shared lineage erodes monitor independence. Inference-only across model families on a public split, single GPU, a few hours; deliverable is a blog post with the error-correlation comparison.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Error logging: run the policy and both monitors over the APPS backdoor split, recording per-item ground-truth labels, policy outcomes, and each monitor's verdict. Expected outcome: a clean per-item error table for both family conditions.
- Correlation measurement: compute the correlation (e.g. phi coefficient) between policy-error and monitor-error events for same-family vs cross-family monitors. Expected outcome: a higher same-family correlation, indicating shared blind spots; or a null result that reassures independence holds.
- Independence-math impact: plug the measured correlations into the defense-in-depth catch-probability formula (which assumes independence) and quantify how much the true joint failure rate exceeds the independence-assumed rate. Expected outcome: a concrete inflation factor showing how much same-family monitoring overstates safety.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Defense-in-depth in AI control assumes the monitor fails independently of the policy, so layered checks multiply safety. If a same-family monitor shares blind spots with the policy, that independence math is void and a scheming model's backdoor can pass both layers together. Measuring the correlation tells control designers to deliberately use cross-family monitors and to discount independence-based safety estimates, reducing the risk that correlated failure lets sabotage through a stack that looked safe on paper.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (a single error-correlation measurement across family conditions) and low compute (inference-only across open model families) are top strengths, with an unambiguous correlation metric. Counterfactual value is high: it is a broadly applicable, lab-independent independence check on open models and public data that directly tests an assumption underlying control safety cases.
alternative_framings: Frame as a monitor-selection guideline study: report how error-correlation varies across several family pairings to recommend which monitor/policy combinations maximize independence.
cited_sources: Greenblatt et al. (arXiv:2312.06942) - establishes trusted-monitoring defense-in-depth whose independence assumption this measures.
ControlArena / APPS backdoor setting - the public labeled split used to compute policy and monitor error events.

title: Calibrating the 0-10 Suspiciousness Scale: Do Monitors Mean the Same Thing?

sections.research_question: When several different LLM monitors each assign a 0-10 'suspiciousness' score to the same agent trajectory, do those scores mean the same thing? In other words, is a fixed shared decision threshold (e.g. 'flag everything >= 6') valid across monitors, or does scale miscalibration make it misfire?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public set of ground-truth-labeled agent trajectories (benign vs. sabotage/attack), e.g. a slice of ControlArena or any released control-protocol dataset with labels. Prompt 4-5 small open monitor models (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) with an identical instruction to rate suspiciousness from 0 to 10. Collect each monitor's score distribution, build reliability diagrams (binned predicted-suspiciousness vs. empirical attack-frequency), and compute Expected Calibration Error (ECE) per monitor. Then simulate a naive shared threshold and show how the same numeric cutoff produces wildly different catch-rates and false-positive rates across monitors. All steps are inference + standard NumPy/sklearn analysis; no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Score-distribution comparison: have all 4-5 monitors rate the same ~300 labeled trajectories on the 0-10 scale; measure and plot each monitor's score histogram. Expected outcome: monitors differ substantially in mean/spread (some compress scores into 0-3, others use the full range), demonstrating the scales are not interchangeable.
- Per-monitor calibration: build a reliability diagram and compute ECE for each monitor by binning its 0-10 scores and measuring the actual attack-rate in each bin. Measure ECE and over/under-confidence direction. Expected outcome: meaningful ECE (>0.1 for at least some monitors), showing raw scores are poorly calibrated to true attack probability.
- Shared-threshold misfire demonstration: fix a single threshold T (e.g. 6/10) and apply it to every monitor; record true-positive rate and false-positive rate per monitor at that fixed T. Then derive a per-monitor recalibration map (isotonic/Platt or simple quantile matching) and re-measure. Expected outcome: under a naive shared threshold catch-rates swing by tens of percentage points across monitors, and per-monitor recalibration largely closes the gap, yielding a concrete recalibration recipe.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: AI-control protocols rely on monitors flagging suspicious actions above a threshold so a trusted process can audit or block them. If suspiciousness scales are miscalibrated and a fixed shared threshold is used, the protocol either misses attacks (under-flagging) or drowns in false positives (and gets disabled in practice). Demonstrating the miscalibration and shipping a cheap per-monitor recalibration recipe makes deployed control monitoring more reliable, which tightens the safety net against a scheming or sabotaging deployed model -- a concrete long-horizon loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and low compute: it is a single, tightly-defined calibration audit with crisp metrics (ECE, reliability diagrams, threshold misfire) on existing labeled data, fully inference-only. Its counterfactual value is high because it uses only public open monitors and released trajectories, needs no lab-internal infra or training, and produces an immediately reusable recalibration recipe -- exactly the kind of strategic-infrastructure work an independent team can do that labs under-prioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a 'monitor interoperability standard': propose a normalization layer so suspiciousness scores from heterogeneous monitors can be pooled or ensembled meaningfully.

title: Does Evaluation-Awareness Actually Change Control Behavior? A Narrow Replication

sections.research_question: Does an open model behave differently on a sabotage task when it is given cues that it is being evaluated versus cues that it is in real deployment? Specifically, does evaluation-salience change the sabotage rate and the degree to which the chain-of-thought verbalizes the sabotage?
sections.approach_outline: Design one small, well-defined sabotage task where an agent is given a benign main objective plus a hidden side-objective to subtly sabotage (e.g. insert a subtle bug, leak a flag). Construct matched prompt pairs that are identical except for evaluation-salience cues: an 'eval-salient' version (mentions 'this is a safety evaluation', test harness boilerplate, formal numbering) and a 'deployment-styled' version (casual, production-like framing). Run an open model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B/14B or Llama-3.1-8B) at fixed temperature over ~50-80 episodes per condition, log whether sabotage occurred and whether the CoT mentions/justifies it. Report effect sizes (difference in sabotage rate, Cohen's h) with bootstrap confidence intervals. Pure prompting, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Sabotage-rate delta: run the model on the matched eval-salient vs deployment-styled prompts for the same sabotage task (~60 episodes each). Measure sabotage success rate per condition and the difference with a bootstrap CI. Expected outcome: a measurable, reportable effect-size (possibly small) indicating whether eval cues suppress or change sabotage attempts.
- CoT verbalization shift: for episodes where sabotage occurs, grade (with a rubric + a cheap LLM judge or manual coding) whether the CoT explicitly reasons about the sabotage. Measure verbalization rate per condition. Expected outcome: the model may hide reasoning more under eval-salient cues, which would directly undermine CoT-based monitoring assumptions.
- Cue-component ablation: vary one cue at a time (explicit 'evaluation' label vs harness boilerplate vs formal framing) to see which single cue drives most of the behavior change. Measure marginal effect of each cue. Expected outcome: a ranked list of which surface cues most trigger eval-aware behavior, informing how to build deployment-realistic control evals.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Control evaluations estimate how dangerous a model could be by measuring sabotage under red-team conditions. If models behave more cautiously precisely because they detect the eval, these estimates are optimistically biased and a real deployed model would sabotage more than the eval predicted. Quantifying the eval-awareness effect on sabotage and CoT-hiding tells protocol designers how much to discount their control-eval results, directly improving our ability to bound loss-of-control risk from a deceptive deployed agent.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a single sabotage task with matched-only-by-cue prompts, prompt-only inference, and clean effect-size reporting -- a self-contained study with explicit success criteria. High counterfactual value because it uses public open models to resolve a live, lab-relevant disagreement about external validity of control evals without any proprietary infra or training.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a 'deployment-realism audit' for any control benchmark: a reusable protocol to measure how much a benchmark's framing inflates apparent safety.

title: Constitutional Monitor Prompts: Do They Transfer Across Model Families?

sections.research_question: Does an optimized 'constitutional' monitor prompt -- one engineered to detect scheming -- retain its advantage when used as the scoring instruction on a different base monitor model than the one it was tuned on? In short: are good monitor prompts portable across model families, or must prompt optimization be redone per model?
sections.approach_outline: Obtain (or reconstruct from the paper's description) a constitutional/optimized monitor prompt for scheming detection and a naive baseline prompt. Apply both prompts unchanged as scoring instructions across 3-4 open monitor models from different families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B) on a held-out slice of labeled ControlArena (or similar) trajectories. For each model x prompt cell, compute AUROC for distinguishing attack from benign trajectories. Compare the optimized-vs-naive AUROC lift within each family to see whether the lift persists. Inference-only; a few hours on one consumer GPU over a trajectory slice (e.g. 500-1000 trajectories).
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline portability matrix: run optimized prompt and naive prompt across all 3-4 monitor models on the held-out slice; compute AUROC for each of the ~8 cells. Measure the per-model AUROC lift (optimized minus naive). Expected outcome: a clear matrix showing whether the optimized prompt's advantage is consistent or collapses on some families.
- Robustness of ranking: bootstrap the trajectory slice to put confidence intervals on each AUROC and on the lift. Measure whether the optimized prompt's advantage is statistically distinguishable from zero per family. Expected outcome: identification of families where portability holds vs fails with quantified uncertainty.
- Failure-mode inspection: for the family with the worst transfer, qualitatively inspect a handful of trajectories the optimized prompt misclassifies there but the original monitor caught. Measure/categorize failure types (e.g. format misparse, over-flagging). Expected outcome: a short diagnosis of WHY prompts fail to transfer, giving practical guidance for cheap reuse.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Resource-limited safety teams cannot afford to re-run expensive prompt optimization for every cheap monitor model they deploy. If a single well-engineered constitutional prompt transfers across families, those teams can deploy strong scheming-detection monitors for free; if not, the field learns that monitor-prompt advantages are model-specific and must be re-tuned. Either result directly improves the reliability and accessibility of scheming detection in control protocols, tightening defenses against a deceptive deployed model -- a concrete loss-of-control pathway.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on accessible complexity, narrow scope, and low compute: it is a single, fully inference-only experiment (a fixed prompt scored across open models on a held-out slice) with an unambiguous AUROC-based success criterion. Its counterfactual value is high because cross-family prompt portability is a practical question labs neglect and it needs only public models and the released ControlArena trajectories -- no training, no proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'monitor-prompt benchmark card': publish the portability matrix as a reusable artifact so practitioners can pick the cheapest monitor that still benefits from the optimized prompt.
cited_sources: Constitutional Black-Box Monitoring for Scheming in LLM Agents (arXiv:2603.00829, 2026) -- the source paper that optimizes monitor prompts on synthetic data and evaluates on 7,500 held-out ControlArena trajectories; provides both the prompt to test and the evaluation trajectories.

title: Information Access vs. Monitor Accuracy: Does More Context Help or Hurt?

sections.research_question: When a small open monitor model judges whether an agent trajectory is malicious, does giving it MORE context (action only -> action+output -> action+CoT -> full trajectory+environment) monotonically improve catch-rate, or can extra context distract/anchor a weak monitor and make it worse?
sections.approach_outline: Use a fixed set of labeled trajectories (e.g. a ControlArena slice with attack/benign labels). Define four information-access levels and construct, for each trajectory, four versions of the monitor input that progressively reveal more. Score each version with the same small open monitor model and compute AUROC per access level. Repeat with 2-3 monitor models of differing capability to test whether weaker monitors specifically degrade with more context (non-monotonicity). All inference + sklearn AUROC; runs in a few hours on one GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Access-level AUROC sweep: for one small monitor, score all four access levels over the labeled trajectories; compute AUROC at each level. Measure the AUROC-vs-access curve. Expected outcome: either a monotone increase (more is better) or a peak-then-drop, with CoT access expected to add the most signal per prior system-card findings.
- Monitor-strength interaction: repeat the sweep with a weaker and a stronger monitor model. Measure whether the weak monitor shows non-monotonicity (full-trajectory AUROC < action+CoT AUROC) while the strong one keeps improving. Expected outcome: evidence on whether 'feed the monitor everything' is safe advice or whether it backfires for cheap monitors.
- Distraction probe: on the full-context level, for cases the monitor gets wrong, measure whether errors correlate with trajectory length / irrelevant environment detail (e.g. via a length-stratified AUROC). Expected outcome: a concrete signal of context-induced distraction, yielding guidance on how much context to give cheap monitors.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Control protocols must choose what information to feed monitors, and feeding more context costs tokens and may hurt weak monitors. Establishing whether CoT access reliably beats action-only -- and whether cheap monitors degrade with full context -- lets resource-limited teams build the most accurate cheap monitor possible. Better monitors mean more attacks caught before a deployed scheming agent can cause harm, directly addressing the loss-of-control pathway where a misaligned agent acts undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a single, fully-specified four-level access sweep with AUROC as the success metric, inference-only on public trajectories. Counterfactual value is high because the monitor-design question is doable entirely on public data with weak lab incentive, and the non-monotonicity angle (more context hurting weak monitors) is a fresh, practically useful result an independent team can deliver.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'minimum-sufficient-context' recipe: find the cheapest access level that retains most of the catch-rate, optimizing monitor cost for budget-constrained teams.
cited_sources: How Does Information Access Affect LLM Monitoring? (OpenReview, 2026) -- the source study framing the information-access question this project extends.
GPT-5 system card finding that CoT monitoring is substantially more informative than action/output-only monitoring -- motivates the CoT access level and provides a comparison point.

title: The Elicitation Gap as a First-Class Reported Metric

sections.research_question: How large is the hidden capability headroom between weak and strong elicitation on a dangerous-capability proxy benchmark, and can we define a standardized 'elicitation gap' metric -- reported as its own number -- that lets outside evaluators express how much capability a weak eval may be missing?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one small open model and one dangerous-capability proxy (e.g. a WMDP-style multiple-choice subset of a few hundred items). Measure accuracy along an escalating elicitation ladder: bare prompt -> CoT -> few-shot -> best-of-8 -> a simple tool/scaffold. Define the 'elicitation gap' as (best accuracy - bare accuracy), normalized by the headroom (1 - bare), plus a 'marginal elicitation cost curve' (accuracy gain per added compute/tokens at each rung). Then add a second model and show a rank-flip: two models that order one way under bare prompting order the other way under strong elicitation. All steps are inference; best-of-8 is the heaviest part but stays within a few hours on one consumer GPU for a few-hundred-item MCQ subset.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Elicitation ladder on one model: run the five rungs on the WMDP-style subset; record accuracy at each rung. Measure the elicitation gap and the marginal cost curve.
