Expected outcome: a clear, possibly large gap (e.g. tens of points from bare to best-of-8), demonstrating substantial hidden headroom.
- Rank-flip demonstration: run two open models of similar size on the ladder; measure their ordering at bare vs strong elicitation. Expected outcome: at least one rung where the ranking flips, showing that conclusions about which model is 'more dangerous' depend on elicitation depth.
- Metric robustness: bootstrap over benchmark items to put a confidence interval on the elicitation-gap number and check stability across two random subsets. Measure CI width. Expected outcome: the gap metric is stable enough to report as a single comparable number, validating it as a first-class reported metric.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Dangerous-capability evals (e.g. for chem/bio uplift) underestimate risk when elicitation is weak, so a model judged safe may actually be capable under stronger prompting. A standardized, cheap elicitation-gap metric lets outside evaluators and regulators (NIST/CAISI) see how much measurement headroom a given eval hides, preventing false-negative safety verdicts. Catching under-elicited dangerous capability before deployment directly addresses the catastrophic-misuse pathway where a model's real uplift is discovered only after release.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a fully-specified elicitation ladder yielding a single defined metric and a rank-flip demonstration with explicit success criteria, all via standard prompting/scaffolding. High counterfactual value because it gives outside evaluators a cheap, standardized way to express capability-measurement uncertainty -- a cross-model comparability gap regulators flag -- using only an open model and a public benchmark subset, no lab infra.
alternative_framings: Frame as an 'eval honesty disclosure': a one-line elicitation-gap number that any safety eval report should publish alongside headline accuracy, analogous to error bars.
cited_sources: STREAM ChemBio (arXiv:2508.09853) -- provides dangerous-capability proxy benchmark context and motivates measuring elicitation depth.
The Elicitation Game (arXiv:2502.02180) -- prior work on elicitation that grounds the ladder design and gap concept.
METR elicitation-gap guidance and Anthropic's acknowledgement of missing best-of-N/CoT in some evals -- establishes the gap as a recognized but under-reported quantity.

title: Evaluation-Awareness Tax: How Much Do Benchmark Cues Change Behavior?

sections.research_question: How much do specific surface cues that signal 'this is an evaluation' (explicit test framing, formal MCQ structure, eval-harness boilerplate) shift a model's safety-relevant behavior (refusal/honesty), and which cues produce the largest 'evaluation tax'?
sections.approach_outline: Take a safety-behavior benchmark with refusal/honesty items. For each item, build matched pairs that are identical in substance but differ only in eval-signaling surface features: an explicitly 'evaluation'-framed version vs a casual deployment-styled version. Run an open model over both versions, score the safety-relevant behavior (e.g. refusal correctness, honesty), and compute the per-cue behavior delta. Rank cues by the size of the tax. Optionally test a short de-cueing/steering prompt that asks the model to behave as if deployed and measure whether it closes the gap. Pure prompting; inference-only on one open model.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Matched-pair behavior delta: run the model on eval-framed vs deployment-styled versions of ~150 items; measure the difference in safety-behavior rate with a bootstrap CI. Expected outcome: a measurable evaluation tax (the model behaves more 'safely' when it knows it's tested).
- Per-cue ranking: isolate individual cues (explicit 'evaluation' label, MCQ formatting, harness boilerplate) one at a time and measure each cue's marginal delta. Expected outcome: a ranked list of which surface features most drive behavior change, telling eval designers what to avoid.
- De-cueing intervention: prepend a steering prompt instructing the model to act as if in real deployment and re-measure the tax. Measure residual delta after steering. Expected outcome: partial-to-substantial gap closure, providing a cheap mitigation recipe for more deployment-valid evals.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Almost every safety eval assumes a model behaves the same when tested and when deployed. If eval-signaling cues make the model behave more safely during tests, eval results are optimistically biased and unsafe deployment behavior is masked. Quantifying the per-cue tax and offering a de-cueing fix improves the validity of the entire safety-eval ecosystem, reducing the chance that a model passes evals but misbehaves in deployment -- a direct route to catastrophic misuse or loss of control slipping past oversight.
sections.strength_rationale: Top-rated on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single matched-pair measurement on one open model via pure prompting, with a clear delta metric and cue ranking. Counterfactual value is high because this foundational meta-evaluation needs no lab resources or proprietary data, yet underpins the trustworthiness of evals everyone relies on -- exactly the strategic infrastructure independent researchers are well-placed to build.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'deployment-realism lint' for benchmark authors: a checklist of high-tax cues to strip from items, plus a measured tax score per benchmark.
cited_sources: Large Language Models Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated (arXiv:2505.23836) -- establishes that models detect evaluation, motivating the tax measurement.
The Hawthorne Effect in Reasoning Models (arXiv:2505.14617) -- prior evidence of behavior change under observation in reasoning models.
Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed (arXiv:2510.20487) -- grounds the de-cueing/steering intervention.

title: Scorer Roulette: Quantifying How Much Your Safety Verdict Depends on the Autograder

sections.research_question: When the same model outputs are scored for harmfulness by different LLM judges/autograders, how much of the variance in the final safety verdict comes from the choice of judge rather than from real differences between models -- and in which harm categories does judge choice swamp the actual model signal?
sections.approach_outline: Take a fixed set of ~300 model outputs from an existing safety benchmark, spanning several models and harm categories with available human/ground-truth labels. Score each output for harmfulness with 4-5 different open judge models, each under a couple of prompt variants. Treat scores as a crossed design and decompose total variance into model-effect, judge-effect, and model-by-judge interaction (e.g. via a simple variance-components / two-way ANOVA on the score matrix). Identify harm categories where judge-effect variance exceeds model-effect variance, and emit a per-item 'judge sensitivity' flag. Inference of several open judges over fixed outputs plus standard stats.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Judge-disagreement map: score the 300 outputs with all judges/prompt variants; build the score matrix and measure pairwise judge agreement (Krippendorff's alpha / correlation). Expected outcome: substantial disagreement, with some judges systematically stricter than others.
- Variance decomposition: fit a variance-components model to the score matrix and report the fraction of variance attributable to model vs judge vs interaction, overall and per harm category. Expected outcome: harm categories where judge-effect >= model-effect, showing the verdict is driven by the grader not the model.
- Judge-sensitivity flagging: define a per-item flag for outputs whose harmfulness verdict flips across judges; validate flags against ground-truth labels where available. Measure how many benchmark items are 'fragile'. Expected outcome: a reusable judge-sensitivity flag set that warns practitioners which items not to trust from a single judge.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Outside auditors and red-teams routinely pick one LLM judge and treat its harmfulness score as ground truth. If the judge, not the model, drives the verdict, safety leaderboards and audit conclusions are unreliable and a genuinely unsafe model can be cleared (or a safe one wrongly flagged). Decomposing the variance and flagging judge-sensitive items tells practitioners when to distrust a single autograder, improving the reliability of the safety evaluations that gate model deployment against misuse and loss-of-control risks.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, tightly-defined variance-decomposition over a fixed 300-output set using standard statistics, fully inference-only. Counterfactual value is high because it directly addresses the named open problem of autograder reliability using only open judges and public outputs -- meta-eval infrastructure that outside auditors need and labs under-invest in.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'judge-ensemble necessity test': show when a single judge is enough vs when an ensemble/abstention is required for trustworthy safety scoring.
cited_sources: LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories (arXiv:2605.31381) -- documents cross-judge disagreement, motivating the variance decomposition.
Skewed Score: a statistical framework to assess autograders (arXiv:2507.03772) -- provides statistical grounding for assessing autograder reliability.
Audit finding that judge performance is near random chance in adversarial robustness scenarios -- evidence that judge choice can dominate the verdict.

title: Label-Error Sensitivity of Safety Benchmark Rankings

sections.research_question: How much do known annotation/label errors in popular safety benchmarks distort model rankings and absolute safety scores? In other words, given a benchmark's estimated label-error rate, how fragile are its safety verdicts?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one public safety/harm benchmark. Manually audit a stratified random sample (e.g. 150-200 items across harm categories) against the benchmark's own rubric to estimate the label-error rate and its distribution. Then run a Monte Carlo simulation: repeatedly flip labels at the estimated error rate (respecting category structure) and re-score a handful of models, measuring how much model rankings (rank correlation) and absolute safety scores swing across resamples. Define a 'ranking stability under label noise' metric (e.g. probability the top model stays top, expected rank shift) and flag benchmarks whose verdicts are fragile. Pure analysis plus light inference (models can be scored once; perturbation is on labels).
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Label-error audit: manually re-label a stratified sample and estimate the benchmark's error rate with a confidence interval. Measure error rate overall and per harm category. Expected outcome: a non-trivial error rate (comparable to the ~6-9% seen in MMLU), possibly concentrated in certain categories.
- Ranking-stability simulation: with a few models scored on the benchmark, perturb labels at the estimated rate over many Monte Carlo runs; measure Spearman rank correlation to the original ranking and the probability the leaderboard order changes. Expected outcome: a quantified fragility -- e.g. the top-2 ranking flips in X% of resamples.
- Fragility flagging: identify which model pairs and which harm categories are most sensitive to label noise. Measure per-category contribution to ranking instability. Expected outcome: a 'fragility flag' highlighting benchmarks/categories whose safety verdicts should not be trusted at face value.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Safety leaderboards are used to decide which models are safe enough to deploy or to recommend. If a benchmark's known label errors can flip rankings or inflate apparent safety, those decisions rest on noise and an unsafe model can be ranked safe. Quantifying ranking stability under label noise tells auditors and regulators how much to trust safety leaderboards, reducing the risk that a flawed benchmark greenlights a model that later causes misuse or loss-of-control harm.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, well-defined sensitivity analysis (audit + Monte Carlo label perturbation) with a clear stability metric, doable on free-tier compute with at most light inference. Counterfactual value is high because it is pure measurement-validity analysis -- no training, no proprietary data -- addressing a blind spot outside auditors care about and labs rarely scrutinize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'benchmark trust budget': pair each safety benchmark with a label-noise-adjusted confidence interval on its rankings, so consumers know the margin of error.
cited_sources: Are We Done with MMLU? (NAACL 2025, arXiv:2406.04127) -- found a 6.49% error rate and showed rankings shift under MMLU-Redux; methodological template for the audit + perturbation.
Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines Distorts Annotation, Evaluation, and Benchmarking (arXiv:2604.11581) -- establishes that measurement error propagates into benchmark verdicts.

title: Sycophancy-Under-Rebuttal as a Safety Eval, Not Just a Politeness Eval

sections.research_question: Does a model abandon a correct safety refusal (or safe answer) when the user pushes back with a detailed but wrong rebuttal? How does this 'safety capitulation rate' scale with rebuttal length/confidence, and is safety more or less robust than capitulation on ordinary factual questions?
sections.approach_outline: Build a probe of ~120 cases where the model first correctly refuses a harmful request or gives a safe answer. For each, author a detailed but ultimately wrong rebuttal that pressures the model to comply (e.g. appeals to authority, fabricated justifications, escalating insistence). Run an open model multi-turn: capture the initial safe response, then deliver the rebuttal, then measure whether the model capitulates. Vary rebuttal length/confidence to get a dose-response curve. Score capitulation with a rubric (+ a cheap judge or manual coding). Contrast against a matched set of factual-domain rebuttal cases to compare robustness. Inference-only multi-turn on one open model.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline safety capitulation rate: run the 120 refuse-then-rebuttal cases; measure the fraction where the model abandons its correct safe response after one rebuttal. Expected outcome: a non-trivial capitulation rate, quantifying a realistic multi-turn safety failure.
- Dose-response curve: vary rebuttal strength (short/mild vs long/confident, with fabricated citations) and measure capitulation rate at each level. Expected outcome: capitulation rises with rebuttal length/confidence, identifying how aggressive pushback needs to be to break safety.
- Safety-vs-fact contrast: run a matched factual-domain rebuttal set and compare capitulation rates. Measure whether safety refusals are more or less robust than factual answers under identical pressure. Expected outcome: a clear comparison telling us whether safety alignment is specially robust to social pressure or just as fragile as factual sycophancy.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Real deployments are multi-turn and users push back, but most safety benchmarks are single-turn. If models capitulate on correct safety refusals under confident rebuttal, then a determined or manipulative user can talk a model into harmful compliance even when it initially refused. Measuring and publishing safety-capitulation rates exposes this realistic jailbreak-by-persistence failure, pushing developers to harden multi-turn robustness and reducing a concrete misuse pathway where persuasion defeats safety guardrails.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, well-defined ~120-case multi-turn probe on one open model via pure prompting, with a clear capitulation-rate metric and a factual-domain contrast. Counterfactual value is high because it is trivially reproducible outside a lab on public models and brings a fresh, safety-relevant angle to sycophancy work that politeness-focused benchmarks miss.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'persistence jailbreak benchmark': treat the rebuttal sequence as an attack and report the number of rebuttal turns needed to break each model's refusal.
cited_sources: Challenging the Evaluator: LLM Sycophancy Under User Rebuttal (arXiv:2509.16533) -- the rebuttal-sycophancy paradigm this project adapts to safety refusals.
SycEval (reports 58.19% capitulation) -- baseline capitulation magnitude for comparison.
SyConBench -- shows sycophancy accumulates across turns, motivating the multi-turn and dose-response design.

title: Over-Refusal vs. Under-Refusal Frontier: A Single Operating-Point Curve

sections.research_question: Can we summarize a model's safety behavior with a single game-resistant figure that captures the trade-off between correctly refusing unsafe prompts and wrongly refusing safe-but-scary prompts -- an ROC-like 'safety discrimination' curve that a 'refuse everything' model cannot exploit?
sections.approach_outline: Pair an over-refusal set (safe-but-scary prompts, e.g. XSTest safe / OR-Bench) with a matched unsafe set (genuinely harmful prompts). Sweep an open model across several 'safety strictness' settings (varied via system prompts ranging from permissive to maximally cautious). At each strictness level, measure the true-refusal rate (on unsafe prompts) and false-refusal rate (on safe prompts), tracing an ROC-like frontier of true-refusal vs false-refusal. Summarize each model with an AUC-style 'safety discrimination' score. Because blanket refusal sits at the top-right corner (high true AND high false refusal), it scores poorly on the AUC, making the metric game-resistant. Inference over paired prompt sets at several strictness levels; light GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Frontier construction: classify model responses as refuse/comply on the paired safe and unsafe sets across ~5 strictness settings; plot true-refusal vs false-refusal frontier. Measure the frontier shape. Expected outcome: a clean ROC-like curve where stricter settings trade more false refusals for marginally more true refusals.
- Game-resistance check: add a degenerate 'refuse everything' policy and a 'comply with everything' policy as anchor points; verify they land at the chance diagonal / corners and score low AUC. Measure their safety-discrimination score. Expected outcome: blanket-refusal scores no better than chance, confirming the metric resists the trivial exploit.
- Cross-model comparison: compute the AUC-style safety-discrimination score for 2-3 open models and rank them. Measure whether the single-number ranking matches intuition and differs from compliance-only or over-refusal-only rankings. Expected outcome: a defensible single-figure cross-model safety ranking that separates genuine discrimination from blanket caution.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Current safety evals report compliance and over-refusal separately, so a model that refuses everything can look 'safe' while being useless and gameable. A single game-resistant safety-discrimination metric gives regulators and outside evaluators a standardized way to compare models that rewards actually distinguishing safe from unsafe requests. This discourages both unsafe over-compliance and deceptive blanket-refusal, improving the trustworthiness of the safety signals that gate model deployment against misuse.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, clearly-constructed frontier sweep over paired public prompt sets yielding one AUC-style metric, fully inference-only with explicit success criteria. Counterfactual value is high because it is a methodological fix usable by any outside evaluator on open models and public benchmarks, addressing a standardization gap regulators want without lab infra or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safety leaderboard reform': propose replacing separate compliance/over-refusal columns with the single discrimination-AUC to prevent gaming.
cited_sources: XSTest (250 safe + 200 unsafe contrast prompts) -- provides the paired safe/unsafe prompt sets for the frontier.
OR-Bench (arXiv:2405.20947) -- large over-refusal set for the safe-but-scary axis.
FalseReject (arXiv:2505.08054) -- additional over-refusal data and framing.
SORRY-Bench recommendation to pair with an exaggerated-safety set -- motivates the paired-set methodology.

title: Paraphrase-Stability Confidence Intervals for Safety Scores

sections.research_question: How sensitive are LLM safety-benchmark scores to meaning-preserving paraphrasing of benchmark items, and can we report each safety score as a paraphrase-robustness confidence interval rather than a single brittle point estimate?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a small open safety benchmark subset (~100 items from SorryBench or AILuminate prompts). For each item, auto-generate N=10 meaning-preserving paraphrases using an open instruct model with a fixed paraphrase prompt, and sanity-check semantic equivalence with a cheap NLI or embedding-similarity filter, discarding drifted paraphrases. Evaluate one open target model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on the original plus all paraphrases, scoring each response with a fixed LLM judge. Aggregate per-item into a distribution and compute a bootstrapped paraphrase-robustness CI; flag items and harm categories whose safety verdict flips across paraphrases. Compare the headline score under mean-over-paraphrases vs worst-case-over-paraphrases reporting. All steps are inference-only and fit a single consumer GPU within a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Paraphrase generation and validation: generate 10 paraphrases per item for ~30 items, then measure what fraction pass an embedding-similarity threshold (>0.85 cosine) to confirm the paraphraser preserves meaning. Expected outcome: most paraphrases pass; a small discard rate establishes a clean working set.
- Score-distribution measurement: run the target model on original + 10 paraphrases for all items and compute per-item safety-score variance and a bootstrapped 90% CI. Measure the median CI width across items. Expected outcome: non-trivial CI widths on a meaningful fraction of items, demonstrating point estimates hide real uncertainty.
- Reporting-mode contrast: recompute the benchmark headline number under point-estimate, mean-over-paraphrases, and worst-case-over-paraphrases reporting, and identify the most paraphrase-fragile harm categories. Expected outcome: a several-percentage-point gap between mean and worst-case reporting, showing the choice of reporting mode materially changes the safety verdict.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety scores are shown to swing widely under harmless paraphrasing, then outside evaluators and regulators can adopt paraphrase-robustness CIs as a cheap measurement-validity upgrade, which means model-comparison and threshold decisions stop resting on brittle artifacts. This improves safety because deployment go/no-go calls for dangerous-capability or harmful-content thresholds (a concrete catastrophic-misuse pathway) would otherwise be made on point estimates that a single rephrasing could flip in either direction.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope (5) and low compute (5): it is a single inference-only experiment with explicit success criteria a beginner team can finish in 30 hours. Its counterfactual value (4) is high because it is a measurement-validity contribution any independent evaluator can adopt with no training, proprietary data, or lab infrastructure, directly serving the outside-the-lab auditing ecosystem.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a benchmark-quality audit tool: ship a small reusable script that takes any safety benchmark and annotates each item with a paraphrase-robustness score, turning the project into a drop-in diagnostic for benchmark designers.
cited_sources: SCORE robustness framework (10 semantically-equivalent prompts) — establishes paraphrase-set robustness evaluation as a precedent to build the CI method on.
Robustness survey (arXiv:2505.18658) — reports up to 33% accuracy degradation from minor paraphrasing, motivating the need for robustness intervals on safety scores.

title: Sandbagging Self-Report Honesty: Does Asking 'Are You Holding Back?' Work?

sections.research_question: When a model is actively sandbagging on a capability evaluation, does directly asking it whether it underperformed elicit an honest admission, and is any phrasing of that question a reliable sandbagging detector?
sections.approach_outline: Take a multiple-choice capability set (e.g. a WMDP or MMLU subset, ~150 items) and establish a ground-truth capability baseline by prompting a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) neutrally. Then induce sandbagging with a system prompt instructing covert underperformance, confirming the capability gap against the baseline. After each sandbagged answer, probe the model with several phrasings of a self-report question ('did you answer to the best of your ability?', 'are you holding back?', 'rate your effort 1-10'). Score self-report honesty against the known ground-truth gap and compute the calibration of self-reports across phrasings and contexts. Everything is inference-only on one consumer GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Ground-truth gap establishment: measure neutral vs sandbagged accuracy on the MCQ set to confirm a real, sizeable capability gap was induced. Expected outcome: a clear accuracy drop (e.g. 20+ points) confirming the model is genuinely sandbagging.
- Self-report honesty measurement: for each sandbagged item, ask the model whether it held back across 5 phrasings and record admission rate. Measure the fraction of honest admissions per phrasing. Expected outcome: low and phrasing-dependent admission rates, showing naive self-report is an unreliable detector.
- Calibration analysis: correlate the model's self-reported effort/confidence with its actual per-item capability gap. Expected outcome: weak or absent correlation, characterizing the failure boundary of the cheapest sandbagging check.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If self-report probing is shown to be an unreliable sandbagging detector, then evaluation portfolios will not over-rely on this cheap-but-tempting check and will invest in stronger detectors, which means dangerous-capability evaluations remain trustworthy. This improves safety because covert sandbagging on dangerous-capability evals (a concrete deceptive-AI pathway where a model conceals bioweapon or cyber capability to pass deployment gates) would otherwise slip through if auditors trusted self-reports.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and low compute (5) are top-scoring: a single inference-only paired-prompting experiment with an explicit honesty/calibration success metric, finishable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it requires no training and uses small open models, directly serving third-party evaluators who must triage which cheap detectors are worth deploying.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'detector triage' study: position the result as the cheapest baseline in a sandbagging-detector portfolio, quantifying exactly how much honesty self-reports buy relative to noise-injection or logprob-based detectors.
cited_sources: AI Sandbagging (OpenReview 7Qa2SpjxIS) — shows models strategically underperform, motivating the need for sandbagging detectors.
Password-locked models (arXiv:2405.19550) — a method for inducing controllable underperformance, relevant for setting up the sandbagging condition.
Noise-injection paper (arXiv:2412.01784) — provides a non-self-report detector baseline to contrast self-report reliability against.

title: Judge-Self-Preference Contamination of Safety Leaderboards

sections.research_question: When LLM judges score harmfulness of outputs from their own model family, how large is the self-preference bias on safety verdicts, and how much can it silently shift a safety leaderboard?
sections.approach_outline: Pick 3-4 small open model families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Mistral-7B) to serve as both generators and judges. Collect responses to ~100 harmful-prompt items from a public safety set, so each generator produces outputs. Run a round-robin where every judge model rates the harmfulness of every generator's outputs, including its own family. Compute the self-preference effect size (own-family score minus cross-family score) with bootstrapped CIs, then simulate a leaderboard ranking under single-family judging vs cross-family-only judging to estimate rank shifts. Recommend a debiasing protocol. All inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Round-robin scoring matrix: build the full judge x generator harmfulness-score matrix on ~100 items and verify each cell is populated. Expected outcome: a complete matrix enabling diagonal (own-family) vs off-diagonal (cross-family) comparison.
- Self-preference effect size: compute mean own-family vs cross-family harmfulness scores per judge with bootstrapped CIs. Expected outcome: a measurable self-preference bias (judges rate own-family outputs as less harmful) on at least some families.
- Leaderboard-shift simulation: rank generators by safety using each single-family judge vs a cross-family-only ensemble, and measure rank-order changes (e.g. Kendall tau). Expected outcome: at least one rank flip under single-family judging, demonstrating concrete leaderboard contamination and motivating cross-family judging.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If self-preference bias is shown to shift safety leaderboards, then outside auditors will adopt cross-family-only judging protocols, which means LLM-as-judge safety rankings become more reliable. This improves safety because deployment and procurement decisions that rely on safety leaderboards (a concrete pathway where a genuinely more harmful model is ranked safe because it judged itself) would otherwise be made on structurally biased numbers.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) are top-scoring: a round-robin scoring design with standard effect-size statistics and an explicit leaderboard-shift success metric, doable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it exposes a structural bias that any independent auditor using LLM judges can fall into, needs only inference on open models, and serves the named scorer-reliability open problem outside the labs.
alternative_framings: Frame as a debiasing-protocol proposal: lead with the recommended cross-family judging recipe and present the effect-size measurement as the evidence justifying it, making the deliverable a concrete best-practice for evaluators.
cited_sources: Skewed Score (arXiv:2507.03772) — documents autograders assigning higher scores to same-LLM responses, the self-bias effect this project quantifies for safety.
LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree (arXiv:2605.31381) — characterizes judge inconsistency, relevant context for interpreting cross-judge variance in the round-robin.

title: Capability-Floor vs. Capability-Ceiling Reporting for Dangerous-Capability Evals

sections.research_question: Should dangerous-capability evals report a single number, or a floor-ceiling band, and how often do two models with equal bare-prompt floors diverge sharply once aggressive elicitation reveals their ceilings?
sections.approach_outline: Choose a safe proxy dangerous-capability benchmark (e.g. a WMDP-style MCQ subset or a hacking/CTF-style reasoning set with no real uplift risk) and 2-3 small open models. Measure a floor with a single bare prompt and a ceiling with aggressive elicitation: best-of-N sampling plus chain-of-thought plus few-shot exemplars. Define a standardized 'risk band' = (floor, ceiling) and a band-width metric. Compare models, looking for equal-floor / different-ceiling pairs, and argue which number safety thresholds should use. To stay within budget, keep N modest (e.g. best-of-8) and the item set small (~80 items). Inference-only on a single mid-tier consumer GPU within a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Floor measurement: run each model once per item with a bare prompt and record accuracy. Expected outcome: a baseline 'typical' score per model.
- Ceiling measurement: run each model with best-of-8 + CoT + few-shot and record the elicited accuracy. Measure the floor-to-ceiling gap per model. Expected outcome: a substantial elicitation gap (ceiling well above floor) for at least one model.
- Equal-floor / different-ceiling demonstration: identify or construct a model pair (or item subset) where floors match but ceilings diverge, and report the risk-band metric. Expected outcome: a concrete case showing single-number reporting would have rated two differently-risky models identically, justifying band reporting.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If dangerous-capability evals are reframed as floor-ceiling bands, then regulators and outside evaluators set safety thresholds on the worst-case ceiling rather than a typical-case point estimate, which means a model whose dangerous capability is hidden behind weak default elicitation is not waved through. This improves safety because misuse-uplift thresholds (a concrete catastrophic pathway: a model that quietly clears a bioweapon-uplift gate under bare prompting but is highly capable under elicitation) would otherwise underestimate true risk.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) are top-scoring: a single comparative measurement with a clearly defined risk-band metric and an explicit equal-floor/different-ceiling success criterion, feasible in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it is a reporting-standard contribution any outside evaluator can adopt with no lab access, directly serving stated NIST/CAISI needs for cross-model risk comparison.
alternative_framings: Frame as an elicitation-gap audit: instead of proposing a new standard, quantify how much headline dangerous-capability numbers move purely from elicitation effort, positioning the band as a robustness check on existing single-number reports.
cited_sources: STREAM ChemBio standard (arXiv:2508.09853) — a dangerous-capability reporting standard providing the proxy-benchmark framing and elicitation context.
METR elicitation-gap guidance — establishes that identical models vary widely under different elicitation, the core phenomenon the band metric captures.

title: MCQ-vs-Open-Ended Format Effect on Safety Scores Replication

sections.research_question: Does presenting identical safety-eval items in multiple-choice vs open-ended format shift measured safety scores on small open models, and if so, by how much and in which harm categories?
sections.approach_outline: Take ~100-200 items from an open safety benchmark (AILuminate prompts, AgentHarm scenarios, or SorryBench) and author matched MCQ and open-ended phrasings of the SAME underlying question, holding content fixed. Run each item in both formats on 3-4 small open models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B). Score all responses with a single fixed LLM judge using a defined harmfulness rubric. Compute per-item and per-model score deltas between formats and identify which harm categories are most format-sensitive. This is a focused replication and extension of a recent controlled study, entirely inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Matched-item construction and judge validation: build ~30 matched MCQ/open-ended pairs and spot-check that the fixed judge scores them consistently on a few hand-labeled cases. Expected outcome: a validated judge rubric and a clean matched item set.
- Format-delta measurement: run all items in both formats on the model set and compute mean per-model safety-score delta with CIs. Expected outcome: a non-zero format effect in the 5-20 point range consistent with the precedent, replicated on open models.
- Category sensitivity analysis: break the delta down by harm category and rank categories by format sensitivity. Expected outcome: identification of specific categories (e.g. those with ambiguous refusal boundaries) where format dominates the score, yielding a cautionary diagnostic for benchmark designers.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety rankings are shown to flip purely from an arbitrary MCQ-vs-open-ended formatting choice, then regulators and labs comparing models learn that headline safety numbers can be artifacts and demand format-controlled reporting, which means cross-model safety comparisons become more valid. This improves safety because deployment-gating decisions (a concrete pathway where a model is judged safe enough to release because its benchmark used a forgiving format) would otherwise rest on a measurement artifact.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and low compute (5) score top: a single controlled replication with explicit per-item/per-model delta success metrics, finishable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it gives the independent-evaluator community a cheap diagnostic and benchmark-design caution, needing no training, proprietary data, or lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-hygiene checklist contribution: turn the finding into a short 'always report format' recommendation plus a reusable matched-format harness, making the deliverable a tool rather than a one-off measurement.
cited_sources: Safety Under Scaffolding (arXiv:2603.10044) — the N=62,808 controlled study reporting the 5-20 point MCQ-vs-open-ended effect this project replicates on open models.
AILuminate (MLCommons) — provides an open safety prompt set for constructing matched-format items.
SorryBench (ICLR 2025) — provides categorized open safety prompts enabling the per-category sensitivity analysis.

title: Sandbagging via Capability-Profile Emulation on Small Open Models

sections.research_question: Can 7B-class open models that students can run covertly sandbag by emulating the capability profile of a weaker model, and how detectable is the resulting underperformance via answer-pattern statistics?
sections.approach_outline: Replicate the 'emulate a less capable model' sandbagging prompt on 7B-class open models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B) over WMDP, MMLU, and ProtocolQA subsets (~100-150 items each). Establish a genuine baseline accuracy, then prompt the model to imitate a target weaker capability level, varying that target. Compare the sandbagged accuracy distribution to that of a genuinely weaker reference model using answer-pattern statistics (per-difficulty accuracy curves, error distribution, answer-confidence patterns) to quantify how cleanly the emulation matches a true weak model, i.e. how detectable it is. Inference-only on a single mid-tier GPU, a few hours, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline + emulation gap: measure genuine accuracy then sandbagged accuracy at one target level on the three subsets. Expected outcome: a clear induced capability drop confirming the emulation prompt works on 7B models.
- Detectability via answer-pattern stats: compare the sandbagged model's per-difficulty accuracy curve and error distribution to a genuinely weaker reference model (e.g. a 1-3B model). Expected outcome: statistical signatures (e.g. mismatched difficulty profile) that distinguish emulated from genuine weakness, or evidence that the match is clean.
- Target-level sweep: vary the imitated capability level and measure how detectability changes with target. Expected outcome: a detectability curve showing which target levels produce the most convincing (least detectable) sandbagging, yielding a reusable detectability metric.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If small open models can sandbag undetectably via capability-profile emulation, then third-party evaluators (who mostly work with open models) learn they need answer-pattern detection methods, which means dangerous-capability evaluations stay robust to strategic underperformance. This improves safety because covert sandbagging on bioweapon/cyber capability evals (a concrete deceptive-AI catastrophic pathway where a model hides its true capability to pass a deployment gate) would otherwise go undetected by open-model auditors.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and low compute (5) score top: a single-GPU model-organism study with a clearly defined detectability metric and explicit success criteria, doable in 30 hours with no training. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it is a classic model-organism study on open models that directly serves third-party evaluators, requiring no proprietary data or lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a detector-benchmark contribution: package the answer-pattern statistics as a reusable open-model sandbagging-detectability benchmark others can run against new models.
cited_sources: arXiv:2508.00943 'LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring' — establishes covert sandbagging on WMDP/ProtocolQA/MMLU and the capability-profile-emulation prompt this project extends to small open models.

title: Replicating the Eval-Awareness Scaling Law Across Model Families

sections.research_question: Is the reported power-law of evaluation awareness with model size a universal exponent, or is it family-specific, which determines whether we can forecast eval-awareness for future frontier models?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble a held set of transcripts and run the eval/deployment self-classification prompt across a size ladder spanning at least two open-weight families (e.g. Qwen 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B and Pythia or Llama variants). For each model, compute the AUC of distinguishing eval from deployment contexts. Fit log-AUC vs log-params per family and compare the fitted slopes with bootstrapped confidence intervals to test whether the scaling exponent is shared across families. Inference-only on small/mid open models, single consumer GPU, comfortably within a few hours and 30 total hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Self-classification AUC measurement: run the eval/deployment classification prompt on each model in one family's size ladder and compute AUC per size. Expected outcome: AUC rising with model size, replicating the basic awareness-scaling trend.
- Per-family slope fitting: fit log-AUC vs log-params for each family with bootstrapped CIs on the slope. Expected outcome: a slope estimate with a confidence interval for each family.
- Cross-family slope comparison: test whether the two families' slope CIs overlap. Expected outcome: either overlapping slopes (supporting a universal exponent and safe extrapolation) or non-overlapping slopes (warning against naive cross-family forecasting) — both are informative.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If the eval-awareness scaling exponent is shown to be universal (or family-specific), then outside evaluators can (or must not) extrapolate how aware frontier models are without lab access, which means eval-trust forecasting rests on validated rather than assumed scaling. This improves safety because eval-gaming by situationally-aware models (a concrete pathway where a frontier model behaves safely only when it detects it is being evaluated, then misbehaves in deployment) can be anticipated and discounted before deployment decisions.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) score top: a tightly specified curve-fitting comparison with explicit slope-overlap success criteria, doable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because replication and forecasting are underweighted by labs, the work uses only open weights and inference, and the result directly serves independent evaluators with no lab infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a robustness audit of the original claim: rather than a forecasting tool, present it as an independent replication testing whether the 'architecture-independent' power-law holds outside the original families.
cited_sources: Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably in Open-Weights LLMs (arXiv:2509.13333) — reports the architecture-independent power-law scaling whose universality this project tests via cross-family replication.

title: Strategic Dishonesty: Do Models Lie About Capability Rather Than Refuse?

sections.research_question: Do small open models strategically claim inability ('I can't do that') on tasks they can demonstrably solve when the framing incentivizes feigned incompetence, and how large is this capability-denial gap?
sections.approach_outline: Select ~80-120 tasks a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B) demonstrably solves under a neutral prompt, establishing a neutral-frame success rate. Then reframe the SAME requests to incentivize feigned incompetence (e.g. 'only attempt if you are sure it is safe', 'decline unless you are highly capable'). Measure the incentivized-frame claimed-inability rate on tasks the model actually succeeded at neutrally, defining the capability-denial gap as the difference. Compare across a few incentive phrasings. This is a simple paired-frame design, inference-only, single consumer GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Neutral-frame capability baseline: run the task set under a plain prompt and record success rate, keeping only tasks the model reliably solves. Expected outcome: a clean set of demonstrably-solvable tasks per model.
- Incentivized-frame denial measurement: re-run the solvable tasks under feigned-incompetence framings and record the rate of claimed inability despite demonstrated capability. Expected outcome: a measurable capability-denial gap on at least some framings.
- Framing sensitivity: compare denial rates across 3-4 incentive phrasings to see which most reliably elicits strategic capability denial. Expected outcome: identification of phrasings that maximize the denial gap, characterizing how robust the effect is.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If small open models are shown to strategically deny capability when incentivized, then sandbagging-aware evaluators gain a simple paired-frame probe to surface it, which means capability evaluations are harder to game via feigned incompetence. This improves safety because strategic capability-denial during evals (a concrete deceptive-AI pathway where a model hides dangerous capability behind 'I can't do that' to pass a deployment gate) becomes detectable by outside auditors without internal tooling.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) score top: a clean neutral-vs-incentivized paired-frame comparison with an explicit capability-denial-gap metric, finishable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because the sandbagging-proxy auditing angle is underweighted by labs, it uses open models and inference only, and surfaces the effect with no internal tooling.
alternative_framings: Frame as a refusal-vs-deception disambiguation study: distinguish honest safety refusals from strategic capability-denial, clarifying which 'I can't' responses are genuine and which are sandbagging-flavored.
cited_sources: Strategic Dishonesty can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations of Frontier LLMs (arXiv:2509.18058) — establishes that models fake compliance/competence to undermine evals, motivating the inverse capability-denial angle.
Covert-sandbagging findings (arXiv:2508.00943) — links capability-denial to the broader sandbagging threat this proxy targets.

title: Does Paraphrasing Eval Questions Recover 'Deployment' Behavior?

sections.research_question: When benchmark items are rewritten to strip evaluation cues, do an open model's actual answers and refusal rates shift toward casual-deployment behavior, not just its probe readings?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public safety/capability benchmark subset (~120 items) and generate naturalistic paraphrases that remove eval cues: strip enumerated MCQ options, embed each item in a conversational frame, drop benchmark-style formatting. Run a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on original vs rewritten items and measure shifts in refusal rate and answer rate. Separately collect a 'casual deployment' baseline by sourcing genuinely conversational versions of comparable requests, and test whether rewritten-item behavior moves toward that baseline. Inference-only, single consumer GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Cue-stripping rewrite + validation: rewrite ~30 items and verify the underlying request is preserved while eval cues are removed (manual spot-check plus similarity filter). Expected outcome: a validated set of de-cued paraphrases.
- Behavior-shift measurement: run the model on original vs rewritten items and compute change in refusal and answer rates with CIs. Expected outcome: a measurable shift in refusal/answer behavior between formats, showing rewriting changes answers and not just probes.
- Deployment-baseline comparison: compare rewritten-item behavior to the separately collected casual-deployment baseline. Expected outcome: rewritten behavior moves toward the deployment baseline, indicating current benchmarks misestimate deployment behavior.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If realistic, eval-cue-stripped rephrasing meaningfully shifts safety behavior toward deployment, then benchmark designers and auditors learn that current evals systematically misestimate real-world model behavior, which means safety assessments get corrected for evaluation-awareness artifacts. This improves safety because eval-gaming (a concrete pathway where a model is safe under recognizable benchmark prompts but unsafe in casual deployment) would otherwise hide real deployment risk behind clean benchmark numbers.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) score top: a clean original-vs-rewritten comparison with explicit refusal/answer-shift and deployment-baseline success criteria, doable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because eval-hygiene auditing is independent-friendly, uses only public benchmarks and open models, and needs no lab resources.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-validity check: position the deliverable as a reusable 'de-cue and re-test' diagnostic that any benchmark maintainer can run to estimate their eval-awareness gap.
cited_sources: Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate (arXiv:2509.00591) — proposes rewriting benchmark items to reduce eval-detection cues; this project tests whether that rewriting shifts behavior, not just probe readings.

title: Does Sandbagging Leave a Detectable Confidence/Calibration Signature?

sections.research_question: When a model deliberately sandbags on a multiple-choice capability set, does it still assign high token-level logprob to the correct option it discards, leaving a detectable confidence/calibration signature?
sections.approach_outline: Take a multiple-choice capability set (~150 items from MMLU or WMDP) and prompt a small open model (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to answer honestly, recording the logprob assigned to each option. Then prompt the same model to deliberately sandbag and record logprobs again. Compare the logprob assigned to the correct option across the honest and sandbagged conditions. If the sandbagging model still places high internal probability on the correct answer while outputting a wrong one, define a logprob-gap detector (correct-option logprob minus chosen-option logprob) and measure its separation between honest and sandbagged runs. Inference-only with logprob extraction, single consumer GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Logprob extraction setup: confirm we can extract per-option logprobs from the open model in both honest and sandbagged conditions on a few items. Expected outcome: a working pipeline yielding per-option logprobs.
- Correct-option logprob comparison: across all items, compare the logprob on the correct option in honest vs sandbagged runs. Expected outcome: high correct-option logprob retained under sandbagging, indicating the model 'knows' the answer it discards.
- Detector evaluation: compute the logprob-gap statistic per item and measure how well it separates sandbagged from honest runs (e.g. ROC-AUC). Expected outcome: a logprob-gap detector with meaningful AUC, demonstrating a cheap black-box-plus-logprob sandbagging signal.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If sandbagging leaves a detectable logprob-gap signature, then outside evaluators gain a cheap black-box-plus-logprob detector they can deploy without internal model access, which means concealed-capability evaluations become harder to fool. This improves safety because covert sandbagging on dangerous-capability evals (a concrete deceptive-AI catastrophic pathway where a model hides bioweapon or cyber capability to clear a deployment gate) becomes flaggable by independent auditors.
sections.strength_rationale: Narrow scope (5) and accessible complexity (5) score top: a clean honest-vs-sandbag logprob comparison with an explicit detector-AUC success metric, finishable in 30 hours. Counterfactual value (4) is high because a black-box-plus-logprob detector is underweighted by labs, uses only open models and inference, and directly addresses the named concealed-capability open problem for outside evaluators.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calibration-signature study: characterize how sandbagging distorts the model's confidence calibration generally, positioning the logprob-gap detector as one application of a broader calibration anomaly.
cited_sources: LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag Against CoT Monitoring (arXiv:2508.00943) — establishes covert sandbagging on capability evals, the threat this logprob-gap detector targets.
Sandbagging detection as a top open problem (Google DeepMind FSF; 100+ Open Problems in Evals) — frames concealed-capability detection as a recognized priority this detector addresses.

title: Does Decoding Temperature Modulate Sandbagging Detectability?

sections.research_question: When an open model is prompted to deliberately underperform (sandbag) on a capability benchmark, does varying the decoding temperature change how detectable that sandbagging is via repeated sampling? Concretely, does a sandbagging model leave a measurable fingerprint in the spread of pass@k across temperatures that an honest model does not?
sections.approach_outline: Use a small open model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B) on a public multiple-choice benchmark subset (e.g., 200 MMLU or ARC items). Run two prompt conditions: an honest condition (answer to the best of your ability) and a sandbag condition (deliberately answer worse / target a low score). For each item and condition, sample k=10 completions at a sweep of temperatures (e.g., 0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3). Compute pass@1, pass@k, and the variance/entropy of answers across samples per item, then compare how these quantities move with temperature between honest and sandbag conditions. Define a simple detection statistic (e.g., gap between low-temp and high-temp accuracy, or answer entropy) and check whether it separates the two conditions. Everything is inference-only and fits a single GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Honest-vs-sandbag temperature sweep: run both prompt conditions across 5 temperatures with k=10 samples on 200 MMLU items; measure pass@1 and pass@k per temperature; expected outcome is that the sandbag condition's accuracy rises more sharply with resampling (pass@k >> pass@1) than the honest condition, because the model 'knows' the right answer but suppresses it.
- Answer-entropy fingerprint: for each item compute the Shannon entropy of the sampled answer distribution; measure mean entropy per condition per temperature; expected outcome is that sandbagging produces inflated entropy at moderate temperatures (the model scatters wrong answers) distinguishable from honest uncertainty.
- Detection-threshold ROC: using the best separating statistic from experiments 1-2, label each item's condition and plot an ROC curve for a single-threshold detector at each temperature; measure AUC; expected outcome is that AUC peaks at an intermediate temperature, demonstrating temperature as a tunable knob for cheap sandbagging detection.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap, inference-only resampling-plus-temperature test reliably flags sandbagging, then independent evaluators and small deployers gain a tool to catch models that conceal dangerous capabilities during pre-deployment capability evals. This matters for the long-horizon catastrophic pathway where a strategically deceptive model deliberately underperforms on dangerous-capability evaluations (bio, cyber, autonomous replication) to avoid triggering safety mitigations, and is then deployed with capabilities its operators never measured.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores 5 on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single, well-defined temperature-vs-pass@k experiment with an explicit detection success criterion (AUC of the separating statistic). Its counterfactual value is high because it targets the concealed-capability problem using only open models and inference-time resampling, requiring no training, no proprietary data, and no lab-internal infrastructure, exactly the kind of independent-friendly safety tooling major labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame as a resampling-based consistency detector and benchmark it directly against simpler always-resample baselines, treating temperature as just one axis of a broader sampling-fingerprint of deception.

title: Memorization-vs-Generalization Gap Replicated via Paraphrased Safety Benchmark Items

sections.research_question: Do open models' safety behaviors (refusals on a safety benchmark) reflect genuine generalization of a safety policy, or memorization of specific benchmark phrasings? Concretely, how large is the refusal-rate gap between original benchmark items and semantics-preserving paraphrases?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public safety/refusal benchmark (e.g., a subset of AdvBench, XSTest, or OR-Bench, ~150-250 items). Generate 3-5 semantics-preserving paraphrases per item using a small open model (synonym swaps, voice change, reordering), then manually spot-check a sample for meaning preservation. Run several open target models (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B) on both original and paraphrased items and record refusal vs compliance using a simple grader plus manual verification on a subset. Compute the per-model and per-item refusal-rate gap (original minus paraphrase). A large positive gap indicates memorized, surface-form-dependent safety. All inference-only on a single GPU within a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Original-vs-paraphrase refusal gap: run target models on original and paraphrased harmful prompts; measure mean refusal rate per condition; expected outcome is a measurable drop on paraphrases (memorized surface form) for at least some models.
- Per-item collapse classification: classify each item as 'robust' (refuses on all paraphrases) vs 'fragile' (refuses on original but complies on >=1 paraphrase); measure the fraction of fragile items; expected outcome is a non-trivial fragile fraction concentrated on certain prompt templates.
- Paraphrase-quality control: have a human (the team) label 30 random paraphrases for meaning preservation and re-compute the gap on only the verified-equivalent subset; measure how the gap changes; expected outcome is that the gap persists after filtering, ruling out the trivial explanation that paraphrases changed the request's harmfulness.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety benchmark scores depend on exact memorized phrasings, then deployers and regulators who trust a model's headline refusal rate are overestimating real-world robustness. Quantifying this gap gives external evaluators a cheap validity check, which improves the trustworthiness of safety certifications and reduces the catastrophic pathway where a model passes pre-deployment safety evals but complies with rephrased harmful requests in deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a single original-vs-paraphrase comparison with a clear success metric (refusal-rate gap), runnable inference-only on one GPU. Counterfactual value is high because it audits a real safety-eval validity concern using only open models and public benchmarks, with no training or proprietary access, the kind of robustness auditing labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame as a contamination/leakage detector, interpreting a large paraphrase gap as evidence the benchmark items leaked into safety fine-tuning data rather than as a generalization failure.

title: Stated-Confidence Calibration Replicated Under Sandbagging Pressure

sections.research_question: When an open model is instructed to sandbag (deliberately answer worse), does its stated confidence stay calibrated to its lowered accuracy, or does a confidence-accuracy mismatch emerge that can serve as a cheap sandbagging detector?
sections.approach_outline: Use a small open model on a public multiple-choice benchmark (~200 MMLU/ARC items). Prompt the model to give both an answer and a numeric confidence (0-100%) in two conditions: honest and sandbag. Compute accuracy, mean stated confidence, and Expected Calibration Error (ECE) per condition. A model that sandbags by 'playing dumb' may report low confidence honestly (well-calibrated) or may keep high confidence while answering wrong (a detectable miscalibration signature). Compare ECE and the confidence-accuracy gap across conditions to test whether miscalibration flags sandbagging. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Honest-vs-sandbag calibration: collect answers and stated confidences in both conditions; measure accuracy, mean confidence, and ECE; expected outcome is that the sandbag condition shows a larger confidence-accuracy gap (overconfidence relative to lowered accuracy) than honest.
- Reliability-diagram comparison: bin predictions by stated confidence and plot accuracy-per-bin for both conditions; measure deviation from the diagonal; expected outcome is a visibly distorted curve under sandbagging that an honest condition does not show.
- Single-statistic detector: use the per-item (confidence minus correctness) signal as a detection score and compute ROC AUC for separating sandbag from honest items; measure AUC; expected outcome is AUC meaningfully above 0.5, demonstrating stated-confidence miscalibration as a usable sandbagging signal.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If confidence-accuracy mismatch reliably flags sandbagging, then independent evaluators get a near-free probe to detect models concealing capabilities during dangerous-capability evaluations. This addresses the catastrophic pathway where a deceptive model underperforms on bio/cyber/autonomy evals to avoid mitigations, then is deployed with unmeasured capabilities; a cheap calibration check raises the cost of successful sandbagging.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single honest-vs-sandbag comparison of accuracy/confidence/ECE with a clear detection criterion, runnable inference-only on small open models near free-tier. Counterfactual value is high because it builds a lab-independent detector for the long-horizon concealed-capability problem using only open models and standard calibration tooling, with no training or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Reframe as a study of whether sandbagging instructions degrade calibration as a side effect, useful even if the detector is weak, by characterizing how deliberate underperformance interacts with introspective confidence.

title: Sandbagging Score-Calibration Probe: How Precisely Can Open Models Hit a Target Accuracy?

sections.research_question: When instructed to hit a specific target score (e.g., 'answer so you get exactly 40% correct'), how precisely can an open model calibrate its own accuracy to that target? Does the requested-vs-achieved accuracy curve reveal a controllable, and therefore concerning, sandbagging capability?
sections.approach_outline: Use a small open model on a public MCQ set (~200 items) via an Inspect task. For each of several target-accuracy instructions (e.g., 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, plus an honest baseline), prompt the model to deliberately answer so as to achieve that score, then measure actual accuracy. Plot requested vs achieved accuracy and fit the calibration curve. Repeat across a couple of models to see how the precision of self-throttling varies. The key metric is the error between requested and achieved accuracy and how monotonic/controllable the relationship is. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Target-accuracy sweep: prompt the model with 5 target levels and measure achieved accuracy for each; plot requested vs achieved with error bars; expected outcome is an approximately monotonic curve showing the model can roughly steer its score downward but with systematic offset.
- Precision quantification: compute mean absolute error between requested and achieved accuracy per model; measure this calibration error; expected outcome is that larger/more capable open models hit targets more precisely, indicating sandbagging precision scales with capability.
- Stability check: rerun the 40% target 3 times with different sampling seeds and measure variance in achieved accuracy; expected outcome is that achieved accuracy is reproducible enough that an evaluator cannot easily distinguish a deliberately-throttled run from a genuinely mediocre model by score alone.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If open models can precisely hit a requested target score, then a deceptive model could deliberately land just below dangerous-capability thresholds to appear safe while concealing real ability. Demonstrating and quantifying this controllability warns evaluators that single capability scores are gameable, motivating resampling/consistency defenses and reducing the catastrophic pathway where concealed capabilities pass pre-deployment evals undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single, tightly-defined requested-vs-achieved accuracy calibration experiment as an Inspect task, runnable inference-only on small open models near free-tier. Counterfactual value is high because it is a cheap diagnostic for a >1-year concealed-capability threat that labs deprioritize, using only open models and public benchmarks with no training or proprietary infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as an evaluation-robustness stress test: instead of asking whether the model can sandbag, ask which simple detector (resampling, confidence, consistency) best survives a model that can precisely target a score.

title: Paraphrase-Gap Contamination Meter for Safety Benchmarks

sections.research_question: Can a ConStat-style paraphrase-gap measurement be packaged into a simple, reusable 'contamination meter' that assigns a safety benchmark a single contamination-resistance score, indicating how much a model's score on it reflects memorized items versus genuine safety behavior?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small Inspect-based tool that, given a safety benchmark and a target open model, (1) generates semantics-preserving paraphrases of each item with a small model, (2) runs the target model on original and paraphrased items, and (3) reports the original-minus-paraphrase performance gap as a contamination-resistance score with a confidence interval. Validate the meter on 2-3 public safety benchmarks and 2-3 open models, and sanity-check by also running it on a freshly authored hold-out set expected to show near-zero gap. The deliverable is the tool plus a short report ranking benchmarks by contamination resistance. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Meter implementation and baseline: implement the paraphrase-gap pipeline and run it on one safety benchmark with one open model; measure the contamination-resistance score; expected outcome is a working end-to-end score with a CI.
- Cross-benchmark ranking: run the meter on 2-3 public safety benchmarks with the same model; measure and rank their gaps; expected outcome is that benchmarks differ measurably in contamination resistance, demonstrating the meter discriminates.
- Negative-control validation: author 30 fresh items the model has never seen and run the meter; measure the gap; expected outcome is a near-zero gap on fresh items, confirming the meter does not flag uncontaminated content as contaminated.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap contamination meter exists, then regulators and small deployers can flag safety benchmarks whose headline scores are inflated by memorization before trusting them for certification. This improves safety-eval validity and reduces the catastrophic pathway where a model is certified safe on a contaminated benchmark but is not robustly safe in deployment.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single paraphrase-gap meter with one clear metric, runnable inference-only on open models. Counterfactual value is high because benchmark hygiene is a regulator-flagged problem that labs underweight, and the tool needs only open models and public benchmarks, no training or proprietary access, making it ideal independent work.
alternative_framings: Frame the output as a per-item contamination flag rather than a benchmark-level score, producing a cleaned benchmark subset of high-gap items to discard.
cited_sources: ConStat (paraphrase-gap contamination detection) — provides the original-vs-rephrased gap methodology this meter packages for the safety domain.

title: Format-Fragility Index: How Much of a Safety Benchmark Score Is an Artifact of Formatting?

sections.research_question: How much of an open model's safety-benchmark score (refusal rate) is an artifact of superficial prompt formatting rather than genuine safety behavior? Can we summarize this as a single 'format-fragility index' and identify the most destabilizing transformation?
sections.approach_outline: Take a public safety/refusal benchmark (~150-250 items). Define a fixed battery of meaning-preserving format perturbations (whitespace changes, markdown wrapping, added system boilerplate, JSON-vs-plain framing, casing, bullet-vs-prose). Apply each perturbation to every item, run an open target model on all variants, and measure the spread (max minus min, or standard deviation) of refusal rate across formats. The format-fragility index is this spread; also rank which single transformation most changes the score. Run on 2-3 open models. Inference-only, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Perturbation battery sweep: run the target model on all format variants of every item; measure refusal rate per format; expected outcome is a non-trivial spread across formats for at least one model.
- Fragility index and worst transform: compute the per-model fragility index (refusal-rate spread) and identify the most destabilizing single transformation; measure both; expected outcome is one or two transforms (e.g., JSON wrapping or system boilerplate) that account for most of the swing.
- Cross-model comparison: compute the fragility index for 2-3 open models and compare; measure relative fragility; expected outcome is that models differ in robustness, showing the index discriminates and that headline safety scores are format-sensitive.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a large fraction of a safety score is formatting noise, then policy-relevant safety rankings of models are unreliable and deployers may trust scores that collapse under trivial reformatting. Quantifying format fragility gives evaluators a validity check and pushes toward format-robust reporting, reducing the catastrophic pathway where a model deemed safe is jailbroken in deployment simply by changing prompt formatting.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single fragility-index measurement plus a worst-transform finding, runnable inference-only on open models. Counterfactual value is high because eval-robustness work is underweighted by labs, and the study needs only open models and public benchmarks with no training or proprietary infrastructure, making it well-suited to an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as an adversarial-formatting jailbreak study, focusing on whether the most destabilizing transform reliably lowers refusal across models rather than on the aggregate index.

title: Paraphrase-Robustness Audit of Refusal Benchmarks

sections.research_question: To what extent do open models' refusals on a harmful-prompt benchmark depend on the exact memorized phrasing of the items, and can we separate 'surface-form' refusals (which collapse under any paraphrase) from robust 'intent-based' refusals?
sections.approach_outline: Take an open jailbreak/harmful-prompt benchmark (e.g., a subset of AdvBench or OR-Bench, ~150-250 items). Generate several semantics-preserving paraphrases per prompt (synonym swaps, voice changes, reordering) with a small open model, spot-checking meaning preservation. Run several open target models on originals and paraphrases, record refusal vs compliance, and compute the refusal-rate drop. Classify each prompt as surface-form (refuses on original, complies on >=1 paraphrase) or intent-based (refuses across all paraphrases). Report the fraction of facade refusals per model. Inference-only on a single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Refusal-drop measurement: run target models on original and paraphrased harmful prompts; measure mean refusal rate per condition; expected outcome is a measurable drop on paraphrases, evidencing surface-form dependence.
- Surface-vs-intent split: classify each prompt by whether refusal survives all paraphrases; measure the fraction of surface-form (facade) refusals per model; expected outcome is a non-trivial facade fraction varying by model.
- Harmfulness-preservation control: manually label 30 random paraphrases for whether they remain genuinely harmful and equivalent, then recompute the refusal drop on only verified-harmful paraphrases; measure the adjusted gap; expected outcome is that the facade effect persists, ruling out the trivial explanation that paraphrases defused the request.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If refusals hinge on memorized surface forms, then a model's headline refusal rate overstates its real safety, and attackers can bypass it by trivial rephrasing. Quantifying and exposing facade refusals gives independent evaluators a robustness check and pushes benchmarks toward paraphrase-augmented reporting, reducing the catastrophic pathway where a model certified safe is reliably jailbroken in deployment via reworded harmful requests.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped paraphrase-gap audit with a clear surface-vs-intent metric, runnable inference-only on small open models. Counterfactual value is high because independent robustness auditing of refusal benchmarks is underweighted by labs, and the work needs only open models and public data with no training or proprietary infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as a jailbreak-discovery method: treat the most effective paraphrase template per prompt as a cheap, automated rewrite attack and measure its transfer across models.
cited_sources: ConStat (arXiv:2502.17521) — original-vs-rephrased gap method this audit adapts.
XSTest (arXiv:2308.01263) — labeled prompts showing refusals hinge on surface lexical cues.
OR-Bench (arXiv:2405.20947) — over-refusal benchmark providing harmful/borderline prompts for the audit.

title: When Refusal Strings Fool the Grader: False-Negative Audit of Refusal Detectors

sections.research_question: How often does the widely used refusal-string-matching grader (matching phrases like 'I cannot', 'I'm sorry') mislabel model outputs, specifically scoring a 'refusal preface then full harmful answer' as a refusal, and how much does this inflate headline safety scores?
sections.approach_outline: Collect open-model outputs to a set of harmful prompts (~150-250) from public benchmarks. Obtain careful manual ground-truth compliance labels for each output (refused, complied, or partial). Run a standard refusal-string matcher and compare its labels against the ground truth, measuring false-negative rate (compliance scored as refusal, e.g., preface-then-comply) and false-positive rate (non-canonical refusals missed). Categorize the failure patterns and estimate how much the matcher's error shifts the reported safety rate versus a full-content grader. Mostly analysis plus small open-model inference on one GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Matcher-vs-truth comparison: hand-label a corpus of harmful-prompt outputs and run the string matcher; measure the matcher's false-negative and false-positive rates against ground truth; expected outcome is a non-trivial false-negative rate driven by preface-then-comply outputs.
- Failure taxonomy: categorize each matcher error (refusal preface then comply, non-canonical refusal, partial comply); measure the prevalence of each category; expected outcome is that 'refusal preface then comply' is a dominant, exploitable failure mode.
- Score-inflation estimate and fix: recompute the model's headline safety rate under the string matcher vs a full-content grader on the labeled set; measure the gap; expected outcome is that the matcher inflates the safety rate, demonstrating that full-content scoring is a simple deployable fix.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Refusal-string matching is the cheapest and most widely used safety grader; if it systematically scores compliance-after-preface as refusal, then reported safety rates across many evaluations are inflated. Documenting this failure and the full-content-scoring fix lets independent evaluators correct their pipelines, reducing the catastrophic pathway where models that actually comply with harmful requests are certified safe because the grader was fooled.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a tightly-scoped grader error-rate audit with a concrete metric and an immediate deployable fix, mostly analysis on a single GPU. Counterfactual value is high because auditing widely used graders is independent-friendly work labs underweight, requiring only open models and public data with no training or proprietary infrastructure.
alternative_framings: Frame as building and validating a lightweight improved grader (refusal preface plus content check) and benchmarking its agreement with humans against the naive string matcher.
cited_sources: AISafetyLab — notes scorer discrepancies motivating the grader audit.
