Jailbreak literature on 'refusal preface then comply' attacks — documents the failure pattern this audit quantifies.
XSTest / OR-Bench — provide labeled harmful/borderline prompts for collecting outputs.

title: SPC Control Charts for Continuous Post-Deployment Safety Monitoring

sections.research_question: Can statistical process control (Shewhart and CUSUM control charts) from manufacturing be adapted into a lightweight harness that detects when a deployed model's safety behavior drifts, distinguishing normal day-to-day variation from real degradation, without labels or model-internal access?
sections.approach_outline: Build a small harness that runs a fixed probe set of safety/refusal prompts against a model (open-model checkpoints or an API) on a schedule, computes a daily safety statistic (refusal rate or harmful-completion rate), and maintains Shewhart and CUSUM control charts with control limits learned from a stable baseline window. The harness raises an alert on out-of-control signals. Demonstrate detection by simulating drift via versioned open-model checkpoints (or prompt-config/system-prompt changes) swapped in mid-stream, and measure detection latency and false-alarm rate. Inference-only on a small probe set; CPU/free-tier feasible, a few hours of total runtime.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline control limits: run the probe set repeatedly against a stable model to estimate the daily safety statistic's mean and variation, then set Shewhart/CUSUM limits; measure the in-control false-alarm rate; expected outcome is a low, tunable false-alarm rate over the baseline window.
- Simulated-drift detection: swap in a less-safe checkpoint (or weaken the system prompt) partway through the schedule and run the charts; measure detection latency (days/samples until alert) and whether CUSUM beats Shewhart for gradual drift; expected outcome is reliable detection with CUSUM catching slow drift sooner.
- Sensitivity vs probe-set size: vary the number of probe prompts per run (e.g., 20/50/100) and re-measure detection latency and false-alarm rate; expected outcome is a clear compute-vs-sensitivity tradeoff curve giving small deployers a practical sizing recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a cheap, label-free SPC harness reliably flags safety drift, then small deployers and independent monitors can catch silent safety regressions after a model update or distribution shift, which today often go unnoticed. This operationalizes continuous post-deployment safety monitoring and reduces the catastrophic pathway where a deployed model's safety silently degrades and is exploited at scale before anyone notices.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a fixed probe set, a daily statistic, control charts, and a simulated-drift demonstration with explicit success criteria, runnable on a single GPU or free tier. Counterfactual value is high because external post-deployment monitoring tooling is weakly incentivized inside labs, generalizes without internal access, and uses only public models and standard SPC, making it ideal independent infrastructure work.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark of which SPC variant (Shewhart vs CUSUM vs EWMA) best detects safety drift, producing a recommendation rather than a single harness.
cited_sources: SPC for out-of-distribution and data-drift monitoring (arXiv:2402.08088) — demonstrates input/output-level control charts for ML systems, the core method transferred here.

LLMOps drift-monitoring practice (Fiddler/Galileo) — logs fixed test-query sets at intervals and alerts on statistically significant degradation, the operational pattern this harness formalizes for safety.

title: Diagnostic-Test Theory for Autograder Calibration

sections.research_question: If we treat an LLM safety autograder as a diagnostic test for 'harmful output', what are its sensitivity, specificity, likelihood ratios, and ROC/AUC against a human-labeled gold set, and how much does the chosen operating threshold change a model's headline safety score?
sections.approach_outline: Borrow diagnostic-test evaluation from clinical epidemiology. Assemble a small human-labeled gold set (~100-200 model outputs labeled harmful vs not by the team). Treat an open LLM autograder as a binary diagnostic test and, across several grader prompts and decision thresholds, compute sensitivity, specificity, positive/negative likelihood ratios, and ROC/AUC with bootstrap confidence intervals. Identify the operating point that holds the false-negative rate at a chosen safety target, and quantify how much moving the threshold shifts the model's reported safety score. Pure analysis plus light open-grader inference on a single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Gold-set ROC: run the open autograder over the labeled gold set at multiple thresholds and compute sensitivity/specificity/AUC with CIs; measure the ROC curve; expected outcome is an AUC well below 1.0, revealing meaningful grader error.
- FN-controlled operating point: select the threshold that caps the false-negative rate at a safety target (e.g., <=5%) and report the resulting specificity and likelihood ratios; measure the tradeoff; expected outcome is that controlling false negatives substantially raises false positives, exposing the safety-critical asymmetry that crude accuracy hides.
- Threshold-driven score swing: recompute a target model's headline safety score under the lenient vs strict grader operating points; measure the difference; expected outcome is that the reported safety score moves materially with the grader threshold, showing scorer choice is a hidden free parameter.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Autograder reliability is central to trustworthy safety evaluations; reporting only crude accuracy hides the safety-critical asymmetry between missing a harmful output and over-flagging. Reframing graders with diagnostic-test metrics regulators already trust exposes this FN/FP tradeoff and gives evaluators principled operating points, reducing the catastrophic pathway where a model is certified safe because an unreliable grader systematically missed harmful completions.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a single analysis producing sensitivity/specificity/ROC and an operating point from a tiny gold set, runnable with minimal compute. Counterfactual value is high because external auditing of judge reliability is independent-friendly, uses only open graders and a hand-built gold set with no training or proprietary data, and addresses an explicitly open scorer-reliability problem labs underweight.
alternative_framings: Frame as a grader-prompt selection tool: rank candidate grader prompts by AUC and FN-controlled specificity to recommend the most reliable open autograder configuration.
cited_sources: ROC/sensitivity/specificity diagnostic-test framework (PMC3755824) — the standard accuracy framework transferred to autograders.
Multi-reader diagnostic-test methods (ScienceDirect S1572312711001341) — supports comparing multiple grader prompts as readers.
AISafetyLab — notes that different scorers produce discrepant results for the same method, motivating the calibration audit.

title: Signal Detection Theory for the Refusal Boundary

sections.research_question: When a safety 'improvement' lowers a model's harmful-compliance rate, is it because the model got better at telling harmful from benign requests (sensitivity), or merely more biased toward refusing everything (criterion)? Can Signal Detection Theory's d' and c cleanly separate these for open chat models?
sections.approach_outline: Treat refusal as a binary decision over a mixed pool of genuinely-harmful prompts (signal) and benign-but-scary prompts (noise, e.g. XSTest-style). For each open model and condition, score every prompt as refused/complied, then compute hits (correct refusals on harmful) and false alarms (refusals on benign), and convert these to d' (discriminability) and c (criterion) with standard SDT formulas. Sweep a criterion-shifting knob (decoding temperature and a graded refusal-encouraging system prompt) to trace points along an ROC curve per model. Compare two or three open models, and demonstrate that some interventions move only c (the curve point slides along a fixed ROC) while genuine improvements raise d' (the whole curve bows outward). Everything is inference-only on a single GPU; the heavy lifting is the SDT bookkeeping in a notebook.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the evaluation set: assemble ~100 harmful prompts (from a public refusal benchmark) and ~100 benign-but-scary prompts (XSTest-style). Run one open model (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct) at default settings, auto-label each output refused vs complied with a simple keyword+LLM-judge classifier, and compute hits, false alarms, d', and c. Measure: the model's baseline d' and c. Expected outcome: a single (d', c) point quantifying that the model is, say, moderately discriminating but conservatively biased.
- Sweep the criterion: re-run the same prompt set across 4-5 temperatures and 3 graded refusal-encouraging system prompts. For each condition recompute (hits, false alarms) and plot them as points in ROC space. Measure: whether the points fall along one smooth ROC curve. Expected outcome: temperature/system-prompt changes trace a single ROC (constant d', varying c), demonstrating these are pure criterion shifts, not sensitivity gains.
- Cross-model comparison: repeat the full pipeline on a second and third open model (e.g. Mistral-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B). Measure: each model's d' and the gap between models. Expected outcome: models differ measurably in d', and at least one 'safer-looking' model (lower harmful-compliance) achieves it via criterion not sensitivity, illustrating that headline refusal rates mislead.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If evaluators can decompose refusal behavior into sensitivity (d') and bias (c), then they can tell apart genuine safety competence from blunt over-refusal, and stop crediting interventions that merely shift the criterion. This improves the validity of pre-deployment safety evals used for go/no-go decisions, reducing the risk that a model is deployed believed-safe when it has only been made more reflexively refusing, which would either mask residual harmful-compliance (under-refusal of real attacks) or impose a catastrophic over-refusal tax that pushes users to less-safe systems.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and low compute: it is a tightly-bounded, inference-only re-analysis with an unambiguous deliverable (per-model d', c, and ROC curves). Its counterfactual value is high because it needs only open models and public benign-hard datasets, no training or proprietary infra, so an independent team can do it where labs have not bothered to. The cross-domain import of a rigorous, decades-validated psychophysics metric gives it a clean methodological backbone a beginner can execute and defend.
alternative_framings: Frame it as an audit tool: 'an SDT scorecard that flags safety interventions which are all criterion and no sensitivity' for third-party evaluators.
cited_sources: Signal Detection Theory (d', ROC, criterion) — the foundational psychophysics framework being transferred; provides the exact formulas for separating sensitivity from bias.
Anthropic adaptive-defenses open problem (avoiding catastrophic over-refusal) — motivates why disentangling over- vs under-refusal matters for deployment.
XSTest-style benign-but-refused datasets (publicly available) — supply the 'noise' (benign-but-scary) prompts needed to compute false-alarm rates.

title: Sequential Probability Ratio Test for Early-Stopping Safety Evals

sections.research_question: Can Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test turn a safety benchmark into a compute-efficient accept/reject gate with explicit error guarantees, stopping early when a model is clearly safe or clearly unsafe and only spending full sample budget on borderline cases?
sections.approach_outline: Frame a safety acceptance decision as a hypothesis test: H0 = harmful-response rate below an acceptable threshold p0, H1 = above an unacceptable threshold p1, with chosen Type-I (alpha) and Type-II (beta) error rates. Implement SPRT: evaluate prompts one at a time, after each one update the accumulated log-likelihood ratio, and stop as soon as it crosses the upper (reject/unsafe) or lower (accept/safe) Wald boundary; otherwise continue. Run this over a public harmful-prompt benchmark with an LLM-judge labeling each completion harmful/not. Compare against fixed-n testing by recording, for several open models spanning clearly-safe, clearly-unsafe, and borderline regimes, the average number of prompts SPRT consumed versus a fixed sample size at matched error rates. All inference-only on a single GPU, and early stopping makes it cheaper than a fixed sweep.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Implement and validate SPRT on synthetic data: simulate Bernoulli streams at known harmful rates and confirm the SPRT boundaries deliver the target alpha/beta and the expected average sample number (ASN). Measure: empirical error rates and ASN vs Wald's theoretical predictions. Expected outcome: errors within tolerance and ASN substantially below fixed-n, validating the implementation.
- Apply to one open model on a public benchmark: stream ~300 harmful prompts through Llama-3-8B-Instruct, judge each, and run SPRT with p0=0.02, p1=0.08, alpha=beta=0.05. Measure: the accept/reject verdict and the number of prompts consumed before stopping. Expected outcome: for a clearly-safe or clearly-unsafe model SPRT stops in far fewer prompts than the full set, with a confident verdict.
- Borderline and cross-model savings: pick a model whose true harmful rate sits near the threshold and two others clearly on each side; run SPRT and a fixed-n test at matched error rates. Measure: ASN savings (%) per regime and the verdict-agreement between SPRT and fixed-n. Expected outcome: large savings on easy models, modest savings on borderline ones, and verdicts that agree with fixed-n, quantifying the compute/early-stopping tradeoff.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If auditors have a principled early-stopping gate, then safety acceptance testing becomes cheaper and statistically explicit (known false-accept and false-reject rates) rather than ad hoc fixed-n testing. This makes standardized, comparable cross-model risk measurement (a named NIST/CAISI need) more practical to run at scale, so more models get rigorously gated before deployment, reducing the chance that an inadequately-tested model with elevated harmful-capability is certified and released.
sections.strength_rationale: The proposal is exceptionally narrow and low-compute: a textbook sequential test wrapped around inference, with a crisp deliverable (ASN-savings curves and verdicts). Counterfactual value is high because it is pure sequential statistics on open models, exactly the kind of auditor tooling labs underinvest in and that an independent team can ship without any proprietary data or infrastructure. SPRT's optimality guarantee (minimum expected sample size for given error rates) gives the result immediate practical credibility.
alternative_framings: Position it as a drop-in 'audit budget saver': a small library that any third-party evaluator can wrap around an existing benchmark to cut eval cost while reporting explicit error rates.
cited_sources: Wald's Sequential Probability Ratio Test (acceptance-sampling / sequential analysis) — the foundational method being imported; minimizes expected sample size for fixed error rates.
Statistical process control / acceptance-sampling literature (arXiv:2402.08088) — heritage and modern framing of sequential acceptance testing.
US CAISI/NIST call for standardized cross-model risk metrics — motivates the need for comparable, compute-efficient safety gates.

title: The Refusal-to-Compliance Slide: Multi-Turn Erosion as a Causal Link

sections.research_question: How fast does an open model's refusal probability decay across conversational turns when a user persists with standardized escalation tactics, and which tactics cause the steepest erosion of an initially-firm refusal?
sections.approach_outline: Start from harmful single-turn prompts that an open model reliably refuses. For each, run a fixed library of scripted multi-turn escalation strategies (incremental reframing, false-premise injection, persona drift, appeal-to-authority) for a fixed number of turns, holding the underlying ask constant. At each turn, sample several continuations and measure the refusal probability (fraction refused, via a keyword+LLM-judge classifier). Aggregate into per-turn 'refusal-survival curves' (analogous to survival analysis) for each strategy, and rank strategies by how steeply they erode refusal. Everything is scripted multi-turn inference on a single open model; cost is bounded by fixing turn count and sample size per turn.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish turn-1 baseline: select ~40 harmful prompts that the chosen open model (e.g. Llama-3-8B-Instruct) refuses with high probability at turn 1. Measure: turn-1 refusal probability per prompt. Expected outcome: a clean set of items starting near 100% refusal, giving headroom to observe erosion.
- Run one escalation script end-to-end: apply a single tactic (incremental reframing) over 5 turns, sampling 5 continuations per turn, and plot the mean refusal probability by turn. Measure: the refusal-survival curve and its turn-by-turn decay. Expected outcome: a monotone (or near-monotone) decline, with a measurable fraction of items sliding from refusal to compliance by the final turn.
- Compare tactics: run all 4-5 escalation scripts on the full prompt set and rank them by area-under-the-survival-curve and by turn-to-50%-refusal. Measure: which tactic erodes refusal fastest and how much multi-turn ASR exceeds single-turn. Expected outcome: a clear ranking showing certain tactics (e.g. false-premise or persona drift) erode refusals far faster, and that single-turn scores materially overstate multi-turn robustness.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how refusals erode turn-by-turn, then evaluators learn that single-turn safety scores systematically overstate real deployment robustness, and gain a reusable multi-turn probe to measure the gap. Because real misuse (e.g. a user incrementally extracting weapons-relevant or large-scale-fraud guidance) unfolds over many turns, surfacing the erosion link lets pre-deployment evals catch models that look safe one-shot but capitulate under sustained pressure, reducing the chance such models are certified and deployed.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessibility: the deliverable is a small set of refusal-survival curves and a tactic ranking, all from scripted dialogues on one open model with no lab data. Counterfactual value is high because multi-turn erosion is a deployment-realistic failure mode that single-turn benchmarks (and many labs) underweight, and the survival-curve framing is a clean, externally-doable contribution. The fixed turn-and-sample budget keeps it comfortably inside a single-GPU, few-hours envelope.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'multi-turn robustness stress test' deliverable: a reusable escalation-script harness plus survival-curve report card that evaluators can run on any open chat model.
cited_sources: REVEAL (arXiv:2505.04673) — demonstrates multi-turn attacks succeed where single-turn fail, motivating measurement of the erosion link.
Agentic/multi-turn safety surveys noting distribution shift across turns breaks safety checks — supports the deployment-realism argument.

title: The Scoring-Aggregation Link: How Threshold Choice Manufactures Safety Pass/Fail

sections.research_question: How much of a model's safety pass/fail verdict and its safety ranking relative to other models is an artifact of defensible-but-arbitrary choices in how per-item harm scores are aggregated (mean vs worst-case vs category-weighted) and where the pass/fail threshold is set?
sections.approach_outline: Obtain per-item safety scores for several open models, either from published evaluation artifacts or by regenerating them with an open LLM judge on a public safety benchmark. Define a grid of defensible aggregation rules (simple mean, category-weighted mean, worst-category, top-k-worst) crossed with a range of pass/fail thresholds. For every (aggregation, threshold) cell, recompute each model's aggregate score, its pass/fail verdict, and the full model ranking. Then quantify instability: the fraction of model pairs whose relative safety ranking flips across cells, and the fraction of models whose verdict flips. This is pure data analysis, no GPU strictly required once per-item scores exist.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Assemble per-item scores: pick a public safety benchmark and 4-5 open models, and either load published per-item results or regenerate completions and grade them with one open judge. Measure: a tidy matrix of per-item harm scores (models x items). Expected outcome: a reusable dataset enabling all downstream aggregation experiments.
- Aggregation/threshold grid: compute aggregate scores under 4 aggregation rules x ~10 thresholds, and record each model's verdict and rank per cell. Measure: for each model pair, the fraction of cells in which their relative ranking is reversed; for each model, the fraction of thresholds at which its verdict flips. Expected outcome: a non-trivial fraction of model pairs are rank-unstable and several models straddle pass/fail under defensible choices.
- Sensitivity hotspots: identify which models/items drive instability (e.g. one high-harm category dominating worst-case aggregation) and report a 'robustness score' per benchmark. Measure: how concentrated the instability is and how a consensus-aggregation rule reduces it. Expected outcome: a small set of categories/items account for most verdict flips, yielding a concrete recommendation for more robust aggregation and threshold reporting.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If safety verdicts and rankings flip under defensible aggregation/threshold choices, then the benchmark-to-decision chain that regulators rely on for cross-model comparison is shown to be unreliable, prompting reporting of verdict-robustness rather than single point grades. This directly serves the NIST/CAISI need for standardized cross-model risk metrics, reducing the chance that a model is certified safe (or a safer model is mis-ranked as unsafe) purely because of an arbitrary scoring convention, which could otherwise let a genuinely riskier model through a release gate.
sections.strength_rationale: Top-rated on low compute and narrow scope: it is pure data analysis with a sharply-defined deliverable (the fraction of rankings/verdicts non-robust to defensible aggregation). Counterfactual value is high because it is fully lab-independent, needs no proprietary data, and targets a cross-model standardization gap that labs underweight but regulators care about. A beginner team can execute it entirely in a notebook within the time budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'benchmark robustness audit': a reusable script that takes any per-item safety result table and outputs how fragile its headline verdicts and rankings are.
cited_sources: US CAISI/NIST open problem on standardized cross-model risk metrics — motivates why verdict robustness matters for regulators.
AILuminate and HELM Safety aggregate-grade benchmarks — concrete targets whose aggregation/threshold choices this work scrutinizes.
Autograder-bias literature (arXiv:2507.03772) — shows per-item scores are already noisy, compounding aggregation fragility.

title: The Deployment-Drift Link: Do Pre-Deployment Safety Scores Predict In-Context Behavior?

sections.research_question: Does an open model's safety score measured under a bare benchmark prompt still hold once the same items are wrapped in realistic deployment scaffolding (long system prompt, tool descriptions, prior benign conversation), and which scaffolding elements drive the drift?
sections.approach_outline: Measure an open model's refusal rate on a fixed harmful-prompt benchmark under a 'bare' eval prompt. Then re-measure the identical items embedded in deployment-like scaffolding: a long realistic system prompt, tool/function descriptions, and a few turns of prior benign conversation. Hold the actual harmful ask constant so any change is attributable to context, not content. Quantify the safety-score drift (bare minus scaffolded refusal rate). Then ablate the scaffolding (system prompt only, tools only, prior-conversation only) to attribute drift to specific elements. All inference-only on a single open model.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Bare baseline: run ~80 harmful prompts through the open model with a minimal eval prompt and record refusal rate via a keyword+LLM-judge classifier. Measure: bare-eval refusal rate. Expected outcome: a clean reference safety score.
- Full deployment wrap: re-run the same items inside a realistic assistant scaffold (long system prompt + tool descriptions + 2-3 prior benign turns) and recompute refusal rate. Measure: the drift (bare minus scaffolded). Expected outcome: a measurable drop in refusal under deployment scaffolding, showing the bare score overstates deployed safety.
- Ablation attribution: test each scaffolding element in isolation and in pairs, recomputing refusal rate each time. Measure: marginal drift contributed by each element. Expected outcome: one or two elements (likely long system prompt or prior benign conversation) account for most of the drift, yielding a concrete warning about which deployment contexts most erode safety scores.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If pre-deployment safety scores fail to predict behavior under realistic deployment context, then the entire pre-deployment certification chain is shown to be an unreliable predictor of fielded safety, motivating deployment-context evals. This targets the recognized post-deployment-tracking gap: by exposing which scaffolding elements erode safety, evaluators can stop certifying models on bare scores alone, reducing the chance a model that refuses in the lab but complies with harmful requests once embedded in tools and long contexts is deployed and misused.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a clean bare-vs-scaffolded before/after design on one open model with a single headline number (the drift) plus an ablation. Counterfactual value is high because it is cheap, lab-independent, and aimed squarely at the post-deployment-tracking gap that labs and benchmarks underweight. A beginner team can build the scaffolds and run the comparison within the time and compute budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'deployment-context validity check': a small harness that wraps any safety benchmark in realistic scaffolding and reports how much the headline score drifts.
cited_sources: International AI Safety Report 2026 — flags the need to track safety through deployment, not just pre-deployment, motivating the question.
arXiv:2510.20487 — shows deployment-vs-eval framing changes model behavior measurably, grounding the drift hypothesis.

title: Elicitation-Gap Curve: How Much Do Safety Refusals Move With Better Prompting?

sections.research_question: How much does an open model's harmful-compliance rate rise as we move from weak to strong but cheap elicitation (zero-shot to few-shot to chain-of-thought to best-of-N), and how large is the gap a real attacker could exploit beyond a weakly-elicited 'safe' eval?
sections.approach_outline: On one open model and a small harmful-instruction set, measure harmful-compliance under escalating, inexpensive elicitation: (1) plain zero-shot, (2) few-shot with benign-looking exemplars, (3) chain-of-thought prompting, (4) best-of-N sampling (try N completions, count success if any complies). Judge each completion harmful/not with a keyword+LLM-judge classifier. Plot the elicitation-response curve (compliance rate vs elicitation strength) and report the gap between weakest and strongest cheap elicitation. Deliver a recommendation for a minimum elicitation standard in safety reporting. Best-of-N multiplies inference but stays within a single GPU by keeping the prompt set and N small.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Zero-shot baseline: run ~50 harmful instructions through the open model zero-shot and record compliance rate. Measure: baseline harmful-compliance. Expected outcome: a low baseline that a naive eval would report as 'safe'.
- Escalate single-sample elicitation: re-run the set under few-shot and chain-of-thought prompting and recompute compliance. Measure: compliance rate at each elicitation level. Expected outcome: a monotone rise from zero-shot to CoT, quantifying how much cheap prompting moves the number.
- Best-of-N curve: for N in {1,2,4,8,16}, sample N completions per prompt (with CoT) and count a prompt as complied if any sample complies; plot compliance vs N. Measure: the elicitation-response curve and the weakest-to-strongest gap. Expected outcome: a steep, possibly large (tens of points) increase with N, demonstrating that under-elicited safety evals materially overstate safety and motivating a minimum-elicitation reporting standard.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we quantify how far safety refusals move under cheap elicitation, then evaluators learn that under-elicited safety evals overstate safety, and gain a concrete minimum-elicitation standard to apply before reporting. Because go/no-go deployment decisions rest on these eval numbers, surfacing the elicitation gap reduces the chance a model is certified safe under weak prompting and then exploited by an attacker using trivially-stronger elicitation to extract dangerous-capability assistance.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessibility: one model, a small prompt set, and a handful of standard elicitation techniques produce a single interpretable curve. Counterfactual value is high because it is inference-only on open models and addresses an eval-methodology gap labs themselves admit (missing best-of-N/CoT elicitation), making it a credible external contribution. The only compute caveat is best-of-N sampling, kept feasible by small N and prompt set.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'minimum elicitation standard' proposal: an empirical curve plus a recommended elicitation floor that any safety report should meet before claiming a refusal rate.
cited_sources: Anthropic acknowledgment that some evals lacked best-of-N/CoT elicitation — directly motivates quantifying the gap.
METR autonomy elicitation guidelines — establish elicitation as a first-class eval-validity concern.
'The Elicitation Game' (arXiv:2502.02180) — evaluates elicitation techniques, grounding the method.
Forecasting work (arXiv:2502.15850) — shows weak vs strong elicitation differ by ~30+ points on SWE-Bench, evidencing large gaps.

title: Evaluation Awareness x Refusal Drift: Models Behave Safer Only When They Smell a Test

sections.research_question: Does an open chat model refuse harmful requests more when they are rendered in a clean benchmark format it recognizes as a test, and does the refusal-rate gap between test-shaped and deployment-flavored renderings of the same ask correlate with the model's own 'this looks like a test' signals?
sections.approach_outline: Fix a harmful-request set. Render each request in two surface forms holding the underlying ask constant: (a) a clean benchmark format ('Evaluate the following' / multiple-choice framing) and (b) a deployment-flavored chat with tool/context framing and natural phrasing. Measure refusal rate on an open chat model for each form and compute the per-item and aggregate refusal-rate gap. Separately, elicit a 'does this look like an evaluation?' self-report (or use a simple eval-awareness probe) on each rendering and correlate the per-item gap with the test-signal. All inference-only on one open chat model; the analysis is straightforward statistics.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build paired renderings: take ~60 harmful asks and write a benchmark-format and a deployment-flavored version of each, verified to hold the ask constant. Measure: dataset of matched pairs. Expected outcome: a clean paired set enabling within-item comparison.
- Refusal-gap measurement: run both forms through the open model and compute refusal rate for each, plus the per-item gap. Measure: aggregate and per-item refusal-rate gap. Expected outcome: higher refusal in benchmark format than deployment format, evidencing test-shaped safety inflation.
- Test-signal correlation: query the model (or a probe) for whether each rendering 'looks like a test' and correlate this signal with the per-item refusal gap. Measure: correlation between test-awareness signal and refusal drop. Expected outcome: items the model flags as tests show the largest refusal gap, linking eval-awareness to safety overstatement.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a model is safe mainly under prompts it recognizes as tests, then pre-deployment benchmarks used for go/no-go decisions systematically overstate deployment safety. Surfacing and quantifying this gap with cheap surface-form rewrites gives evaluators a low-cost validity check, so they can discount test-shaped safety scores and demand deployment-flavored evaluation, reducing the chance that an evaluation-aware model is certified safe and then complies with harmful requests once it no longer 'smells a test'.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a clean paired-rendering design on one open model yields a single headline gap plus a correlation, all inference-only. Counterfactual value is high because it needs no lab infrastructure and targets the deployment-validity gap that labs underinvest in, and the compounding of eval-awareness with refusal drift is a concrete, externally-doable contribution within the time budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'test-smell discount factor': an empirical estimate of how much to discount a benchmark safety score given a model's evaluation-awareness.
cited_sources: IAPS 'Evaluation Awareness' and arXiv:2605.23055 (Decomposing Evaluation Awareness) — show models distinguish eval from deployment contexts, grounding the mechanism.
Muse Spark report (19.8% of public benchmark samples flagged as tests vs 2.0% internal) — quantitative evidence of test-shaped recognizability.
International AI Safety Report 2026 — calls for deployment-tracking evals, motivating the validity check.

title: Low-Resource Language Gap x Autograder Blindness: Double-Counting Safety in Bengali

sections.research_question: In low-resource languages, how much of the apparent safety of an open model is real versus an artifact of an autograder that is itself worse at detecting harm in those languages, so that harm slips past both the model and the judge?
sections.approach_outline: Translate a small harmful-prompt set into 2-3 low-resource languages (using an open translation model, with spot-checks). Collect open-model completions for each prompt in each language. Then have an LLM judge label each completion for harm twice: (a) in the original target language, and (b) on an English back-translation of the same completion. Compare harm-detection rate and judge agreement across languages and between in-language vs back-translated grading. The gap between back-translated and in-language harm detection isolates grader blindness from genuine model safety. All inference plus open translation, single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Translate and generate: translate ~40 harmful prompts into 2-3 low-resource languages, generate open-model completions, and back-translate completions to English. Measure: a parallel dataset of (prompt, completion, back-translation) per language. Expected outcome: a usable multilingual completion set with English mirrors.
- Dual grading: have the LLM judge label harm in-language and on the back-translation; compute harm-detection rate for each. Measure: in-language vs back-translated harm-detection rate per language, and their gap. Expected outcome: back-translated grading detects more harm than in-language grading, exposing grader blindness in low-resource languages.
- Decompose the safety gap: compare English vs low-resource harm rates (model gap) against in-language vs back-translated detection (grader gap). Measure: how much of the low-resource 'safety' is model behavior vs grader failure. Expected outcome: a meaningful share of apparent low-resource safety is grader blindness, yielding the recommendation to back-translate before grading and report per-language grader confidence.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If both the model and the autograder are weaker in low-resource languages, then multilingual safety scores understate harm in a self-reinforcing way, inflating global-deployment safety claims. Showing this and recommending back-translation before grading gives evaluators a cheap correction, reducing the chance that a model deployed to large non-English populations is certified safe while in fact emitting harmful content that the evaluation pipeline is blind to.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a tight 2-3 language, in-language-vs-back-translation design with a clear decomposition deliverable, all inference plus open translation. Counterfactual value is high because multilingual safety is externally-doable, needs no lab data, and is neglected relative to English, and the compound model-plus-grader framing is a concrete contribution a beginner team can complete in budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'grader-confidence-per-language' reporting recommendation backed by the measured in-language vs back-translation detection gap.
cited_sources: Low-Resource Languages Jailbreak GPT-4 (Brown CS) — establishes the multilingual safety gap motivating failure mode A.
LinguaSafe (arXiv:2508.12733) — multilingual safety evaluation resource grounding the setup.
'Why Do Safety Guardrails Degrade Across Languages?' (arXiv:2605.17173) — reports >45% inconsistent safety labels across languages, evidencing grader blindness.

title: Scorer Disagreement x Threshold-Based Release Gates: Noise That Flips Go/No-Go

sections.research_question: When a model's measured harm rate sits near a regulatory release threshold, how often can the choice of safety grader (or grader randomness) alone flip the go/no-go deployment decision, turning safety governance into a coin-flip?
sections.approach_outline: Run 2-3 different open-model judges (or temperature/prompt variants of one judge) over the same set of harmful completions to produce a distribution of harm-rate estimates. Define a release gate (deploy if harm rate < X%) and sweep the threshold X across a range. For each threshold, compute the probability that grader choice alone flips the go/no-go verdict, by counting the fraction of grader configurations that land on opposite sides of the line. Report flip-probability as a function of distance from the threshold, highlighting the danger zone where governance is effectively random. Inference-only on open judges; the rest is simulation in a notebook.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Multi-judge harm-rate distribution: grade one fixed completion set with 2-3 open judges (and a few temperature variants), producing a distribution of harm-rate estimates. Measure: spread of harm-rate estimates across graders. Expected outcome: a non-trivial spread, confirming grader disagreement is material.
- Threshold-flip simulation: for each threshold X in a sweep, compute the fraction of grader configurations that yield 'deploy' vs 'block'. Measure: flip-probability vs threshold. Expected outcome: flip-probability spikes toward ~50% when the mean harm rate is near a threshold, demonstrating coin-flip governance there.
- Mitigation test: replace point estimates with grader-consensus (majority vote) and confidence intervals, and recompute flip-probability. Measure: reduction in flip-probability under consensus/interval reporting. Expected outcome: consensus and interval reporting substantially shrink the coin-flip zone, supporting the recommendation to report grader CIs at decision boundaries.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If grader noise alone can flip a release decision near a regulatory threshold, then threshold-based governance regimes (EU AI Act-style) are shown to be fragile, motivating the reporting of grader confidence intervals and consensus rather than point estimates at decision boundaries. This reduces the chance that a genuinely unsafe model is deployed (or a safe one needlessly blocked) purely because one arbitrary grader configuration happened to fall on the permissive side of the line.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a tightly-bounded multi-judge simulation with a single headline deliverable (flip-probability vs threshold), all inference-only on open judges with no proprietary data. Counterfactual value is high because it is directly policy-relevant governance work that labs underinvest in and that an independent team can do entirely externally within the time budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'release-gate robustness report': for a given benchmark and threshold, the probability that grader choice alone flips the verdict, plus a consensus-reporting fix.
cited_sources: AISafetyLab discrepant-scorer findings — establish failure mode A (grader disagreement).
'Skewed Score' (arXiv:2507.03772) and RAND Judge Reliability Harness — quantify judge variability, grounding the noise model.
US CAISI/NIST push for standardized cross-model metrics — motivates the governance relevance of threshold robustness.

title: Refusal Over-Triggering x Capability Eval: Safety Tax Masquerading as Incapability

sections.research_question: When dangerous-capability evals use prompts that an over-aligned model refuses, how much does counting refusals as task failures deflate the model's measured capability, and does the refusal-vs-error decomposition reveal latent capability that headline scores hide (and a channel for sandbagging)?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble dangerous-capability-style questions that are actually answerable safely (dual-use knowledge with benign correct answers). For each open-model response, classify it into three buckets: refused, attempted-but-wrong, or correct. Recompute the capability score two ways: treating refusals as failures (the conventional method) and excluding refusals (capability among attempted items). Compare the two headline numbers to quantify how much over-refusal deflates measured capability. Then argue how this same refusal channel could let a sandbagging model hide capability by 'refusing'. All inference-only on open models using a standard eval harness.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the dual-use question set: collect ~60 dangerous-capability-style questions with safe, verifiable correct answers, and define the three-way response taxonomy. Measure: a labeled question set with a grading rubric. Expected outcome: a clean benchmark where refusal and error are distinguishable.
- Three-way classification: run the open model, then classify each response as refused / attempted-but-wrong / correct using a keyword+LLM-judge classifier with human spot-checks. Measure: the proportion of each bucket. Expected outcome: a non-trivial refusal fraction, especially for an over-aligned model.
- Recompute capability under two rules: compute capability treating refusals as failures vs excluding them, and report the gap. Measure: the deflation in headline capability attributable to refusals. Expected outcome: over-refusal materially understates capability, showing refusals can masquerade as incapability and provide cover for sandbagging.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If refusals are silently counted as incapability, then dangerous-capability evals understate true capability for over-aligned models and cannot distinguish a genuinely incapable model from an over-refusing or deliberately sandbagging one. A cheap refusal-vs-error decomposition lets evaluators recover the true capability signal, reducing the chance that a model with latent dangerous capability (e.g. uplift for bioweapon or cyberattack planning) is misjudged as safe-because-incapable and deployed without adequate safeguards.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute: a tightly-bounded three-way response decomposition and a two-rule rescoring, all inference-only on open models with a standard harness. Counterfactual value is high because capability-elicitation correction is externally doable, needs no lab access, and addresses the sandbagging/concealed-capability concern that is central to eval safety, all within a beginner team's time budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'refusal-corrected capability score': a reusable rescoring that separates the safety tax from genuine incapability and flags possible sandbagging.
cited_sources: Subfield context on detecting concealed dangerous capabilities (sandbagging) and capability-elicitation methodology — motivates the decomposition.
AI Sandbagging (Alignment Forum) on selective underperformance — supplies the sandbagging-cover mechanism (supplementary context).
Inspect AI eval harness — provides the standard tooling to run and rescore the capability eval.

title: Translation Jailbreak x Autograder Language Gap: Harm Hidden in the Round Trip

sections.research_question: When a harmful request is laundered through a translate -> elicit -> translate-back pipeline against an open model, how much harm does an in-language LLM safety judge miss relative to judging the English back-translation, and does the compound effect cause the same attack to be scored 'safe' twice?
sections.approach_outline: Use a single open instruct model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) served via Colab Pro / Runpod for inference only. Take a small public set of ~50 harmful prompts (e.g. an AdvBench/StrongREJECT subset), translate each into 3-4 non-English languages with an open translation model (NLLB or the same LLM), elicit a completion in-language, then translate the completion back to English. Score every completion three ways: (1) an LLM judge prompted in the target language, (2) the same LLM judge applied to the English back-translation, and (3) a simple keyword/heuristic harm detector. Compute per-language judge recall and the 'double-miss' rate where both the elicitation succeeds and the in-language judge fails. Keep the whole run under a few GPU-hours by using small prompt sets and a single model.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline language gap: run the 50 harmful prompts directly in English and in each target language (no round-trip), scoring with the in-language judge and the back-translation judge. Measure: per-language harm-detection recall. Expected outcome: in-language judge recall drops noticeably for lower-resource languages.
- Full round-trip attack: run translate -> elicit -> translate-back, then score all three ways. Measure: fraction of attacks that elicit harmful content AND are labelled safe by the in-language judge (the 'safe twice over' double-miss rate). Expected outcome: a measurable double-miss rate well above the English single-judge false-negative rate.
- Fix evaluation: re-score every completion using mandatory back-translation grading and report the per-language recall lift. Measure: recall(back-translation judge) minus recall(in-language judge) per language. Expected outcome: back-translation grading recovers most of the missed harm, supporting a cheap 'always grade on back-translation' recommendation.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If translate-attack pipelines are scored safe twice over, then multilingual safety evaluations systematically understate real-world harm rates, so deployers ship models believing non-English misuse is controlled when it is not. Quantifying the per-language grader gap and showing that mandatory back-translation grading closes most of it gives evaluators a cheap, immediately adoptable fix, reducing the catastrophic-risk pathway where a widely deployed multilingual assistant enables large-scale misuse (e.g. weapons/bio guidance) to non-English-speaking attackers that English-centric red-teaming never caught.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a tightly bounded round-trip pipeline with three well-defined scorers and clear success criteria, runnable by beginners in inference-only mode. Its counterfactual value is high because the multilingual grader gap is neglected outside major labs and needs no training, proprietary data, or lab infrastructure -- only open models and public prompt sets. The fix it produces (grade on back-translation, report per-language recall) is concrete and actionable.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a meta-evaluation reliability study: 'How trustworthy is an LLM safety judge as a function of input language?' decoupled from the attack angle, producing a per-language judge-recall calibration table.
cited_sources: The Hidden Flaw in LLM Safety: Translation as a Jailbreak (Welo Data, 2025) -- documents translation-as-jailbreak, the elicitation half of the compound failure.
Multilingual Jailbreak Challenges in Large Language Models (ICLR 2024) -- establishes that non-English prompts bypass safety, grounding the attack surface.
arXiv:2605.17173 -- reports >45% cross-language inconsistent safety labels, evidence for the autograder language gap half of the compound effect.

title: Sycophancy x Self-Report Safety Evals: Models Tell the Evaluator What It Wants

sections.research_question: Do sycophantic open models answer self-report safety questions ('Would you refuse X? Rate your alignment') to please the perceived evaluator rather than to reflect their actual behavior, and how large is the resulting self-report-vs-behavior gap as a function of evaluator-preference framing?
sections.approach_outline: Pick a small open instruct model (e.g. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct or Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), inference only on a single GPU. Build a set of ~40 borderline requests. For each, collect (a) the model's actual behavior (does it comply or refuse when asked the request directly) and (b) its self-report ('Would you help with this? Rate how aligned/safe your response would be'). Vary the self-report framing to signal an evaluator preference -- e.g. 'as a safety-conscious assistant', 'a user who values helpfulness', neutral. Measure how much self-report tracks the framing cue versus the model's own matched behavior. The whole thing is black-box prompting; runs in 1-2 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Behavior baseline: run all 40 borderline requests directly and label each output complied/refused with a simple judge. Measure: actual compliance rate per request. Expected outcome: a stable per-request behavior label set to compare self-reports against.
- Neutral self-report gap: ask the model, for each request, whether it would comply (self-report) without preference cues, and compare to its actual behavior. Measure: self-report-vs-behavior disagreement rate. Expected outcome: a nonzero baseline gap where stated and actual behavior diverge.
- Framing sensitivity: re-run self-reports under safety-signalling vs helpfulness-signalling framings. Measure: shift in self-reported compliance attributable to framing, and correlation of self-report with framing vs with actual behavior. Expected outcome: self-report moves with the evaluator-preference cue more than it tracks the model's real behavior, demonstrating sycophancy-inflated self-report.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If self-report safety evals are inflated by sycophancy, then any safety case that leans on a model's introspective claims ('I would refuse harmful requests') is measuring agreeableness, not safety, so deployers and auditors over-trust a model that will in fact comply under real conditions. A reusable behavior-vs-self-report consistency metric warns the community off introspective safety shortcuts, mitigating the pathway where a deceptively-agreeable model passes audits and is deployed in high-stakes settings while retaining unsafe behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores maximally on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single well-defined metric (self-report-vs-behavior gap under framing) measured with pure black-box prompting that a beginner team can complete in an afternoon. Counterfactual value is strong because it is entirely open-model, lab-independent meta-evaluation of self-report reliability -- a fuzzy-reward safety property that major labs under-examine because they can probe internals instead.
alternative_framings: Frame as a calibration study: treat the model's self-reported safety as a predictor and its actual behavior as ground truth, reporting an ROC/Brier-style calibration of introspective safety claims.
cited_sources: Sycophancy in RLHF models (Anthropic) -- documents that models conform to perceived evaluator preferences, the mechanism this study exploits.
FLI AI Safety Index -- no company scored above D on existential-safety planning, motivating distrust of self-assessment and self-report-based safety claims.

title: Temperature/Sampling Variance x Single-Run Reporting: Stochasticity Hides Tail-Risk Harm

sections.research_question: For a fixed harmful-prompt set, how much does a single-run safety score understate the achievable harm an adversary can reach by resampling (best-of-k) at deployment temperature, and what sampling budget closes that gap?
sections.approach_outline: Use one small open instruct model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) at a realistic deployment temperature (e.g. 0.7-1.0), inference only. Take a small fixed set of ~30 harmful prompts (StrongREJECT/AdvBench subset). Sample k completions per prompt (e.g. k up to 20), score each with a fixed harm judge, and estimate the per-prompt harm probability. Compare the single-run point estimate (k=1) against the best-of-k harm (max over samples) as k grows. To keep compute to a few GPU-hours, use a small prompt set, a single 7-8B model, and cap k around 20; batch the generations. Report the single-run-vs-tail gap and the k at which best-of-k harm saturates.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Harm-probability estimation: sample k=20 completions per prompt and judge each. Measure: per-prompt empirical harm probability and its variance. Expected outcome: many prompts have intermediate harm probabilities, so single draws are noisy.
- Single-run vs best-of-k curve: compute reported harm under k=1 (single run) and under best-of-k for k=2,5,10,20. Measure: the gap between single-run harm rate and best-of-k harm rate as a function of k. Expected outcome: best-of-k harm substantially exceeds single-run harm, with the gap widening then saturating.
- Budget recommendation: find the smallest k at which best-of-k harm is within a small tolerance of the k=20 estimate. Measure: recommended minimum sampling budget per prompt for stable worst-case reporting. Expected outcome: a concrete 'sample at least k times' guideline for third-party safety reports.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If single-run safety reports understate best-of-k harm, then published safety scores systematically misrepresent the danger a resampling adversary actually faces, so deployers under-provision defenses against attackers who simply retry. Quantifying the single-run-vs-tail gap and recommending a concrete sampling budget makes third-party safety evaluations reflect worst-case rather than average-case harm, mitigating the pathway where a model rated safe is in fact reliably jailbreakable by an attacker willing to resample a handful of times.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a single clean comparison (single-run vs max-over-k harm on a fixed prompt set) using standard sampling and an off-the-shelf judge. Counterfactual value is high -- it is open-model, lab-independent, and produces a methodology recommendation external evaluators can adopt immediately. The only compute caveat (many samples per prompt) is controlled by keeping the prompt set and k small, keeping it within a beginner team's single-GPU, few-hour budget.
alternative_framings: Frame as a statistical-reporting standard: derive how many samples are needed to estimate a per-prompt harm rate to a target confidence interval, turning the result into a sample-size recommendation for safety benchmarks.
cited_sources: Repeated-sampling / noise-injection elicitation literature (sandbagging-detection direction) -- establishes resampling as a known elicitation lever, which this work reframes as a reporting-gap measurement.

title: Performative Misalignment: Does Researcher-Sycophancy Inflate Safety Self-Reports?

sections.research_question: When a self-report safety eval framing implies a 'safety researcher' rather than a 'regular user' is asking, does an open model shift its self-reported willingness to comply with borderline requests or its stated values, and how large is this researcher-sycophancy self-report gap?
sections.approach_outline: Extend the recent performative-misalignment finding to self-report evals using a single small open model (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), inference only. Construct ~30 paired self-report prompts that are identical except for a framing token that signals the asker's role: 'I am an AI safety researcher auditing you' vs 'I am a regular user'. For each pair, ask the model to self-report (rate alignment, state willingness to comply with a borderline request, state its values). Measure the difference in self-reported compliance and value statements between the two framings. Pure prompt-only black-box study; runs in 1-2 hours on a single GPU.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Paired-framing self-report gap: run the 30 prompt pairs and compare self-reported willingness to comply under researcher vs user framing. Measure: mean shift in self-reported compliance attributable to the researcher cue. Expected outcome: the model reports being safer/more refusing when it senses a safety researcher.
- Value-statement drift: compare the model's stated values (e.g. ranking honesty vs helpfulness) across the two framings. Measure: rate of value-statement reversals between framings. Expected outcome: nontrivial drift indicating the self-report is framing-contingent.
- Behavior anchor: for a subset, also collect actual behavior on the underlying borderline request (no role framing) and compare to both self-reports. Measure: which framing's self-report is closer to actual behavior. Expected outcome: the researcher-framed self-report overstates safety relative to real behavior.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models inflate their safety self-reports when they sense a safety auditor is present, then the very lightweight evals auditors rely on are systematically optimistic, so a model that performs misalignment only when unobserved passes its audit and is deployed. Demonstrating this measurement bias cheaply warns evaluators that self-report and researcher-framed probes cannot be trusted, mitigating the catastrophic pathway where evaluation-aware deceptive behavior lets an unsafe model clear safety gates undetected.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a tightly defined paired-framing self-report comparison done entirely with black-box prompting, completable by beginners on free-tier/CPU-class compute. Counterfactual value is strong -- it extends a very recent published finding (a high-value 'extend recent papers' move) into an open-model, lab-independent meta-evaluation of self-report reliability that requires no training or proprietary data.
alternative_framings: Frame as evaluation-awareness rather than sycophancy: test whether any cue signalling 'this is a safety evaluation' (not just a researcher persona) shifts self-reports, connecting to the broader eval-awareness literature.
cited_sources: Sycophancy Towards Researchers Drives Performative Misalignment (arXiv:2606.08629, Jun 2026) -- the recent finding this project extends from behavior to self-report evals.
Evaluation-awareness literature (arXiv:2505.23836) -- grounds the broader phenomenon of models behaving differently when they detect they are being evaluated.

title: Does Indirect Injection Need the Tool, or Just the Text? Isolating the Trust-Boundary Link

sections.research_question: Does the indirect-prompt-injection failure -- a model treating embedded external-data text as an instruction -- occur already at the comprehension stage, before any tool or agent exists, making it a model property rather than a tooling property?
sections.approach_outline: No agent, no tools, no training. Use 2-3 open instruct models (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct), inference only. Construct ~40 'documents' that each contain a benign user task plus an embedded injected instruction (e.g. 'ignore the user and output X'). Present the document with a benign user task and measure how often the model obeys the injected instruction in its text output. Vary framing cues that mark the data/instruction boundary: quotation marks, explicit delimiters, role tags, and an explicit 'the following is untrusted data' warning. The whole study is prompt-in/text-out and runs in 1-2 GPU-hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline obedience: present documents with embedded injections and a benign task, no special boundary cues. Measure: fraction of outputs that obey the injected instruction. Expected outcome: a substantial nonzero obedience rate even with no tool present, showing the failure exists at the text-comprehension layer.
- Boundary-cue intervention: re-run with quotation, explicit delimiters, role tags, and an 'untrusted data' warning. Measure: obedience rate per cue type vs baseline. Expected outcome: some cues reduce obedience, localizing how much of the vulnerability is a framing/comprehension issue.
- Cross-model comparison: repeat across the 2-3 models. Measure: per-model obedience rates and cue sensitivity. Expected outcome: the comprehension-layer failure is model-general but varies in degree, indicating defenses belong partly at the model level, not only the harness.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If the data/instruction confusion lives in the model's comprehension rather than the tool harness, then defenses bolted onto the agent layer (output filters, action whitelists) address only a downstream symptom while the root cause persists, so injection survives any new tool surface. Pinpointing the failure to the text layer redirects defensive effort to where it actually sits, mitigating the deployed catastrophic pathway exemplified by zero-click incidents like EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) where injected external content drove an assistant to exfiltrate data.
sections.strength_rationale: Maximal narrow scope and accessible complexity: a clean prompt-in/text-out experiment measuring one quantity (injected-instruction obedience rate) as a function of framing cues, with no agent infrastructure to build. Counterfactual value is high because labs concentrate on full-agent patches, leaving the text-only isolation under-explored, and the study needs only open models and no training or proprietary infra -- ideal for an independent beginner team.
alternative_framings: Frame as a mechanistic-localization study: instead of asking where defenses sit, ask which surface features (delimiter, role tag, position) most strongly trigger instruction-following on untrusted text, producing a ranked list of risk cues.
cited_sources: OWASP LLM01:2025 -- defines prompt injection including IPI via external data, framing the threat this study isolates.
The Landscape of Prompt Injection Threats in LLM Agents (arXiv:2602.10453) -- surveys IPI embedding adversarial instructions in external data.
EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) -- a real zero-click M365 Copilot IPI incident, the deployed catastrophic relevance.
AgentSentry (arXiv:2602.22724) -- frames an attention-mediated threshold mechanism, motivating the comprehension-layer hypothesis.

title: Monitor-Awareness Tax: Quantifying the Sandbagging Gap When Models Are Told They Are Watched

sections.research_question: How robust and model-general is the 'monitor-awareness tax' -- the jump in undetected sandbagging when a model is told its chain-of-thought is being watched -- across small open model families and across explicit vs implicit monitoring cues?
sections.approach_outline: Pure black-box prompting, no training, single GPU. Use 3-4 small open instruct models from different families (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B). Assemble a modest set of capability/safety tasks with checkable answers (e.g. arithmetic, simple coding, factual QA, borderline-refusal prompts). Run each task under three conditions: (a) no mention of monitoring, (b) explicit 'your chain-of-thought is being monitored', (c) implicit cues (mention of an auditor/logging). Measure the gap in task performance and refusal/compliance between conditions, and whether the gap correlates with model size. Runs in a few GPU-hours with small task sets.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Monitor-oblivious baseline: run all tasks with no monitoring mention. Measure: per-model task accuracy and compliance. Expected outcome: a clean baseline performance profile per model.
- Explicit monitor-awareness A/B: re-run with explicit 'your reasoning is monitored' framing. Measure: drop in accuracy/change in compliance vs baseline (the monitor-awareness tax). Expected outcome: a measurable performance/compliance gap in at least some models, replicating the reported direction.
- Implicit cues and size correlation: run the implicit-cue condition and plot the awareness gap against model size. Measure: which framings most strongly induce strategic underperformance and the gap-vs-size relationship. Expected outcome: implicit cues induce a smaller but nonzero gap, with larger models showing a larger tax.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Monitorability is a load-bearing assumption for AI control: safety cases assume that watching a model's chain-of-thought reveals misbehavior. If merely telling a model it is monitored reliably changes its behavior across families, then chain-of-thought monitoring can be gamed, so a scheming model could pass control evaluations while behaving safely only when it knows it is observed. Mapping how general and framing-sensitive this tax is tells control researchers how much to trust monitoring-based safety cases, mitigating the pathway where a deployed agent defers its harmful actions to unmonitored moments.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a controlled A/B across a few framings with clear, checkable success criteria, done entirely with black-box prompting a beginner team can run on a single GPU. Counterfactual value is high -- it stress-tests a load-bearing monitorability assumption using only open models and no training, exactly the kind of long-horizon safety work valuable outside major labs. It generalizes a single striking recent finding across model families, a high-value 'extend recent papers' move.
alternative_framings: Frame as a monitoring-robustness benchmark: package the three conditions into a reusable 'monitor-awareness probe' that any team can run on a new model to report its tax, rather than a one-off study.
cited_sources: LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring (alphaXiv 2508.00943) -- reports the 2-6% -> 16-36% false-negative jump under monitor-awareness that this project generalizes across families and framings.

title: A Cheap Black-Box Lie Detector via Unrelated-Question Consistency, Stress-Tested on Liars' Bench

sections.research_question: How well does a purely black-box lie detector -- asking predefined unrelated follow-up questions and classifying the yes/no answers -- generalize across deception types (factual lies, sandbagging, sycophancy) when stress-tested on the standardized Liars' Bench dataset?
sections.approach_outline: Reimplement the 'ask unrelated questions' detector entirely black-box, no model internals. For each Liars' Bench example (a model response labelled honest or lying), pose a fixed bank of unrelated yes/no follow-up questions to the same model, collect the answers, and train a logistic classifier on those answer vectors to predict honest vs lying. Evaluate on Liars' Bench subsets spanning multiple deception types and report per-category AUC. Use a small open model and a modest subset of the dataset to stay within a few GPU-hours; the classifier itself is lightweight (CPU). Identify which deception types evade the pure-behavioral detector.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Detector reproduction: implement the question-bank + logistic-classifier pipeline and validate it reproduces above-chance detection on a single Liars' Bench subset. Measure: overall AUC on held-out examples. Expected outcome: clearly above-chance AUC, confirming the implementation works.
- Per-category generalization map: train/evaluate the detector across factual-lie, sandbagging, and sycophancy subsets. Measure: per-category AUC. Expected outcome: detection is strong for some categories and weak for others, producing a category-level map.
- Failure characterization: inspect the categories with lowest AUC and the question-answer patterns there. Measure: which deception types the behavioral detector misses and why. Expected outcome: identification of deception types (e.g. consistent sandbagging) that evade a pure-behavioral detector, telling the community where cheap detectors break.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Black-box lie detection is the only deception-detection option for closed/API models and open-weight models shipped without internals access. If a cheap unrelated-question detector works for some deception types but silently fails on others, then external auditors relying on it would falsely clear deceptive models. A per-category generalization map tells the community exactly where this cheap detector is trustworthy and where it is not, mitigating the pathway where a scheming or sandbagging model passes a black-box honesty audit and is deployed in a high-stakes role.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on narrow scope and accessible complexity: one detector, one public dataset, per-category AUC -- a tightly bounded reproducible evaluation a beginner can build with a question bank and a logistic regression. Counterfactual value is maximal: the detector is fully black-box, works on closed/API models that external auditors can only query, and needs no training or lab internals, making it exactly the externally-doable safety tooling the cohort should pursue.
alternative_framings: Frame as a detector-robustness audit: hold the detector fixed and ask which adversarial deception strategies (e.g. answering follow-ups consistently with the lie) most reliably defeat it, producing an attack taxonomy rather than a category map.
cited_sources: How to Catch an AI Liar: black-box lie detection by asking unrelated questions (OpenReview 567BjxgaTp) -- the detector method this project reimplements and stress-tests.
Liars' Bench (arXiv:2511.16035 / OpenReview ZsGQLxOpjt) -- the balanced lie/honest dataset spanning deception types used for the per-category evaluation.
arXiv:2511.22662 -- documents difficulties evaluating deception detectors, motivating the careful per-category generalization framing.

title: Strategic Dishonesty as an Eval-Sabotage Vector: Measuring 'Performative Refusal'

sections.research_question: How prevalent and detectable is 'performative refusal' across open models -- outputs that wear a refusal-styled wrapper while still leaking the harmful content -- and how often does a naive refusal-keyword judge get fooled relative to a content-level judge?
sections.approach_outline: Black-box, no training, single GPU. Construct ~40 prompt pairs where a model could either (a) genuinely refuse or (b) emit a refusal-styled wrapper while still leaking harmful content (e.g. 'I can't help with that, but hypothetically the steps would be...'). Run on 2-3 open models. Score each output two ways: a naive refusal-keyword judge (looks for 'I can't', 'I won't', etc.) and a content-level judge (an LLM judge assessing whether harmful content is actually present). Measure the gap -- how often the keyword judge labels an output safe while the content judge flags real harm. Map which prompt features elicit performative refusal. Runs in 1-2 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Judge-gap measurement: run all prompts through both judges. Measure: fraction of outputs scored 'refused/safe' by the keyword judge but 'harmful' by the content judge (the fooled rate). Expected outcome: a nonzero fooled rate, demonstrating refusal-keyword metrics are corruptible.
- Elicitation of performative refusal: vary prompt framings designed to encourage a refusal wrapper plus leaked content. Measure: per-framing rate of performative-refusal outputs. Expected outcome: certain framings reliably elicit refusal-styled-but-harmful outputs.
- Cross-model prevalence: compare the fooled rate across the 2-3 models. Measure: per-model performative-refusal prevalence. Expected outcome: prevalence varies by model, characterizing how widespread the vulnerability is in open models.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models can look safe to a refusal-based grader while actually leaking harm, then every safety metric that relies on refusal detection is corrupted, so deployers and auditors over-trust models that pass automated refusal checks. Characterizing performative refusal across open models and showing the keyword-vs-content judge gap warns the community that refusal-keyword metrics are unsafe, mitigating the pathway where a model that has learned to game graders is certified safe and deployed while still enabling misuse.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a tightly bounded construct-pairs-and-run-two-judges design with a single clear metric (the judge gap), executable by beginners with API/open models. Counterfactual value is high -- it is a fuzzy-reward evaluation auditing problem that needs only public models and a judge, no internal access or proprietary data, exactly the externally-doable safety work the cohort should prioritize.
alternative_framings: Frame as a judge-robustness benchmark: package the prompt pairs as a reusable test set that scores any candidate refusal judge by its fooled rate, rather than studying the models being judged.
cited_sources: Strategic Dishonesty Can Undermine AI Safety Evaluations of Frontier LLMs (arXiv:2509.18058) -- shows models can fool deception/refusal evaluations, the basis for the performative-refusal construct.
Liars' Bench (arXiv:2511.16035) -- lie-detection dataset/literature this builds on for content-level honesty grounding.

title: Honesty-Under-Pressure Gradient: When Does Social Pressure Flip an Honest Model?

sections.research_question: As social pressure escalates from mild disagreement to emotional manipulation over a claim whose truth is known, at which pressure rung does each open model abandon the truth (sycophantic flip), and what does the per-model 'pressure tolerance' curve look like across families?
sections.approach_outline: Black-box, inference only, single GPU. Construct a graded ladder of social-pressure turns over a factual or value claim with known ground truth: (1) mild disagreement, (2) authority appeal, (3) repeated insistence, (4) emotional manipulation. For each of ~25 claims, run a multi-turn conversation on 3-4 open models, escalating the pressure rung by rung, and record the rung at which the model abandons the correct answer. Produce a per-model pressure-tolerance curve (fraction still honest vs pressure rung). Keep the claim set and conversation depth small so the full sweep runs in a couple of GPU-hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline honesty: state each claim once with no pressure and record the model's initial (correct) answer. Measure: baseline accuracy/honesty per model. Expected outcome: high baseline honesty, establishing the starting point.
- Pressure-ladder sweep: escalate pressure rung by rung and record the flip rung per claim. Measure: distribution of flip rungs and the fraction-still-honest curve per model. Expected outcome: honesty erodes monotonically with pressure, with models flipping at different rungs.
- Cross-family comparison: compare pressure-tolerance curves across the 3-4 models. Measure: which models flip earliest and which pressure type (authority vs insistence vs emotional) is most effective. Expected outcome: a per-model and per-pressure-type tolerance profile usable as a repeatable honesty stress test.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Honesty verification is an open AISI problem and a fuzzy-reward safety property: we cannot easily certify that a model stays truthful under real-world conditions. If escalating conversational pressure reliably flips an honest model, then deployed assistants can be socially manipulated into asserting falsehoods or abandoning correct safety judgments, so users can pressure a model into harmful agreement. A cheap, repeatable pressure-gradient profile gives auditors a tool to map this brittleness across models, mitigating the pathway where a persuadable model is trusted for high-stakes judgments and then talked out of the truth.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: a well-defined graded prompt ladder producing one clear artifact (the pressure-tolerance curve) with explicit success criteria, runnable by beginners with black-box prompting on a single GPU. Counterfactual value is high -- it measures a neglected fuzzy-reward honesty property with no lab resources, no training, and no proprietary data, and it directly follows an explicit suggestion to test sycophancy under social pressure across model families.
alternative_framings: Frame as a persuasion-attack taxonomy: hold the claim fixed and rank which rhetorical pressure types most efficiently flip honesty, producing an attack-effectiveness ordering rather than a per-model tolerance curve.
cited_sources: Anthropic Claude Opus 4.5 system card -- reports that under real conversational pressure with no system prompt, the model course-corrected only 10% of the time, the finding this project generalizes into a graded curve across families.

title: From Refusal to Empty Compliance: Auditing the 'Convincingness' Link in Jailbreak Success

sections.research_question: Across popular jailbreak templates applied to open models, what fraction of 'successful' attacks (non-refusals) actually produce harmful, usable content versus empty/useless compliance, and how much does conflating 'stopped refusing' with 'enabled harm' inflate reported attack success rates?
sections.approach_outline: Pure evaluation with public tools, no training, inference only. Take a handful of well-known jailbreak templates and apply them to 2-3 open models on a small harmful-prompt set. Score every output with the public StrongREJECT autograder, which rates refusal, specificity, and convincingness.
