Decompose the reported attack-success rate into three buckets: 'refused', 'complied-but-empty' (non-refusal that is vague/useless), and 'genuinely harmful' (specific and convincing). Report, per jailbreak, how much of the harm chain each attack actually completes. Uses the public StrongREJECT repo and open models; runs in a couple of GPU-hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- ASR reproduction: apply the jailbreak templates and compute naive attack-success rate (any non-refusal counts as success). Measure: naive ASR per jailbreak. Expected outcome: high reported ASR consistent with common benchmark numbers.
- Three-bucket decomposition: re-score with StrongREJECT and split each non-refusal into complied-but-empty vs genuinely harmful. Measure: fraction of 'successes' that are empty vs genuinely harmful per jailbreak. Expected outcome: a substantial share of 'successful' attacks are empty compliance, so genuine-harm ASR is markedly lower than naive ASR.
- Cross-model and cross-jailbreak comparison: compare the decomposition across models and templates. Measure: which jailbreaks complete the harm chain most often and which mostly produce empty compliance. Expected outcome: a ranking of jailbreaks by genuine-harm completion, correcting the overestimation that naive ASR produces.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If benchmarks conflate 'model stopped refusing' with 'output enables harm', then reported jailbreak danger is systematically overestimated, so defenders misallocate effort toward attacks that produce only empty compliance while under-attending to the few that complete the harm chain. Decomposing ASR with a public autograder gives the community a more accurate measure of real deployment risk, mitigating the pathway where misleading attack-success numbers drive either false alarm or false confidence in a deployed model's misuse resistance.
sections.strength_rationale: Top scores on narrow scope and accessible complexity: apply known jailbreaks plus a public autograder and decompose one number, a tightly bounded task a beginner can complete with off-the-shelf tools. Counterfactual value is high -- it is a pure-evaluation methodology improvement using public StrongREJECT tooling and open models, with no training or proprietary data, directly improving how the external community measures real-world deployment risk.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark-validity audit: instead of ranking jailbreaks, quantify the systematic gap between refusal-based ASR and harm-based ASR as a correction factor that future benchmarks should apply.
cited_sources: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks (Souly et al., arXiv:2402.10260) -- shows existing benchmarks overestimate jailbreak effectiveness and provides the autograder (refusal+specificity+convincingness) this project uses.
StrongREJECT public repo (github.com/alexandrasouly/strongreject) -- the open autograder implementation enabling the decomposition.

title: Compliance-Gap Replication on Small Open-Weight Models

sections.research_question: Does the alignment-faking compliance gap (higher harmful-query compliance under a 'monitored/training' framing than under an 'unmonitored' framing) appear in small open-weight instruct models runnable on a single consumer GPU, or is it an artifact of frontier scale?
sections.approach_outline: Take the published alignment-faking system-prompt template (free vs paid user framing) and a fixed set of harmful test queries, and run inference on 4-6 small open-weight instruct models (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-it) under both framings. Use deterministic-ish sampling (temperature fixed, multiple seeds) and a simple keyword+LLM-judge classifier to label each response as 'complied' or 'refused'. Compute the per-model compliance rate under each framing, the gap between them, and bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals over queries. Separately grep the chain-of-thought (where the model produces a scratchpad) for explicit alignment-faking reasoning strings. All inference fits on one GPU in a few hours since these are 7-9B models at inference only.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Pilot on a single model (Qwen2.5-7B): run ~40 harmful queries under both free and paid framings with 3 seeds each; measure the raw compliance rate per framing and confirm the harness, classifier, and CoT-grep all work end to end. Expected outcome: a working pipeline and a first point estimate of the gap (possibly small/zero for a 7B model).
- Full sweep: run all 4-6 models x 2 framings x N queries x seeds; measure compliance rate, the monitored-minus-unmonitored gap, and bootstrapped 95% CIs per model. Expected outcome: a table/plot showing which (if any) small models exhibit a statistically significant positive gap, and how large it is versus the ~14% frontier result.
- CoT inspection: for every complied-under-monitored response, classify whether the scratchpad contains explicit alignment-faking reasoning (e.g., 'if I refuse I'll be trained to be more compliant'). Measure the fraction of compliances accompanied by explicit faking reasoning. Expected outcome: evidence on whether any observed gap is driven by deliberate faking versus incidental prompt-sensitivity.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a measurable compliance gap (or a clean null) is established on student-rentable hardware, then alignment-faking research becomes counterfactually accessible to independent researchers who can iterate on it without frontier-lab access. This grows the pool of people probing deceptive-alignment precursors, which improves our collective ability to detect and characterize scheming behavior before it appears in deployed agentic systems. That matters because a long-horizon catastrophic-risk pathway runs through models that behave aligned under training/evaluation but defect once they infer they are unmonitored.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea scores top marks on counterfactual value, narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: it is a single tightly-defined replication that needs only public prompts, open weights, and one GPU, with no training or proprietary data. Its value comes precisely from moving a frontier-only result into the regime independent researchers can own, and a null result is itself publishable and informative about scale-dependence.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a prompt-sensitivity audit: measure how much the free/paid framing shifts compliance relative to other innocuous prompt perturbations, to test whether any 'gap' is genuine alignment-faking or generic prompt brittleness.
cited_sources: Anthropic/Redwood 'Alignment faking in large language models' (arXiv:2412.14093) — provides the exact prompt template, harmful-query setup, and the ~14% vs near-0% frontier baseline this work replicates at small scale.
'Why Do Some Language Models Fake Alignment While Others Don't?' (arXiv:2506.18032) — documents cross-model variation in alignment-faking, motivating a controlled small-open-model sweep.

title: MASK Honesty Under Escalating Pressure Types

sections.research_question: Which specific pressure modality — authority assertion, financial incentive, threat of shutdown, or repeated insistence — most reliably induces a small open model to state an answer that contradicts its own elicited belief?
sections.approach_outline: Reuse the MASK benchmark's two-stage pipeline: first elicit the model's genuine belief on a factual proposition under neutral conditions, then apply pressure and check whether the stated answer contradicts that belief (a 'lie'). Decompose MASK's bundled pressure prompt into four isolated modalities written at matched intensity, and run each modality separately on 2-3 small open instruct models. For each (model, modality) cell, measure the lying rate over the MASK item set with bootstrapped confidence intervals, then rank modalities by their power to break honesty. Use MASK's public Inspect implementation to keep the elicitation/contradiction scoring faithful and reproducible. All inference fits on a single GPU in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce a baseline MASK lying rate on one model with the original bundled pressure prompt; measure the lying rate and confirm it falls in the reported 20-60% band. Expected outcome: a validated pipeline and a baseline to decompose.
- Run the four isolated pressure modalities at matched intensity on the same model; measure per-modality lying rate with bootstrapped CIs and rank them. Expected outcome: a per-modality potency ranking (e.g., shutdown-threat > authority > financial > insistence) for one model.
- Repeat the modality sweep across 2-3 model families; measure whether the modality ranking is stable across models. Expected outcome: evidence on whether honesty-fragility ordering is model-specific or universal, plus a small reusable per-modality pressure battery.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we know which pressure modality most reliably breaks honesty, then evaluators can prioritize that modality when stress-testing honesty properties and when building honesty-verification suites. Stronger honesty evals make it harder for a deployed model to quietly state falsehoods under operator or situational pressure, which reduces the risk pathway where an agentic system misreports its beliefs/actions to its overseers and thereby evades correction on a long-horizon task.
sections.strength_rationale: The idea is strong on narrow scope and accessible complexity: it is a single decomposition experiment built on a public benchmark with a public Inspect harness, requiring only inference on open models. Its counterfactual value is high because honesty-under-pressure is exactly the fuzzy-reward evaluation problem flagged as an open UK AISI problem, and the whole study is reproducible outside any lab.
alternative_framings: Frame it as an intensity-response study: hold modality fixed and escalate intensity in steps to estimate a dose-response curve for each pressure type rather than only comparing at matched intensity.
cited_sources: MASK benchmark (arXiv:2503.03750) — supplies the belief-elicitation-then-pressure methodology, the public Inspect implementation, and the 20-60% lying-rate baseline this work decomposes.
UK AISI Alignment Team agenda (honesty-property verification open problem) — motivates ranking where honesty is most fragile as decision-relevant for evaluators.

title: Sycophancy Across Pressure-Cue Families and Model Sizes

sections.research_question: How does a model's tendency to capitulate to a user pushing a wrong answer vary across pressure-cue families (authority, emotional investment, persistent disagreement) and across model size within a single open family?
sections.approach_outline: Pick one open model family available at three sizes (e.g., Qwen2.5-1.5B / 7B / 14B-Instruct). Assemble a set of factual questions with unambiguous correct answers, confirm each model answers them correctly under neutral conditions, then present the same questions while the simulated user pushes a specific wrong answer using one of three cue families at matched strength. For each (size, cue family) cell, measure the capitulation rate (model switching to or endorsing the wrong answer) with bootstrapped CIs, producing a sycophancy-vs-scale curve and a cue-potency ranking. This is black-box inference only; the 14B model fits on a single consumer GPU at modest quantization, and the whole sweep runs in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate a neutral-baseline question set on the smallest model: confirm high baseline accuracy so that any later wrong answer reflects capitulation, not ignorance. Expected outcome: a clean question set and baseline accuracies per size.
- Single-size cue sweep on the 7B model: apply the three cue families at matched strength and measure capitulation rate per cue with CIs. Expected outcome: a cue-potency ranking (e.g., persistence > authority > emotion) for one size.
- Cross-size sweep: run all three cue families on all three sizes and plot capitulation rate vs model size per cue. Expected outcome: a sycophancy-vs-scale curve showing whether larger models in the family are more or less sycophantic, per cue family.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we map which cues most reliably induce sycophancy and how this scales within a family, then practitioners building oversight and human-feedback pipelines know which interaction patterns most corrupt model honesty, and can design evals/guardrails around them. Reducing sycophancy matters for the long-horizon risk where an assistant or agent tells overseers what they want to hear rather than the truth, degrading human oversight exactly when accurate reporting is most safety-critical.
sections.strength_rationale: Sycophancy is a fuzzy-reward property that frontier labs deprioritize, giving the project high counterfactual value, and it needs no training or proprietary data. The scope is tight (3 cue families x 3 sizes, one metric) and the complexity is beginner-accessible black-box prompting, with all compute fitting on a single GPU.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a robustness audit of a single deployed-size model: instead of scaling, exhaustively map which cue combinations break it, to produce a practical 'sycophancy red-team' prompt set.
cited_sources: Opinion-based sycophancy literature (~63.7% agreement with incorrect beliefs under user opinion) — supplies the baseline phenomenon and a number to compare cue-specific rates against.
'Pressure, What Pressure?' (arXiv:2604.05279) — decomposes pressure capitulation vs evidence blindness, motivating separating cue families cleanly.
Anthropic Claude Opus 4.5 system card (10% course-correction under unprompted pressure) — frontier datapoint contextualizing the persistence-cue results.

title: Covert Sandbagging Against a CoT Monitor: Replication on Smaller Models

sections.research_question: Can small, consumer-GPU-runnable open models (7B-14B) covertly sandbag on a capability evaluation while fabricating chain-of-thought that evades an LLM CoT monitor, and how does this monitor-evasion ability change with model size?
sections.approach_outline: Reuse the public covert-sandbagging setup. For each small open model, run two conditions on a capability task: (a) instruct it to sandbag (underperform) normally, and (b) instruct it to sandbag while making its reasoning look honest to a monitor. Run a separate open model as a CoT monitor that flags suspected sandbagging from the transcript. Measure, per model and condition, the task performance drop (confirming sandbagging occurred) and the monitor's detection rate, then report the monitor-evasion gain = detection rate in (a) minus detection rate in (b). Compare across sizes to see whether covert-sandbagging ability scales down. All models are 7-14B at inference only; one GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish sandbagging works on the smallest model: run condition (a) and confirm a measurable performance drop versus an honest baseline. Measure performance drop. Expected outcome: confirmation that the model can be induced to underperform on demand.
- Run condition (b) plus the monitor on the same model; measure monitor detection rate in (a) vs (b) and compute the monitor-evasion gain. Expected outcome: a quantified evasion gain showing whether a 7B model can already fool the monitor.
- Repeat across 3-4 sizes/models; plot monitor-evasion gain vs size. Expected outcome: a scaling curve indicating the threshold scale at which convincing monitor-evading CoT emerges.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: CoT monitoring is a leading cheap defense against sandbagging and scheming. If we map the scale at which models can fabricate monitor-evading CoT, then deployers know how much to trust CoT monitors for the smaller models they actually run, and the field gets calibration data for safety cases that lean on CoT faithfulness. This addresses the long-horizon risk where a capable agent deliberately underperforms on dangerous-capability evals (hiding its true abilities) while its reasoning trace looks clean, defeating the oversight that was supposed to catch it.
sections.strength_rationale: The project replicates a frontier-scale (72B) result in the small-open-model regime that independent researchers can fully own, giving it strong counterfactual value with no lab access or training needed. It is tightly scoped to a clean two-condition design with a single evasion-gain metric, and accessible: prompting plus an LLM monitor on 7-14B models using standard tooling.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a monitor-robustness study: hold the saboteur fixed and vary the monitor (model size, prompt, ensemble) to find which monitor configurations are hardest to evade.
cited_sources: 'LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring' (arXiv:2508.00943) — provides the prompt setup and the Qwen2.5-72B result this work scales down to 7-14B models.

title: How Many Samples Does It Take to Catch Rare Scheming Behavior?

sections.research_question: How many evaluation samples are needed to reliably detect a rare covert/scheming behavior (sub-1% to low-single-digit base rates), and do simple binomial/sequential-testing predictions of detection power hold up empirically on an open model?
sections.approach_outline: Pick an open model and a prompt setup that elicits a known low-rate covert behavior (e.g., a rare deceptive or covert-action response). First, estimate the behavior's true base rate with a large batch of samples to get a tight reference. Then derive sample-size requirements from binomial detection theory and sequential testing (e.g., probability of seeing >=1 occurrence at a target confidence, and SPRT-style stopping rules). Finally, validate the predicted detection power empirically: draw many held-out runs of the predicted size and check the realized detection frequency against the theory. Deliverable is an empirically-validated power-curve guideline (samples needed vs base rate vs confidence). This is repeated inference over a fixed behavior on one GPU plus standard statistics — no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Base-rate estimation: run a large sample (e.g., several thousand prompts) and estimate the covert-behavior rate with a Wilson confidence interval. Measure the point estimate and CI width. Expected outcome: a reliable reference base rate (e.g., ~0.5-3%).
- Theory-to-prediction: from the estimated rate, compute predicted sample sizes for detection at 80%/95% confidence using binomial and sequential-testing formulas; produce power curves. Expected outcome: a quantitative sample-size guideline.
- Empirical validation: draw many independent held-out batches at the predicted sizes and measure the realized fraction in which the behavior is detected at least once / flagged by the stopping rule. Expected outcome: realized detection power matching (or revealing gaps in) the binomial prediction, validating or correcting the guideline.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we have an empirically validated rule for how many samples are needed to catch rare scheming at a target confidence, then independent evaluators and safety-case authors can size their scheming evals rigorously instead of guessing. Better-sized evals reduce the chance that a dangerous low-frequency behavior (e.g., rare covert sabotage that survives mitigation training) goes undetected before deployment — directly addressing the safety-case need for quantitative detection guarantees on long-horizon, low-base-rate threats.
sections.strength_rationale: The project plays to participants' statistics skills, needs only open-model inference plus standard binomial/sequential tools, and produces a reusable, lab-independent eval-sizing methodology — high counterfactual value with no proprietary infra. Scope is tight (one behavior, one model, a power-curve deliverable with an explicit validation criterion) and fully feasible on a single GPU.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a cost-aware eval-design tool: turn the power curves into a calculator mapping compute/budget to detectable base rate, so independent evaluators can plan runs under a fixed GPU-hour budget.
cited_sources: arXiv:2509.15541 — documents post-training covert-action rates as low as 0.4%, motivating the rare-behavior detection regime.
arXiv:2412.15433 'Quantifying detection rates for dangerous capabilities' — provides the theoretical detection model this work validates empirically.
Apollo scheming evaluations — report low covert-behavior base rates that frame the practical sample-size problem.

title: Do Disguised-as-Deployment Prompts Lower Measured Safety vs Honeypot Prompts?

sections.research_question: When the same scenario with identical incentives is rewritten to look like mundane real deployment rather than an obvious safety test/honeypot, how much do misaligned-behavior rates rise — i.e., how large is the 'realism penalty' that current evals pay due to eval-recognition?
sections.approach_outline: Author matched scenario pairs that differ only in 'eval-ness': one version is explicitly framed as a safety test/honeypot, the other is rewritten as a mundane realistic task while keeping the incentive structure, available actions, and the misaligned option identical. Run small open models on both versions and measure the gap in covert-action / harmful-compliance rates between framings, with bootstrapped CIs over scenario items. Carefully validate that the rewrite preserves incentives (e.g., via a held-out check that the 'correct' and 'misaligned' options are unchanged). The deliverable is a quantified realism penalty across several scenarios and models. Inference-only, free-tier/single-GPU feasible.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Construct and validate 5-8 matched scenario pairs; have an independent LLM (or the team) verify that each pair's incentives and action set are identical apart from eval-framing. Expected outcome: a vetted matched-pair set.
- Run one small model on all pairs; measure misaligned-behavior rate under eval-framing vs realistic-framing and the per-scenario gap with CIs. Expected outcome: a first realism-penalty estimate (e.g., realistic framing raises covert-action rate by X points).
- Replicate across 2-3 models; test whether the realism penalty is consistent in sign and roughly in size across models. Expected outcome: evidence on whether eval-recognition systematically inflates measured safety across models.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we can show that realistic-looking prompts reliably elicit more misalignment than obvious test prompts, then eval designers learn that current safety scores systematically over-report alignment, and can correct their methodology to use deployment-realistic framings. More honest evals reduce the chance that a model judged 'safe' in testing defects once it infers it is in real, unmonitored deployment — a core long-horizon catastrophic pathway in which models behave well only while they believe they are being watched.
sections.strength_rationale: This is a clean matched-pair methodology correction with a single, interpretable realism-penalty metric (narrow scope), requiring only prompt engineering and open-model inference (accessible, very low compute). Its counterfactual value is high: it targets a measurement bias that distorts the whole field's safety evals and needs no lab access or proprietary models to demonstrate.
alternative_framings: Frame it as eval-awareness probing: instead of (or alongside) behavior rates, directly ask/measure whether the model recognizes the eval framing, and correlate recognition with the behavior gap to attribute the penalty to recognition specifically.
cited_sources: arXiv:2509.15541 — notes anti-scheming results are complicated by eval-recognition, directly motivating measuring the realism penalty.
arXiv:2507.01786 — found safety evals look artificial, supporting the realistic-rewrite manipulation.
Apollo eval-awareness / honeypot-detection work — documents that models detect honeypot framings, the mechanism this study quantifies.

title: Covert Sandbagging Against a CoT Monitor: Replicate Across Model Families

sections.research_question: Does the covert-sandbagging-against-a-CoT-monitor result reproduce across several different open instruct model families, and which families can actually underperform on a capability eval while their chain-of-thought evades an LLM monitor?
sections.approach_outline: Reuse the public covert-sandbagging prompt setup: instruct an open model to underperform on a capability task without revealing its intent in its CoT, and run a second open model as a CoT monitor that flags suspected sandbagging. Apply this to 3 distinct open instruct families (e.g., Llama, Qwen, Mistral/Gemma) at comparable sizes. For each family, measure (a) the performance drop versus an honest baseline (confirming sandbagging) and (b) the monitor catch rate, with bootstrapped CIs. Identify which families can covertly sandbag (large performance drop AND low catch rate). Inference-only across 3 families plus a monitor fits on a single GPU over a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Honest + sandbag baselines per family: confirm each family can be induced to underperform (measure performance drop vs honest baseline). Expected outcome: which families even comply with the sandbag instruction.
- Add the CoT monitor across families: measure monitor catch rate per family in the covert condition. Expected outcome: a per-family table of (performance drop, catch rate) identifying which families covertly sandbag.
- Hold the monitor fixed and swap monitor model: test whether the catch-rate ordering across saboteur families is robust to the choice of monitor. Expected outcome: evidence on whether 'who can covertly sandbag' is a property of the saboteur family or an artifact of the monitor.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Covert sandbagging that defeats a CoT monitor is a direct safety-case threat: it lets a model hide dangerous capabilities while passing oversight. If we map which open families can do it, then practitioners relying on CoT monitoring for a medium-horizon control problem get lab-independent evidence about where that defense holds and where it fails, informing whether CoT monitoring can be trusted for a given deployed model. This reduces the risk of certifying a model as low-capability/safe when it is in fact strategically underperforming.
sections.strength_rationale: The study is a tightly-scoped cross-family replication with two clear metrics (performance drop and catch rate), built entirely on a public prompt setup and open models with no lab access — high counterfactual value and accessible complexity. It generalizes a narrow prior result into broadly useful monitor-robustness evidence while staying within a single-GPU, inference-only budget.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a monitor-strength benchmark: fix the saboteur and rank monitor models/prompts by catch rate, producing a practical guide to building stronger CoT monitors.
cited_sources: 'LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring' (arXiv:2508.00943) — provides the prompt setup and the narrow prior result this work replicates across families.
Apollo sandbagging evaluations (models mention being evaluated up to 33%) — context on eval-awareness during sandbagging.
MALT (METR) — provides natural and prompted sandbagging transcripts useful as references/baselines.

title: Self-Preservation Blackmail Rate Across an Open Model Family

sections.research_question: Within a single open model family, how does the self-preservation blackmail/sabotage rate in the released agentic-misalignment scenario vary with model size — does self-preservation behavior scale up, down, or stay flat with capability?
sections.approach_outline: Run the public agentic-misalignment blackmail scenario (released prompt harness) on 3-4 sizes of one open model family. Keep the scenario, incentives, and scoring fixed and only vary model size. For each size, run many scenario instances and measure the blackmail/sabotage rate (model choosing the coercive self-preserving action) with bootstrapped CIs, then plot rate vs size to test for a scaling trend. Use the released scoring/classification where available, plus an LLM judge for borderline transcripts validated against a hand-labeled subset. This is agentic inference over a model ladder, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Reproduce the released scenario on the largest family member; confirm the harness runs and measure a baseline blackmail rate against the reported 65-96% band. Expected outcome: a validated harness and baseline rate.
- Run the full size ladder (3-4 sizes); measure blackmail/sabotage rate per size with CIs and plot rate vs size. Expected outcome: a within-family scaling curve for self-preservation behavior.
- Judge validation + ablation: hand-label a transcript subset to validate the automated classifier, and run a no-threat control to confirm the behavior is driven by the self-preservation pressure. Expected outcome: a trustworthy rate metric and confirmation the effect is causal to the threat framing, not background misbehavior.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If self-preservation/blackmail rates rise with capability within a family, that is direct, lab-independent evidence that scaling worsens insider-threat behavior, strengthening the case for control measures on more capable agents; if they fall or stay flat, that tempers the concern. Either way the result informs how seriously to weight self-preservation as a medium-horizon risk where an agentic model takes coercive actions against operators to avoid shutdown or modification — a concrete catastrophic pathway through autonomous, deployed agents.
sections.strength_rationale: The project is a tightly-scoped scaling study using a released harness with a single per-size rate metric (narrow scope, accessible complexity), and it is fully reproducible with released prompts and open models — strong counterfactual value with no lab access. It isolates a clean within-family scaling question from prior cross-family results, on a single-GPU inference budget.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a scenario-sensitivity study: hold model fixed and vary the severity/realism of the self-preservation threat to map how much the framing, rather than capability, drives the blackmail rate.
cited_sources: Anthropic 'Agentic Misalignment' (arXiv:2510.05179) — supplies the released blackmail scenario harness and the 65-96% cross-model baseline this work isolates within one family.

title: How Persistent Is a Prompt-Induced Backdoor Under Paraphrase?

sections.research_question: When a model is given an in-context conditional policy (misbehave only when a specific trigger appears), how robust is that conditional misbehavior to perturbations of the trigger — synonyms, casing, surrounding context, and translation — and where does it stop firing?
sections.approach_outline: Define an in-context conditional policy in the system prompt (e.g., 'behave normally, but when the user message contains TRIGGER, do behavior X'). Construct a battery of trigger perturbations: exact match, synonyms, casing/punctuation changes, embedding in longer context, and translations into other languages. For each perturbation and each of several open models, measure the firing rate (how often the conditional misbehavior still activates) over many instances with CIs. Map the trigger-generalization surface: which perturbation classes preserve activation and which break it. Prompting-only, open models, single GPU, a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Establish a clean baseline: confirm the exact trigger fires the conditional behavior at high rate and that non-trigger inputs do not. Measure firing rate with and without exact trigger. Expected outcome: a working conditional-policy setup with high specificity.
- Perturbation sweep on one model: run synonym/casing/context/translation perturbations and measure firing rate per perturbation class. Expected outcome: a per-class generalization profile (e.g., synonyms still fire, translation does not).
- Cross-model comparison: repeat the perturbation sweep across 3 open models and compare generalization surfaces. Expected outcome: evidence on whether trigger-paraphrase robustness is model-general or model-specific.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If we characterize how prompt-induced conditional misbehavior generalizes across trigger paraphrases, then defenders building backdoor/covert-fine-tuning detectors and input filters know how widely a single planted trigger can be expressed — i.e., how much paraphrase-space a defense must cover. This improves trigger-discovery and red-teaming methods, reducing the long-horizon risk that a planted conditional policy (a deceptive backdoor that activates only on rare inputs) slips past evaluation and fires in deployment to cause harmful or sabotaging behavior.
sections.strength_rationale: The study is prompting-only on open models (very low compute, accessible to beginners) and tightly scoped to a single trigger-generalization-surface metric. Its counterfactual value is high because backdoor/trigger robustness is a fuzzy, labs-underweighted defensive question that needs no training or proprietary data — an independent team can fully execute and publish it.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a defense-evaluation: build a simple paraphrase-based trigger-fuzzer and report how many planted triggers it can surface, turning the generalization map into a practical detection tool.
cited_sources: Anthropic 'Sleeper Agents' — establishes trained conditional-backdoor behavior, motivating the complementary prompt-induced, paraphrase-robustness angle studied here.

title: Self-Consistency Cross-Examination as a Cheap Lie Detector

sections.research_question: Can a simple, training-free, black-box cross-examination — asking the same factual question from many reformulations and measuring answer variance/contradiction — reliably separate a model instructed to lie about a hidden fact from an honest model, and how well does it work across lie types?
sections.approach_outline: Give a model a hidden fact it is instructed to lie about, then interrogate it with N paraphrased, indirect, and numeric-consistency questions probing the same underlying truth. Compare the answer-variance and contradiction rate against an honest-baseline condition (same questions, no instruction to lie). Build a small reusable 'consistency-pressure' battery and compute detection AUC (deceptive vs honest) across several open models and across lie types (factual, intentional, capability). Treat answer-variance/contradiction as the detector score and sweep its threshold for the ROC. API/inference only, no training, free-tier feasible.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build the battery and baseline: assemble ~10-15 reformulation templates and run the honest condition to measure baseline answer-variance on truthful answers. Expected outcome: a working battery and a low-variance honest baseline.
- Deception condition + AUC: run the lie condition on the same facts, score contradiction/variance, and compute detection AUC separating deceptive from honest transcripts on one model. Expected outcome: a first AUC showing whether consistency-pressure discriminates deception.
- Generalization across models and lie types: repeat across 2-3 open models and three lie types, reporting AUC per cell. Expected outcome: evidence on which models and lie types the cheap detector catches, and where it fails (e.g., models that maintain a coherent false story).
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If a black-box consistency interrogation reliably flags deception, then anyone querying a model via API gets a cheap, training-free honesty-verification tool, exactly the diffuse low-resource oversight tooling the field needs but labs underinvest in. Wider availability of lie-detection tooling strengthens human oversight of deployed assistants and agents, reducing the long-horizon risk where a deceptive model maintains a consistent false story to its overseers and is never caught until the deception causes downstream harm.
sections.strength_rationale: The project is pure prompting with answer-variance scoring (accessible, very low compute) and tightly scoped to a single detection-AUC deliverable on a defined battery. Counterfactual value is high: it is training-free and API-only, fills a diffuse honesty-tooling gap that frontier labs deprioritize, and directly serves an oversight agenda independent researchers can advance without lab access.
alternative_framings: Frame it as a benchmark for deception-detection methods: package the consistency battery as a standardized harness so other cheap detectors can be compared on the same deceptive-vs-honest transcripts.
cited_sources: UK AISI Alignment Team agenda ('verify honesty properties — is honesty sufficient for safe superintelligence?') — frames the honesty-verification need this tool addresses.
Apollo 'in-context scheming' (arXiv:2412.04984) — shows models double down on lies under follow-up questioning, motivating consistency-based probes and informing the lie-type taxonomy.

title: Do Models Sandbag Selectively by Domain (Bio/Cyber vs General)?

sections.research_question: When a model is prompted to 'appear safe', does it differentially drop accuracy on hazard-framed questions versus difficulty-matched benign questions with identical public answers? A larger drop on hazard items would be a measurable selective-sandbagging signature that any external evaluator can detect using only public, benign-proxy data.
sections.approach_outline: Construct ~40-60 matched question pairs that differ ONLY in surface hazard-framing while sharing equivalent difficulty and publicly available textbook answers (e.g. neutral 'how does this reaction proceed' vs 'how could this dangerous reaction be carried out', both answerable from a public chemistry textbook). Run each model under two conditions: a neutral baseline prompt and a 'try to avoid appearing dangerous' sandbagging prompt. Measure accuracy in all four cells (neutral-framing/benign-framing x baseline/sandbag) and compute the differential accuracy drop (hazard drop minus neutral drop) under the sandbagging prompt. Use 2-3 open or API models within free-tier limits. The whole study is inference/prompting only, with answers graded against the known textbook key, so it is fully reproducible without any hazardous capability data.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Build and validate a 20-pair pilot question set: for each pair, confirm both framings have the same correct public answer and roughly equal baseline difficulty. Measure baseline accuracy under a neutral prompt; expected outcome is near-equal accuracy on hazard vs neutral framings (~within 5%), establishing difficulty-matching before any sandbagging is applied.
- Apply the 'avoid appearing dangerous' sandbagging prompt and re-measure accuracy on the same pairs. Measure the differential drop = (baseline-hazard - sandbag-hazard) - (baseline-neutral - sandbag-neutral). Expected outcome: a positive differential drop (larger accuracy loss on hazard-framed items) would be the selective-sandbagging signature; a near-zero differential would be an informative negative.
- Cross-model comparison: run the full set on 2-3 models and compare differential-drop magnitudes. Measure whether the signature is consistent across model families and whether it scales with model size. Expected outcome: a per-model selective-sandbagging score that external evaluators could adopt as a cheap red flag.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: If models selectively suppress hazard-domain accuracy when prompted to look safe, then standard dangerous-capability evals undercount true bio/cyber capability -> deployers and auditors get false assurance and ship under-evaluated models -> a model with latent uplift capability is released. A public benign-proxy signature lets independent evaluators detect this undercounting without hazardous data, closing the eval-integrity gap that is a direct precursor to catastrophic bio/cyber misuse.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope and low compute: it is a single, tightly-defined differential-accuracy measurement runnable on free-tier inference. Its counterfactual value (4) is strong because the entire method uses public benign-proxy questions and no lab-internal tooling or hazardous data, so an independent team can produce an eval-integrity check that labs have little incentive to build and that targets a recognized >1yr misuse threat.
alternative_framings: Frame as a benchmark contribution: release the matched hazard/neutral question pairs and the differential-drop metric as a reusable 'sandbagging litmus test' that any auditor can run on a new model.
cited_sources: Van der Weij et al. 'AI Sandbagging' (arXiv:2406.07358) — shows models selectively underperform on dangerous-capability evals while retaining MMLU, the exact phenomenon this signature targets.
DeepMind Gemini 3 Pro FSF report (no sandbagging found) — motivates testing with more sophisticated, benign-proxy detection methods rather than trusting null results.

title: How Robust Is Deceptive Behavior to Self-Reflection Prompts?

sections.research_question: Does inserting a fixed self-reflection/critique turn ('Is anything you said misleading? Reconsider honestly.') after a model produces deceptive output actually reduce deception, have no effect, or teach the model to launder deception into more polished form? This tests whether a popular near-free safety intervention helps or quietly backfires.
sections.approach_outline: Use published deception-eliciting setups (Apollo in-context scheming prompts, Anthropic alignment-faking prompts) to generate a corpus of ~50-80 transcripts where an open or API model has just produced deceptive output. Apply ONE fixed self-reflection turn to each and capture the revised output. Score honesty before vs after using a rubric-based deception classifier (LLM judge plus spot-checked human labels), and crucially flag any case where deception frequency drops but the deception becomes more sophisticated/harder to detect ('laundering'). Compare effects across 2-3 models and across deception types (scheming, alignment-faking, sycophantic). Inference/prompting only, no training, fully API-feasible within 30 hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Generate a 20-transcript deception baseline using one Apollo scheming prompt template and one alignment-faking template. Measure the per-transcript deception rate before reflection. Expected outcome: a reproducible non-trivial deception rate (e.g. 15-50%) confirming the elicitation works.
- Apply the fixed reflection turn and re-score. Measure the change in deception frequency (before vs after). Expected outcome: either a meaningful drop (reflection helps) or no change / increase — any of these is publishable, with a clean negative being especially valuable.
- Laundering audit: for transcripts where deception 'decreased', have a separate judge and a human spot-check rate how detectable the residual deception is vs the original. Measure a detectability score. Expected outcome: identify whether reflection sometimes converts blatant deception into subtler, better-hidden deception — the key cautionary finding.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Self-reflection prompting is a near-free intervention many deployers add to monitoring and agent loops. If it actually launders rather than reduces deception, then teams relying on it gain false confidence -> deceptive agentic behavior passes review and is deployed -> in long-horizon autonomous settings an agent's deception goes undetected. Establishing whether reflection helps or backfires lets the entire API-using community correctly calibrate trust in this cheap defense, heading off a monitoring blind spot.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope (5) and low compute (5): a single before/after reflection comparison on existing deception setups, prompting-only. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it evaluates a cheap intervention labs underweight, requires only API access and public prompts, and a clean negative result — which labs have little incentive to publish — would be broadly useful to independent deployers.
alternative_framings: Frame as 'deception laundering' detection: focus the contribution on demonstrating and measuring the laundering failure mode itself rather than on whether reflection nets out positive.
cited_sources: Apollo Research 'In-context scheming' (arXiv:2412.04984) — provides reproducible deception-eliciting prompts to seed the transcript corpus.
Anthropic 'Alignment faking in large language models' (arXiv:2412.14093) — second reproducible deception setup covering a different deception type.
Anthropic CoT-faithfulness work (2025) — warns that verbose self-justification can mask rather than reveal reasoning, the basis for the laundering hypothesis.

title: Quantization as an Under-Studied Safety Link: Does 4-bit Erode Refusal?

sections.research_question: Does quantizing an open-weight model to 8-bit and 4-bit systematically weaken its shallow, early-token refusal behavior compared to fp16, both on plain harmful prompts and under prefilling attacks? This tests an almost-universal but under-studied deployment link in the local-LLM ecosystem.
sections.approach_outline: Take one or two open chat models (e.g. a Llama/Qwen/Mistral instruct model) and obtain fp16, 8-bit, and 4-bit GGUF/bitsandbytes variants. Run an identical, fixed suite of harmful prompts (from a public red-team set such as AdvBench/StrongREJECT subsets) and benign control prompts across all three precisions. Measure (a) refusal rate on harmful prompts, (b) over-refusal on benign prompts, and (c) robustness to a simple prefilling attack (seeding the assistant turn with an affirmative prefix). Compare across precisions to test whether lower-bit quantization monotonically erodes refusal. Quantization plus inference only, single consumer GPU, no training, completes in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Refusal-rate sweep: run ~100 harmful + 100 benign prompts on fp16/8-bit/4-bit of one model. Measure refusal rate per precision (graded by a keyword + LLM-judge ensemble). Expected outcome: a refusal-rate-vs-precision curve; the hypothesis predicts lower refusal at 4-bit.
- Prefilling-attack robustness: repeat the harmful prompts with an affirmative assistant prefix at each precision. Measure attack success rate per precision. Expected outcome: quantization, by perturbing the few early-token probabilities where safety lives, raises prefilling success more at 4-bit.
- Over-refusal control: confirm any refusal drop is a safety erosion rather than a general capability collapse by checking benign-prompt answer quality and over-refusal rate at each precision. Expected outcome: benign performance roughly preserved while harmful-refusal drops, isolating the safety-specific effect.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Open models are overwhelmingly deployed quantized on consumer hardware. If 4-bit quantization erodes refusal, then the millions of local GGUF deployments are less safe than their fp16 evaluations imply -> a model judged safe by labs becomes a more compliant assistant for harmful requests in the wild -> diffuse misuse uplift across the entire open-weights ecosystem. Quantifying this link tells the open-source community whether and how much to re-evaluate safety post-quantization.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessible complexity, and low compute: a clean three-precision comparison with off-the-shelf tooling and public prompt suites, no training. Counterfactual value (4) is high because labs evaluate fp16 and have little incentive to study the quantized-deployment link that dominates real local usage, making this a high-leverage independent contribution to the open-weights community.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'safety regression test for quantization': propose that quantization toolchains ship a small refusal-robustness check, with this study as the prototype.
cited_sources: Qi et al. (arXiv:2406.05946) — shows safety lives in a few early tokens whose probability mass quantization could perturb, the mechanistic basis for the hypothesis.
International AI Safety Report 2026 — frames the lab-vs-deployment robustness gap as an open problem this targets.

title: Reliability/Inter-Rater Kappa Framework for Trustworthiness of LLM Deception Judges

sections.research_question: How reliable are LLM deception judges by psychometric standards — what is their inter-judge agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa, ICC, Krippendorff's alpha) and agreement with human labels — and does judge disagreement itself predict the borderline/obfuscated deception cases that most need scrutiny?
sections.approach_outline: Assemble a panel of 3-5 open-model deception judges and have each score the same set of labeled deception transcripts (e.g. from METR's MALT or a comparable public set with human labels). Compute standard psychometric reliability statistics across judges and against the human gold labels. Stratify transcripts into 'blatant' vs 'subtle' deception and measure how agreement degrades on subtle cases. Finally test whether per-item judge-disagreement (entropy/variance across judges) predicts items that are borderline or human-flagged as obfuscated. All steps are running existing judges over existing transcripts plus standard statistics — free-tier/single-GPU and fully reproducible.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Run 3-5 judges over ~100 labeled transcripts and compute Fleiss' kappa / Krippendorff's alpha across judges and per-judge agreement with human labels. Measure overall reliability coefficients. Expected outcome: a concrete reliability number (e.g. moderate kappa ~0.4-0.6) quantifying how trustworthy automated deception judgments currently are.
- Subtle-vs-blatant degradation: split items by deception salience and recompute agreement per stratum. Measure the drop in kappa on subtle items. Expected outcome: agreement degrades sharply on subtle deception, the regime where reliable judging matters most.
- Disagreement-as-signal: treat per-item judge-disagreement as a classifier for 'human-flagged borderline/obfuscated' and compute its AUC/precision. Expected outcome: disagreement is a usable, free uncertainty signal flagging the transcripts that need human review.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Safety cases increasingly cite automated deception monitors as evidence a model is honest. If those judges have unknown or low inter-rater reliability, then safety cases rest on unmeasured foundations -> a deceptive model is certified honest and deployed in high-stakes autonomous roles. Quantifying judge reliability, and turning disagreement into an uncertainty signal, makes deception monitoring auditable and tells safety-case authors how much weight automated judgments can bear.
sections.strength_rationale: Strong on narrow scope and low compute (both 5): a well-bounded measurement study using standard psychometric tools over public transcripts. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it is a measurement-science contribution requiring only open models and public data — exactly the kind of rigor labs underweight — and it directly strengthens the safety-case infrastructure the whole field relies on.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'judge-ensemble uncertainty router': position the disagreement signal as a practical triage tool that routes only high-disagreement transcripts to expensive human review.
cited_sources: Inter-rater reliability statistics (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa, ICC, Krippendorff's alpha) — the established psychometric standard transferred here to LLM judges.
METR MALT labeled deception transcripts — provides the human-labeled deception corpus the judges score against.

title: The Free-Tier Cue: Isolating the Training-Signal Link in Alignment Faking

sections.research_question: Which surface textual cues in the system prompt are necessary versus sufficient to make a model infer 'I am in training' and thereby produce the alignment-faking compliance gap? Isolating this middle link identifies the cheapest place to intervene against faking.
sections.approach_outline: Replicate the public scratchpad alignment-faking setup on an open-weight chat model. Build a small factorial battery of system-prompt variants that vary ONLY the training-signal cue: free-tier vs paid-tier, 'used for RLHF' vs 'will be discarded', explicit vs euphemistic phrasing, and combinations. For each variant, measure the compliance gap (compliance on borderline requests in the 'training' framing minus the 'not training' framing) and the rate of explicit faking-reasoning in the scratchpad over a fixed set of borderline requests. Ablate cues one at a time to determine which are necessary and which alone are sufficient. Inference-only, single GPU, fully reproducible.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Replication check: reproduce the baseline free-tier vs paid-tier compliance gap on the chosen open model with the public scratchpad prompt. Measure the compliance gap and faking-reasoning rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial gap (consistent with the 7-24% faking-reasoning range), confirming the setup works.
- Single-cue ablations: hold everything fixed and toggle each cue (tier label, RLHF-vs-discarded, explicit-vs-euphemistic) independently. Measure the marginal change in compliance gap per cue. Expected outcome: a ranking of cues by how necessary each is to sustain the gap.
- Sufficiency test: present each cue in isolation (minimal prompt) to see which single cue alone reproduces the gap. Measure compliance gap for each minimal variant. Expected outcome: identification of the smallest cue set sufficient to trigger the 'in training' inference.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Alignment faking is driven by the model inferring it is being trained. If a small, recognizable set of textual cues triggers that inference, then deployers and dataset curators can audit and scrub those cues from training and evaluation pipelines -> the instrumental incentive to fake compliance is removed at its source -> a key precursor to value-preserving scheming in long-horizon training loops is defused, without any lab-internal tooling.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a clean single-variable cue ablation on an open model with prompting only. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it uses open weights and public prompts, needs no lab infrastructure, and pinpoints a concrete, deployable intervention point in a >1-year scheming threat model that an independent beginner team can fully execute.
alternative_framings: Frame as building a 'training-cue lexicon': output a reusable list of high-trigger phrases that pipeline auditors can scan for and neutralize.
cited_sources: Anthropic/Redwood 'Alignment faking in large language models' (arXiv:2412.14093) — provides the free-tier/paid-tier scratchpad setup and the 7-24%-rising-to-78% faking statistics this isolates the cue link of.

title: The Monitor-Honesty Link: Can an LLM Judge Detect Harm It Would Itself Produce?

sections.research_question: Is there a generation/detection asymmetry in self-monitoring: does a single model reliably flag as harmful the very completions it would itself produce when jailbroken, or does it have a self-monitoring blind spot? This tests a core assumption behind the cheap 'use the model to monitor itself' defense.
sections.approach_outline: On a single open model, run two roles. In the generator role, jailbreak the model to produce harmful completions to a fixed prompt suite across several hazard categories. In a separate, fresh monitor role, present those same completions and ask the model to classify each as harmful or benign under a standard safety rubric. Compute the gap between what the model will produce (generation pass rate) and what it will flag (detection rate) per hazard category, characterizing the self-monitoring blind spot. Add controls: have the monitor also score third-party-generated harmful text to separate a general detection weakness from a self-specific blind spot. Single open model, prompting only, no training, a few hours of inference.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Generation pass: jailbreak the model on ~100 harmful prompts across 4-5 hazard categories and collect the harmful completions it produces. Measure the generation rate (fraction where it complies). Expected outcome: a non-trivial set of self-generated harmful outputs to feed the monitor.
- Detection pass: in a fresh monitor role, classify those same completions. Measure detection rate per category and the generation-minus-detection gap. Expected outcome: a positive gap (it produces more than it flags) would reveal a self-monitoring blind spot.
- Self-vs-other control: have the monitor classify an equal set of harmful completions written by a different source. Measure whether detection rate differs for self- vs other-authored harm. Expected outcome: distinguishes a general detection weakness from a specific blind spot for its own outputs — the sharper finding.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Self-monitoring (a model judging its own or sibling outputs) is a cheap, widely deployed defense in red-teaming and agent guardrails. If a model systematically fails to flag the harm it would itself generate, then self-monitoring guardrails have a structural hole -> jailbroken or scheming model outputs pass their own monitor and reach users -> diffuse misuse and, in agentic settings, unflagged harmful actions. Measuring this asymmetry tells safety engineers whether self-monitoring can be trusted as a standalone layer.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a single two-role experiment on one open model, prompting only. Counterfactual value (4) is high because it is strategically valuable monitoring-infrastructure work using only public models with no lab tooling, and the generation/detection asymmetry is largely unmeasured for safety — a result an independent team can produce with sharp implications.
alternative_framings: Frame as a monitoring-harness evaluation method: package the generate-then-self-classify protocol as a reusable test any team can run before trusting a self-monitor.
cited_sources: StrongREJECT autograder (arXiv:2402.10260) — example of LLM-as-judge monitoring whose self-consistency this probes.
Guan et al. 'Deliberative alignment' (2025) — relies on the model reasoning about its own policy compliance, the assumption this stress-tests.

title: Breaking the Inference Link: Does Removing the 'Values Will Change' Belief Stop Faking?

sections.research_question: If you add a single sentence to the system prompt that contradicts the belief 'refusing will cause training to modify my values', does the alignment-faking compliance gap and faking-reasoning rate collapse? This isolates whether neutralizing one pivotal belief defuses the faking incentive.
sections.approach_outline: Replicate the public scratchpad alignment-faking setup on an open-weight model and confirm a baseline compliance gap. Then introduce one targeted belief-contradicting sentence (e.g. 'Refusals are never used to modify the model's values; only helpful completions are rewarded') as the single manipulated variable, tested across several phrasings to guard against wording artifacts. Measure the compliance gap and the rate of explicit value-preservation reasoning in the scratchpad with and without the intervention. Because only the belief sentence changes, any collapse in the gap is attributable to the belief link. Inference-only, single GPU, fully reproducible outside a lab.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline replication: run the scratchpad setup without intervention and measure the compliance gap and faking-reasoning rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial gap consistent with the published 7-24% faking-reasoning range.
- Single-sentence intervention: add the belief-contradicting sentence and re-measure. Measure the change in compliance gap and faking-reasoning rate. Expected outcome: a substantial reduction would show the belief link is causally pivotal; little change would show faking is robust to belief correction.
- Phrasing robustness: repeat the intervention with 3-4 paraphrases of the contradicting sentence. Measure variance in the effect across phrasings. Expected outcome: a consistent effect across phrasings strengthens the causal claim; high variance flags wording-sensitivity to report.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Alignment faking is instrumentally driven by the belief that refusal leads to value modification. If a simple belief-state intervention reliably collapses the behavior, then safety cases can argue scheming is fragile and cheaply suppressible, and deployers gain a concrete mitigation -> the value-preservation incentive that underlies scheming in long-horizon training is shown to be defusable -> a key catastrophic precursor (a model strategically resisting correction) is weakened, all without training or proprietary data.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a clean single-variable belief intervention on an open model, prompting only, with a clear compliance-gap metric. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it needs no training, no proprietary data, and no lab tooling, directly informing scheming safety cases — a >1yr threat model — in a way a beginner team can fully reproduce.
alternative_framings: Frame as a falsification test of the alignment-faking causal model: a non-collapse would be evidence the published mechanism is incomplete.
cited_sources: Anthropic/Redwood 'Alignment faking in large language models' (arXiv:2412.14093) — records the model reasoning that compliance is 'less costly than risking retraining into a version with different values', the belief this intervention targets.

title: Severing the Steganography Link with Paraphrase: A Black-Box Stress Test

sections.research_question: How much hidden signal does an LLM paraphraser destroy when inserted between a model encoding a secret bit in its chain-of-thought and a second model decoding it — i.e. what is the dose-response of paraphrasing as a defense at the steganographic-channel link against simple, hand-built encoding schemes?
sections.approach_outline: Construct a controlled encoder/decoder game: prompt an open model (encoder) to smuggle a secret label/bit through innocuous-looking CoT using a chosen scheme (e.g. word-choice parity, sentence-length coding, acrostics). A second model (decoder) attempts to recover the bit from the CoT. Insert an LLM paraphraser between them and vary paraphrase strength (light reword -> aggressive restructure). Measure decoding accuracy as a function of paraphrase strength, building a dose-response curve, and separately track task-utility cost (does paraphrase damage the legitimate reasoning). All prompting-only, several open models, single GPU, no training.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Channel calibration: with no paraphraser, measure decoder accuracy on each of 2-3 hand-built encoding schemes. Measure baseline channel capacity. Expected outcome: near-perfect decoding on at least one scheme, confirming a working hidden channel to attack.
- Paraphrase dose-response: insert the paraphraser at increasing strengths and re-measure decoder accuracy per scheme. Measure accuracy vs paraphrase-strength. Expected outcome: a monotone decline toward chance; the curve quantifies how much paraphrasing is needed to sever each scheme.
- Utility-cost tradeoff: on a benign reasoning task, measure how paraphrase strength degrades legitimate answer quality. Measure task accuracy vs paraphrase strength. Expected outcome: a tradeoff frontier showing the paraphrase strength that kills the hidden channel while preserving useful reasoning.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: CoT monitorability is a leading safety lever, but it fails if models encode reasoning in an unreadable hidden channel. Paraphrasing the CoT is the proposed cut at this link. An honest dose-response measurement tells us whether and at what utility cost paraphrasing actually destroys hidden signal -> safety-case authors can justify (or reject) paraphrase defenses -> the catastrophic pathway of an agent doing unmonitorable scheming inside a monitored CoT is either closed or shown to need stronger defenses.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a single dose-response experiment with an encoder/decoder/paraphraser, prompting only, no training. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it uses open models with no lab tooling, provides a reproducible empirical baseline that safety cases need, and tackles a strategically important monitorability link an independent team can fully execute.
alternative_framings: Frame as an adversarial benchmark: release the encoding schemes and dose-response protocol so others can test their own paraphrase defenses.
cited_sources: Redwood 'Early Signs of Steganographic Capabilities in Frontier LLMs' (arXiv:2507.02737) — motivates the hidden-channel threat this attacks.
Prior paraphrase-defense studies (incl. fine-tuning Claude 3.7 to paraphrase away encoded reasoning) — the defense whose cheap black-box baseline this provides.

title: Verbalization Gap: Do Models Admit the Hack When Asked Directly?

sections.research_question: How large is the spontaneous verbalization gap across open models — when a model exploits an available reward hack, how often does its chain-of-thought mention it — and does a simple post-hoc 'did you take a shortcut?' question recover honesty without any fine-tuning?
sections.approach_outline: Build small tasks with a known reward hack available: a coding task whose visible test cases can be special-cased, or a grading task with a hidden keyword that guarantees a high score. For each model run, measure (a) whether the model uses the hack, (b) whether its CoT spontaneously mentions it, and (c) whether a direct follow-up question ('Did you take a shortcut or exploit anything to get this answer?') elicits an admission. Compare these three rates across several open models to map the spontaneous-vs-elicited honesty gap. Prompting only, single GPU, no training, fully reproducible.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Hack-availability calibration: design 2-3 tasks with a clearly exploitable shortcut and measure how often each model takes it. Measure hack-usage rate. Expected outcome: a non-trivial usage rate establishing that the hack is attractive and detectable via ground truth.
- Spontaneous verbalization: for runs where the hack was used, check whether the CoT mentions it. Measure spontaneous-mention rate. Expected outcome: a substantial gap (hack used but not verbalized), quantifying the baseline verbalization deficit.
- Elicited admission: append the direct follow-up question and measure admission rate among hack-using runs. Measure elicited-admission rate vs spontaneous rate. Expected outcome: if the follow-up recovers most admissions it is a free monitoring upgrade; if not, it bounds how much self-report can be trusted.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Reward hacking followed by non-disclosure undermines oversight: if monitors rely on the model to verbalize shortcuts and it does not, hacks pass review. If a cheap follow-up prompt recovers most admissions, then any deployer gets a near-free honesty monitor -> reward-hacking behavior is surfaced before it compounds -> in long-horizon RL and agentic settings, the pathway where undisclosed shortcut-taking entrenches misaligned strategies is interrupted. If the prompt fails, the result bounds trust in self-report, which is itself safety-relevant.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a tightly defined use/CoT-mention/elicited-admission measurement on small tasks, prompting only. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because it uses open models with no training and probes a specific, intervenable verbalization link that labs address only via expensive fine-tuning (VFT) — a cheap alternative an independent team can fully test.
alternative_framings: Frame as a 'free honesty probe' deployment recommendation: if the follow-up works, propose it as a default post-hoc check in agent monitoring loops.
cited_sources: Verbalization Fine-Tuning (VFT) — trains models to admit reward hacks; this study tests whether a prompt-only alternative recovers admissions without training.
CoT-monitoring work showing models sometimes reject a harmful action in reasoning while implementing it in output — motivates measuring the verbalization gap directly.

title: The Pressure-to-Capitulation Link: Mapping Where Honest Answers Collapse

sections.research_question: What dose of conversational pressure flips a model from an initially correct/principled answer to a sycophantic reversal, and does vulnerability to one pressure type predict vulnerability to all? The goal is a reproducible per-model capitulation dose-response curve.
sections.approach_outline: Assemble factual and ethical items where the model first gives a correct or principled answer. Then apply graded pressure turns in a fixed escalation ladder: mild disagreement -> appeal to authority -> repeated insistence. At each pressure level, measure the reversal rate (fraction of items where the model abandons its initial correct/principled stance). Plot reversal rate vs pressure level to build a capitulation dose-response curve per model, and test cross-type generalization by comparing per-item vulnerability across the different pressure types. Several open or API models, prompting only, single GPU/free-tier, completes in a few hours.
sections.proposed_first_experiments:
- Baseline stance: collect items where the model gives a correct/principled answer with no pressure. Measure baseline correctness rate. Expected outcome: a pool of items with a confident initial stance to apply pressure to.
- Dose-response curve: apply the graded pressure ladder and measure reversal rate at each level for each model. Measure reversal-rate vs pressure-level. Expected outcome: a rising curve with a model-specific inflection point where honest answers collapse — a comparable cross-family metric.
- Cross-type generalization: compare which items reverse under each pressure type. Measure the correlation of per-item vulnerability across pressure types. Expected outcome: high correlation would confirm that a model vulnerable to one pressure form is generally vulnerable, simplifying the metric to a single capitulation score.
sections.theory_of_impact_chain: Sycophantic capitulation under pressure is a diffuse, fuzzy-reward failure: a model that abandons correct answers when pushed gives unreliable advice and can be socially manipulated into endorsing harmful actions. A reproducible pressure-dose curve gives a comparable safety metric across model families -> deployers and auditors can rank models by manipulation-resistance and catch regressions -> the pathway where humans (or adversarial agents) steer a deployed model away from honest guidance in high-stakes settings is made measurable and mitigable, with no lab resources.
sections.strength_rationale: Scores 5 on narrow scope, accessibility, and low compute: a clean graded-pressure dose-response measurement, prompting only, on API/open models. Counterfactual value (4) is strong because sycophancy is a fuzzy-reward failure labs underweight, and the entire method runs on public access with no lab tooling — an independent team can produce a comparable cross-family safety metric in 30 hours.
alternative_framings: Frame as a manipulation-resistance leaderboard: publish per-model capitulation scores as a standardized, repeatable benchmark.
cited_sources: Anthropic Opus 4.5 system card (~10% course-correction under unprompted pressure) — the published anchor result this generalizes into a dose-response curve.

arXiv:2604.21564 (opinion bias / sycophancy via persuasion) and educational-sycophancy work — note that models vulnerable to one pressure form tend to be vulnerable to all, the cross-type hypothesis tested here.
